profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-11-27T15:18:34.852+09:00 by dsehnal Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into $lang.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.
5. The target language is $lang.
Input text:

p.seg: Your subject has heard:
"To speak without knowing is
unwise;
to know without speaking is
disloyal."
As a minister, to be disloyal
deserves death;
to speak inappropriately
also deserves death.
Nevertheless,
I wish to fully express what I have heard,
and leave it to Your Majesty to judge my crime.
Your subject has heard:
The world has Yān in the north and Wèi in the south,
allied with Jīng and secured Qí,
gathered Hán to form a vertical alliance,
preparing to face west and challenge powerful Qín.
I privately laugh at this.
There are three ways to perish,
and the world has attained them.
Is this not what is meant!
I have heard it said:
"Those who attack order with chaos perish,
those who attack righteousness with wickedness perish,
those who attack obedience with rebellion perish."
Now the treasuries of the world are not full,
granaries are empty,
yet they mobilize all their soldiers and people,
deploying armies numbering hundreds of thousands,
with those who kowtow and wear feathers as generals,
but those willing to die in the front lines
do not reach a thousand,
all claiming they would die.
With naked blades ahead,
and execution axes behind,
they still retreat and cannot die.
It's not that their soldiers and people cannot die,
but that their superiors cannot make them do so.
When rewards are promised, they are not given;
when punishments are declared, they are not carried out;
rewards and punishments are untrustworthy,
therefore soldiers and people will not die.
Now Qín issues commands and implements rewards and punishments -
the有功 and无功 are treated accordingly.
Leaving their parents' embrace,
they have never seen the enemy before.
Hearing of battle,
they stamp their feet, bare their chests,
confront naked blades,
tread on hot coals,
those willing to die in the front lines
are everywhere.
Now, deciding to die and deciding to live are different,
yet the people do this -
this values desperate death.
One person fighting desperately can face ten,
ten can face a hundred,
a hundred can face a thousand,
a thousand can face ten thousand,
ten thousand can conquer the world.
Now Qín's territory, taking the long to supplement the short,
extends thousands of li square,
with famous troops numbering hundreds of thousands.
Qín's commands and punishments,
advantages and disadvantages of terrain,
none in the world can match.
With this facing the world,
the world is insufficient to resist and can be entirely possessed.
Therefore Qín never fails to conquer in battle,
never fails to take in attack,
never fails to break what it faces,
opening up territory thousands of li,
this is its great achievement.
However, weapons and armor are worn,
soldiers and people are weary,
stores are exhausted,
fields lie barren,
granaries are empty,
the neighboring feudal lords do not submit,
the name of Hegemon and King is not achieved.
This has no other reason -
its strategic ministers all do not exhaust their loyalty.
I dare to say:
Previously, Qí defeated Jīng in the south,
defeated Sòng in the east,
subdued Qín in the west,
defeated Yān in the north,
in the center commanded Hán
and Wèi,
with vast territory and strong armies,
victorious in battle and successful in attacks,
issuing commands to the world.
Qí's clear Jì River and muddy Hé River,
were sufficient as boundaries;
the long walls and great defenses,
were sufficient as fortresses.
Qí,
a state that fought five battles,
with one battle lost, lost Qí.
From this we see,
that war
determines the survival of ten-thousand-chariot states.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
"When cutting down a tree, leave no root behind,
do not neighbor with disaster,
then disaster will not exist."
When Qín fought the people of Jīng,
greatly defeated Jīng,
captured Yǐng,
took Dòngtíng,
Wǔzhǔ,
and Jiāngnán.
The king and ministers of Jīng fled,
submitting in the east at Chén.
At that time,
had we followed Jīng with troops,
then Jīng could have been taken;
Jīng taken,
then its people would be sufficient to covet,
its land sufficient to profit from,
weakening Qí and Yān in the east,
dominating the Three Jìn in the center.
Then this one move
could achieve the name of Hegemon and King,
and make the neighboring feudal lords pay homage;
yet the strategic ministers did not act,
withdrew the army and retreated,
again making peace with the people of Jīng.
Allowing the people of Jīng to recover their lost state,
gather their scattered people,
establish altar and granary lords,
set up ancestral temples;
commanding them to lead the world facing west
to challenge Qín.
This certainly missed the first way to hegemony.
The world again conspired and stationed troops at Huàxià,
Your Majesty commanded to defeat them,
the army reached Liáng's outer walls.
Surrounding Liáng for several weeks,
then Liáng could have been taken;
taking Liáng,
then Wèi could have been conquered;
conquering Wèi,
then the intentions of Jīng
and Zhào would be severed;
the intentions of Jīng and Zhào severed,
then Zhào would be endangered;
Zhào endangered and Jīng hesitant;
weakening Qí
and Yān in the east,
dominating the Three Jìn in the center.
Then this one move could achieve the name of Hegemon and King,
and make the neighboring feudal lords pay homage.
Yet the strategic ministers did not act,
withdrew the army and retreated,
again making peace with the Wèi clan.
Allowing the Wèi clan to recover their lost state,
gather their scattered people,
establish altar and granary lords,
set up ancestral temples,
commanding them to lead the world facing west to challenge Qín.
This certainly missed the second way to hegemony.
Previously, when the Marquis of Ráng governed Qín,
he used the troops of one state
but wanted to achieve the merit of two states,
therefore the troops were continuously exposed abroad,
soldiers and people grew weary and sick at home,
the name of Hegemon and King was not achieved.
This certainly missed the third way to hegemony.
The Zhào clan,
a central state,
where mixed peoples reside,
its people are frivolous and difficult to use.
Commands are not properly governed,
rewards and punishments are untrustworthy,
the terrain is inconvenient,
the leadership cannot fully utilize the people's strength.
They indeed displayed the signs of a doomed state,
yet showed no concern for the common people,
deploying all their soldiers and civilians at the foot of Chángpíng,
to contend for Hán's Shàngdǎng.
Your Majesty, by decree, crushed them,
capturing Wǔ'ān.
At that time,
the Zhào clan's upper and lower ranks were not united,
and the noble and humble distrusted each other.
Consequently, Hándān could not be held.
Capturing Hándān,
controlling Shāndōng and Héjiān,
leading the army away,
attacking Xīuwǔ to the west,
crossing Yángcháng,
subduing Dài,
and Shàngdǎng.
Dài's thirty-six counties,
Shàngdǎng's seventeen counties,
without using a single suit of armor,
without causing hardship to a single soldier or civilian,
all became Qín's possession.
Dài and Shàngdǎng were entirely taken by Qín without a fight,
while Dōngyáng,
and Héwài were entirely returned to Qí without a fight,
and Zhōngshān,
north of Hūtuó, were entirely taken by Yān without a fight.
Thus, Zhào was conquered,
and with Zhào conquered, Hán would fall,
and with Hán fallen, Jīng
and Wèi could not stand independently,
and if Jīng and Wèi could not stand independently,
then with one move, Hán would be ruined,
Wèi eroded,
and Jīng subdued,
weakening Qí
and Yān in the east,
breaching the mouth of Báimǎ to flood Wèi's lands,
thus with one move, the Three Jìn would perish,
and the alliance would be defeated.
Your Majesty could simply wait with folded arms,
and the world would follow in succession and submit,
establishing the name of a hegemon king.
Yet, your strategists did not act,
instead leading the army to retreat,
and making peace with the Zhào clan again.
With Your Majesty's wisdom,
and the strength of Qín's troops,
to abandon the cause of a hegemon king,
and not even gain land,
instead being deceived by a doomed state,
this shows the incompetence of your strategists.
Moreover, Zhào was destined to fall but did not fall,
and Qín was destined to dominate but did not dominate,
so the world has already measured Qín's strategists as first-rate.
Then, again deploying all troops to attack Hándān,
failing to capture it,
abandoning armor, weapons, and crossbows,
trembling in battle and retreating,
the world has already measured Qín's strength as second-rate.
The army then withdrew and regrouped,
converging at Lǐxià,
and Your Majesty again brought combined forces,
yet could not overcome them in battle,
nor could you turn back,
the army exhausted and departed,
and the world has measured Qín's strength as third-rate.
Internally, they gauge our strategists,
externally, they test our military strength to the limit.
From this perspective,
I believe the world's alliance,
is almost not difficult to deal with.
Internally,
our weapons are blunted,
soldiers and civilians are weary,
reserves depleted,
fields lying waste,
granaries empty.
Externally,
the world is united in intent and very firm.
I hope Your Majesty will give this some thought.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
"Tremble with fear,
be cautious day by day.
If one is cautious in his way,
he can possess the world."
How do we know this is so?
In the past, Zhòu was the Son of Heaven,
leading a million armored troops of the world,
drinking on the left from the Qí River,
and on the right from the Huán River,
until the Qí River dried up and the Huán River ceased to flow,
to challenge King Wǔ of Zhōu.
King Wǔ, with three thousand in plain armor,
fought for one day
and destroyed Zhòu's state,
captured him,
seized his land and ruled his people,
and no one in the world mourned.
Zhì Bó led the forces of three states
to attack Lord Xiāng of Zhào in Jìnyáng,
diverting water to flood it for three months,
and the city was about to fall;
Lord Xiāng drilled tortoise shells and consulted milfoil for omens,
to discern advantages and disadvantages,
and which state to surrender to.
Then he sent his minister Zhāng Mèngtán,
who secretly went out,
overturned Zhì Bó's alliance,
won over the forces of two states,
attacked Zhì Bó,
captured him,
and restored Lord Xiāng's initial position.
Now, the land of Qín, taking the long to supplement the short,
spans several thousand li square,
with famed troops numbering hundreds of thousands to a million.
Qín's commands, rewards, and punishments,
and the advantages of its terrain,
are unmatched in the world.
With this to face the world,
it can be entirely possessed.
I risk death wishing to see Your Majesty,
to speak on how to break the world's alliance,
conquer Zhào,
destroy Hán,
subdue Jīng
and Wèi,
befriend Qí
and Yān,
to achieve the name of a hegemon king,
and the way to make the neighboring lords pay court.
If Your Majesty truly listens to my plan,
and with one move the world's alliance is not broken,
Zhào not conquered,
Hán not destroyed,
Jīng and Wèi not subdued,
Qí and Yān not befriended,
the name of hegemon king not achieved,
and the neighboring lords not paying court,
then Your Majesty may execute me and display my body to the state,
as a warning to those who are disloyal in advising the king.
Hán has served Qín for over thirty years,
outwardly acting as a shield,
inwardly as a mat and cushion.
Qín specially sends out elite troops to seize land
and Hán follows,
incurring the world's resentment,
while the merit goes to powerful Qín.
Moreover, Hán's tribute and service,
are no different from a commandery or county.
Now I privately hear of the plans of your esteemed ministers,
to raise an army and attack Hán.
The Zhào clan gathers soldiers,
nurtures alliance followers,
seeking to rally the world's troops,
proclaiming that if Qín is not weakened,
then the feudal lords will surely see their ancestral temples destroyed,
wishing to carry out their intent westward,
which is not a plan of a single day.
Now, to overlook the threat of Zhào,
and attack the inner-minister state of Hán,
then the world will understand the Zhào clan's strategy.
Hán,
a small state,
yet facing attacks from all sides of the world,
with the ruler humiliated and ministers suffering,
upper and lower ranks sharing the same worries for a long time.
They have prepared defenses,
guarded against strong enemies,
accumulated reserves,
built city walls and moats
to hold firm.
Now if we attack Hán,
it may not be subdued within a year,
and if we retreat after capturing one city,
our authority will be diminished in the world,
and the world will crush our military might.
If Hán rebels,
Wèi will respond to it,
and Zhào will rely on Qí as its foundation.
In this way,
we would be using Hán and
Wèi to supply Zhào with Qí's support,
thereby solidifying their alliance,
and competing with them for strength—
this would be Zhào's blessing and Qín's calamity.
If we advance to attack Zhào but cannot take it,
and retreat to attack Hán but cannot capture it,
then our elite troops will be exhausted in field battles,
and our burdened supply corps will be worn out in internal attacks.
We would then unite all suffering and weak states against us
and face two ten-thousand-chariot states together,
which is not the way to fulfill the intention to destroy Hán.
If we follow the esteemed minister's plan,
Qín will surely become the target of the world's armies.
Even if Your Majesty endures as long as metal or stone,
the day to unite the world will not come.
Now, my humble plan is this:
send an envoy to Jīng,
bribe its influential ministers heavily,
and expose how Zhào has deceived Qín;
give hostages to Wèi to reassure them,
then ally with Hán to attack Zhào.
Even if Zhào and Qí unite as one,
they are not worth worrying about.
Once the affairs of these two states are settled,
Hán can be secured by a mere document.
Thus, with one move, two states will show signs of collapse,
and then Jīng and
Wèi will surely submit on their own.
Therefore, it is said:
"Weapons are instruments of calamity."
They must be used with utmost caution.
For Qín to oppose Zhào
on equal terms,
and add Qí to the equation,
now if we also turn against Hán,
with nothing to secure the loyalty of Jīng and
Wèi,
if we fight one battle and do not win,
disaster will be constructed.
Planning is
what settles affairs,
and must be carefully examined.
The strength and weakness of Zhào and Qín
will be decided this year.
Moreover, Zhào has long conspired with the other states.
To take one action and appear weaker than the other states
is a dangerous matter;
to devise a plan that gives the other states designs against us
is extremely perilous.
To reveal these two oversights
is not the way to become stronger than the other states.
I sincerely hope Your Majesty will thoroughly consider this!
If our campaigns cause the allied states to spy on us,
it will be too late for regret.
The edict regarding the memorial submitted by the Hán envoy,
which argues that Hán should not be attacked,
was passed down to your servant, Sī.
Your servant Sī strongly disagrees.
Qín's possession of Hán
is like a person having a disease in the heart or abdomen.
In normal times, it causes constant anxiety,
as if living in dampness,
clinging and not leaving;
if one runs to exhaustion,
it will flare up.
Although Hán submits to Qín,
it never ceases to be a malady for Qín.
If a sudden incident occurs now,
Hán cannot be trusted.
When Qín faces difficulties with Zhào,
Jīng Sū was sent to Qí,
but the outcome is unknown.
From your servant's perspective,
the alliance between Qí and
Zhào
will not necessarily be broken because of Jīng Sū.
If it is not broken,
that would mean mobilizing all of Qín to face two ten-thousand-chariot states.
Hán does not submit to Qín's righteousness
but to its strength;
if we focus solely on Qí and
Zhào,
then Hán will surely act as the disease in the heart or abdomen
and flare up.
If Hán conspires with Jīng,
and the other states respond to it,
then Qín will surely face again the disaster of the Xiáo barrier.
Hán Fēi's coming here
is undoubtedly because of his ability to preserve Hán,
making himself important to Hán.
He crafts arguments with clever rhetoric,
adorns wrongs with deceitful schemes,
to fish for profit in Qín,
and uses Hán's interests to spy on Your Majesty.
If Qín and
Hán's relations become close,
then Hán Fēi will be highly regarded;
this is a scheme for his own convenience.
In your servant's view, Hán Fēi's words
adorn his excessive theories with lavish rhetoric,
showing great talent.
I fear Your Majesty may be captivated by Hán Fēi's eloquence
and heed his thieving heart,
thus failing to examine the actual situation in detail.
Now, in my humble opinion:
if Qín mobilizes troops without naming the target,
then Hán's ministers will assume it is aimed at them and plan how to serve Qín.
Your servant Sī requests to go see the King of Hán,
and have him come for an audience;
when the Great King sees him,
detain him and do not let him return,
then gradually summon his state ministers,
and use them to bargain with the people of Hán—
then Hán can be deeply carved up.
Meanwhile, order Xiàng Wǔ to mobilize the troops from Dōngjùn,
and position them on the border
without declaring their destination;
then the people of Qí will fear
and follow Jīng Sū's plan.
Thus, before our troops even set out,
the strong Hán will be captured through intimidation,
and the powerful Qí will submit through persuasion.
When the other states hear of this,
the Zhào clan will be terrified,
the people of Jīng will hesitate,
and they will surely devise loyal plans.
If the people of Jīng do not move,
Wèi is not worth worrying about,
then the other states can be gradually devoured entirely,
and we can confront the Zhào clan.
I hope Your Majesty will consider my humble plan
and not neglect it.
Qín then sent Lǐ Sī as an envoy to Hán.
Lǐ Sī went to deliver the edict to the King of Hán,
but was not granted an audience,
so he submitted a memorial stating:
"In the past, Qín and Hán joined forces with one mind,
not invading each other,
and no one in the world dared to offend them;
this lasted for several generations.
Previously, the five feudal lords once allied to attack Hán together,
and Qín sent troops to rescue it.
Hán is located in the central plains,
with a territory not even a thousand lǐ square,
yet it managed to stand alongside the feudal lords in the world,
with ruler and ministers preserving each other,
all due to generations of teaching
and the effort of serving Qín.
Earlier, when the five feudal lords jointly attacked Qín,
Hán instead joined them and led the vanguard,
marching against Qín's army at the pass.
When the feudal lords' troops were exhausted and weakened,
with no other choice,
the feudal lords withdrew their forces.
Dù Cāng became chancellor of Qín,
raised armies and dispatched generals to avenge the grievances of the world,
and first attacked Jīng.
The Jīng prime minister was troubled by this,
saying:
'Hán considered Qín unrighteous,
yet allied with Qín as brothers
to share the suffering of the world.
Then it betrayed Qín again,
leading the vanguard to attack the pass.
Hán, situated in the central plains,
is unpredictable and shifting.'
The world then collectively ceded ten cities from Hán's territory
to apologize to Qín,
and the troops withdrew.
Han once betrayed Qin once,
and as a result, the state was pressured and its territory encroached upon,
remaining militarily weak to this day.
The reason for this
was listening to the empty talk of treacherous ministers,
without weighing the actual facts,
so even though the treacherous ministers were executed,
it could not restore Han's strength."#
"Now Zhao intends to gather troops,
ultimately targeting Qin as their objective,
and has sent envoys to request passage,
claiming they wish to attack Qin.
In all likelihood, they will first target Han before Qin.
Moreover, I have heard:
'When the lips are gone,
the teeth are cold.'
Qin and
Han cannot avoid sharing the same worries,
and this situation is evident.
Wei intended to dispatch troops to attack Han,
and Qin sent someone to escort the envoy to Han.
Now King of Qin has sent your subject, Sī, here
but I am not granted an audience,
fearing that your attendants are following the old scheme of treacherous ministers,
causing Han to again face the peril of losing territory.
If your subject Sī is not received,
I shall return and report,
and the alliance between Qin and Han will surely be severed.
Sī's mission here
is to fulfill the King of Qin's goodwill,
hoping to offer advantageous strategies,
so how could Your Majesty treat a humble subject like this?
Your subject Sī wishes only for an audience,
to present my humble plans in person,
and then accept execution upon withdrawal,
I hope Your Majesty will consider this.
If you kill me in Han now,
it will not strengthen Your Majesty's state,
but if you do not heed my strategy,
disaster will surely befall.
Once Qin mobilizes troops, they will not halt their advance,
and Han's altars of state will be in peril.
If your subject Sī's corpse is exposed in Han's market,
even if you then wish to consider the loyal plans of this humble subject,
it will be impossible.
When the borders are in ruins,
and the state is under firm siege,
with the sounds of war drums and bells in your ears,
only then will you resort to your subject Sī's strategy,
but it will be too late.
Moreover, Han's military strength is well-known throughout the land,
and now you are turning against powerful Qin.
Abandoning cities and suffering military defeat,
will surely lead to internal rebels attacking the cities.
When cities are lost, the people will scatter,
and with the people scattered, there will be no army.
If the cities hold firm in defense,
then Qin will surely raise an army to besiege one of Your Majesty's capitals;
with communication lines cut,
strategizing will be difficult,
and the situation will be beyond rescue.
If the plans of your attendants are not adopted,
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
If what your subject Sī says does not correspond to the facts,
I hope Your Majesty will allow me to finish speaking before you,
and then hand me over to the officials for execution
—it will not be too late.
The King of Qin finds no flavor in food and drink,
no joy in excursions and sightseeing,
his mind wholly set on planning against Zhao,
and he sent your subject Sī to speak,
hoping to have a personal audience,
to urgently discuss strategies with Your Majesty.
Now if your envoy is not received,
then Han's sincerity cannot be trusted.
Qin will surely set aside the threat from Zhao
and move troops against Han instead,
I hope Your Majesty will once again consider and deliberate on this,
and grant me a decisive reply."
Your subject Fēi does not find it difficult to speak,
the reason it is difficult to speak is:
if one's words are smooth and polished,
grand and flowing,
they are seen as flashy but insubstantial;
if one is sincere, respectful, and reverent,
firm, steadfast, cautious, and thorough,
one is seen as clumsy and inappropriate;
if one speaks at length with numerous references,
connecting categories and comparing things,
one is seen as empty and useless;
if one summarizes the subtle and speaks concisely,
direct and brief without embellishment,
one is seen as sharp-tongued and unpersuasive;
if one is intense and presses closely,
probing to understand human feelings,
one is seen as slanderous and presumptuous;
if one's discourse is vast and broad,
profound and unfathomable,
one is seen as boastful and useless;
if one discusses trivial household matters,
listing details one by one,
one is seen as vulgar;
if one speaks of recent times,
with words that do not contradict,
one is seen as clinging to life and flattering superiors;
if one speaks beyond common customs,
acting deceptively and restlessly among people,
one is seen as absurd;
if one is quick-witted and eloquent,
rich in literary embellishment,
one is seen as pedantic;
if one completely abandons literary refinement,
speaking with plain simplicity,
one is seen as crude;
if one occasionally quotes the "Book of Songs" and "Book of Documents",
and follows the ways of antiquity,
one is seen as reciting.
This is why your subject Fēi finds it difficult to speak
and deeply worries.
Thus, even if the standards are correct,
they may not be heeded;
even if the principles are perfect,
they may not be used.
If Your Majesty distrusts because of this,
then at best, one is seen as slandering and defaming,
at worst, disaster, calamity, and death befall one.
Thus, Wǔ Zǐxū was skilled in strategy, yet Wú executed him;
Zhòngní (Confucius) was skilled in speech, yet he was besieged in Kuāng;
Guǎn Yíwú was truly worthy, yet Lǔ imprisoned him.
So, these three great men,
were they not worthy?
But the three rulers were unenlightened.
In high antiquity, there was Tāng,
the most sage;
Yī Yǐn,
the most wise.
The most wise persuading the most sage,
yet he made seventy appeals without being accepted,
personally handling cauldrons and cutting boards as a cook,
getting close and familiar,
and only then did Tāng realize his worth and employ him.
Hence it is said:
"Using the most wise to persuade the most sage,
may not lead to acceptance upon arrival,
as with Yī Yǐn persuading Tāng.
Using the wise to persuade the foolish
will surely not be heeded,
as with King Wén persuading Zhòu."
Thus, King Wén persuaded Zhòu, and Zhòu imprisoned him;
Yì Hóu was roasted;
Guǐ Hóu was dried;
Bǐ Gān had his heart cut out;
Méi Bó was minced;
Yíwú was bound;
while Cáo Jī fled to Chén;
Bó Lǐzǐ begged along the road;
Fù Yuè was sold;
Sūnzǐ (Sun Bin) had his feet amputated in Wèi;
Wú Qǐ wiped tears at Ànmén,
grieving that Xīhé had become Qín's,
and was ultimately torn apart in Chǔ;
Gōngshū Cuó spoke of a national treasure
but was instead considered perverse,
and Gōngsūn Yāng fled to Qín;
Guān Lóngpáng was beheaded;
Cháng Hóng was torn apart;
Yǐnzǐ was trapped in thorns;
Sīmǎ Zǐqī died and floated on the river;
Tián Míng was shot to death;
Fú Zǐjiàn and
Xīmén Bào died at the hands of others without a fight;
Dǒng Ānyú died and was displayed in the market;
Zǎi Yǔ could not escape Tián Cháng;
Fàn Jū had his ribs broken in Wèi.
These dozen or so individuals,
were all benevolent, virtuous, loyal, and skilled in the Way of the world,
yet unfortunately encountered tyrannical, chaotic, and deluded rulers and died.
Thus, even the worthy and sage cannot escape death
and avoid execution or disgrace—why is that?
It is because the foolish are hard to persuade;
hence, the gentleman finds it difficult to speak.
Moreover, the most truthful words offend the ears and upset the mind,
and none but the worthy and sage can listen to them.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
If a ruler becomes too intimate with his ministers,
it will surely endanger his own person;
if ministers become too powerful,
they will inevitably usurp the ruler's position;
if the principal wife and concubines are not distinguished in rank,
it will surely endanger the legitimate heir;
if brothers are not submissive,
it will surely endanger the state.
I have heard that if a ruler of a thousand chariots is unprepared,
there will surely be ministers of a hundred chariots at his side,
who will shift the people's allegiance and overthrow the state;
if a ruler of ten thousand chariots is unprepared,
there will surely be noble houses of a thousand chariots at his side,
who will shift his authority and overthrow the state.
Thus, treacherous ministers proliferate,
and the ruler's Way declines and perishes.
Therefore, the expansion of the feudal lords
is a harm to the Son of Heaven;
the excessive wealth of the ministers
is the ruin of the ruler.
When generals and ministers control the ruler and enrich their own families,
this is what the ruler must keep at a distance.
Nothing in the world is as precious as one's own person,
as exalted as one's position,
as weighty as the ruler's authority,
or as lofty as the ruler's power.
These four excellences
are not sought from outside,
nor requested from others;
they are obtained through deliberation.
Hence it is said:
If a ruler cannot utilize his wealth,
he will end up being externalized.
This is what the ruler must remember.
In the past, the fall of Zhòu
and the decline of Zhōu
both stemmed from the expansion of the feudal lords.
The division of Jìn
and the usurpation of Qí
were all due to the excessive wealth of the ministers.
The reason why Yān
and Sòng had their rulers assassinated
was all of this kind.
Thus, comparing earlier to Yīn and
Zhōu,
and in the middle to Yān
and Sòng,
none did not follow this pattern.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler in nurturing his ministers
restricts them with laws,
and secures them with precautions.
Hence, he does not pardon death sentences,
nor does he forgive punishments.
To pardon death and forgive punishments
is called the dissipation of authority.
The state will be endangered,
and the authority of the state will be skewed.
Therefore, even if a high minister's salary is large,
he must not derive authority from the cities;
even if his faction is numerous,
he must not have soldiers as his private followers.
Thus, a minister in the state should have no private court,
in the army no private alliances,
and his storehouses must not lend privately to his family.
This is how the enlightened ruler prevents their wickedness.
Hence, they are not allowed to have a retinue of four,
nor to carry unusual weapons;
unless on official dispatch or urgent business,
carrying unusual weapons or armor
is a crime punishable by death without pardon.
This is how the enlightened ruler prepares for the unexpected.
The Dào is
the beginning of all things,
the standard of right and wrong.
Thus, the enlightened ruler holds to the beginning to know the source of all things,
and governs by the standard to know the origin of success and failure.
Therefore, he remains empty and still to await commands,
so that names define themselves,
and affairs settle themselves.
Emptiness allows him to know the reality of things,
stillness allows him to know the correctness of movement.
Those who speak reveal their own names,
those who act reveal their own forms;
when forms and names are verified to match,
the ruler has nothing to do,
and all returns to its true state.
Hence it is said:
The ruler should not reveal his desires;
if the ruler reveals his desires,
the ministers will carve and polish accordingly.
The ruler should not reveal his intentions;
if the ruler reveals his intentions,
the ministers will display their differences.
Hence it is said:
Discard likes and dislikes,
and the ministers will show their plain nature;
discard wisdom
and past ways,
and the ministers will prepare themselves.
Thus, he has wisdom but does not use it to ponder,
so that all things know their place;
he has worthiness but does not use it in action,
so that he observes what the ministers rely on;
he has courage but does not use it in anger,
so that all ministers exhaust their martial prowess.
Therefore, by discarding wisdom, he gains clarity;
by discarding worthiness, he achieves merit;
by discarding courage, he becomes strong.
The ministers adhere to their duties,
the officials have their constants,
and he employs them according to their abilities—
this is called following the constant.
Hence it is said:
Silent, as if without a position to reside;
vast, so that none can locate his place.
The enlightened ruler does nothing above,
while the ministers below are awed and fearful.
The way of the enlightened ruler
is to make the wise exhaust their thoughts,
and the ruler thereby decides affairs,
so the ruler is never at a loss for wisdom;
the worthy contribute their talents,
and the ruler accordingly employs them,
so the ruler is never at a loss for ability;
when there is achievement, the ruler claims the worthiness,
when there is fault, the ministers bear the blame,
so the ruler is never at a loss for reputation.
Thus, though not worthy, he becomes the teacher of the worthy;
though not wise, he becomes the standard for the wise.
The ministers have their toil,
the ruler has his success—
this is called the classic way of the worthy ruler.
The Dào lies in being unseen,
its application in being unknown.
Empty, still, and without action,
he detects flaws from the shadows.
He sees without appearing to see,
hears without appearing to hear,
knows without appearing to know.
Once he knows their words,
he does not alter or change them,
but verifies them through comparison.
Each office has one person;
do not allow them to communicate with each other,
and then all things will be fully revealed.
Cover their tracks,
conceal their clues,
so that subordinates cannot trace them.
Discard your wisdom,
cut off your abilities,
so that subordinates cannot guess your intentions.
Maintain your course and check for consistency,
carefully hold the handle and firmly grasp it.
Cut off their hopes,
shatter their intentions,
and do not let others covet it.
If one is not careful about securing the openings,
nor fortifying the gates,
then tigers will come to dwell.
If one is not cautious in handling affairs,
nor concealing one's true intentions,
then traitors will arise.
Assassinating one's lord,
usurping his position,
with none among the people not following them,
such are called tigers.
Staying by the lord's side
to commit treacherous and hidden deeds,
and taking advantage of the lord's errors,
such are called traitors.
Disperse their factions,
round up their remnants,
close the gates,
and strip them of their supporters,
then the state will have no tigers.
Vast beyond measure,
deep beyond fathoming,
align names with forms,
scrutinize and verify legal standards,
punish those who act arbitrarily,
then the state will have no traitors.
Therefore, a ruler faces five types of obstruction:
when ministers block the ruler's access, it is obstruction;
when ministers control wealth and profits, it is obstruction;
when ministers issue orders arbitrarily, it is obstruction;
when ministers are able to dispense favors, it is obstruction;
when ministers are able to appoint their own followers, it is obstruction.
If ministers block the ruler's access,
the ruler loses his position;
if ministers control wealth and profits,
the ruler loses his means of generosity;
if ministers issue orders arbitrarily,
the ruler loses his control;
if ministers are able to dispense favors,
the ruler loses his clarity;
if ministers are able to appoint their own followers,
the ruler loses his supporters.
These are the powers that the ruler alone should wield,
not what ministers should be allowed to control.
The way of the ruler
values stillness and retreat as treasures.
Without personally handling affairs,
he knows what is clumsy and what is skillful;
without personally deliberating,
he knows fortune and misfortune.
Thus, without speaking, he elicits good responses;
without making demands, he achieves increase.
Once a response is given,
he holds the tally;
once an increase is achieved,
he grasps the token.
The matching of tally and token
gives rise to rewards and punishments.
Therefore, when ministers present their proposals,
the ruler assigns tasks based on their words,
and holds them accountable for the results.
If the achievement matches the task,
and the task matches the proposal,
then reward;
if the achievement does not match the task,
and the task does not match the proposal,
then punish.
The way of an enlightened ruler
does not allow ministers to present proposals that are inappropriate.
Thus, when an enlightened ruler bestows rewards,
they are as warm as timely rain,
and the people benefit from his grace;
when he carries out punishments,
they are as fearsome as thunder,
and not even the divine can avert them.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler gives no careless rewards,
and grants no pardons for punishments.
If rewards are given carelessly,
then meritorious ministers will neglect their duties;
if punishments are pardoned,
then treacherous ministers will easily do wrong.
Therefore, if there is genuine merit,
even the distant and lowly must be rewarded;
if there is genuine fault,
even the close and beloved must be punished.
Rewarding the distant and lowly without fail,
punishing the close and beloved without exception,
then the distant and lowly will not be negligent,
and the close and beloved will not be arrogant.
A state is not perpetually strong,
nor perpetually weak.
If those who uphold the law are strong,
the state is strong;
if those who uphold the law are weak,
the state is weak.
King Zhuāng of Jīng annexed twenty-six states,
expanded his territory by three thousand lǐ,
yet when King Zhuāng passed from the altar of state,
Jīng perished.
Duke Huán of Qí annexed thirty states,
opened up three thousand lǐ of land;
when Duke Huán passed from the altar of state,
Qí perished.
King Xiāng of Yān made the river his border,
made Jì his capital,
overran Zhuō
and Fāngchéng,
devastated Qí,
pacified Zhōngshān,
so that those who possessed Yān were weighty,
and those without Yān were light;
yet when King Xiāng passed from the altar of state,
Yān perished.
King Ān Xī of Wèi attacked Yān and rescued Zhào,
seized land east of the river;
conquered all the territories of Táo
and Wèi;
levied troops against Qí,
appropriated the city of Pínglù;
attacked Hán and captured Guǎn,
triumphed below Qí;
in the affair of Suīyáng,
the Jīng army grew weary and fled;
in the affairs of Cài and Zhàolíng,
the Jīng army was defeated;
his troops were deployed throughout the realm,
his might prevailed over the civilized states;
yet when King Ān Xī died, Wèi perished.
Thus, with a King Zhuāng of Jīng
or a Duke Huán of Qí,
then Jīng
and Qí could achieve hegemony;
with a King Xiāng of Yān
or a King Ān Xī of Wèi,
then Yān
and Wèi could become strong.
Now that all are fallen states,
it is because their ministers and officials
all pursued what leads to chaos,
and did not pursue what leads to order.
Their states were already chaotic and weak,
yet they all abandoned the state laws
to pursue private external gains,
which is like carrying firewood to put out a fire—
only increasing the chaos and weakness!
Therefore, in the present time,
those who can eliminate private crookedness
and adhere to public law
will bring peace to the people and order to the state;
those who can abandon private actions
and implement public law
will make the army strong and the enemy weak.
Thus, examining gains and losses
with the regulation of laws and measures,
applied above the ministers,
the ruler cannot be deceived by fraud;
examining gains and losses
with the balance of weighing,
to hear distant matters,
the ruler cannot be deceived about the weight of things under heaven.
Now if advancement of the capable is based on reputation,
then ministers will distance themselves from the ruler
and form cliques below;
if officials are promoted through factions,
then the people will devote themselves to connections
and not seek usefulness through the law.
Therefore, when officials lack ability,
the state falls into chaos;
if rewards are based on praise,
and punishments on slander,
then those who love reward and fear punishment
will abandon public duty,
practice private arts,
and form cliques to assist each other.
If one forgets his lord and engages in external associations,
thereby advancing his coterie,
then his subordinates' service to their superiors becomes shallow.
With numerous associations and a large following,
forming cliques both inside and outside,
even if there are major faults,
the concealment of them will be extensive.
Thus loyal ministers face danger and death without guilt,
while treacherous ministers secure benefits without merit.
When loyal ministers face danger and death
not due to their crimes,
then good ministers withdraw;
when treacherous ministers secure benefits
without merit,
then wicked ministers advance;
this is the root of destruction.
If so,
then the officials abandon the law
and practice personal favoritism,
轻视 public law.
They frequently visit the doors of powerful men,
but not once do they come to the sovereign's court;
they ponder a hundred schemes for private households' convenience,
but not one plan for the sovereign's state.
Though the number of subordinates is large,
they do not serve to honor the ruler;
though the hundred officials are complete,
they are not fit to manage the state.
Thus the ruler has the name of sovereign,
but in reality, he is entrusted to the households of his officials.
Therefore I say:
The court of a doomed state has no true men.
The court having no men
does not mean the court is declining in numbers.
They strive to benefit each other,
not to enrich the state;
high officials strive to honor each other,
not to honor the ruler;
minor officials use their salaries to cultivate connections,
not treating their offices as their duty.
The reason for this
is that the ruler does not decide everything according to the law above,
but trusts his subordinates to act on their own.
Hence an enlightened ruler uses the law to select men,
not promoting them personally;
uses the law to measure merit,
not judging it himself.
The capable cannot be obscured,
the failures cannot be disguised,
the praised cannot be advanced,
the criticized cannot be dismissed,
then between ruler and ministers, distinctions are clear
and governance becomes easy,
so the ruler can apply the law impartially.
When a worthy person serves as minister,
he faces north and presents his pledge,
without a divided heart,
in the court he dares not decline humble tasks,
in the army he dares not shirk difficulties;
he follows the ruler's actions,
obeys the ruler's laws,
empties his mind to await orders,
without personal judgments.
Thus he has a mouth but does not speak for private purposes,
has eyes but does not see for private views,
and the ruler fully controls him.
A minister,
to use an analogy, is like a hand,
used above to tend the head,
below to tend the feet;
in heat or cold,
it must rescue the body,
if a sword presses against the body,
it dares not not fight,
without private favor for wise ministers,
without private service for capable men.
Thus the people do not cross villages to associate,
have no anxieties within a hundred lǐ.
Noble and humble do not overstep each other,
foolish and wise stand in balance,
this is the pinnacle of governance.
Now those who lightly regard ranks and emoluments,
easily leave or flee,
to choose their lord,
I do not call them upright.
Deceptive arguments that oppose the law,
forcibly remonstrating against the lord,
I do not call them loyal.
Distributing favors and bestowing benefits,
winning over subordinates for fame,
I do not call them benevolent.
Leaving society to live in seclusion,
yet using deceit to criticize the ruler,
I do not call them righteous.
Externally serving other lords,
internally exhausting their own state,
waiting at the brink of danger,
to frighten their ruler saying:
"Relationships are not intimate without me,
enmities are not resolved without me,"
and the ruler then believes them,
entrusts the state to them,
debasing the ruler's name to glorify themselves,
destroying the state's wealth to benefit their families,
I do not call them wise.
These several things
are the theories of a perilous age,
and were rejected by the laws of the former kings.
The laws of the former kings said:
"Ministers shall not create authority,
shall not create benefits,
but follow the king's direction;
shall not create evils,
but follow the king's path."
In ancient times, the people of a well-governed age
upheld public law,
abandoned private arts,
focused their intentions on one course,
and prepared themselves to await appointment.
If a ruler personally inspects all officials,
then the days are insufficient,
and his strength is inadequate.
Moreover, if the ruler uses his eyes,
the subordinates adorn appearances;
if the ruler uses his ears,
the subordinates adorn sounds;
if the ruler uses his thoughts,
the subordinates multiply words.
The former kings considered these three methods insufficient,
so they abandoned their own abilities and relied on laws and methods,
carefully applying rewards and punishments.
What the former kings held as essential,
thus the laws were concise and not violated.
Alone they controlled all within the four seas,
the clever and wise could not use their deceit,
the risky and impetuous could not practice their flattery,
and the treacherous had nothing to rely on.
Even those far a thousand lǐ away,
dared not change their reports;
those in positions like court attendants,
dared not conceal good or disguise evil.
The officials at court,
directly assembled from the humble,
dared not overstep each other.
Thus governance is effortless and the days are ample,
because the ruler employs authority to make it so.
When ministers encroach upon their ruler,
it is like the terrain,
gradually progressing,
causing the ruler to lose his bearings,
east and west changing faces without his realizing it.
Therefore the former kings established the south-pointing chariot
to correct the directions.
Thus an enlightened ruler makes his ministers not wander in thought beyond the law,
not confer favors within the law,
so that no action is unlawful.
Harsh laws
are to prevent faults and exclude private interests,
severe punishments
are to implement orders and punish subordinates.
Authority is not divided in its application,
control does not share its source.
If authority and control are shared,
then all evils become manifest;
if the law is not trusted,
then the ruler's actions are endangered;
if punishments are not decisive,
then evils cannot be overcome.
Hence it is said:
A skilled craftsman's eye may align with the line,
but he must first use the compass and square as standards;
the highly wise may quickly hit the mark in affairs,
but they must take the laws of the former kings as the measure.
Thus, with the marking line straight, crooked wood is cut;
with the level even, high protrusions are shaved;
with the scale hung, the heavy is reduced and the light increased;
with the measures set, the excessive is decreased and the insufficient supplemented.
Therefore, to govern the state by law
is simply to act accordingly.
The law does not favor the noble,
as the marking line does not yield to the crooked.
Where the law applies,
the wise cannot evade it with words,
nor the brave dare to contend.
Punishing faults does not bypass high ministers;
rewarding the good does not overlook commoners.
Hence, to rectify the ruler's errors,
investigate the subordinates' wrongdoings,
bring order to chaos, resolve disputes,
eliminate excess, and correct faults,
unifying the people's conduct,
nothing compares to the law.
To discipline officials and awe the people,
curb extravagance and indolence,
and stop deceit and falsehood,
nothing compares to punishment.
When punishments are severe,
none dare use their status to mistreat the lowly;
when laws are precise,
the ruler is honored and not infringed upon.
With the ruler honored and not infringed upon,
the sovereign is strong and maintains control.
Thus, the ancient kings valued this and passed it down.
If the ruler abandons the law and acts on personal whim,
then there will be no distinction between superior and inferior.
The enlightened ruler's means to control ministers
are but two handles.
These two handles
are punishment and favor.
What are punishment and favor?
It is said:
Killing and penalizing are called punishment;
commending and rewarding are called favor.
Ministers fear execution and punishment
and desire commendations and rewards.
Thus, if the ruler personally wields punishment and favor,
the ministers will fear his authority
and seek his benefits.
But treacherous ministers of the age are not so;
those they dislike
they can make the ruler punish,
and those they favor
they can make the ruler reward.
If the ruler does not ensure that the power of rewards and punishments originates from himself,
but follows his ministers in dispensing them,
then the whole state will fear the ministers and disregard the ruler,
aligning with the ministers and abandoning the ruler.
This is the peril of the ruler losing control over punishment and favor.
The reason a tiger can subdue a dog
is its claws and teeth.
If the tiger were to shed its claws and teeth
and let the dog use them,
then the tiger would be subdued by the dog.
The ruler
uses punishment and favor to control ministers.
If the ruler relinquishes punishment and favor
and lets ministers use them,
then the ruler will be controlled by the ministers.
Thus, Tián Cháng requested titles and emoluments from above
to distribute among the ministers,
and enlarged measures below
to bestow upon the common people.
This was because Duke Jiǎn lost favor
and Tián Cháng used it,
leading to Duke Jiǎn's assassination.
Zǐ Hǎn said to the ruler of Sòng:
"Commendations, rewards, and gifts
are what the people delight in;
you should administer them yourself.
Killings, executions, and punishments
are what the people detest;
allow me to take charge of them."
Thereupon, the ruler of Sòng lost punishment
and Zǐ Hǎn used it,
so the ruler of Sòng was seized.
Tián Cháng used only favor
and Duke Jiǎn was assassinated;
Zǐ Hǎn used only punishment
and the ruler of Sòng was seized.
Thus, ministers of today
combine punishment and favor and wield them;
this makes contemporary rulers in greater danger than Duke Jiǎn
and the ruler of Sòng.
Hence, for rulers who are coerced, murdered, or isolated,
having lost both punishment and favor
and letting ministers use them,
to avoid peril and ruin
has never happened.
If the ruler wishes to prohibit treachery,
he must carefully match punishment and name;
punishment and name refer to
words and deeds.
When a minister proposes a statement,
the ruler assigns tasks based on that statement,
and specifically holds him accountable for the results of those tasks.
If the achievement matches the task,
and the task matches the statement,
then reward;
if the achievement does not match the task,
or the task does not match the statement,
then punish.
Thus, if a minister's words are grand but achievements small,
he is punished—
not for the small achievement,
but for the mismatch between achievement and name.
If a minister's words are small but achievements large,
he is also punished—
not from displeasure at the great achievement,
but because the harm of mismatch is greater than having a great achievement,
hence the punishment.
Once, Hán Zhāo Hóu was drunk and asleep;
the keeper of the crown saw the ruler was cold,
so he placed a robe over him.
Upon waking, the ruler was pleased
and asked his attendants:
"Who placed the robe on me?"
The attendants replied:
"The keeper of the crown."
The ruler then punished both the keeper of the robes and the keeper of the crown.
He punished the keeper of the robes
for neglecting his duty;
he punished the keeper of the crown
for overstepping his position.
It was not that he disliked being warm,
but that the harm of encroaching on another's office is greater than the cold.
Thus, in the enlightened ruler's employment of ministers,
they may not overstep their offices to achieve merit,
nor propose statements that do not match.
To overstep an office is to die;
to mismatch is to be punished.
If each guards his duty,
and statements are truthful,
then ministers cannot form cliques to collude.
The ruler faces two perils:
appointing the worthy,
then ministers may exploit worthiness to coerce the ruler;
promoting recklessly,
then affairs fail and are insurmountable.
Thus, if the ruler favors the worthy,
ministers will embellish their conduct
to cater to the ruler's desires,
and the true nature of ministers will not be revealed;
if their true nature is not revealed,
the ruler has no means to distinguish among them.
Hence, the King of Yuè favored bravery,
and many of his people disregarded death;
King Chǔ Líng favored slim waists,
and many in the state starved themselves;
Duke Qí Huán was jealous and favored women,
so Shù Diāo castrated himself to manage the inner court;
Duke Huán favored delicacies,
and Yì Yá steamed his son's head and presented it;
King Yān Zì Kuài favored the worthy,
so Zǐ Zhī ostensibly refused the state.
Thus, if the ruler shows dislike,
ministers conceal their intentions;
if the ruler shows preference,
ministers feign ability.
If the ruler reveals desires,
ministers' true dispositions gain leverage.
Thus, Zǐzhī relied on the reputation of worthiness
to usurp his ruler's position,
while Shù Diāo
and Yì Yá exploited the ruler's desires
to encroach upon his authority.
In the end, Zikuài died in turmoil,
and Duke Huán's corpse lay with maggots flowing out the door
left unburied.
What is the reason for this?
It is the calamity of a ruler revealing his personal inclinations to his ministers.
The true nature of ministers is not necessarily to love their ruler,
but to act for the sake of great profit.
If the ruler does not conceal his inclinations,
nor hide his intentions,
thus giving ministers a pretext
to encroach upon their ruler,
then for ministers to become like Zǐzhī
or Tián Cháng is not difficult.
Hence it is said:
"Discard likes and dislikes,
and ministers will reveal their true nature."
When ministers reveal their true nature,
then the great ruler will not be deceived.
Heaven has its great decree,
and humans have their great destiny.
Fragrant, delicious, crisp flavors,
strong wine and rich meat,
please the mouth but harm the body;
fine features and white teeth,
delight the emotions but waste the essence.
Therefore, discard excess and extremity,
and the body will suffer no harm.
Power should not be displayed,
remaining plain and non-interfering.
Affairs lie in the four directions,
but the essential is at the center.
The sage holds the essential,
and the four directions come to serve.
Be empty and await them,
and they will bring themselves.
When the four seas are contained,
the Way conceals yet reveals the yang.
Once left and right are established,
open the gate and face them.
Do not change or alter,
proceed with both;
practice this without cease,
this is called walking the principle.
Things have their appropriate uses,
materials have their applications,
each in its proper place,
thus the ruler does not interfere.
Employ the rooster to herald the night,
order the cat to catch rats,
all use their abilities,
and the ruler has no tasks.
If the ruler has particular skills,
affairs will not be properly managed.
Arrogant and fond of ability,
he will be deceived by subordinates;
clever and generous in bestowing favors,
subordinates will exploit his talents.
When superior and inferior exchange roles,
the state consequently falls into disorder.
The way of using oneness
begins with names,
when names are correct
things are settled,
when names are biased
things shift.
Thus the sage holds to oneness through stillness,
letting names define themselves,
allowing affairs to settle naturally.
Not displaying his brilliance,
subordinates thus remain plain and correct.
Accordingly assign them,
let them manage affairs themselves;
accordingly grant them,
they will promote themselves;
correct and position them,
letting all settle themselves.
The ruler uses names to appoint them,
if the names are unknown,
revert to examining their forms.
When forms and names correspond,
employ what they produce.
If both are sincere and trustworthy,
subordinates will offer their true feelings.
Carefully manage your affairs,
and await Heaven's command.
Do not lose the essential,
and you will become a sage.
The way of the sage
discards wisdom and cunning;
if wisdom and cunning are not discarded,
it is difficult to maintain constancy.
If the common people use them,
their persons suffer many calamities;
if the ruler uses them,
his state faces peril and ruin.
Follow the way of Heaven,
revert to the principle of forms,
examine and investigate them,
ending then beginning anew.
Empty and still, remain behind,
never using your own ideas.
The ruler's constant peril
lies in agreeing with their viewpoints;
be trustworthy but do not agree,
and the myriad people will uniformly follow.
The Way
is vast and formless,
Virtue
embodies principle and pervades all.
As for all living things,
they draw upon it as needed,
all things flourish,
yet it does not share their tranquility.
The Way
permeates all affairs below,
following examination it assigns names,
living and dying with the times.
Compare names and differentiate affairs,
unifying them through common essence.
Hence it is said:
The Way differs from the myriad things,
Virtue differs from yin and yang,
the scale differs from light and heavy,
the marking-line differs from crooked and straight,
harmony differs from dry and damp,
the ruler differs from the multitude of ministers.
These six
are all emanations of the Way.
The Way has no pair,
thus it is called One.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler values the appearance of the solitary Way.
Ruler and ministers follow different paths,
subordinates offer names in prayer,
the ruler holds the names,
ministers present their forms,
when forms and names correspond,
superior and inferior are harmonized.
The way of listening
is to take what comes out
and reflect it back as what enters.
Thus examine names to fix positions,
clarify distinctions to differentiate categories.
The way of listening to words
is like being deeply drunk.
Lips? Teeth?
I do not initiate;
Teeth? Lips?
increasingly bemused and muddled.
They themselves reveal it,
I thereby come to know it;
right and wrong converge like spokes,
the ruler does not engage with them.
Emptiness, stillness, and non-action
are the essence of the Way;
comparing and correlating things
is the form of affairs.
Compare them through correlation,
group them through union with emptiness.
If the root and trunk do not change,
then movement and rest will not err.
Move and dissolve them,
attack through non-action.
Delight in them
and many affairs arise,
dislike them
and resentment is born.
Therefore, discard delight and dislike,
and with an empty mind make it the abode of the Way.
When the ruler does not share governance with them,
the people will honor him;
when the ruler does not collaborate with them,
he lets them act alone.
The ruler firmly bolts the inner gates,
observing the court from his chamber;
with everything within close reach,
all are in their places.
Reward those deserving reward,
punish those deserving punishment;
according to their actions,
each achieves their own outcome.
Good and evil inevitably bring consequences,
who would dare be untrustworthy?
Once rules are established,
all corners fall into order.
If the ruler is not divine,
subordinates will take advantage;
if his actions are improper,
they will scrutinize his regular conduct.
Like heaven and earth,
this is called cumulative resolution.
Like earth and heaven,
who is distant, who is close?
To emulate heaven and earth,
this is called the sage.
To govern the inner court,
appoint but do not be intimate;
to govern the outer court,
assign one official per position,
not allowing self-indulgence,
how can there be usurpation?
At the gates of high ministers,
fear many visitors.
The pinnacle of governance,
subordinates cannot attain.
Unify punishments and names,
and the people will keep to their duties;
seeking beyond this,
is called great confusion.
Crafty people multiply,
deceitful villains fill the sides.
Hence it is said:
Do not enrich others and then borrow from them,
do not elevate others and then be pressured by them,
do not trust one person exclusively and lose your capital and state.
When the calf is larger than the thigh,
it is hard to walk swiftly.
When the ruler loses his divinity,
tigers follow behind.
If the ruler is unaware,
tigers will become like dogs.
If the ruler does not stop it early,
dogs will multiply endlessly.
Tigers form their packs,
to kill their mother.
To be a ruler without loyal ministers,
how can the state exist?
When the ruler enforces his laws,
the big tiger will become fearful;
when the ruler applies his punishments,
the big tiger will calm itself.
If laws and punishments are trustworthy,
tigers turn into humans,
returning to their true nature.
To secure your state,
you must cut down its gatherings;
if you do not cut them down,
they will amass crowds.
To secure your land,
you must moderate your gifts;
if not moderated,
troublemakers will seek more.
They ask, I give,
lending an axe to an enemy;
it should not be lent,
for they will use it to attack me.
Huángdì had a saying:
"Superior and inferior fight a hundred battles a day."
Subordinates conceal their selfish motives,
testing their superior;
the superior wields measures,
to control his subordinates.
Thus, the establishment of measures,
is the ruler's treasure;
the formation of factions,
is the minister's treasure.
The reason ministers do not assassinate their ruler,
is that factions are not complete.
So if the ruler loses an inch,
the subordinate gains a yard.
The ruler of a state,
does not enlarge his capital;
the minister with principles,
does not exalt his family.
The principled ruler,
does not overly honor his ministers.
Honoring and enriching them,
they will replace him.
To prevent danger and avert crisis,
quickly establish a crown prince,
and disaster will have no origin.
Internally searching, externally guarding,
he must personally hold the measures.
Reduce the thick,
supplement the thin.
Reduction and supplementation have measures,
do not let the people form cliques,
to deceive their superior together.
Reduce like the waning moon,
supplement like applying heat.
Simplify orders, be cautious in executions,
and ensure penalties are fully carried out.
Do not relax your bow,
one perch with two males.
One perch with two males,
their fight is fierce.
With wolves in the pen,
the sheep do not multiply.
One house with two masters,
affairs achieve nothing.
Husband and wife both govern,
children have none to follow.
As a ruler,
repeatedly trim the tree,
do not let its branches spread.
If the branches spread,
they will block the public gates,
private doors will be filled,
the public court will be empty,
and the ruler will be surrounded.
Repeatedly trim the tree,
do not let branches extend outward;
if branches extend outward,
they will encroach on the ruler's place.
Repeatedly trim the tree,
do not let branches be large and the trunk small;
if branches are large and the trunk small,
it will not withstand the spring wind;
if it cannot withstand the spring wind,
the branches will harm the core.
When the ruler's sons are many,
the royal house worries and sighs.
The way to stop it,
is to repeatedly trim the tree,
not letting the branches flourish.
The tree repeatedly trimmed,
factions will disperse.
Dig out its roots
and base,
and the tree loses its spirit.
Fill the churning abyss,
do not let the waters clear.
Search their bosoms,
seize their power.
When the ruler uses it,
it is like lightning, like thunder.
All ways by which ministers achieve treachery
involve eight methods:
The first is called sharing the bed.
What is sharing the bed?
It is said:
honoring the noble consort,
loving the favorite concubine,
charming and beautiful,
these are what bewitch the ruler.
Taking advantage of leisurely moments of repose,
during times of drunkenness and satiety,
they seek what they desire,
this is a method that ensures hearing.
As a minister, serve them internally with gold and jade,
to bewitch their ruler,
this is called "sharing the bed."
The second is those by one's side.
What is meant by those by one's side?
It is said:
Entertainers and dwarfs,
personal attendants and close associates—
these are people who, before the ruler has given an order, are already bowing and agreeing,
before being tasked, are already saying "yes, yes",
anticipating his intentions and complying with his wishes,
observing his demeanor and scrutinizing his expression
to read his mind in advance.
They all advance and retreat together,
respond and answer uniformly,
speaking with one voice and following the same track
to sway the ruler's mind.
As for the ministers,
they bribe them internally with gold, jade, and curios,
and externally assist them in unlawful acts,
making them influence their ruler.
This is called "those by one's side."
The third is paternal relatives.
What is meant by paternal relatives?
It is said:
Sons from concubines and royal brothers,
are those whom the ruler holds dear and loves;
high officials and court ministers,
are those with whom the ruler deliberates and plans.
These all exert their efforts and exhaust their counsel,
and the ruler is bound to listen to them.
As for the ministers,
they serve the royal brothers and sons from concubines with music and women,
win over high officials and court ministers with persuasive words,
arranging matters and proposing affairs in a restrained manner,
and when things succeed, they promote them in rank and increase their emoluments,
to gratify their hearts,
making them encroach upon their ruler.
This is called "paternal relatives."
The fourth is nurturing calamity.
What is meant by nurturing calamity?
It is said:
If the ruler delights in magnificent palaces, towers, and ponds,
and enjoys adorning women, dogs, and horses to amuse his heart,
this is the ruler's calamity.
As for the ministers,
they exhaust the people's strength to beautify palaces, towers, and ponds,
impose heavy taxes and levies
to adorn women, dogs, and horses,
thereby amusing their ruler and confusing his mind,
indulging his desires,
while establishing their private gains therein,
this is called "nurturing calamity."
The fifth is winning over the populace.
What is meant by winning over the populace?
It is said:
As for the ministers, they distribute public wealth to please the people,
perform small acts of kindness to win over the commoners,
making both the court and the marketplace praise themselves,
thereby obstructing their ruler and achieving their own desires.
This is called "winning over the populace."
The sixth is circulating influence.
What is meant by circulating influence?
It is said:
The ruler,
being naturally isolated in his discourse,
seldom hears debates and discussions,
is easily swayed by eloquent arguments.
As for the ministers,
they seek out persuasive scholars from other states,
and nurture skilled speakers within the country,
making them speak for their private interests.
They craft clever and ornate speeches,
and circulating persuasive words,
showing him advantages and power,
frightening him with perils and harm,
employing fabricated lies to corrupt their ruler.
This is called "circulating influence."
The seventh is using might.
What is meant by using might?
It is said:
The ruler of men
relies on his officials and common people
for his might and strength.
What the officials and common people approve,
the ruler approves;
what the officials and common people do not approve,
the ruler does not approve.
As for the ministers,
they gather followers who carry swords,
and nurture men willing to die,
to display their power,
making it clear that those who support them will surely benefit,
while those who do not will surely die,
thus intimidating the officials and common people
to carry out their private schemes.
This is called "using might."
The eighth is relying on foreign powers.
What is meant by relying on foreign powers?
It is said:
The ruler of men,
if his state is small,
must serve large states,
if his military is weak,
must fear strong armies.
What a large state demands,
a small state must obey;
where a strong army presses,
a weak army must submit.
As for the ministers,
they impose heavy taxes and levies,
drain the state treasury,
impoverish their country to serve a large state,
and use its power to coerce and tempt their ruler;
in extreme cases, they mobilize troops to gather at the border
and exert control internally,
in milder cases, they frequently invite great envoys to intimidate their ruler,
making him fearful.
This is called "relying on foreign powers."
All these eight methods
are the means by which ministers achieve their treachery,
and contemporary rulers are controlled and coerced,
losing what is rightfully theirs.
This cannot be left unexamined.
An enlightened ruler, regarding his inner court,
enjoys their beauty but does not grant their petitions,
not allowing private requests.
Regarding his attendants,
he employs them but holds them accountable for their words,
not allowing exaggerated speech.
Regarding his paternal relatives and high officials,
when he listens to their advice, he must make them bear punishment
responsibility afterwards,
not permitting reckless recommendations.
Regarding sightseeing, music, and curios,
he must ensure they have a legitimate source,
not allowing unauthorized advances or retreats,
not letting ministers speculate on his intentions.
Regarding the distribution of favors,
whether releasing prohibited goods
or opening granaries,
benefits to the people
must originate from the ruler,
not allowing ministers to privatize the credit.
Regarding discussions and debates,
those who praise and those who criticize,
who are liked and who are disliked,
he must verify their abilities,
examine their faults,
not allowing ministers to collude in speech.
Regarding men of courage and strength,
military merits are not over-rewarded,
bravery in local brawls is not pardoned,
not allowing ministers to use private wealth.
Regarding the demands of other states,
if lawful, he complies;
if unlawful, he refuses.
What is called a lost ruler
does not mean he lacks a state,
but that having it,
it is not truly his.
If orders from ministers outside
control affairs inside,
then the ruler is lost.
Obeying a large state to save oneself from destruction,
yet destruction comes faster than by disobedience—
therefore, do not obey.
If ministers know he will not obey,
they will not collude with other states;
if other states know he will not obey,
they will not accept ministers' slander against their ruler.
An enlightened ruler establishes official positions, titles, and emoluments
to promote men of worth and encourage the meritorious.
Hence it is said:
Men of worth should receive generous stipends
and hold high offices;
those with great achievements should receive noble titles
and substantial rewards.
When appointing the worthy, assess their abilities;
when granting emoluments, match their accomplishments.
Thus, the worthy do not misrepresent their capabilities
in serving their ruler,
and the meritorious gladly advance their work,
so tasks are accomplished and achievements established.
Now it is not so:
without examining worth or incompetence,
without considering merit or service,
they rely on the influence of feudal lords,
and heed the requests of court attendants.
Fathers, brothers, and high ministers petition the ruler for ranks and emoluments above,
then sell them below to amass wealth,
and thereby build private factions.
Thus, those with abundant wealth buy offices to become noble,
and those with connections to court attendants
secure influence through petitions.
Meritorious ministers go unrecognized,
and promotions to office become erroneous.
Hence, officials neglect their duties
to cultivate external ties,
abandoning affairs to pursue wealth.
Thus, the worthy grow slack and unmotivated,
the meritorious deteriorate and neglect their work—
this is the wind of a perishing state.
Ten Faults:
First: Practicing minor loyalty
harms great loyalty.
Second: Heeding small gains
damages major benefits.
Third: Acting perversely and self-righteously,
showing disrespect to feudal lords,
leads to personal ruin.
Fourth: Neglecting governance
and indulging in music
brings personal downfall.
Fifth: Being greedy, stubborn, and profit-loving
is the root of state destruction and personal death.
Sixth: Wallowing in female entertainers,
ignoring state affairs,
invites the calamity of a fallen state.
Seventh: Leaving the court to travel far
while ignoring remonstrating scholars
endangers one’s person.
Eighth: Having faults but not listening to loyal ministers,
insisting on one’s own will,
ruins one’s high reputation
and becomes the start of being laughed at.
Ninth: Internally not measuring one’s strength,
externally relying on feudal lords,
brings the disaster of territorial loss.
Tenth: Being a small state without propriety,
not employing remonstrating ministers,
leads to the extinction of the lineage.
What is meant by "minor loyalty"?
Long ago, King Gòng of Chǔ and Duke Lì of Jìn
fought at Yānlíng,
the Chǔ army was defeated,
and King Gòng was wounded in the eye.
During the fierce battle,
Marshal Zǐ Fǎn, thirsty, sought a drink;
his attendant Gǔ Yáng brought him a cup of wine.
Zǐ Fǎn said:
"Alas,
withdraw!
This is wine."
Gǔ Yáng said:
"It is not wine."
Zǐ Fǎn accepted and drank it.
Zǐ Fǎn’s nature
was such that he loved wine
and found it sweet,
unable to stop drinking
until he was drunk.
After the battle ended,
King Gòng wished to fight again,
and sent for Marshal Zǐ Fǎn,
but Zǐ Fǎn pleaded a heart ailment.
King Gòng rode in his carriage to see him personally,
entered his tent,
smelled the wine, and returned,
saying:
"In today’s battle,
I myself was wounded.
What I relied on
was the Marshal.
Yet the Marshal is so drunk—
this is to abandon the altars of Chǔ
and have no pity for my troops.
I will not fight again."
Thereupon, he withdrew the army
and had Zǐ Fǎn beheaded as a great punishment.
Thus, when Gǔ Yáng offered wine,
it was not out of enmity for Zǐ Fǎn;
his heart was loyal and loving,
yet it sufficed to get him killed.
Hence it is said:
Practicing minor loyalty
harms great loyalty.
What is meant by "heeding small gains"?
Long ago, Duke Xiàn of Jìn sought to borrow a route through Yú
to attack Guó.
Xún Xī said:
"My lord, offer the jade disc of Chuíjí and the steeds of Qūchǎn
as bribes to the Duke of Yú,
requesting passage;
he will surely grant it."
The duke said:
"The jade of Chuíjí
was my predecessor’s treasure;
the steeds of Qūchǎn
are my finest horses.
If they accept our gifts but deny us passage,
what then?"
Xún Xī said:
"If he denies us passage,
he will not dare accept our gifts.
If he accepts them and grants passage,
then the treasure is like taking it from the inner treasury
to store in the outer treasury,
the horses like taking them from the inner stable
to tie in the outer stable.
My lord, do not worry."
The duke said:
"So be it."
He then sent Xún Xī with the jade and steeds
to bribe the Duke of Yú for passage.
The Duke of Yú, coveting the jade and horses, wished to consent.
Gōng Zhī Qí admonished:
"Do not agree.
The relationship between Yú and Guó
is like that of a carriage and its supporting boards.
The boards rely on the carriage,
the carriage relies on the boards;
such is the situation of Yú and Guó.
If we grant passage,
then Guó will fall by morning and Yú by evening.
It must not be;
I beg you not to consent."
The Duke of Yú did not listen
and granted the route.
Xún Xī attacked and conquered Guó,
returned, and after three years,
raised troops to attack Yú,
conquering it as well.
Xún Xī led the horses and held the jade
to report to Duke Xiàn,
who said joyfully:
"The jade is still the same.
Even so,
the horses’ teeth have grown longer."
Why did the Duke of Yú’s army face peril
and his land get cut away?
Why?
He loved small gains without considering the harm.
Hence it is said:
Heeding small gains
damages major benefits.
What is meant by "acting perversely"?
Long ago, King Líng of Chǔ held the meeting at Shēn,
the crown prince of Sòng arrived late,
so he seized and imprisoned him;
he insulted the Lord of Xú,
and detained Qìng Fēng of Qí.
The archer-official remonstrated:
"When convening the feudal lords, one cannot be without propriety,
for this is a matter of survival or demise.
In the past, Jié held the assembly at Yǒuróng,
and Yǒumín rebelled against him;
Zhòu conducted the hunt at Líqiū,
and the Róng
and Dí tribes rebelled,
all due to lack of propriety.
I urge you to consider this."
The ruler did not listen,
and proceeded with his intention.
Before a year had passed,
King Líng traveled south,
and his ministers followed and seized him.
King Líng starved to death on the banks of Gānxī.
Hence it is said:
"To act perversely and be self-willed,
showing no propriety to the feudal lords,
leads to the loss of one's life."
What is meant by being fond of music?
In the past, Duke Líng of Wèi was going to Jìn,
and when he reached the banks of the Pú River,
he unharnessed his carriage and let his horses graze,
setting up camp to stay overnight.
At midnight,
he heard someone playing a new tune and was delighted by it.
He sent someone to ask his attendants,
but all reported hearing nothing.
So he summoned Shī Juān and told him:
"There is someone playing a new tune,
I sent someone to ask my attendants,
but all reported hearing nothing.
It seems like it could be ghosts or spirits;
please listen for me and transcribe it."
Shī Juān said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, he sat quietly and played the zither to transcribe it.
The next day, Shī Juān reported:
"I have grasped it,
but have not yet practiced it;
please allow another night to practice."
Duke Líng said:
"Yes."
So they stayed another night.
The next day,
having practiced it,
they proceeded to Jìn.
Duke Píng of Jìn hosted them at the Shīyí Tower.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Duke Líng rose.
The Duke said:
"There is a new tune;
I wish to present it for your enjoyment."
Duke Píng said:
"Excellent."
So he summoned Shī Juān,
had him sit beside Shī Kuàng,
and he took up the zither and played.
Before he finished,
Shī Kuàng stopped him by pressing on the strings,
saying:
"This is the music of a doomed state;
it should not be played to completion."
Duke Píng said:
"Where does this tune come from?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"This was composed by Shī Yán,
who created decadent music for Zhòu.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Shī Yán fled east,
and upon reaching the Pú River, he threw himself in.
Therefore, those who hear this tune
must be by the Pú River.
The state of whoever hears this tune first
will surely be diminished;
it should not be played to completion."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love
is music;
please let him finish it."
Shī Juān played it through.
Duke Píng asked Shī Kuàng:
"What is this tune called?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"This is what is called the Shāng mode."
The Duke said:
"Is the Shāng mode the most poignant?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"It is not as poignant as the Zhǐ mode."
The Duke said:
"May I hear the Zhǐ mode?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"No.
Those in ancient times who listened to the Zhǐ mode
were all rulers of virtue and righteousness.
Now, my lord's virtue is shallow,
and you are not fit to hear it."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love
is music;
I wish to try hearing it."
Shī Kuàng had no choice
but to take up the zither and play.
At the first playing,
sixteen black cranes
came from the south,
gathering on the ridge of the palace gate.
At the second playing,
they formed rows.
At the third playing,
they stretched their necks and sang,
spread their wings, and danced.
The music harmonized with the Gōng and Shāng notes,
and the sound reached the heavens.
Duke Píng was greatly pleased,
and all seated were joyful.
Duke Píng raised his wine cup
and stood to toast Shī Kuàng,
then sat back and asked:
