"Is no music more poignant than the Zhǐ mode?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"It is not as poignant as the Jué mode."
Duke Píng said:
"May I hear the Jué mode?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"No.
In the past, Huángdì assembled ghosts and spirits
on Mount Tài,
riding an ivory chariot drawn by six蛟龙,
with Bìfāng at the reins,
Chīyóu leading the way,
the Wind Earl sweeping ahead,
the Rain Master sprinkling the path,
tigers and wolves in front,
ghosts and spirits behind,
soaring snakes crouching on the ground,
phoenixes covering above,
gathering all ghosts and spirits,
and composed the Jué mode.
Now, my lord's virtue is shallow,
and you are not fit to hear it.
If you hear it,
I fear disaster may follow."
Duke Píng said:
"I am old;
what I love is music,
and I wish to hear it to the end."
Shī Kuàng had no choice but to play it.
At the first playing,
black clouds arose from the northwest;
at the second playing,
a great wind came,
followed by heavy rain,
tearing the curtains,
shattering the sacrificial vessels,
and breaking the tiles on the corridor roof.
Those seated scattered and fled;
Duke Píng was terrified,
and crouched among the corridor rooms.
Jìn suffered a great drought,
leaving the land barren for three years.
Duke Píng himself became afflicted with illness.
Hence it is said:
"To neglect governance
and incessantly indulge in the five tones
leads to personal ruin."
What is meant by greed and obstinacy?
Long ago, Zhì Bó Yáo led Zhào,
Hán, and Wèi
to attack Fàn and
Zhōngháng,
exterminating them.
Upon returning,
he rested his troops for several years,
then sent a messenger to request territory from Hán.
Hán Kāngzǐ wished to refuse,
but Duàn Guī advised:
"You must grant it.
For Zhì Bó's character
is covetous and arrogantly stubborn.
If he comes requesting land and is refused,
he will surely turn his troops against Hán.
My lord should grant it.
Once granted, he'll grow accustomed,
and will request land from other states.
Those states will likely refuse,
and if they refuse,
Zhì Bó will surely attack them.
Thus,
Hán can avoid calamity
and await changes in the situation."
Kāngzǐ said:
"Agreed."
He then ordered an envoy to present one county of ten thousand households
to Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó was pleased,
and again sent someone to request territory from Wèi.
Xuānzǐ wished to refuse,
but Zhào Jiā advised:
"He requested land from Hán,
and Hán granted it.
Now he requests land from Wèi.
If Wèi refuses,
then Wèi would be strengthening itself internally
while provoking Zhì Bó externally.
If we don't give,
he will surely deploy troops against Wèi.
Better to grant it."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Agreed."
He then ordered someone to present one county of ten thousand households
to Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó again sent someone to Zhào to request the lands of Cài and
Gāoláng,
but Zhào Xiāngzǐ refused.
Zhì Bó then secretly allied with Hán and Wèi,
planning to attack Zhào.
Xiāngzǐ summoned Zhāng Mèngtán and told him:
"Zhì Bó's character
shows surface friendship but underlying alienation.
He has sent messengers three times to Hán and Wèi
while I have not participated,
so he will surely deploy troops against me.
Where should I establish myself securely?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:[69"Dǒng Yānwū,
a talented minister of Lord Jiǎn,
governed Jìnyáng,
and Yǐn Duó continued his methods.
Their remaining teachings still survive.
My lord should settle in Jìnyáng."
The lord said:
"Agreed."
He then summoned Yánlíng Shēng,
ordering him to lead the chariots and cavalry
ahead to Jìnyáng,
while the lord followed.
When the lord arrived,
he inspected the city walls and the stores of the five offices.
The walls were in disrepair,
the granaries held no accumulated grain,
the treasury had no stored money,
the armory contained no armor or weapons,
and the city lacked defensive equipment.
Xiāngzǐ grew fearful,
and summoned Zhāng Mèngtán:
"I have inspected the city walls
and the stores of the five offices,
all are inadequately prepared.
How shall I respond to the enemy?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"I have heard that when sages govern,
they store wealth among the people,
not in government treasuries,
focusing on cultivating education
rather than building city walls.
My lord should issue orders
commanding the people to keep three years' food for themselves,
with surplus grain deposited in the granaries;
keep three years' supplies for themselves,
with surplus money deposited in the treasury;
and those with extra labor
should be ordered to repair the city walls."
The lord issued the orders that evening,
and the next day,
the granaries could not hold all the grain,
the treasury had accumulated money,
and the armory received armor and weapons.
After five days, the city walls were repaired,
and defensive preparations were complete.
The lord summoned Zhāng Mèngtán and asked:
"Our city walls are repaired,
defenses are prepared,
money and grain are sufficient,
armor and weapons are abundant,
but what shall we do about having no arrows?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"I heard that when Dǒngzǐ governed Jìnyáng,
the walls of the ducal residence
were all made of reeds, mugwort, and thorn bushes,
with some thorns growing over ten feet high.
My lord can dig them up and use them."
So they dug them up and tested them,
finding their hardness unmatched even by the strongest bamboo arrows
from Jùnlù.
The lord said:
"We have enough arrows now,
but what shall we do about having no metal?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"I heard that when Dǒngzǐ governed Jìnyáng,
the halls of the ducal residence and official buildings
all used refined copper for pillars and bases.
My lord can dig them up and use them."
So they dug them up and used them,
obtaining surplus metal.
Orders were established,
defenses were prepared.
The troops of the three states indeed arrived.
They then ascended Jìnyáng's walls,
and battle commenced.
For three months they couldn't capture it.
So they spread their armies and besieged it,
diverting water from the Jìnyáng River to flood it,
besieging Jìnyáng for three years.
Those in the city nested like birds to live,
hung cauldrons to cook,
as supplies and food were nearly exhausted,
and officers grew weak and ill.
Xiāngzǐ told Zhāng Mèngtán:
"Food supplies are depleted,
resources exhausted,
officers weak and ill,
I fear we cannot hold out!
I wish to surrender the city,
but to which state should we surrender?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"I have heard that
if one cannot preserve what is perishing,
or secure what is endangered,
then there's no value in wisdom.
If my lord abandons this plan,
I request to try slipping out secretly
to meet the lords of
Hán and Wèi."
Zhāng Mèngtán met the lords of Hán
and Wèi, saying:
"I have heard that when the lips perish, the teeth feel cold.
Now Zhì Bó leads you two lords to attack Zhào,
and Zhào will perish.
When Zhào perishes,
you two lords will be next."
The two lords said:
"We know this is so.
However,
Zhì Bó's character
is crude at heart and shows little affection.
If our plot is discovered,
disaster will surely befall us.
What can be done about this?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"If the plan comes from the mouths of you two lords,
and enters only my ears,
no one else will know of it."
The two lords then made a pact with Zhāng Mèngtán
for the revolt of the three armies,
setting the date with him.
That night, they sent Mèngtán into Jìnyáng,
to report the two lords' planned revolt.
Xiāngzǐ welcomed Mèngtán and bowed to him twice,
both fearful and joyful.
After the two lords had sent Zhāng Mèngtán according to their agreement,
they went to court to see Zhì Bó and then left,
meeting Zhì Guò outside the main gate.
Zhì Guò found their expressions strange,
so he went in to see Zhì Bó and said:
"The two lords appear to be about to change their allegiance."
The lord said:
"How so?"
He replied:
"They walk proudly and their intentions seem lofty,
not like their usual demeanor.
My lord, you should act before they do."
The lord said:
"I have made a careful pact with the two leaders,
to destroy Zhào and divide its land into three.
The reason I treat them with intimacy
ensures they will not betray or deceive me.
Our troops have been stationed at Jìnyáng for three years,
and now we are about to capture it any day,
and share in its benefits.
How could they have other intentions?
It must not be so.
You should set aside your worries,
and do not speak of this again."
The next morning,
the two leaders again attended court and then left,
and again met Zhì Guò at the main gate.
Zhì Guò went in to see and said:
"My lord, did you tell the two leaders what I said?"
The lord said:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"Today when the two leaders left court,
they saw me and their expressions changed,
and they kept looking at me.
This surely means there will be a change.
My lord, you should kill them."
The lord said:
"You should stop and say no more."
Zhì Guò said:
"That won't do.
You must kill them.
If you cannot kill them,
then draw them closer to you."
The lord said:
"How can I draw them closer?"
Zhì Guò said:
"Wèi Xuānzǐ's strategist is named Zhào Jiā,
and Hán Kāngzǐ's strategist is named Duàn Guī.
Both can influence their lords' plans.
My lord, you should make an agreement with the two lords
that after destroying the state of Zhào,
you will enfeoff these two men
each with a county of ten thousand households.
If you do this,
then the hearts of the two leaders will not change."
Zhì Bó said:
"After destroying Zhào and dividing its land into three,
and then enfeoffing these two men
each with a county of ten thousand households,
what I get will be less.
This cannot be done."
Seeing that his advice was not heeded,
Zhì Guò left,
and changed his clan name to Fǔ.
On the appointed night,
the Zhào clan killed the officials guarding the dikes
and breached them to flood Zhì Bó's army.
Zhì Bó's army was thrown into chaos trying to deal with the flood,
while Hán and Wèi attacked from the flanks,
and Xiāngzǐ led his troops to assault them from the front,
decisively defeating Zhì Bó's army
and capturing Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó died and his army was destroyed,
his state was divided into three,
and he became the laughingstock of the world.
Therefore it is said:
Greed, stubbornness, and a love of profit
are the roots of the destruction of states and the loss of life.
What is meant by indulgence in female musicians?
In the past, the Róng king sent Yóu Yú
on a diplomatic mission to Qín.
Duke Mù asked him:
"I have often heard of the Way,
but have never seen it with my own eyes.
I would like to hear how the enlightened rulers of old gained and lost their states."
Yóu Yú replied:
"I have heard it said:
They usually gained them through frugality,
and lost them through extravagance."
Duke Mù said:
"I have not disgraced myself in asking you about the Way,
yet you answer me with frugality—
why is that?"
Yóu Yú replied:
"I have heard that in ancient times, when Yáo possessed the world,
he ate from earthen bowls,
and drank from earthen vessels.
His territory extended south to Jiāozhǐ,
north to Yōudū,
and east and west to where the sun and moon rise and set.
None failed to submit and serve him.
When Yáo abdicated the world,
Yú Shǔn received it.
He made eating vessels
by cutting mountain timber and shaping it,
carving and smoothing the marks,
and applying lacquer and ink on them,
then transporting them to the palace to be used as eating vessels.
The feudal lords considered this more extravagant,
and thirteen states refused to submit.
Shǔn abdicated the world and passed it to Yǔ.
Yǔ made sacrificial vessels,
lacquering the outside black,
and painting the inside red.
He used plain silk for cushions,
and mats with patterned edges.
Wine cups were adorned with colors,
and ritual vessels were decorated.
This was even more extravagant,
and thirty-three states refused to submit.
After the Xià dynasty perished,
the Yīn people received the world,
and made grand carriages,
adorned with nine tassels.
Eating vessels were carved and polished,
wine cups were engraved,
white jade adorned the steps and whitewash the courtyards,
and cushions and mats bore carved patterns.
This was even more extravagant,
and fifty-three states refused to submit.
When the noblemen all know ornate decorations,
those who wish to submit become fewer.
Therefore I say:
Frugality is the Way."
After Yóu Yú left,
the duke summoned the Neìshǐ Liào and told him:
"I have heard that if a neighboring state has a sage,
it is a worry for the rival state.
Now Yóu Yú
is a sage.
I am troubled by this.
What should I do?"
Neìshǐ Liào said:
"I have heard that the Róng king's dwelling place
is remote and the roads are long,
and he has not heard the music of the Central States.
My lord, you should send him female musicians
to disrupt his governance,
and then ask for an extension of Yóu Yú's stay,
to create distance for his admonitions.
When there is a rift between the ruler and his minister,
then you can plan against them."
The lord said:
"Agreed."
He then sent Neìshǐ Liào
to present sixteen female musicians to the Róng king,
and at the same time requested an extension for Yóu Yú's stay.
The Róng king agreed,
and upon seeing the female musicians, he was delighted by them.
He set up banquets with lavish drinking,
spending his days listening to music,
and did not move his court for a whole year,
causing half of his oxen and horses to perish.
Yóu Yú returned,
and thereupon remonstrated with the Róng king,
but the Róng king would not listen.
Yóu Yú then left and went to Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín welcomed him and appointed him as a high minister,
inquiring about the military strength and topography of the Róng.
Having obtained this information,
he raised an army and attacked them,
annexing twelve states,
and expanding the territory by a thousand li.
Hence it is said:
"To be infatuated with female musicians,
and neglect the governance of the state,
is the calamity that leads to the state's downfall."
What is meant by 'leaving the court and traveling far'?
In the past, Duke Jǐng of Qí traveled to the sea
and enjoyed it.
He issued an order to his ministers, saying:
"Whoever speaks of returning shall die."
Yán Zhuōjù said:
"Your Majesty enjoys traveling by the sea,
but what if there are subjects plotting against the state?
Even if Your Majesty enjoys it,
how will you retain it?"
Duke Jǐng of Qí said:
"I have decreed that
'whoever speaks of returning shall die.'
Now you have violated my decree."
He seized a spear and was about to strike him.
Yán Zhuōjù said:
"In the past, Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgàn.
Now, even if Your Majesty kills me,
I would be the third such victim.
My words are for the state,
not for myself."
He stretched out his neck forward and said:
"Strike me, Your Majesty!"
The ruler then laid down the spear,
hastened to his carriage, and returned.
Within three days,
he heard that there were people in the state plotting
not to allow Duke Jǐng of Qí back in.
The reason Duke Jǐng of Qí was able to retain the state of Qí
was due to the efforts of Yán Zhuōjù.
Hence it is said:
"To leave the court and travel far
is a path that endangers oneself."
What is meant by
'having faults but not listening to loyal ministers'?
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí nine times assembled the feudal lords,
unifying and rectifying the world,
becoming the leader of the Five Hegemons,
with Guǎn Zhòng assisting him.
Guǎn Zhòng grew old,
and could no longer handle affairs,
so he retired to his home.
Duke Huán went to him and asked:
"Father Zhòng, you are ill at home,
and if unfortunately you do not recover from this illness,
to whom should the government be transferred?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am old,
and should not be consulted.
Nevertheless,
I have heard that
no one knows a minister better than his ruler,
and no one knows a son better than his father.
May Your Majesty try to decide with your own heart."
The ruler said:
"How about Bào Shūyá?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not acceptable.
Bào Shūyá's character
is rigid, stubborn, and harshly aggressive.
Rigidity leads to oppressing the people with violence,
stubbornness means he cannot win the people's hearts,
and harsh aggression means his subordinates will not serve him willingly.
His mind is without fear,
so he is not an assistant for a hegemon."
The Duke said:
"Then how about Shù Diāo?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not acceptable.
In human nature, none do not love their own bodies.
Your Majesty is jealous and fond of the inner harem,
and Shù Diāo castrated himself to manage the inner court.
If he does not love his own body,
how can he love his ruler?"
The Duke said:
"Then how about Wèi's Prince Kāifāng?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not acceptable.
The distance between Qí and Wèi is no more than ten days' journey.
Kāifāng, in serving his ruler,
and wishing to please Your Majesty,
did not return to see his parents for fifteen years.
This goes against human nature.
If he is not close to his own parents,
how can he be close to his ruler?"
The Duke said:
"Then how about Yì Yá?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Not acceptable.
Yì Yá managed the flavors for Your Majesty,
and the only thing Your Majesty had not tasted was human flesh.
Yì Yá steamed his own son's head and presented it to you,
as you know.
In human nature, none do not love their own children.
Now he steamed his son to make a meal for Your Majesty.
If he does not love his own son,
how can he love his ruler?"
The Duke said:
"Then who is suitable?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Xí Péng is suitable.
His character
is firm within and incorruptible without,
with few desires and much trustworthiness.
Firmness within
makes him sufficient to set an example,
incorruptibility without
enables him to bear great responsibilities,
few desires
allow him to govern the masses,
and much trustworthiness
enables him to befriend neighboring states.
He is an assistant for a hegemon,
may Your Majesty employ him."
The ruler said:
"Agreed."
After a little over a year,
Guǎn Zhòng died,
and the ruler did not use Xí Péng
but instead relied on Shù Diāo.
Diāo was in power for three years,
and when Duke Huán traveled south to Tángfù,
Shù Diāo led Yì Yá,
Wèi's Prince Kāifāng, and other ministers in rebellion.
Duke Huán died of thirst and starvation in his southern gate chamber,
a room guarded by the Duke's own men,
his body left unburied for three months,
with worms emerging from the door.
Thus, though Duke Huán's armies had roamed the world unchecked,
and he was the leader of the Five Hegemons,
he ultimately was murdered by his own ministers,
his high reputation destroyed,
and became a laughingstock of the world.
Why?
Because of the fault of not following Guǎn Zhòng's advice.
Hence it is said:
"To have faults but not listen to loyal ministers,
insisting on one's own will,
leads to the destruction of one's high reputation,
and becomes the beginning of being laughed at by others."
What is meant by 'not measuring one's strength internally'?
In the past, when Qín attacked Yíyáng,
the Hán clan was in crisis.
Gōngzhòng Péng said to the ruler of Hán:
"Allied states cannot be relied upon.
Why not seek peace with Qín through Zhāng Yí?
Offer them a famous city as a bribe,
and ally south with them to attack Chǔ.
This way, the threat from Qín is resolved,
and the harm is transferred to Chǔ."
The Duke said:
"Good."
Then he urged Gōng Zhòng to proceed,
intending to make peace with Qin to the west.
When the King of Chu heard of this,
he became alarmed,
summoned Chén Zhěn and told him:
"Hán Péng is about to make peace with Qin to the west,
what should we do now?"
Chén Zhěn said:
"If Qin obtains a capital city from Hán,
and drives forth its trained troops,
with Qin and Hán united to face Chu to the south,
this is what the King of Qin seeks through temple sacrifices,
and it will certainly harm Chu.
Your Majesty should quickly dispatch trusted ministers,
with many chariots,
and heavy bribes,
to present to Hán, saying:
'Although my state is small,
all its soldiers have been mobilized,
and I hope your great state will show good faith towards Qin.
I therefore wish your great state would send envoys to enter our territory
and observe the mobilization of Chu's troops.'"
Hán sent an envoy to Chu,
and the King of Chu accordingly dispatched chariots and cavalry,
arraying them along the lower road,
and said to the Hán envoy:
"Report to the Lord of Hán,
saying that the troops of my humble state are now about to enter your territory."
The envoy returned and reported to the Lord of Hán,
who was greatly pleased,
and stopped Gōng Zhòng.
Gōng Zhòng said:
"This will not do.
The one who can truly harm us
is Qin,
while the one who rescues us in name only
is Chu.
To heed the empty words of Chu
and make light of the real disaster from powerful Qin
is to endanger the foundation of the state."
The Lord of Hán would not listen.
Gōng Zhòng angrily returned home,
and did not attend court for ten days.
The situation at Yìyáng grew more critical,
and the Lord of Hán ordered envoys to hasten the troops from Chu,
with their carriages and canopies in constant sight
but ultimately no troops arrived.
Yìyáng was indeed captured,
and they became the laughingstock of the feudal lords.
Hence it is said:
Internally not measuring one's strength,
externally relying on the feudal lords—
this is the calamity that leads to the reduction of the state.
What is meant by a small state being without propriety?
Long ago, Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn was fleeing exile,
and passed through Cáo,
where the Lord of Cáo bared his body to watch him.
Lí Fùjī and Shū Zhān were in attendance before him.
Shū Zhān said to the Lord of Cáo:
"I observe that the Prince of Jìn
is no ordinary man.
If Your Majesty treats him without propriety,
should he someday return to his state and raise an army,
I fear it would bring harm to Cáo.
Your Majesty would do better to kill him."
The Lord of Cáo would not listen.
Lí Fùjī returned home unhappy,
and his wife asked him:
"You return from outside with an unhappy expression,
why is that?"
Fùjī said:
"I have heard that
when good fortune does not come,
calamity comes to involve me.
Today our lord summoned the Prince of Jìn,
and treated him without propriety.
I was present,
and therefore I am unhappy."
His wife said:
"I observe that the Prince of Jìn
is a ruler of ten thousand chariots;
his attendants
are ministers of ten thousand chariots.
Now in dire straits and fleeing exile, he passes through Cáo,
and Cáo treats him without propriety.
If he returns to his state,
he will surely punish those without propriety,
and Cáo will be the first.
Why do you not beforehand show him your difference?"
Fùjī said:
"Very well."
He filled a pot with gold,
filled it with food,
placed a jade disc on top,
and at night had someone deliver it to the prince.
The prince received the messenger,
bowed twice,
accepted the food but declined the jade.
The prince went from Cáo to Chǔ,
and from Chǔ to Qín.
After being in Qín for three years,
Duke Mù of Qín summoned his ministers
and deliberated, saying:
"Long ago, Duke Xiàn of Jìn associated with me,
and all the feudal lords knew of it.
Duke Xiàn unfortunately left his ministers,
and it has been ten years since.
His successor is unworthy,
I fear this will cause
his ancestral temple to go uncleansed
and the altars of soil and grain to receive no sacrifices.
If I do not stabilize this situation,
it would not be the way to maintain associations with others.
I wish to support Chóng'ěr and install him in Jìn,
what do you think?"
The ministers all said:
"Good."
The duke accordingly raised troops,
with five hundred armored chariots,
two thousand fine cavalry,
and fifty thousand foot soldiers,
supported Chóng'ěr and entered him into Jìn,
establishing him as the Lord of Jìn.
Three years after Chóng'ěr ascended the throne,
he raised troops and attacked Cáo.
He then sent someone to inform the Lord of Cáo, saying:
"Hang Shū Zhān and expel him from the city,
and I will kill him and make of him a great example."
He also sent someone to inform Lí Fùjī, saying:
"The army is approaching the city,
I know you will not oppose me.
Mark out the lane where you live,
and I will issue an order,
commanding the army not to dare violate it."
When the people of Cáo heard this,
they led their relatives
and sought protection in Lí Fùjī's lane—over seven hundred families.
This is the use of propriety.
Thus Cáo,
a small state,
and pressed between Jìn and Chǔ,
its lord's peril was like piled eggs,
yet he treated others with impropriety,
this is why its line was cut off.
Hence it is said:
A small state without propriety,
that does not heed remonstrating ministers,
is in a situation to have its line cut off.
Men of wisdom and strategy
must have far-sighted and clear discernment;
without clear discernment,
they cannot illuminate private schemes;
men capable in law
must be resolute and firm of integrity;
without firm integrity,
they cannot correct villainy.
A minister who follows orders in conducting affairs,
and governs officials according to law,
is not what is called a powerful man.
A powerful man
acts without orders and on his own authority,
impairs the law to benefit himself,
drains the state to convenience his family,
and has the power to obtain his lord's favor—
this is what is called a powerful man.
Men of wisdom and strategy, with clear discernment,
if heard and employed,
can illuminate the hidden affairs of powerful men;
men capable in law, with firm integrity,
if heard and employed,
can correct the villainous conduct of powerful men.
Therefore, when men of wisdom and method are employed,
then the powerful ministers will certainly be outside the bounds of law.
Thus, men of wisdom and law
are irreconcilable enemies with those in power.
When those in power monopolize crucial affairs,
then both internal and external officials serve them.
Hence, if the feudal lords do not rely on them,
their affairs will not be attended to,
so rival states plead for them;
if the hundred officials do not rely on them,
their careers will not advance,
so all ministers serve them;
if the court attendants do not rely on them,
they cannot get close to the ruler,
so the ruler's intimates conceal for them;
if the scholars do not rely on them,
their stipends will be meager and their courtesy humble,
so the scholars speak for them.
These four types of supporters
are how treacherous ministers adorn themselves.
Powerful men cannot be loyal to their ruler
and recommend their enemies,
and the ruler cannot bypass these four supporters
to clearly perceive his ministers,
thus the ruler becomes increasingly obscured
while the great ministers grow more powerful.
Generally, those in power
are rarely not trusted and loved by the ruler,
and moreover, they are familiar and old acquaintances.
As for迎合 the ruler's heart,
sharing his likes and dislikes,
this is naturally how they advance themselves.
Their official positions are noble and weighty,
their cliques are numerous,
and the whole state pleads for them.
Then, the men of method and technique
who wish to approach the superior
have no trusted or beloved kinship,
nor the favor of familiarity;
moreover, they will use the words of method and technique
to correct the ruler's biased heart,
which is contrary to the ruler's will.
Their position is lowly and humble,
without faction, isolated and alone.
To contend with the intimate, trusted, and beloved from a distant position,
the odds are insurmountable;
to contend as newcomers with the familiar and old,
the odds are insurmountable;
to contend with opposing views
against those who share likes and dislikes,
the odds are insurmountable;
to contend from light and humble against the noble and weighty,
the odds are insurmountable;
to contend with a single mouth against a whole state,
the odds are insurmountable.
Men of method and technique
hold these five insurmountable positions,
waiting for years without even gaining an audience;
while those in power ride on five advantageous resources,
and alone persuade the ruler morning and evening.
So, by what means can men of method and technique advance,
and when can the ruler become enlightened?
Thus, with resources surely insurmountable
and situations irreconcilable,
how can men of method and technique
avoid danger?
Those who can be falsely accused of crimes
are executed by public law;
those who cannot be implicated with crimes
are assassinated by private swords.
Thus, those who clarify methods and techniques but oppose the ruler
either die by official execution,
or inevitably perish by private swords.
Those who form cliques and deceive the ruler,
and twist words for private convenience,
are certainly trusted by the powerful.
So, those who can be credited with achievements
are honored with official titles;
those who cannot be adorned with fine reputations
are empowered with external authority.
Thus, those who deceive the ruler and flock to private gates
either gain prominence through official titles,
or become powerful through external authority.
Now, if the ruler executes without verification,
and bestows ranks and emoluments without seeing merit,
how can men of method and technique
risk death to present their ideas?
How would treacherous ministers willingly retreat when in profit?
Thus, the ruler becomes increasingly humbled,
while private gates grow more esteemed.
Although Yuè is wealthy and militarily strong,
the rulers of the central states all know it is of no benefit to them,
saying:
"It is not within my control."
Now, those who possess a state,
though their land is vast and people numerous,
if the ruler is blocked and obscured,
and great ministers monopolize power,
then their state is like Yuè.
They know it is not like Yuè,
but do not realize their state is not like their own,
failing to perceive the similarity.
The reason people say Qí perished
is not that its land and cities vanished.
The Lǚ clan lost control,
and the Tián clan took over;
the reason people say Jìn perished
is also not that its land and cities vanished,
but that the Jī clan lost control,
and the six ministers monopolized it.
Now, if great ministers hold the handle of power and decide alone,
and the ruler does not know to reclaim it,
this shows the ruler's lack of clarity.
Those who share the same illness as the dead
cannot live;
those who engage in the same practices as perished states
cannot survive.
Now, following in the footsteps of Qí and Jìn,
and wishing the state to be secure and enduring,
is impossible.
Generally, the difficulty in implementing methods and techniques
is not only for states of ten thousand chariots,
but also for those of a thousand chariots.
The ruler's attendants are not necessarily wise,
yet when the ruler finds someone wise and listens to him,
he then discusses that person's words with his attendants,
which is like discussing wisdom with fools.
The ruler's attendants are not necessarily worthy,
yet when the ruler finds someone worthy and honors him,
he then discusses that person's conduct with his attendants,
which is like discussing worthiness with the unworthy.
If the wise have their decisions judged by fools,
and worthy men have their conduct evaluated by the unworthy,
then the wise and worthy will feel ashamed, and the ruler's judgments will be perverse.
Among ministers who desire official positions,
the cultivated men maintain integrity to secure themselves,
and the wise men promote their careers through governance and debate.
The cultivated men cannot bribe others,
relying on their purity,
and even more, they cannot govern by bending the law,
thus the cultivated and wise do not serve the attendants,
nor do they heed personal solicitations.
The ruler's attendants,
whose conduct is not like Bóyí's,
if their demands are not met,
and bribes do not come,
then the efforts of purity and debate cease,
and slanderous accusations arise.
The achievements of governance and debate
are controlled by the intimate favorites,
and the conduct of purity and integrity
is decided by slander and praise,
then the cultivated and wise officials are discarded,
and the ruler's clarity is blocked.
If not judging wisdom and conduct by merit,
nor verifying crimes through comparison and evidence,
but listening to the words of intimate attendants,
then incapable men will be at court,
and foolish, corrupt officials will hold office.
The peril for a state of ten thousand chariots
is that the great ministers are too powerful;
the peril for a state of a thousand chariots
is that the attendants are too trusted:
these are the common worries of rulers.
Moreover, when a minister commits a great crime,
it is the ruler's great fault,
for the interests of minister and ruler are opposed.
How can this be made clear?
I say:
The ruler's benefit lies in appointing officials based on their abilities,
while the ministers' benefit lies in obtaining positions despite their incompetence;
the ruler's benefit lies in granting ranks and emoluments for meritorious service,
while the ministers' benefit lies in gaining wealth and honor without achievements;
the ruler's benefit lies in having outstanding talents exercise their abilities,
while the ministers' benefit lies in forming cliques for private gain.
Hence, the state's territory diminishes while private households grow rich,
the sovereign is humbled while the ministers gain power.
Thus, the ruler loses authority while the ministers seize the state,
the sovereign is reduced to a vassal,
while the chief minister holds the tally of authority.
This is how ministers deceive the ruler to serve their private interests.
Therefore, among the powerful ministers of the present age,
those who can maintain their favor
when the ruler changes the political situation
are fewer than two or three out of ten.
What is the reason for this?
The crimes of ministers are great.
Ministers who commit great crimes
act deceptively toward their ruler,
and their offenses deserve death.
Wise men, with far-sighted vision
and fear of death,
will certainly not follow powerful men;
virtuous men, cultivating integrity
and ashamed to join treacherous ministers in deceiving their ruler,
will certainly not follow powerful ministers.
Thus, the followers of those in power
are either foolish and unaware of danger,
or corrupt and unashamed of wickedness.
Powerful ministers rally these foolish and corrupt men,
joining with them above to deceive the ruler,
and below to seize profits and exploit the people,
forming cliques and conspiracies,
speaking with one voice,
deluding the ruler and undermining laws,
confusing officials and commoners,
endangering the state and diminishing its territory,
bringing toil and disgrace upon the sovereign,
these are great crimes.
When ministers commit great crimes and the ruler fails to restrain them,
this is a great failure.
If the ruler above commits great failures,
and ministers below commit great crimes,
to expect the state not to perish
is impossible.
Generally, the difficulties of persuasion:
It is not the difficulty of knowing enough to persuade,
nor the difficulty of articulating my thoughts clearly,
nor the difficulty of daring to express myself fully and exhaustively.
The true difficulty of persuasion
lies in knowing the mind of the person being persuaded,
and tailoring my persuasion to match it.
If the persuaded seeks lofty reputation,
but I persuade him with substantial profit,
I will be seen as lowly and treated with contempt,
and inevitably cast aside.
If the persuaded seeks substantial profit,
but I persuade him with lofty reputation,
I will be seen as impractical and detached from reality,
and inevitably not accepted.
If the persuaded secretly seeks profit
while overtly pursuing reputation,
and I persuade him with reputation,
he will outwardly accept me
but actually distance himself;
if I persuade him with profit,
he will secretly adopt my advice while overtly rejecting me.
This cannot be overlooked.
Affairs succeed through secrecy,
and fail through disclosure.
It may not be that I personally disclosed it,
but if my words touch upon concealed matters,
in such cases, I am endangered.
If he overtly undertakes one matter,
but actually aims to achieve another purpose,
and the persuader not only knows the overt action
but also understands the true intent,
in such cases, I am endangered.
If I plan an unusual matter appropriately,
and a wise man deduces it from external signs,
and the matter is leaked,
he will certainly attribute it to me,
in such cases, I am endangered.
If the favor and intimacy are not yet deep,
yet I speak with utmost knowledge,
and if my advice is followed with success,
my merit will be forgotten;
if it fails and brings defeat,
I will be suspected,
in such cases, I am endangered.
If a noble person has faults,
and the persuader explicitly appeals to ritual and righteousness, exposing his errors,
in such cases, I am endangered.
If a noble person has a successful plan and wishes to claim credit,
and the persuader is aware of it,
in such cases, I am endangered.
If I press him to do what he cannot,
or stop him from what he cannot cease,
in such cases, I am endangered.
Thus, if I discuss great men with him,
he will think I am driving a wedge;
if I discuss minor figures,
he will think I am trading on influence.
If I discuss his favorites,
he will think I am seeking leverage;
if I discuss those he dislikes,
he will think I am testing him.
If I am concise and direct,
he will think me unwise and dismiss me as clumsy;
if I am detailed and broad in argument,
he will think me verbose and tedious.
If I outline matters and state my ideas briefly,
he will say I am timid and incomplete;
if I consider affairs broadly and freely,
he will say I am rustic and arrogant.
These difficulties of persuasion
must be understood.
The essence of persuasion
lies in knowing how to glorify what the person prides himself on
and minimize what he is ashamed of.
If he has private urgings,
I must present them as matters of public righteousness
and encourage him.
If he has base intentions
but cannot restrain himself,
the persuader should embellish their good aspects
and minimize his reluctance to act.
If he has lofty aspirations,
but realistically cannot achieve them,
the persuader should point out the drawbacks
and show the faults,
praising his decision not to proceed.
If he wishes to boast of his intelligence and ability,
then cite similar cases from different events,
providing ample groundwork,
letting him draw ideas from me,
while pretending ignorance
to enhance his wisdom.
If I wish to present words that preserve him,
I must justify them with fine names,
while subtly showing they align with his private interests.
If I wish to陈述危害之事,
I should emphasize the criticism
while subtly indicating how it relates to his personal concerns.
Praise others who share his conduct;
advise on different matters that align with his plans.
If someone shares his flaws,
I must strongly emphasize that they are harmless;
if someone shares his failures,
I must clearly justify that they are not mistakes.
If he prides himself on his strength,
do not confront him with difficulties;
if he boasts of his decisiveness,
do not anger him by pointing out errors;
if he considers his plans wise,
do not embarrass him with past failures.
In general, avoid contradicting his ideas,
and let your words not cause friction,
then you can fully exercise your wisdom and eloquence.
By this method, you can achieve
close rapport without suspicion
and express yourself completely.
Yǐ Yǐn served as a cook,
Bǎilǐ Xī was a slave,
both used these positions to approach their rulers.
These two men
were both sages.
Yet they still had to humble themselves to advance,
showing how demeaning it was.
Now if my words could gain me such humble positions
and enable me to be heard and employed to save the age,
this would not be shameful for a capable scholar.
When much time has passed,
and the ruler's favor has deepened,
one can plan deeply without suspicion,
argue frankly without punishment,
then clearly analyze advantages and disadvantages to achieve merit,
and directly point out right and wrong to cultivate one's character.
Maintaining this relationship,
this is the success of persuasion.
Previously, Duke Wǔ of Zhèng wanted to attack Hú,
so he first married his daughter to the ruler of Hú to please him.
Then he asked his ministers:
"I wish to use military force,
who should we attack?"
Minister Guān Qísi replied:
"Hú can be attacked."
Duke Wǔ angrily executed him,
saying:
"Hú
is our brother state.
You suggest attacking it,
why?"
The ruler of Hú heard this,
believing Zhèng was friendly toward him,
and thus made no preparations against Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng attacked Hú by surprise,
and conquered it.
In Sòng there was a wealthy man,
whose wall collapsed during rain.
His son said:
"If not repaired,
thieves will surely come."
His neighbor's father said the same.
That evening, he indeed lost much wealth.
The family highly praised their son's wisdom,
but suspected the neighbor's father.
Both speakers were correct in their advice,
yet the serious case led to execution,
the minor case to suspicion,
showing the difficulty lies not in knowing,
but in how knowledge is applied.
Thus Rào Cháo's words were appropriate,
he was considered sage in Jìn,
but executed in Qín,
this cannot be ignored.
Previously, Mí Zǐxiá was favored by the ruler of Wèi.
In Wèi's laws:
stealing the ruler's carriage warranted foot-amputation.
When Mí Zǐxiá's mother fell ill,
someone went at night to inform him,
Mí Zǐxiá pretended to command the ruler's carriage to go out.
The ruler heard and praised him,
saying:
"How filial!
For his mother's sake,
he forgot the punishment of foot-amputation."
Another day,
while touring an orchard with the ruler,
he ate a peach and found it sweet,
not finishing it,
he offered half to the ruler.
The ruler said:
"How he loves me!
He forgot his own taste to offer me the peach."
When Mí Zǐxiá's looks faded and favor waned,
and he offended the ruler,
the ruler said:
"This man once stole my carriage,
and once gave me his leftover peach."
Thus Mí Zǐxiá's conduct hadn't changed from before,
but what previously earned praise later brought punishment,
due to the change in affection and dislike.
So when favored by the ruler,
one's wisdom seems fitting and brings closer ties;
when disliked by the ruler,
one's wisdom seems inappropriate and brings alienation.
Therefore, those who advise and persuade
must consider the ruler's affections before speaking.
The dragon as a creature
can be tamed and ridden when gentle;
but beneath its throat are reverse scales measuring a foot,
if anyone touches them,
it will certainly kill.
The ruler also has reverse scales,
if the persuader can avoid touching them,
he nearly succeeds.
The Chǔ man Hé Shì found a jade rough in Chǔ mountains,
and presented it to King Lì.
King Lì had jade craftsmen examine it.
The craftsmen said:
"It's stone."
The king considered Hé deceptive,
and amputated his left foot.
When King Lì died,
King Wǔ succeeded.
Hé again presented his rough to King Wǔ.
King Wǔ had jade craftsmen examine it.
Again they said:
"It's stone."
The king again considered Hé deceptive,
and amputated his right foot.
When King Wǔ died,
King Wén succeeded.
Hé then held his rough and wept below Chǔ mountains,
for three days and nights,
until tears exhausted and blood flowed.
The king heard this,
sent someone to ask the reason,
saying:
"Many in the world suffer amputation,
why do you weep so bitterly?"
Hé replied:
"I weep not for amputation,
but that precious jade is called stone,
a loyal man is named deceiver,
this is why I weep."
The king then had jade craftsmen cut the rough
and obtained treasure,
thus naming it
"Hé Shì's Jade."
Pearls and jade
are what rulers urgently desire.
Though Hé presented an unpolished rough,
it harmed the ruler not;
yet both feet were amputated
before the treasure was recognized,
so difficult is treasure's recognition.
Now rulers' regard for law and method
may not match their desire for Hé's jade,
yet they restrict ministers and people's selfish evils.
Thus those with the Way escape punishment
only because the ruler's rough remains unpresented.
When the ruler employs method,
great ministers cannot monopolize decisions,
court favorites dare not peddle influence;
when officials enforce law,
vagrants turn to farming,
and wandering scholars face battle dangers;
thus law and method
become what ministers and people curse.
Unless the ruler can oppose ministers' opinions,
transcend commoners' slander,
and independently follow the Way's words,
then scholars of law and method
may die,
but the Way will never be recognized.
Previously Wú Qǐ instructed King Dào of Chǔ about Chǔ's customs:
"Ministers hold too much power,
enfeoffed lords are too numerous.
If this continues,
they oppress the ruler above
and abuse the people below,
this is the way to impoverish the state and weaken the military.
Better to confiscate ranks and stipends
from enfeoffed lords' descendants after three generations,
reduce various officials' salaries and ranks,
cut unnecessary redundant positions,
to support selected and trained soldiers."
King Dào of Chǔ passed away within a year of implementing Wú Qǐ's reforms,
and Wú Qǐ was torn apart by chariots in Chǔ.
Shāng Yāng advised Duke Xiào of Qín to organize the people into interconnected groups of five and ten,
establish a system for reporting offenses and sharing punishment,
burn the Books of Songs and Documents
to make laws and decrees clear,
block private requests
to promote public service,
restrict wandering scholars
and honor those engaged in farming and warfare.
Duke Xiào implemented these policies,
which brought security and respect to the ruler
and prosperity and strength to the state.
After eight years, he passed away,
and Shāng Yāng was torn apart by chariots in Qín.
Chǔ failed to employ Wú Qǐ and thus declined into chaos,
while Qín practiced Shāng Yāng's laws and became prosperous and strong.
The words of these two men were indeed fitting,
yet why were they
torn apart and
dismembered?
Because high officials oppose strict laws
and the common people dislike orderly governance.
In the present age,
high officials are greedier for power,
the common people are more content with chaos,
surpassing even the customs of Qín
and Chǔ,
and rulers lack the discernment of King Dào
or Duke Xiào.
How, then, can proponents of law and statecraft
endure the dangers these two faced
to promote their own methods?
This is why the world lacks a hegemon or true king.
All treacherous ministers seek to align with the ruler's desires
to gain favor and influence.
Thus, whatever the ruler approves,
they praise;
whatever the ruler dislikes,
they condemn.
Generally, people
agree with those who share their preferences
and oppose those who differ.
What ministers praise
aligns with the ruler's approval—
this is called shared preference;
what ministers condemn
aligns with the ruler's disapproval—
this is called shared rejection.
For preferences and rejections to align
yet opposition to arise
is unheard of.
This is how ministers gain trust and favor.
When treacherous ministers
leverage this favor
to slander or praise other officials for advancement,
if the ruler lacks statecraft to control them
or verification to scrutinize them,
they will trust present words
based on past agreement,
enabling favored ministers to deceive the ruler
and serve their own interests.
Thus, the ruler is inevitably deceived above,
and ministers grow powerful below,
becoming what are called domineering ministers.
When a state has domineering ministers,
subordinates cannot fully use their talents
to express loyalty,
and officials cannot uphold the law
to achieve merit.
How can this be demonstrated?
People gravitate toward safety and benefit
and flee harm and danger—
this is human nature.
Now, ministers who exert themselves for merit
and devote their wisdom to loyalty
face personal hardship and family poverty,
with father and son suffering harm;
those who deceive the ruler for profit
and bribe powerful ministers
gain high status and family wealth,
with father and son enjoying benefits.
Who would abandon safety and benefit
for harm and danger?
If governance is so flawed,
yet the ruler expects subordinates to be free of treachery
and officials to uphold the law,
it is clearly impossible.
Thus, those close to the ruler,
knowing honesty cannot bring safety or benefit,
will surely say:
"If I serve my superior with loyalty and honesty,
accumulating merit to seek security,
it is like a blind person
trying to distinguish black from white—
hopeless.
If I follow the Way, practice righteousness,
avoid chasing wealth and status,
and serve my superior to seek security,
it is like a deaf person
trying to discern clear and muddled sounds—
even more hopeless.
Since neither approach brings security,
how can I avoid colluding with others,
deceiving my ruler,
and acting treacherously
to please the powerful?"
They will inevitably disregard their duty to the ruler.
Other officials, knowing uprightness cannot bring security,
will surely say:
"If I serve my superior with integrity to seek security,
it is like trying to draw squares and circles
without a compass or square—
hopeless.
If I uphold the law, avoid cliques, and perform official duties
to seek security,
it is like scratching my head with my foot—
even more hopeless.
Since neither approach brings security,
how can I avoid abandoning the law for personal gain
to please the powerful?"
They will inevitably disregard the ruler's laws.
Thus, many serve the powerful for personal gain,
while few serve the ruler according to the law.
Hence, the ruler is isolated above
while ministers form cliques below,
as when Tián Chéng assassinated Duke Jiǎn of Qí.
A minister skilled in statecraft
can present measured policies,
clarify the ruler's laws above,
and suppress treacherous ministers below,
thereby honoring the ruler and securing the state.
If such policies are presented and accepted,
rewards and punishments will surely follow.
If the ruler truly understands the methods of sages,
not indulging in popular opinions,
judging right and wrong by aligning names with realities,
and verifying statements through evidence,
then those close to him,
knowing deceit cannot bring security,
will surely say:
"If I do not abandon treacherous, selfish acts
and instead serve my ruler with all my effort and wisdom,
but resort to collusion and false praise or slander
to seek security,
it is like carrying a heavy burden
into an unfathomable abyss
and hoping to survive—
hopeless."
Other officials, knowing
treacherous profiteering cannot bring security,
will surely say:
"If I do not serve with integrity and uphold the law,
but instead twist the law with a corrupt heart
for personal gain,
it is like climbing a high peak
and falling into a steep ravine
while hoping to survive—
hopeless."
With the path to safety and danger so clear,
how could those close to the ruler deceive him with empty words,
and how would officials dare to exploit the people through greed?
Thus, ministers can express loyalty without obstruction,
and subordinates can fulfill their duties without resentment.
This is how Guǎn Zhòng governed Qí
and Shāng Yāng strengthened Qín.
From this perspective,
when sages govern a state,
they inherently have ways to make people unable not to be loyal,
not relying on others to love them willingly.
Relying on others to love one willingly
is perilous,
while relying on making it impossible for them not to act
is secure.
If the relationship between ruler and minister lacks the intimacy of blood ties,
and the path of integrity can bring benefits,
then ministers will exert their efforts to serve their lord;
if the path of integrity cannot ensure safety,
then ministers will act selfishly
to interfere with the ruler.
An enlightened ruler understands this,
therefore he establishes systems of reward and punishment
to demonstrate them to the world.
Thus, although the ruler
does not personally instruct all officials,
nor visually search for evildoers,
the state is already well-governed.
A ruler
does not need eyes like Lí Lóu
to be considered clear-sighted,
nor ears like Shī Kuàng
to be considered keen-hearing.
If one relies solely on one's own eyesight,
depending on vision for clarity,
what one sees will be limited,
this is not a method that prevents deception.
If one relies solely on one's own hearing,
depending on ears for acuity,
what one hears will be scarce,
this is not a way to avoid being deceived.
An enlightened ruler
makes the world inevitably serve as his eyes,
makes the world inevitably serve as his ears.
Thus, while residing deep within the palace
his illumination shines throughout the four seas,
and the world cannot obscure or deceive him -
why is this?
Because the ways of darkness and disorder are abandoned
while the momentum of clarity and acuity prevails.
Therefore, those skilled at utilizing circumstances
bring security to the state,
while those unaware of leveraging circumstances
bring danger to the state.
In ancient Qín customs,
rulers and ministers abandoned laws and served private interests,
thus the state fell into chaos, military weakened
and the ruler became humbled.
Shāng Jūn advised Qín Xiàogōng to reform laws
and change customs to clarify public justice,
rewarding reports of crimes,
restricting non-essential activities
while benefiting fundamental enterprises.
At that time,
the people of Qín were accustomed to old practices where the guilty
could obtain pardon,
and the meritless could gain honor and prominence,
thus they lightly violated the new laws.
Thereupon, those who violated them faced certain severe punishment,
while those who reported crimes received generous and reliable rewards.
Thus no criminal could escape
and many were punished,
the people resented bitterly
and numerous complaints were heard daily.
Xiàogōng did not heed them,
but proceeded with Shāng Jūn's laws.
Later the people realized that crimes would surely be punished,
and many reported private offenses,
thus none among the people dared transgress,
and punishments found no application.
Therefore the state became orderly and military strong,
territories expanded and the ruler respected.
The reason for this outcome
was heavy punishment for concealed crimes,
and generous rewards for reporting offenses.
This is also the way to make the world inevitably
serve as one's eyes and ears.
The methods for achieving perfect governance are clear,
yet scholars of the world remain unaware.
Moreover, the foolish scholars of the world,
all ignorant of the realities of order and chaos,
chatter endlessly reciting ancient books,
thereby disrupting contemporary governance;
their wisdom insufficient to avoid pitfall traps,
yet they recklessly criticize those with true methods.
Those who listen to their words face danger,
those who employ their plans encounter chaos,
this represents the height of foolishness
and the extreme of calamity.
Though both share the reputation
of being debaters and speakers,
their actual difference is vast,
this is a case of identical names
but fundamentally different realities.
When comparing worldly foolish scholars
to those with true methods,
it's like comparing anthills to great mountains,
the distance between them is immense.
Whereas the sage,
examines the reality of right and wrong,
investigates the circumstances of order and chaos.
Therefore in governing the state,
he rectifies and clarifies laws,
implements severe punishments,
aiming to save the masses from chaos,
eliminate the world's calamities,
ensuring the strong don't oppress the weak,
the many don't brutalize the few,
the elderly can live out their lives,
the young and orphaned can grow up,
borders remain unviolated,
ruler and minister maintain mutual affection,
father and son preserve each other,
without the peril of death, capture or enslavement -
this represents the greatest achievement.
Foolish people don't understand this,
instead considering it tyranny.
Fools naturally desire order yet hate the means to achieve it,
all detest danger yet love what creates danger.
How do we know this?
Because severe punishments and heavy penalties,
though hated by the people,
are what bring order to the state;
while pitying the people and lightening punishments,
though loved by the people,
are what bring danger to the state.
When sages establish laws for the state,
they necessarily go against worldly trends,
while conforming to the Way and its Power.
Those who understand this
align with righteousness but differ from customs;
those who don't understand
differ from righteousness but align with customs.
When few in the world understand,
then righteousness becomes wrong.
Occupying an unrighteous position,
suffering the slander of many mouths,
drowning in contemporary opinions,
yet hoping to face a stern Son of Heaven and seek safety -
isn't this nearly impossible!
This is why men of wisdom die without achieving recognition in the world.
Lord Chūnshēn, younger brother of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
had a beloved concubine named Yú,
while his legitimate wife had a son named Jiǎ.
Yú wanted her lord to abandon his wife,
so she injured her own body
and showed it to the lord while weeping,
saying:
"To be your concubine
is great fortune.
However,
pleasing the lady is incompatible with serving you,
and pleasing you is incompatible with serving the lady.
I am naturally incompetent,
my abilities insufficient to please both masters,
the situation makes mutual satisfaction impossible -
rather than dying at the lady's place,
better to receive death before you.
If I am granted death,
and you later favor others around you,
I beg you to investigate thoroughly,
lest you become others' laughingstock."
The lord thus believed Concubine Yú's deception,
and abandoned his legitimate wife.
Yú further wanted to kill Jiǎ
and establish her own son as heir,
so she tore the lining of her intimate garment,
showed it to the lord while weeping,
saying:
"I have enjoyed your favor for long,
Jiǎ couldn't possibly be unaware,
yet now he tried to force himself upon me.
I struggled with him,
until he tore my clothes -
this son's lack of filial piety
couldn't be greater than this."
The lord became enraged,
and killed Jiǎ.
Thus, the wife was abandoned due to the deceit of the concubine Yú,
and the son died because of it.
From this perspective,
a father's love for his son
can still be destroyed and harmed.
The relationship between ruler and minister
lacks the intimacy of father and son,
and the slanderous words of ministers
are not limited to the mouth of one concubine.
Why wonder that the worthy and sage are executed!
This is why Shāng Jūn was torn apart by chariots in Qín,
and Wú Qǐ was dismembered in Chǔ.
All ministers,
if guilty, naturally do not wish to be punished,
and those without merit all desire honor and prominence.
But when a sage governs the state,
rewards are not given to the meritless,
and punishment is invariably carried out against the guilty.
However, those who possess methods and strategies
are inevitably harmed by the treacherous ministers around them,
and only an enlightened ruler can heed them.
Scholars of the age persuade rulers,
not saying
"utilize the power of authority
to suppress treacherous and wicked ministers,"
but all saying
"benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and love are sufficient."
Rulers of the age admire the name of benevolence and righteousness
without examining its reality,
hence in major cases the state perishes and the ruler dies,
in minor cases territory is lost and the ruler is humbled.
How to illustrate this?
Giving to the impoverished,
this is what the age calls benevolence and righteousness;
pitying the common people
and being unwilling to punish,
this is what the age calls kindness and love.
Now, if one gives to the impoverished,
then the meritless gain rewards;
if one is unwilling to punish,
then the violent and disorderly do not cease.
If the state has those without merit who gain rewards,
then the people will not externally strive to face the enemy and take heads,
nor internally urgently labor in farming,
but all will wish to use wealth to serve the rich and powerful,
perform private good deeds to establish reputation,
in order to obtain high office and generous salaries.
Thus, treacherous and selfish ministers multiply,
and violent and disorderly elements prevail more,
what awaits but destruction?
Severe penalties
are what the people fear;
heavy punishments
are what the people detest.
Therefore, the sage
displays what they fear
to prohibit their wickedness,
establishes what they detest
to prevent their treachery,
so the state is secure and violent disorder does not arise.
I thereby demonstrate that benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and love are insufficient for use,
while severe penalties and heavy punishments can govern the state.
Without the threat of the whip,
or the preparation of bit and bridle,
even Zào Fù could not subdue a horse;
without the standards of compass and square,
the straightness of the ink line,
even Wáng Ěr could not form circles and squares;
without the power of authority,
the methods of reward and punishment,
even Yáo and Shùn could not achieve governance.
Now rulers of the age all lightly dismiss heavy punishments and severe penalties,
practice kindness and love,
yet desire the achievements of hegemony and kingship,
this too is unattainable.
Therefore, those skilled as rulers
clarify rewards and establish benefits to encourage the people,
causing them to be rewarded for merit
and not bestowed with benevolence and righteousness;
use severe penalties and heavy punishments to prohibit them,
causing them to be punished for crime
and not exempted due to kindness and love.
Thus, the meritless do not hope,
and the guilty do not侥幸.
Relying on rhinoceros-hide carriages and fine horses,
one can overcome the difficulties of land and steep obstacles;
riding the safety of boats,
wielding the advantage of oars,
one can traverse the perils of rivers and waterways;
grasping the methods of law and statecraft,
implementing heavy punishments and severe penalties,
one can attain the achievements of hegemony and kingship.
The possession of law, statecraft, rewards, and punishments in governing a state
is like having rhinoceros-hide carriages and fine horses for land travel,
or light boats and handy oars for water travel,
those who ride them thereby achieve success.
Yī Yǐn obtained them,
and Tāng became king;
Guǎn Zhòng obtained them,
and Qí achieved hegemony;
Shāng Jūn obtained them,
and Qín grew strong.
These three men,
all understood the methods of hegemony and kingship,
discerned the techniques for order and strength,
and were not constrained by世俗之言;
fitting the intentions of the enlightened rulers of their time,
they were directly appointed as commoners,
established in positions as ministers and chancellors;
occupying their posts and governing the state,
they had the reality of honoring the ruler and expanding territory;
these are called truly valuable ministers.
Tāng obtained Yī Yǐn,
and with a hundred lǐ of land became the Son of Heaven;
Huán Gōng obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
became one of the Five Hegemons,
nine times assembled the feudal lords,
and unified and corrected the world;
Xiào Gōng obtained Shāng Jūn,
territory was expanded,
and military strength increased.
Therefore, with loyal ministers,
externally there is no worry of enemy states,
internally no anxiety of rebellious ministers,
long-lasting peace under heaven,
and fame passed down to later ages—
these are called loyal ministers.
As for Yù Ràng being a minister to Zhì Bó,
above he could not persuade his ruler to
understand the principles of laws, methods, and measures
to avoid the calamity of disaster,
below he could not lead and control the masses
to secure his state.
When Xiāng Zǐ killed Zhì Bó,
Yù Ràng then blackened his body and cut off his nose,
disfiguring his appearance,
to seek revenge for Zhì Bó against Xiāng Zǐ.
Although this involved mutilating his body and sacrificing his life
for the name of loyalty to his ruler,
in reality it benefited Zhì Bó
as little as the tip of an autumn hair.
This is what I look down upon,
yet rulers of the age consider it loyalty and esteem it.
In ancient times, there were Bó Yí and Shū Qí,
to whom King Wǔ offered the world but they refused,
and the two starved to death on the hills of Shǒuyáng.
Such ministers,
unafraid of heavy punishment,
uninterested in great rewards,
cannot be restrained by penalties,
nor motivated by rewards—
these are called useless ministers.
I despise and reject them,
yet rulers of the age praise and seek them.
A proverb says:
"The leper pities the king."
This is an irreverent saying.
Nevertheless,
ancient proverbs are not empty,
and cannot be unexamined.
This refers to rulers who are robbed and killed.
If a ruler lacks laws and methods
to control his ministers,
even with long life and fine talent,
ministers will still gain power,
monopolize affairs, and decide arbitrarily,
each pursuing their private interests.
And fearing that the worthy, the elders, and the heroic
might借用 the ruler's power
to restrict and punish them,
they thus kill the worthy and elder and install the young and weak,
depose the rightful heir and establish the unrighteous.
Therefore, the "Spring and Autumn Annals" recorded it as follows:
"Prince Wéi of Chǔ was about to go on a diplomatic mission to Zhèng,
but before he had left the country,
he heard that the king was ill and returned.
Taking the opportunity to inquire about the king's illness,
he strangled and killed the king with the strings of his own crown,
and subsequently installed himself as king.
In Qí, Cuī Zhù's wife was beautiful,
and Duke Zhuāng had an affair with her,
frequently visiting Cuī's residence.
When the duke went there,
Cuī's follower Jiǎ Jǔ led Cuī's men to attack the duke.
The duke entered the chamber,
begged to share the state with Cuī,
but Cuī refused;
the duke then asked to commit suicide in the temple,
but Cuī again would not listen.
The duke then fled,
climbing over the northern wall.
Jiǎ Jǔ shot the duke,
hitting his thigh,
the duke fell,
Cuī's men hacked the duke to death with spears,
and installed his brother, Duke Jǐng."
In recent times, we have witnessed:
Lì Duì's control of Zhào,
starving the lord father for a hundred days until he died;
Nào Chǐ's control of Qí,
pulling out King Mǐn's sinews,
hanging him on the temple beam,
where he died overnight.
Thus, although a leper may suffer from ulcers, sores, and abscesses,
compared with the Spring and Autumn period,
he has not reached the point of being strangled or shot in the thigh;
compared with recent times,
he has not reached the point of starving to death or having his sinews pulled out.
Therefore, the lords who are robbed and killed or meet death,
the worry and fear in their hearts,
the pain and suffering in their bodies,
must be worse than that of a leper.
From this perspective,
even saying "the leper pities the king" is acceptable.
Whenever the ruler's state is small but the families are great,
his power is light but his ministers' is heavy,
it can lead to ruin.
Neglecting laws and prohibitions
while focusing on schemes and calculations,
neglecting internal governance
and relying on external alliances,
can lead to ruin.
When ministers engage in scholarly pursuits,
heirs favor debate,
merchants hoard wealth abroad,
and commoners rely on weapons,
it can lead to ruin.
Fondness for palaces, towers, and ponds,
indulging in carriages, fine clothes, and curios,
exhausting and impoverishing the people,
squeezing and wasting resources,
can lead to ruin.
Observing astrological dates,
serving ghosts and spirits,
believing in divination,
and indulging in sacrifices,
can lead to ruin.
Appointing based on rank without verification,
relying on one person as the sole channel,
can lead to ruin.
If official posts can be obtained through influence,
and titles and emoluments through bribery,
it can lead to ruin.
Indecisive and achieving nothing,
weak and irresolute,
unable to decide likes and dislikes,
and having no firm stance,
can lead to ruin.
Insatiably greedy,
eager for profit and gain,
can lead to ruin.
Fond of extravagant words inconsistent with the law,
enjoying sophistry without seeking utility,
indulging in ornate language regardless of results,
can lead to ruin.
Superficial and easily seen through,
leaky and unable to conceal,
incapable of secrecy,
and leaking conversations among ministers,
can lead to ruin.
Stubborn and unyielding,
obstinate and fond of winning arguments,
disregarding the state
and acting recklessly with overconfidence,
can lead to ruin.
Relying on distant allies
while neglecting nearby neighbors,
depending on rescue by the powerful,
and insulting neighboring states,
can lead to ruin.
When sojourners and foreign guests,
with substantial wealth abroad,
interfere with state plans above,
and meddle in people's affairs below,
it can lead to ruin.
When the people trust the minister more,
and subordinates do not respect their superior,
and the ruler favors and trusts him but cannot remove him,
it can lead to ruin.
When talents within the state are not employed,
but external scholars are sought,
not evaluating by merit,
but preferring to appoint based on reputation,
and elevating sojourners to override established norms,
it can lead to ruin.
Disregarding the legitimate heir,
letting secondary sons contend for power,
with the crown prince undecided when the ruler dies,
can lead to ruin.
Overconfident and unrepentant,
chaotic yet self-praising,
not assessing domestic resources
but underestimating neighboring enemies,
can lead to ruin.
A small state not staying humble,
weak yet unafraid of the strong,
discourteous and insulting to great neighbors,
greedy, stubborn, and inept in diplomacy,
can lead to ruin.
Once the crown prince is established,
marrying a wife from a powerful enemy as the queen,
endangers the crown prince,
and causes ministers to change loyalties;
when ministers change loyalties,
it can lead to ruin.
Timid and weak in defense,
foreseeing early but soft-hearted and cowardly,
knowing what should be done,
but hesitating to act,
can lead to ruin.
When the ruler is abroad and the state appoints a replacement,
or the hostage crown prince has not returned
and the ruler changes the heir,
this causes the state to split;
when the state splits,
it can lead to ruin.
Humiliating high officials and being overly familiar with them,
punishing and killing commoners contrary to reason,
breeding resentment and shame
that fester and lead to treachery;
when treachery arises,
it can lead to ruin.
When two ministers hold equal power,
relatives are numerous and strong,
forming internal cliques and external alliances to contend for influence,
it can lead to ruin.
Listening to the words of concubines,
employing the wisdom of favorites,
causing internal and external grief and resentment
while repeatedly acting unlawfully,
can lead to ruin.
Disrespecting high officials,
showing discourtesy to elders,
oppressing the people with toil,
killing the innocent,
can lead to ruin.
Fond of using cunning to distort laws,
often mixing personal conduct with public affairs,
frequently changing laws and prohibitions,
issuing numerous orders,
can lead to ruin.
Having no secure territory,
poorly built city walls,
no accumulated reserves,
scarce resources,
lacking preparations for defense and offense
yet lightly engaging in attacks,
can lead to ruin.
When the royal lineage is short-lived,
the ruler frequently passes away,
infants become sovereigns,
high officials monopolize power,
establishing sojourners as factions,
and repeatedly cede territory to maintain alliances,
can lead to ruin.
When the crown prince is overly honored and prominent,
his followers are numerous and powerful,
he maintains many connections with major states,
and his authority is established early,
can lead to ruin.
Being narrow-minded and impatient,
rash and easily provoked to action,
furious and impulsive without considering consequences,
can lead to ruin.
When the ruler is frequently angered and fond of using military force,
neglects fundamental training and underestimates warfare,
can lead to ruin.
When high ministers envy each other,
great officials become overly powerful,
rely externally on enemy states,
oppress internally the common people,
attack personal enemies,
yet the ruler fails to punish them,
can lead to ruin.
When the ruler is unworthy while collateral relatives are virtuous,
the crown prince is insignificant while the庶子 are strong,
officials are weak while the people are unruly,
thus the state becomes restless;
a restless state
can lead to ruin.
Harboring grudges without expressing them,
leaving crimes unpunished,
causing ministers to secretly resent
and grow increasingly anxious and fearful,
with prolonged uncertainty,
can lead to ruin.
When military commanders are given excessive authority,
border governors are overly honored,
they act arbitrarily without authorization,
making decisions without seeking permission,
can lead to ruin.
When the queen engages in debauchery,
the queen mother hoards filth,
internal and external affairs are confused,
men and women lack distinction,
this is called having two rulers.
Having two rulers
can lead to ruin.
When the queen is demeaned while concubines are exalted,
the crown prince is humble while the庶子 are honored,
the prime minister is slighted while ushers are empowered,
thus internal and external relations become discordant.
Discord between internal and external
can lead to ruin.
When high ministers are excessively noble,
factions are numerous and strong,
they obstruct the ruler's decisions
and heavily monopolize state affairs,
can lead to ruin.
When officials of private families are employed,
descendants of military merit are dismissed,
local favorites are promoted,
meritorious service in office is neglected,
valuing private conduct and belittling public achievements,
can lead to ruin.
When the state treasury is empty while ministers are wealthy,
registered households are poor while sojourners are rich,
farmers and soldiers are distressed,
while non-essential workers prosper,
can lead to ruin.
Seeing great advantages but not pursuing them,
hearing of calamities but making no preparations,
being superficial in matters of contention and defense,
yet striving to adorn oneself with benevolence and righteousness,
can lead to ruin.
Not practicing the filial piety of a ruler,
but admiring that of a commoner,
disregarding the state's interests,
and obeying the queen mother's orders,
with women governing the state,
and eunuchs holding power,
can lead to ruin.
Eloquent in speech but lawless,
intelligent in mind but lacking method,
the ruler highly capable
yet not acting according to laws and measures,
can lead to ruin.
When close ministers advance and old associates retreat,
the unworthy hold power while the virtuous remain hidden,
the meritless are honored and the laboring are demeaned,
thus the subordinates resent.
Resentful subordinates
can lead to ruin.
When paternal relatives and high ministers receive emoluments exceeding their merits,
their insignia and robes surpass their ranks,
their palaces and provisions are excessively extravagant,
and the ruler does not restrain them,
then the ministers' desires become boundless.
Boundless desires of ministers
can lead to ruin.
When the ruler's sons-in-law and grandsons live among the people,
yet violently oppress their neighbors,
can lead to ruin.
Signs of ruin
do not mean certain ruin,
but indicate the possibility of ruin.
For two Yáo cannot both be kings,
two Jié cannot both be destroyed.
The mechanism of ruin or kingship
necessarily lies in their governance or chaos,
and the imbalance of their strength and weakness.
A tree breaks necessarily through worms,
a wall collapses necessarily through cracks.
Yet though a tree may be worm-eaten,
without a strong wind it will not break;
though a wall may have cracks,
without heavy rain it will not collapse.
The ruler of a ten-thousand-chariot state
who can master methods and implement laws,
becoming the wind and rain to the ruler showing signs of ruin,
will find it not difficult to unite the world.
The ruler has three safeguards.
If the three safeguards are complete,
then the state is secure and his person glorious;
if the three safeguards are incomplete,
then the state is endangered and his person imperiled.
What are the three safeguards?
When ministers discuss the faults of those in power,
the errors of administrators,
and the true conditions among officials,
if the ruler does not keep them confidential
but leaks them to his close favorites and capable men,
then ministers who wish to speak out
dare not fail to accommodate the minds of these close favorites and capable men,
before they can report to the ruler.
Thus, those who speak honestly and directly
cannot gain audience,
and loyalty and integrity daily become estranged.
In loving a person,
he does not solely benefit him,
but waits for praise before benefiting him;
in hating a person,
he does not solely harm him,
but waits for criticism before harming him.
Thus, the ruler has no authority
and importance lies with his attendants.
Disliking the toil of self-governance,
he allows the changing allegiances of ministers like spokes to a hub,
thereby transferring the handle of power and shifting its basis,
so that the mechanism of life and death,
the essence of giving and taking
rests with the high ministers;
such is encroachment.
This is called the three safeguards being incomplete.
If the three safeguards are incomplete,
it is a sign of being overthrown and killed.
Generally, there are three types of overthrow:
there is open overthrow,
administrative overthrow,
and punitive overthrow.
When a minister attains the dignity of a high official,
he externally manipulates the state's vital interests to control other officials,
ensuring that all affairs both internal and external
cannot proceed without his approval.
Even if there are worthy and virtuous men,
those who oppose him will inevitably meet with disaster,
while those who comply will certainly receive blessings.
Consequently, none of the officials dare to remain loyal to the ruler or concerned for the state
so as to contend over the benefits and harms to the altars of soil and grain.
Even if the ruler is worthy,
he cannot plan alone,
and if the ministers dare not be loyal to their sovereign,
then the state becomes a lost state.
This is called "a state without ministers."
When a state has no ministers,
is it because the court lacks officials
or the courtiers are few in number?
The ministers cling to their salaries and cultivate connections,
pursuing private paths instead of devoting public loyalty—
this is called "enlightened usurpation."
They trade on favor to monopolize power,
feigning external affairs to overcome internal ones,
distorting the appearances of fortune, misfortune, gain, and loss,
to cater to the ruler's likes and dislikes.
If the ruler listens to them,
he demeans himself and neglects the state to support them;
when affairs fail, they share the calamity with the ruler,
but when success is achieved, the minister alone monopolizes it.
All those in positions of power,
united in heart and word, speak of their merits;
then those who speak ill of them to the ruler will not be believed—
this is called "usurpation through affairs."
As for the control of prisons,
the enforcement of prohibitions and punishments,
if ministers seize these,
this is called "usurpation through punishments."
If the three safeguards are incomplete,
then the three usurpations arise;
if the three safeguards are complete,
then the three usurpations cease.
When the three usurpations are blocked,
then one can become king.
The ruler's flaw lies in trusting others;
trusting others,
he is then controlled by them.
A minister's relation to his ruler
is not one of flesh and blood kinship;
he is bound by circumstances and has no choice but to serve.
Therefore, as a minister,
he spies on his ruler's mind without a moment's rest,
while the ruler idly and arrogantly resides above—
this is why in the world there are those who coerce rulers
