and assassinate their lords.
If a ruler greatly trusts his son,
then treacherous ministers can exploit the son
to achieve their private ends,
as when Lì Duì tutored the King of Zhào
and starved Lord Fù.
If a ruler greatly trusts his wife,
then treacherous ministers can exploit the wife
to achieve their private ends,
as when Yōu Shī tutored Lì Jī
to kill Shēnshēng and establish Xī Qí.
Given that even one as close as a wife and as dear as a son
cannot be trusted,
then there is no one else who can be trusted.
Moreover, for the lord of ten thousand chariots
or the ruler of a thousand chariots,
there are among the queen, consorts, wives, and the legitimate son designated as heir
some who desire their ruler's early death.
How do we know this is so?
Between husband and wife,
there is no natural bond of flesh and blood;
if loved, they are close;
if not loved, they become distant.
As the saying goes:
"The child of a beloved mother is held."
Conversely, then,
the child of a hated mother is cast aside.
A man at fifty
has not yet lost his fondness for beauty,
but a woman at thirty has already declined in looks.
When a woman with fading beauty serves a husband fond of beauty,
she herself is distanced and demeaned,
and her son is doubted as the successor—
this is why queens,
consorts, and wives hope for their ruler's death.
Only when the mother becomes queen and the son becomes ruler
are orders invariably carried out,
prohibitions universally observed,
the pleasures of intimacy undiminished from the former ruler,
and control over ten thousand chariots assured without doubt—
this is why methods like poison and strangulation are employed.
Thus, the "Táo Zuǒ Chūnqiū" says:
"Rulers who die of illness cannot account for half."
If the ruler is unaware of this,
then disorder finds ample support.
Therefore it is said:
When many profit from a ruler's death,
the ruler is in peril.
Thus, Wáng Liáng loved horses,
and King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè loved his people,
all for the sake of battle and speed.
A physician willingly sucks a patient's wound,
holding their blood in his mouth,
not out of flesh and blood kinship,
but because of the benefit involved.
So, when a carriage-maker finishes a carriage,
he wishes people wealth and honor;
when a coffin-maker finishes a coffin,
he wishes people an early death.
It is not that the carriage-maker is kind and the coffin-maker wicked;
if people are not noble,
the carriage won't sell;
if people do not die,
the coffin won't be bought.
Their intent is not to hate people,
but their profit lies in people's death.
Thus, when factions form around the queen,
consorts, and the heir apparent,
they desire the ruler's death,
for if the ruler does not die,
their power is not secure.
Their intent is not to hate the ruler,
but their profit lies in the ruler's death.
Therefore, the ruler must pay heed to those who profit from his death.
Just as the sun and moon have halos surrounding them,
the real danger lies within;
guard against those you dislike,
for calamity often comes from those you love.
Hence, an enlightened king
does not undertake unverified matters,
nor consume unusual food;
he listens distantly and observes closely
to examine failures inside and out,
scrutinizes concordant and differing words
to discern the divisions of cliques;
he compares and verifies evidence
to hold accountable the truth of statements;
he holds the later to respond to the former,
applies the law to govern the multitude,
and considers all aspects to cross-examine.
Scholars receive no undeserved rewards,
and none overstep their conduct;
executions must be fitting,
crimes not pardoned,
so that treachery and evil have no place for their private schemes.
If corvée labor is heavy, the people suffer;
if the people suffer, powerful influences arise;
if powerful influences arise, exemptions and remissions increase;
if exemptions increase, the nobility grow rich.
To enrich the noble by afflicting the people,
and to foster influence that empowers ministers,
is not a long-term benefit for the world.
Therefore it is said:
If corvée labor is light, the people are at ease;
if the people are at ease, subordinates hold no heavy power;
if subordinates hold no heavy power,
then powerful influences are extinguished;
if powerful influences are extinguished, virtue resides with the superior.
Now, it is clear that water overcomes fire,
yet if a cauldron or pot intervenes,
the water above boils dry,
while the fire below burns fiercely—
water loses its means of victory.
Now, governing to prohibit treachery is even clearer than this,
yet if the ministers in charge of law act like the cauldron,
then the law remains bright only in the mind,
but has already lost its means of prohibiting treachery.
In ancient traditions,
as recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
those who violate laws and commit rebellions to become great traitors
have always emerged from among the high-ranking ministers.
Yet the laws and decrees are established,
and punishments are enforced,
often targeting the lowly and humble.
Thus, the people lose all hope,
with nowhere to voice their grievances.
Ministers form cliques,
concealing the truth from the ruler and uniting as one,
appearing hostile in public while privately colluding,
to feign selflessness,
acting as each other's eyes and ears,
awaiting the ruler's vulnerabilities.
The ruler remains obscured,
unable to hear the truth,
holding the title of sovereign but lacking real power,
while ministers monopolize the law and act arbitrarily—
this was the case with the King of Zhōu.
If power is partially delegated to them,
the positions of ruler and subject are reversed.
This illustrates that ministers must not be entrusted with authority.
The ruler's error lies in
having already appointed ministers,
yet also relying on those not appointed
to check them.
This leads the latter to oppose the appointed ministers,
and the ruler ends up being controlled by the unappointed.
Now, those relied upon to check others
are the very ones who were previously checked.
If the ruler fails to clarify laws
to restrain the ministers' power,
he cannot gain the trust of the common people.
If the ruler abandons the law and uses ministers to check each other,
those who favor each other will form cliques and praise one another,
while those who despise each other will form factions and slander one another.
With slander and praise conflicting,
the ruler becomes confused and disordered.
As for ministers,
without reputation and solicitations,
they cannot advance;
without defying laws and acting autocratically,
they cannot assert authority;
without feigning loyalty and trustworthiness,
they cannot evade restrictions.
These three
are the tools that delude the ruler and corrupt the law.
The ruler must ensure that ministers,
though possessing wisdom and ability,
cannot defy laws or act autocratically;
though having virtuous conduct,
cannot claim merit before achieving results;
though appearing loyal and trustworthy,
cannot escape legal restraints—
this is what is called clarifying the law.
The ruler may be misled by affairs or
blocked by words—
both must be carefully examined.
Ministers who easily propose affairs,
demanding few resources,
deceive the ruler with their plans.
If the ruler is misled and fails to scrutinize,
and thus over-praises them,
then the ministers end up controlling the ruler through affairs.
This is called being misled;
those misled by affairs are trapped in calamity.
If their proposals are modest
but the costs in retreat are high,
even if they achieve results,
their initial claims are untruthful.
Untruthfulness should be punished;
if achievements are not rewarded,
then no minister will dare embellish words
to delude the ruler.
The way of the ruler is to ensure that
ministers' earlier words do not contradict later ones,
and later words do not contradict earlier ones.
Even if affairs succeed,
they must be held accountable for inconsistencies—
this is called governing subordinates.
When a minister proposes a plan to the ruler
and fears criticism,
he first spreads a narrative saying:
"Those who oppose this plan
are envious of it."
If the ruler internalizes this,
he stops listening to other ministers;
if ministers fear this claim,
they dare not discuss affairs.
With both dynamics at play,
loyal ministers are ignored,
and only flattering ministers are trusted.
This is called being blocked by words;
those blocked by words are controlled by ministers.
The way of the ruler is to impose
accountability for speaking
and accountability for not speaking.
Those who speak without basis or evidence
bear the responsibility for their words;
those who avoid duty through silence
while holding high positions
bear the responsibility for their silence.
The ruler must ensure that speaking ministers
clarify their points
to verify their claims,
and question silent ministers about their choices
to hold them accountable.
Then, no minister will dare speak recklessly,
nor remain silent arbitrarily,
for both speech and silence carry responsibility.
If the ruler desires to undertake an affair
without understanding its full context,
but openly reveals his intentions,
those who act on it
will not benefit
and will inevitably bring harm in return.
Those who understand this
follow principle and abandon desire.
In undertaking affairs, there is a principle:
if the benefits are many
and the costs few,
it may be done.
Deluded rulers do otherwise;
they consider only the benefits,
ignoring the costs.
Even if costs double the benefits,
they remain unaware of the harm,
thus gaining in name but losing in substance.
In such cases, the achievement is small
while the harm is great.
Truly, an achievement
must have great benefits
and small costs
to be deemed worthy.
If great costs go unpunished
and minor gains are rewarded,
ministers will incur great expenses
for trivial achievements,
and when small successes are made,
the ruler also suffers harm.
Those ignorant of governance insist:
"Do not change antiquity,
do not alter conventions."
Whether to change or not,
the sage does not blindly follow—
he rectifies governance accordingly.
Thus, the immutability of antiquity
and the permanence of conventions
depend on their applicability to the present.
If Yī Yǐn had not changed the Yīn dynasty,
or Tài Gōng the Zhōu dynasty,
then Tāng
and Wǔ would not have become kings.
If Guǎn Zhòng had not reformed Qí,
or Guō Yǎn not transformed Jìn,
then Huán
and Wén would not have become hegemons.
Those who resist changing antiquity
fear disturbing the people's comfort.
Yet preserving antiquity unchanged
perpetuates the path of chaos;
catering to popular sentiment
indulges treacherous conduct.
If the people are ignorant and unaware of disorder,
and the ruler is timid and unable to reform,
governance fails.
The ruler,
with clarity understanding governance,
must enforce it strictly.
Thus, even if it opposes the people's wishes, he must establish order.
The explanation lies in
Lord Shāng's internal and external affairs where iron-tipped spears
and heavy shields were prepared as precautions.
Thus, when Guō Yǎn began his governance,
Duke Wén had official troops;
when Guǎn Zhòng began his governance,
Duke Huán had armed chariots,
as preparations to warn the people.
Hence, foolish and indolent people,
suffering from minor expenses and forgetting great benefits,
led to Yín Hǔ receiving slander.
And those who fear minor changes and lose long-term advantages,
caused Zōu Jiǎ to criticize military campaigns.
Accustomed to chaos and tolerant of order,
thus the people of Zhèng could not return.
Drilling tortoise shells and counting stalks,
the omen said "greatly auspicious,"
yet the one who attacked Yān
was Zhào.
Drilling tortoise shells and counting stalks,
the omen said "greatly auspicious,"
yet the one who attacked Zhào
was Yān.
Jù Xīn's service to Yān,
brought no merit and endangered the state;
Zōu Yǎn's service to Yān,
brought no merit and severed the state's path.
Zhào first succeeded against Yān,
later succeeded against Qí,
the state was in chaos yet its arrogance grew,
considering itself equal to Qín,
not because Zhào's tortoise was divine
but because Yān's tortoise was deceptive.
Zhào again drilled tortoise shells and counted stalks
to attack Yān northward,
intending to coerce Yān to oppose Qín,
the omen said "greatly auspicious."
They began attacking Dàliáng
when Qín advanced from Shàngdǎng,
their troops reached Lí and six cities were captured.
Reaching Yángchéng,
Qín had taken Yè.
When Páng Yuán led troops south,
then Zhàng was completely lost.
Therefore, I say:
Although Zhào's tortoise lacked foresight regarding Yān,
it should have seen the near threat from Qín.
Qín, with its "greatly auspicious,"
gained actual territory,
and had justification for rescuing Yān.
Zhào, with its
"greatly auspicious,"
suffered land loss and military humiliation,
and its ruler died in despair.
Again, not because Qín's tortoise was divine
but because Zhào's tortoise was deceptive.
In earlier times,
Wèi spent years attacking eastward, exhausting Táo and Wèi,
then years facing westward and losing its state,
not because Fēnglóng, Wǔxíng, Tàiyī, Wángxiàng,
Shètí, Liùshén, Wǔkuò, Tiānhé, Yīnqiāng, Suìxīng
were in the west for years,
nor because Tiānquē, Húnì, Xíngxīng,
Yínghuò, Kuítái were in the east for years.
Thus, it is said:
Tortoise stalks, ghosts, and spirits cannot determine victory,
positions and directions
cannot dictate battle outcomes.
Yet relying on them,
there is no greater folly.
In ancient times, the former kings devoted efforts to亲近 the people,
and focused on clarifying laws.
When laws are clear,
loyal ministers are encouraged;
when punishments are certain,
treacherous ministers are restrained.
With loyalty encouraged and treachery restrained,
the land expands and the ruler is honored—
as in Qín's case.
Ministers forming cliques and colluding
to obscure the right path,
practicing selfish crookedness
leading to land loss and ruler debasement—
as in the states east of the mountains.
The weak and disordered perish,
such is human nature.
The well-governed and strong rule,
such is the ancient way.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè relied on a large auspicious tortoise
to fight Wú but did not prevail,
becoming a captive and serving in Wú;
upon returning to his state, he abandoned the tortoise,
clarified laws and亲近 the people
to take revenge on Wú,
and then Fūchāi was captured.
Thus, those relying on ghosts and spirits neglect laws,
those relying on other states endanger their own.
Cáo relied on Qí and did not heed Sòng,
Qí attacked Jīng and Sòng destroyed Cáo.
Xíng relied on Wú and did not heed Qí,
Yuè attacked Wú and Qí destroyed Xíng.
Xǔ relied on Jīng and did not heed Wèi,
Jīng attacked Sòng and Wèi destroyed Xǔ,
Zhèng relied on Wèi and did not heed Hán,
Wèi attacked Jīng and Hán destroyed Zhèng.
Now Hán is a small state relying on large ones,
the ruler is negligent and listens to Qín
and Wèi, depends on Qí and Jīng for support,
yet small states perish even more.
Thus, relying on others cannot expand territory,
but Hán does not see this.
Jīng attacked Wèi and sent troops to Xǔ and Yān,
Qí attacked Rén and Hù and weakened Wèi,
yet it was insufficient to save Zhèng,
and Hán remains unaware.
These are all cases of not clarifying laws and prohibitions
to govern their states,
relying on external forces
to the demise of their altars of grain and soil.
Therefore, I say:
Understanding the methods of governance,
even a small state
can be wealthy;
with respectful and trustworthy rewards and punishments,
even a sparse population
can be strong.
If rewards and punishments lack measure,
even a large state,
with weak military,
its land is not truly its land,
its people not truly its people.
Without land and people,
even Yáo and Shùn could not rule as kings,
nor could the Three Dynasties become strong.
If rulers bestow excessively,
and ministers take without merit,
abandoning laws
to speak of the achievements of ancient kings and wise rulers,
the ruler entrusts the state to them.
Therefore, I say:
This is desiring ancient merits,
rewarding modern people with ancient standards.
The ruler bestows excessively,
and ministers take without merit.
When the ruler bestows excessively,
ministers become opportunistic;
when ministers take without merit,
merit loses its honor.
Those without merit receiving rewards
lead to depleted resources and popular resentment;
depleted resources and popular resentment
cause the people not to exert their full efforts.
Hence, excessive rewards lose the people,
excessive punishments
make the people unafraid.
Rewards fail to encourage,
punishments fail to restrain,
then even a large state
is surely in peril.
Thus it is said:
Petty wisdom should not be tasked with planning,
minor loyalty should not be entrusted with upholding laws.
When King Gōng of Jīng battled Duke Lì of Jìn at Yānlíng,
the Jīng army was defeated,
and King Gōng was wounded.
In the heat of battle,
Minister of War Zǐ Fǎn, thirsty, sought a drink,
His friend Shù Gǔyáng offered him a cup of wine.
Zǐ Fǎn said:
"Take it away,
this is wine."
Shù Gǔyáng said:
"It is not."
Zǐ Fǎn accepted and drank it.
Zǐ Fǎn was a man fond of wine,
found it sweet,
could not keep it from his mouth,
and lay down drunk.
King Gōng wished to resume battle and discuss plans,
sent someone to summon Zǐ Fǎn,
but Zǐ Fǎn excused himself due to a heart ailment.
King Gōng rode in his carriage to see him,
entered the tent,
smelled the stench of wine and turned back,
saying:
"In today's battle,
my own eyes witnessed the wounds,
what I relied on was the Marshal,
yet the Marshal is like this,
this is to destroy the state of Jīng's altars of land and grain
and have no pity for my people.
I have no one with whom to resume the fight."
He disbanded the army and left,
and had Zǐ Fǎn executed as a great punishment.
Therefore it is said:
Shù Gǔyáng's offering of wine,
was not because he intended to harm Zǐ Fǎn,
but genuinely out of loyal affection for him,
yet it precisely sufficed to kill him, that is all.
This is an act of minor loyalty
that undermines great loyalty.
Therefore it is said:
Minor loyalty
is the enemy of great loyalty.
If minor loyalty is allowed to govern the law,
then crimes will surely be pardoned out of mutual affection,
which brings ease to those below,
yet it harms the governance of the people.
When Wèi was just establishing its laws clearly,
following statutes and orders,
the meritorious were always rewarded,
the guilty were always punished,
it strongly upheld the world,
and its might extended to the neighboring states;
but when the laws were neglected,
and rewards given arbitrarily,
the state daily declined.
When Zhào was just clarifying its state regulations,
following the great army's ways,
it had numerous people and strong soldiers,
and expanded its territory against Qí and Yān;
but when the state regulations were neglected,
and those employed were weak,
the state daily declined.
When Yān was just upholding the law diligently,
and officials' judgments were careful,
it made counties in the east from Qí,
and in the south took all the land of Zhōngshān;
but when the upholding of law was lost,
and official judgments were not used,
with factions contending,
decisions following subordinates,
then the army weakened and territory was reduced,
and the state was controlled by neighboring enemies.
Therefore it is said:
Those who clarify the law are strong,
those who neglect the law are weak.
The distinction between strength and weakness is so clear,
yet the rulers of the age do not act accordingly,
so the states' decline is fitting.
A saying goes:
"If a family has constant occupations,
though hungry, they do not starve;
if a state has constant laws,
though in danger, it does not perish."
Now, if constant laws are abandoned for private whims,
then ministers will adorn themselves with wisdom and ability;
if ministers adorn themselves with wisdom and ability,
then laws and prohibitions are not established.
This allows the way of arbitrary opinions to prevail,
and the way of governing the state to be abandoned.
The way of governing the state
is to remove what harms the law,
then one is not misled by wisdom and ability,
nor deceived by fame and reputation.
In the past, Shùn sent officials to control the flood,
and those who acted before orders
were killed by Shùn;
Yǔ convened the lords at Huìjī,
and the lord of Fángfēng who arrived late was executed by Yǔ.
From this we see,
those who act before orders are killed,
those who come after orders are executed,
thus the ancients valued following orders first.
Therefore, a mirror held steady remains clear and undisturbed,
and beauty and ugliness are compared accordingly;
a scale held steady remains balanced and undisturbed,
and lightness and heaviness are weighed accordingly.
If the mirror is shaken,
it cannot be clear,
if the scale is shaken,
it cannot be balanced,
such is the nature of law.
Therefore, the former kings took the Way as constant,
and law as fundamental.
When the foundation is orderly, reputation is honored;
when the foundation is chaotic, reputation is cut off.
All wisdom and ability, clarity and understanding,
if there is a basis, proceed;
if not, stop.
Thus wisdom and ability alone on the Way
cannot be transmitted to others.
But the Way and law are all-encompassing,
while wisdom and ability are often flawed.
Hanging a scale lets one know level,
setting a compass lets one know round,
this is the all-encompassing Way.
An enlightened ruler makes the people adhere to the Way,
thus they are at ease yet achieve merit.
Abandoning the compass for cleverness,
abandoning the law for wisdom,
is the way of confusion and chaos.
A chaotic ruler makes the people adorn themselves with wisdom,
not understanding the Way,
thus they toil without merit.
Abandoning laws and prohibitions to heed requests and visits,
ministers sell offices above,
and seek rewards below,
thus benefits lie in private households
and authority rests with the ministers.
Therefore, the people have no heart to exhaust their strength in serving the ruler,
but strive to network with superiors.
When the people prefer networking above,
then goods and wealth flow upward,
and the clever-tongued are employed.
If so,
then the meritorious become fewer.
Treacherous ministers advance more
while capable ministers retreat,
then the ruler is confused and does not know what to do,
and the people gather without knowing the way.
These are the faults of abandoning laws and prohibitions, neglecting merit and toil, promoting fame and reputation, and heeding requests and visits.
All those who undermine the law
surely devise deceit and rely on things
to gain intimacy,
and also like to speak of what is rare in the world.
This is how tyrannical and chaotic rulers are misled,
and how ministers and worthy assistants are encroached upon.
Therefore, if ministers praise the merits of Yī Yǐn
and Guǎn Zhòng,
they have grounds to defy the law and adorn themselves with wisdom;
if they praise the loyalty of Bǐ Gān and Wǔ Zǐxū who were killed for it,
they have excuses to resent forceful remonstrance.
Praising the wise above,
and decrying tyranny below,
cannot be taken as examples,
such things must be prohibited.
The ruler establishes laws believing them right,
yet now many ministers establish their private wisdom
to deem the law wrong,
this is using wisdom for evil,
surpassing the law to set up wisdom.
Such must be prohibited,
this is the ruler's way.
The way of an enlightened ruler
must clarify the distinction between public and private,
make laws and institutions clear,
and eliminate private favors.
That orders must be carried out and
prohibitions must be enforced
is the public duty of the ruler;
to insist on personal pursuits,
be trustworthy among friends,
not be swayed by rewards,
nor deterred by punishments,
is the private duty of ministers.
When private duty prevails, chaos ensues;
when public duty prevails, order reigns;
hence, there is a distinction between public and private.
Ministers have private motives
and public duties.
Cultivating oneself with purity
and acting with impartiality and righteousness,
holding office without selfishness—
this is the public duty of ministers;
engaging in corrupt conduct and indulging desires,
seeking personal comfort and family gain—
this is the private motive of ministers.
When an enlightened ruler is in power,
ministers abandon private motives
and fulfill public duties;
when a chaotic ruler is in power,
ministers discard public duties
and pursue private motives.
Thus, ruler and minister have different minds:
the ruler employs strategy to retain ministers,
and ministers use strategy to serve the ruler.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is one of calculation.
To harm oneself for the benefit of the state
is something a minister will not do;
to harm the state for the benefit of ministers
is something a ruler will not undertake.
The nature of a minister
is to avoid self-harm without gain;
the nature of a ruler
is to reject harm to the state, showing no favoritism.
The ruler and minister
are united by calculation.
As for facing danger with unwavering resolve to die,
exhausting wisdom and strength,
it is done for the sake of law.
Therefore, the ancient kings established clear rewards to encourage it,
and strict punishments to intimidate.
When rewards and punishments are clear,
the people will exhaust themselves unto death;
when the people exhaust themselves unto death,
the military strengthens and the ruler is honored.
If rewards and punishments are not carefully observed,
the people will seek gains without merit,
and offenders may escape by luck,
leading to a weak military and a humbled ruler.
Thus, the ancient kings and their worthy assistants
exhausted their efforts and wisdom.
Hence it is said:
"The distinction between public and private must be clear,
laws and prohibitions must be rigorous;
the ancient kings understood this."
Virtue is internal;
acquisition is external.
"The highest virtue does not appear as virtue"
means that the spirit is not distracted by externals.
When the spirit is not distracted by externals,
the self is preserved whole;
preserving the self whole is called virtue.
Virtue is the attainment of self.
All virtue
is gathered through non-action,
accomplished through non-desire;
it is stabilized by non-thinking,
and solidified by non-use.
To act and desire
leaves virtue no abode;
without an abode,
it is not whole.
Using and thinking about it
makes it unstable;
instability
leads to ineffectiveness,
and ineffectiveness
arises from [a focus on] virtue.
To focus on virtue is to have no virtue;
not focusing on virtue is to have virtue.
Therefore it is said:
"The highest virtue does not appear as virtue,
thus it possesses virtue."
The reason for valuing non-action and non-thinking as emptiness
is that the mind is unconstrained.
Those without method
thus take non-action and non-thinking as emptiness.
But if one deliberately takes non-action and non-thinking as emptiness,
the mind constantly remembers emptiness,
which is being constrained by the pursuit of emptiness.
Emptiness means the mind is unconstrained.
If constrained by the pursuit of emptiness,
it is not true emptiness.
For the empty-minded, non-action
does not treat non-action as a constant rule.
Not treating non-action as a constant rule
leads to emptiness;
emptiness
results in abundant virtue;
abundant virtue is called the highest virtue.
Hence it is said:
"The highest virtue takes no action
yet nothing is left undone."
Benevolence means
a heart that joyfully loves others;
it rejoices in others' good fortune
and grieves at others' misfortune;
it arises from an irrepressible inner impulse,
not seeking reward.
Therefore it is said:
"The highest benevolence acts without ulterior motive."
Righteousness pertains to
the affairs between ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
the distinctions between father and son, noble and humble,
the interactions between acquaintances and friends,
and the divisions between close and distant, inner and outer.
It is fitting for a minister to serve the ruler,
for an inferior to cherish the superior,
for a son to serve the father,
for the humble to respect the noble,
for friends to assist each other,
and for the close to be inner and the distant outer.
Righteousness means
what is fitting,
and acting accordingly.
Therefore it is said:
"The highest righteousness acts with deliberate purpose."
Ritual is
the expression of emotions,
the refinement of various righteous acts,
the interactions between ruler and minister, father and son,
and what distinguishes noble from humble, worthy from unworthy.
When inner feelings are held without expression,
rapid steps and low bows make them clear;
when genuine love is unknown,
kind words and elaborate speeches convey it.
Ritual is
the external adornment that expresses the internal.
Therefore it is said:
"Ritual expresses emotions."
When people are moved by external things,
they do not know it is ritual for self-cultivation.
The multitude practices ritual
to honor others,
hence it waxes and wanes.
The noble person practices ritual
for self-cultivation;
for self-cultivation,
hence it is revered as the highest ritual;
the highest ritual is revered,
while the multitude is divided,
so they cannot respond in kind;
unable to respond,
therefore it is said:
"The highest ritual acts, but none respond."
Though the multitude is divided,
the sage's return to reverence and respect,
fulfilling the rituals of hand and foot,
does not wane.
Therefore it is said:
"He rolls up his sleeves and still practices it."
The Way accumulates, and accumulation yields achievements;
Virtue is
the achievement of the Way.
Achievements have substance, and substance radiates brilliance;
Benevolence is
the radiance of Virtue.
Radiance has luster, and luster manifests in affairs;
Righteousness is
the affair of Benevolence.
Affairs involve ritual,
and ritual is adorned with refinement;
Ritual is
the refinement of Righteousness.
Hence it is said:
"When the Way is lost, Virtue is lost;
when Virtue is lost, Benevolence is lost;
when Benevolence is lost, Righteousness is lost;
when Righteousness is lost, Ritual is lost."
Ritual is the outward display of emotions,
refinement is the ornamentation of substance.
The noble person embraces emotions and discards appearances,
values substance and dislikes ornamentation.
Those who rely on appearances to judge emotions
have base emotions;
those who require ornamentation to assess substance
have decaying substance.
How can this be argued?
The Héshì jade
is not adorned with five colors,
the Suíhóu pearl
is not decorated with silver and gold.
Their substance is supremely beautiful,
no object can sufficiently adorn them.
When things require adornment to become valuable,
their substance is not beautiful.
Thus between father and son,
their ritual is simple and unadorned,
hence it is said
ritual is sparse.
All things cannot flourish simultaneously,
as with yīn and yáng;
principles contend and yield,
as with authority and virtue.
Substantial depth has sparse appearance,
as in the ritual between father and son.
From this perspective,
elaborate ritual
indicates the decline of sincere heart.
Thus those who practice ritual
are channeling people's simple hearts,
yet when common people perform ritual,
they feel slighted if others respond lightly,
and resentful if there is no response.
Now those who practice ritual
channel people's simple hearts,
yet provide grounds for mutual reproach -
how can this avoid contention?
Contention leads to chaos,
hence it is said:
"Ritual is
the thinning of loyalty and trust,
and the beginning of chaos."
Acting before things and moving before principles is called foreknowledge.
Foreknowledge is
baseless conjecture without connection to reality.
How can this be argued?
Zhān Hé sat,
with disciples attending him,
when an ox lowed outside the gate.
A disciple said:
"It is a black ox with a white forehead."
Zhān Hé said:
"Yes,
it is a black ox,
but the white is on its horns."
Someone was sent to look,
and indeed it was a black ox with cloth wrapped around its horns.
Using Zhān's technique
to captivate people's minds
is flashy but perilous.
Hence it is said:
"It is the ostentation of the Way."
If we set aside Zhān's observation
and have a simple child look,
he would also know it was a black ox
with cloth wrapped around its horns.
Thus with all Zhān's observation,
mental strain and spiritual exhaustion,
he ultimately achieved the same as a simple child -
therefore it is said
"the beginning of foolishness."
Hence it is said:
"Foreknowledge is
the ostentation of the Way,
and the beginning of foolishness."
The so-called
"great man"
refers to the greatness of his wisdom.
The so-called
"dwelling in thickness, not in thinness"
means practicing genuine feelings
and abandoning ritual appearances.
The so-called
"dwelling in substance, not in ostentation"
means necessarily following principles, not taking shortcuts.
The so-called
"rejecting that and taking this"
means discarding appearances and shortcuts,
and embracing principle-following and genuine feelings.
Hence it is said:
"Reject that and take this."
When people encounter misfortune
their hearts fear and dread,
when hearts fear and dread
their conduct becomes upright,
when conduct is upright
thought becomes thorough,
when thought is thorough
they grasp the principles of affairs.
When conduct is upright
there is no harm or misfortune,
when there is no harm or misfortune
they live out their natural lifespan;
when they grasp the principles of affairs
they necessarily achieve success.
Living out one's natural lifespan
means completeness and longevity;
necessarily achieving success
means wealth and honor.
Longevity, completeness, wealth and honor are called blessing.
Yet blessing originates from having misfortune,
hence it is said:
"Misfortune is where blessing leans."
Thus achievement is accomplished.
When people have blessing
wealth and honor arrive,
when wealth and honor arrive
food and clothing become luxurious,
when food and clothing become luxurious
arrogance arises in the heart,
when arrogance arises in the heart
conduct becomes depraved and actions abandon principle.
When conduct becomes depraved
the body meets premature death,
when actions abandon principle
there is no achievement of success.
Having internal calamities of death and premature demise,
and external lack of successful reputation
is great misfortune.
Yet misfortune fundamentally arises from having blessing,
hence it is said:
"Blessing is where misfortune lurks."
Those who follow the Way and principles in their actions
can accomplish anything.
Being able to accomplish anything means
at best achieving the尊势 of the Son of Heaven,
at least easily obtaining the ranks and emoluments of ministers and generals.
Those who abandon the Way and principles and act recklessly,
even if they have the尊势 of the Son of Heaven or feudal lords above,
and below possess the wealth of Yīdùn,
Táozhū,
or diviners,
will still lose their people
and forfeit their wealth and resources.
Common people lightly abandon the Way and principles
and easily act recklessly
because they don't understand how profound and great are misfortune and blessing,
and how vast and far-reaching is the Way.
Hence the admonition:
"Who knows their ultimate extent?"
Everyone desires wealth, honor, and longevity,
yet none can avoid the calamities of poverty, low status, death, or premature demise.
If one must have wealth, honor, and longevity,
but ends up with poverty, low status, death, or premature demise,
this means they cannot reach what they wish to attain.
All those who lose the path to their desires and act recklessly are called lost;
being lost, they cannot reach what they wish to attain.
Now, the multitude cannot reach what they wish to attain,
hence it is said:
"Lost."
That the multitude cannot reach what they wish to attain
has been so from the division of heaven and earth until now.
Therefore, it is said:
"Human confusion
has indeed lasted for a long time."
What is called 'squareness'
is the correspondence between inner and outer,
the alignment of words and actions.
What is called 'incorruptibility'
is the commitment to life and death,
and indifference to material wealth.
What is called 'uprightness'
is righteousness that must be just,
with a public-minded heart, not biased toward factions.
What is called 'brilliance'
is high official rank and nobility,
and splendid robes.
Now, the person who possesses the Dào,
though both inwardly and outwardly faithful and compliant,
does not use it to slander the impoverished or fallen;
though willing to die for principles and indifferent to wealth,
does not use it to insult the weary or shame the poor;
though righteous and impartial, not factional,
does not use it to eliminate the wicked or blame the selfish;
though powerful and finely dressed,
does not use it to boast to the lowly or deceive the poor.
What is the reason for this?
If those who have lost their way
were willing to listen, learn, and inquire of the wise,
they would not become lost.
Now, the reason the multitude desires success
but instead meets with failure
stems from not understanding the principles
and refusing to ask the wise or listen to the capable.
The multitude refuses to ask the wise
or listen to the capable,
and if the sage forcibly imposes the consequences of their failures upon them,
they resent it.
The multitude is many and the sage few;
the few cannot overcome the many—
that is the nature of numbers.
Now, to act in a way that makes one an enemy of all under heaven
is not the way to preserve one's life or achieve longevity.
Therefore, one acts with measured steps
and raises them accordingly.
Hence it is said:
"Square but not cutting,
incorruptible but not injurious,
upright but not unrestrained,
brilliant but not dazzling."
Acute hearing and clear vision, intelligence and wisdom are of heaven;
movement, stillness, thought, and reflection are of man.
Man,
relying on heaven's clarity to see,
depending on heaven's acuity to hear,
and leaning on heaven's wisdom to think and reflect.
Thus, if vision is strained,
the eyes become unclear;
if hearing is pushed to extremes,
the ears become dull;
if thought and reflection are excessive,
knowledge and awareness become disordered.
If the eyes are unclear,
they cannot distinguish black from white;
if the ears are dull,
they cannot differentiate clear and muddy sounds;
if knowledge is disordered,
one cannot discern the grounds of gain and loss.
Eyes that cannot distinguish the colors of black and white
are called blind;
ears that cannot differentiate clear and muddy sounds
are called deaf;
a mind that cannot discern the grounds of gain and loss
is called mad.
Blind,
one cannot avoid the dangers of the daytime;
deaf,
one cannot know the harm of thunderclaps;
mad,
one cannot escape the calamities of human laws and decrees.
What the text calls "governing people"
means regulating the rhythm of movement and stillness,
and reducing the expenditure of thought and reflection.
What it calls
"serving heaven"
means not exhausting the power of acute hearing and clear vision,
and not fully taxing one's knowledge and awareness.
If one exhausts them fully,
then the spirit is heavily spent;
if the spirit is heavily spent,
the calamities of blindness, deafness, confusion, and madness arrive.
Therefore, one is sparing.
Being sparing means
cherishing one's vital spirit,
and being frugal with one's knowledge and awareness.
Hence it is said:
"In governing people and serving heaven, there is nothing like being sparing."
The multitude uses their spirit agitatedly;
agitation leads to much expenditure,
and much expenditure is called extravagance.
The sage uses their spirit calmly;
calm leads to little expenditure,
and little expenditure is called sparing.
Sparing is a method
born from the principles of the Dào.
To be able to be sparing
is to follow the Dào
and submit to principle.
The multitude, encountering distress,
falling into calamity,
still do not know to withdraw,
and do not submit to the principles of the Dào.
The sage, even before seeing the form of calamity,
emptily and naturally submits to the principles of the Dào,
thereby achieving early submission.
Therefore, it is said:
"To be sparing
is to achieve early submission."
One who knows how to govern people
keeps their thoughts and reflections calm;
one who knows how to serve heaven
keeps their senses empty.
With thoughts and reflections calm,
so virtue does not depart;
with senses empty,
then harmonious energy daily enters.
Hence it is said:
"Accumulate virtue repeatedly."
To be able to make old virtue not depart
and new harmonious energy arrive daily
is due to early submission.
Therefore, it is said:
"Early submission
is called accumulating virtue repeatedly."
Accumulating virtue leads to the spirit becoming calm;
the spirit calm leads to harmony increasing;
harmony increasing leads to plans succeeding;
plans succeeding lead to the ability to master all things;
able to master all things,
then in battle, it is easy to defeat the enemy;
easy to defeat the enemy in battle
ensures that one's strategies surely overshadow the age.
With strategies surely overshadowing the age,
therefore it is said:
"There is nothing unconquerable."
Being unconquerable stems from accumulating virtue repeatedly,
hence it is said:
"Accumulating virtue repeatedly
then there is nothing unconquerable."
Easy victory in battle
leads to uniting and possessing all under heaven;
strategies overshadowing the age
ensure that the people follow.
Advancing to unite all under heaven
and retreating to be followed by the people,
the method is so profound
that the multitude cannot see its beginning or end.
Unable to see its beginning or end,
therefore none can know its limit.
Hence it is said:
"Being unconquerable
then none can know its limit."
If a state is established only to perish later,
or a person lives only to meet calamity afterwards,
one cannot be said to truly possess their state,
nor to preserve their person.
To truly possess one's state,
one must be able to secure its altars of soil and grain;
to preserve one's person,
one must be able to live out their natural lifespan,
and only then can it be said that they truly possess their state,
and preserve their person.
Those who can possess their state
and preserve their person
must embody the Dào.
Embodying the Dào
leads to profound wisdom,
profound wisdom
enables far-reaching foresight,
and with far-reaching foresight,
no one can perceive their ultimate limits.
Only by making others unable to see the ultimate extent of their affairs,
being unseen in the ultimate extent of their affairs,
can one preserve their person
and possess their state.
Hence it is said:
"None know their ultimate limits.
When none know their ultimate limits,
one can possess the state."
What is called
"the mother of possessing the state"
— mother
refers to the Dào.
The Dào
gives birth to the means by which the state is possessed;
since it is the means by which the state is possessed,
it is called "the mother of possessing the state."
The Dào,
when applied in interacting with the world,
ensures long establishment of life,
and enduring maintenance of blessings.
Therefore it is said:
"Having the mother of the state,
one can endure long."
Trees have spreading roots
and taproots.
The taproot
is what the texts call the "dǐ."
The dǐ
is what enables the tree to establish its life;
the spreading roots
are what enable the tree to sustain its life.
Virtue
is what enables humans to establish their lives;
blessings
are what enable humans to sustain their lives.
Those who establish themselves on principle
maintain their blessings long,
hence it is said:
"Deepen its roots."
Those who embody the Dào
see their lives grow long,
hence it is said:
"Secure its dǐ."
With the dǐ secured,
life grows;
with roots deepened,
vision lasts long.
Therefore it is said:
"Deepen its roots,
secure its dǐ,
this is the way to long life and enduring vision."
If craftsmen frequently change their trades,
they lose their efficiency;
if workers are often moved about,
they lose their productivity.
For one worker,
losing half a day daily,
in ten days amounts to losing five man-days of work.
For ten thousand workers,
losing half a day daily,
in ten days amounts to losing fifty thousand man-days of work.
Thus, the more people frequently change occupations,
the greater the number affected,
and the larger the loss incurred.
Whenever laws and decrees are altered,
advantages and disadvantages shift,
and when advantages and disadvantages shift,
the people's pursuits change;
changing pursuits is called changing occupations.
Therefore, reasoning from principle,
mobilizing the masses frequently
leads to little success;
moving large vessels often
causes much damage;
stirring small fish repeatedly while cooking
ruins their gloss;
governing a large state with frequent legal changes
makes the people suffer,
hence a ruler with the Dào values tranquility,
and does not emphasize changing laws.
Thus it is said:
"Governing a large state is like cooking small fish."
When ill, people value physicians;
when in calamity, they fear ghosts.
When a sage is in power,
the people have few desires;
with few desires,
their blood and qì are regulated and their actions follow reason,
and with reasoned actions, they encounter few calamities.
When internally free from the harms of boils, ulcers, and hemorrhoids,
and externally from the calamities of punishments and legal executions,
they pay little heed to ghosts.
Hence it is said:
"When the Dào is used to oversee the world,
its ghosts are not supernatural."
The people in a well-governed age
do not harm each other with ghosts and spirits.
Therefore it is said:
"Not that their ghosts are not supernatural,
but that their supernaturalness does not harm people."
Ghostly afflictions
— when they cause illness, it is called ghosts harming people;
when people exorcise them,
it is called people harming ghosts.
When people violate laws and decrees,
it is called the people harming the ruler;
when the ruler punishes or executes people,
it is called the ruler harming the people.
If the people do not break the law,
then the ruler does not carry out punishments;
the ruler not carrying out punishments
is called the ruler not harming people.
Therefore it is said:
"The sage also does not harm the people."
When the ruler and the people do not harm each other,
and humans and ghosts do not injure one another,
it is said:
"Neither harms the other."
When the people dare not break the law,
the ruler internally needs not use punishments,
and externally does not exploit their property and livelihood.
The ruler internally not using punishments,
and externally not exploiting their property and livelihood,
allows the people to multiply.
The people multiplying and stores accumulating abundantly
— the people multiplying and stores accumulating abundantly
is called having virtue.
All so-called afflictions
occur when the húnpò depart and the jīngshén become disordered;
with disordered jīngshén, there is no virtue.
If ghosts do not afflict people,
the húnpò do not depart,
and if the húnpò do not depart,
the jīngshén are not disordered;
jīngshén not being disordered is called having virtue.
When the ruler's stores are abundant
and ghosts do not disturb the people's jīngshén,
then virtue entirely resides with the people.
Hence it is said:
"When neither harms the other,
virtue converges upon both."
This means that virtue flourishes both above and below
and all returns to the people.
A ruler with the Dào
has no enemies or grudges with neighboring states externally,
and bestows virtuous favor upon the people internally.
Having no enemies or grudges with neighboring states externally
means he treats other feudal lords with courtesy and righteousness.
Bestowing virtuous favor upon the people internally
means he governs human affairs with focus on fundamentals.
Treating feudal lords with courtesy and righteousness
leads to few military campaigns;
governing the people's affairs with focus on fundamentals
stops extravagance and waste.
The primary utility of horses lies in
external military provisions
and internal indulgence in extravagance.
Now, a ruler who follows the Dào
externally minimizes the use of military forces
and internally prohibits excessive luxury.
The sovereign does not employ horses in battles or pursuits,
and the people do not use horses for distant indulgence
or transporting goods;
their accumulated efforts are solely devoted to farmland,
and focusing efforts on farmland
necessarily involves fertilization and irrigation.
Hence it is said:
"When the world follows the Dào,
warhorses are retired to fertilize the fields."
When a ruler lacks the Dào,
he internally brutalizes his people
and externally invades and deceives neighboring states.
Internal brutality
leads to the exhaustion of people's livelihoods,
while external aggression
causes frequent military conflicts.
With livelihoods exhausted,
livestock diminish;
with frequent wars,
soldiers are depleted.
Diminished livestock
results in scarcity of warhorses,
and depleted soldiers
bring the army to peril.
When warhorses are scarce,
broodmares are conscripted;
when the army is in danger,
even close ministers are enlisted.
Horses are
crucial for military purposes;
the suburbs
signify proximity.
Now, the means to supply the army come from broodmares and close ministers.
Therefore it is said:
"When the world lacks the Dào,
warhorses are bred in the suburbs."
When humans have desires,
their plans become disordered;
disordered plans
intensify desires,
intensified desires
allow evil thoughts to prevail,
prevailing evil thoughts
disrupt the normal course of affairs,
and such disruption
gives rise to calamities.
From this perspective,
calamities stem from evil thoughts,
which are tempted by desirable things.
Things that are desirable
in advancement teach good people to commit treachery,
and in retreat cause virtuous people to suffer misfortune.
When treachery arises,
it encroaches upon and weakens the ruler above,
and when misfortune arrives,
the common people are often harmed.
Thus, desirable things
both encroach upon the ruler above and harm the people below.
To encroach upon the ruler and harm the people
is a grave offense.
Hence it is said:
"No disaster is greater than desirability."
Therefore, the sage is not drawn by the five colors,
nor indulges in music and pleasures;
the enlightened ruler scorns luxuries and rejects excessive beauty.
Humans lack fur or feathers,
so without clothing, they cannot withstand the cold;
unconnected to heaven above
and unrooted in earth below,
with intestines and stomach as their foundation,
without food, they cannot survive;
thus, they cannot avoid having desires for profit.
If the heart of desire for profit is not eliminated,
it becomes a worry for one's person.
Therefore, the sage wears enough to withstand cold,
eats enough to satisfy hunger,
and then has no worries.
Ordinary people are not like this;
whether greatly as feudal lords
or with surplus wealth of a thousand gold,
their anxiety to obtain more remains unremoved.
Convicts may be pardoned,
death-row inmates sometimes live,
but the worries of those who do not know contentment are never resolved in their lifetime.
Hence it is said:
"No disaster is greater than not knowing contentment."
Thus, excessive desire for profit brings more worry,
worry leads to illness;
illness arises and wisdom declines,
wisdom declining
results in loss of measure;
loss of measure
leads to reckless actions,
reckless actions
bring about calamities.
When calamities arrive,
illness afflicts internally,
internal affliction
causes pain and misfortune to press externally,
external pressure of pain and misfortune
mixes suffering within the intestines and stomach.
When suffering mixes within the intestines and stomach,
the harm to a person is profound.
Profound harm leads to retreat and self-blame,
and self-blame arises from the desire for profit.
Therefore it is said:
"No blame is more profound than that from desire for profit."
The Dào is
that by which all things are as they are,
and that with which all principles accord.
Principles are
the patterns that form things;
the Dào is
that by which all things are accomplished.
Hence it is said:
"The Dào
is what orders things."
Things have principles,
and cannot encroach upon each other;
things have principles
and cannot encroach upon each other,
thus principles serve as the regulators of things.
All things have different principles,
yet the Dào fully accords with the principles of all things,
so it cannot but transform;
cannot but transform,
thus it has no constant course.
Having no constant course,
therefore life and death draw from it,
all wisdom considers it,
and all affairs rise and fall by it.
Heaven attains it to be high,
earth attains it to store,
the Northern Dipper attains it to establish its majesty,
the sun and moon attain it to maintain their light,
the five constants attain it to secure their positions,
the constellations attain it to align their courses,
the four seasons attain it to govern their changing energies,
Xuānyuán attained it to rule over the four directions,
Chìsōng attained it to unite with heaven and earth,
and sages attain it to accomplish cultural achievements.
The Dào
is wise with Yáo and Shùn,
mad with Jiēyú,
perishes with Jié and Zhòu,
and prospers with Tāng and Wǔ.
Consider it near,
and it roams to the four extremes;
consider it far,
and it is always by our side;
consider it dark,
yet its light is brilliant;
consider it bright,
yet its substance is obscure.
It accomplishes the work of heaven and earth,
harmonizes and transforms like thunder,
and all things within the universe
rely on it for completion.
The true nature of the Dào
is unconstrained and formless,
soft and weak, adapting to the times,
corresponding with principles.
All things attain it to die,
attain it to live;
all affairs attain it to fail,
attain it to succeed.
The Way is likened to water:
a drowning person who drinks too much of it will die,
while a thirsty person who drinks just enough will live.
It is likened to swords and halberds:
a fool using them to vent anger brings about disaster,
while a sage employing them to punish tyranny achieves blessings.
Thus, through it, one may obtain death,
through it, life,
through it, failure,
through it, success.
People rarely see a live elephant,
but upon finding the bones of a dead one,
they refer to its picture to imagine it alive.
Hence, all that people conceive in their minds
is called "image."
Now, although the Way cannot be heard or seen,
the sage grasps its manifested effects
to infer its form.
Therefore, it is said:
"It is a form without form,
an image without substance."
As for principles,
they involve distinctions of square and round, short and long,
coarse and fine, hard and brittle.
Thus, only after principles are established can the Way be apprehended.
Hence, established principles encompass preservation and destruction,
death and life,
flourishing and decline.
Things that alternate between existence and extinction,
sudden death and sudden life,
initially flourishing and later declining
cannot be called constant.
Only that which is born with the splitting of heaven and earth,
and remains undying and undecaying even when heaven and earth dissipate, is called "constant."
And the constant
undergoes no change,
has no fixed principle.
Having no fixed principle,
it is not confined to a constant location;
therefore, it cannot be described.
The sage observes its profound emptiness,
applies its universal movement,
and forcibly names it
"the Way,"
so that it can be discussed.
Hence, it is said:
"The Way that can be spoken of
is not the constant Way."
Humans begin with life and end with death.
The beginning is called emergence,
the end is called entrance.
Thus, it is said:
"Emerging into life, entering into death."
The human body has three hundred sixty joints,
four limbs and nine orifices,
which are its major components.
The four limbs and nine orifices total thirteen,
and the movements and stillness of these thirteen
are all associated with life.
Association implies following,
so it is said:
"The followers of life are thirteen in number."
Upon death,
these thirteen components all return
and become associated with death,
so the followers of death also number thirteen.
Therefore, it is said:
"The followers of life are thirteen,
the followers of death are thirteen."
In general, as people live and thrive,
the living are inherently active;
exhaustion of activity leads to depletion.
If activity does not cease,
this means depletion without end.
Depletion without end
leads to the exhaustion of life;
exhaustion of life is called death.
Thus, these thirteen components
all become grounds for dying.
Hence, it is said:
"In people's lives,
they live and are active;
their activity all leads to the grounds of death,
amounting to thirteen."
Therefore, the sage cherishes the vital spirit
and values dwelling in stillness.
Not cherishing the vital spirit
nor valuing dwelling in stillness
is far worse than the harm from rhinoceroses and tigers.
For rhinoceroses and tigers have their territories,
and their movements and rest have their times.
Avoid their territories
and observe their times,
and one can escape the harm of rhinoceroses and tigers.
People only know that rhinoceroses and tigers have claws and horns,
but do not realize that all things have claws and horns,
thus failing to avoid the harm from all things.
How can this be argued?
When seasonal rains fall and gather,
the open wilds are quiet,
yet if one trespasses mountains and rivers at dawn or dusk,
the claws and horns of wind and dew will harm them.
Serving superiors without loyalty,
lightly violating prohibitions and orders,
then the claws and horns of penal law will harm them.
Living in the community without restraint,
hatred and love without measure,
then the claws and horns of conflict and fighting will harm them.
Desires and cravings without limit,
movement and rest without moderation,
then the claws and horns of boils and abscesses will harm them.
Fond of using private cunning while abandoning the principles of the Way,
then the claws and horns of traps and snares will harm them.
Rhinoceroses and tigers have their territories,
and all harms have their origins.
Avoid their territories,
block their origins,
and one can escape all harms.
As for weapons and armor,
they are means to prepare against harm.
Those who value life,
even when entering the army,
have no mind of angry contention.
Having no mind of angry contention,
then there is no need for the preparations to rescue from harm.
This does not only refer to armies in the wild.
When the sage moves through the world,
having no mind to harm others,
then surely no one will harm them.
With no one to harm them,
they do not prepare against others.
Hence, it is said:
"Traveling on land, one does not encounter rhinoceroses or tigers."
Entering the mountains,
they do not rely on preparations to rescue from harm.
Therefore, it is said:
"Entering the army, one does not prepare armor and weapons."
Keeping far from all harms,
thus it is said:
"The rhinoceros has nowhere to thrust its horn,
the tiger has nowhere to plant its claws,
weapons have nowhere to admit their blades."
Making no preparations yet certainly suffering no harm—
this is the principle of heaven and earth.
Embodying the Way of heaven and earth,
therefore it is said:
"There is no ground of death."
Moving without encountering the ground of death
is called "excelling in nurturing life."
Those who love their children are tender towards them;
those who value life are tender towards their own bodies;
those who esteem achievement are tender towards their tasks.
A compassionate mother towards her young child
strives to bring him blessings;
striving to bring him blessings
means working to remove his misfortunes;
working to remove his misfortunes
leads to thorough deliberation;
thorough deliberation
results in grasping the principles of affairs;
grasping the principles of affairs
ensures certain success;
certain success
means acting without doubt;
acting without doubt is called courage.
The sage, in dealing with all matters,
is entirely like the compassionate mother thinking for her young child,
thus perceiving the path that must be taken.
Perceiving the path that must be taken brings clarity,
and in undertaking affairs, they also act without doubt;
acting without doubt is called courage.
Compassion gives rise to courage,
hence it is said:
"Through compassion,
one can be brave."
Duke Zhōu stated:
"If the freezing in winter is not solid,
then the growth of plants in spring and summer
will not be lush."
Heaven and earth cannot constantly indulge in extravagance and waste,
how much less can humans?
Thus, all things must have their rise and decline,
all affairs must have their relaxation and tension,
the state must have both civil and military aspects,
and governance must have rewards and punishments.
Therefore, when the wise man uses his wealth frugally,
his household becomes rich;
when the sage treasures his spirit,
his essence becomes abundant;
when the ruler values his soldiers in war,
the people become numerous,
and with numerous people,
the state becomes vast.
Hence it is raised as a saying:
"Through frugality,
one can achieve breadth."
All things that have form are easy to shape,
easy to cut.
How is this argued?
Having form
means having shortness and length,
having shortness and length
means having smallness and largeness,
having smallness and largeness,
means having squareness and roundness;
having squareness and roundness,
means having hardness and brittleness;
having hardness and brittleness,
means having lightness and heaviness;
having lightness and heaviness,
means having whiteness and blackness.
Shortness and length, smallness and largeness, squareness and roundness, hardness and brittleness,
lightness and heaviness, whiteness and blackness are called principles,
and once principles are established, things are easy to cut.
Thus, deliberating in the great hall before speaking
ensures establishment,
as those skilled in strategic discussion know.
Therefore, to achieve squareness or roundness
by following the compass and square,
the success of all tasks takes form.
And all things have their compass and square,
while deliberating speakers
calculate according to these standards.
The sage completely follows the compass and square of all things,
hence it is said:
"I dare not take the lead in the world."
Not daring to take the lead in the world,
then no affair is left unmanaged,
no achievement is left unaccomplished,
and one's deliberations are sure to surpass the age,
so even if one wishes not to hold high office,
how could it be possible?
Holding high office is called becoming the leader of accomplished affairs.
Therefore, it is said:
"Not daring to take the lead in the world,
thus one can become the leader of accomplished affairs."
Those compassionate towards their children
dare not cut off food and clothing,
those compassionate towards themselves
dare not deviate from laws and measures,
those compassionate towards squareness and roundness
dare not abandon the compass and square.
Thus, when facing troops,
showing compassion to officers and soldiers
leads to victory over the enemy,
and compassion towards equipment
makes the city walls solid.
Hence it is said:
"Through compassion,
in battle one wins,
in defense one holds firm."
Those who can fully preserve themselves
and completely follow the principles of all things
are bound to possess innate nature.
Innate nature
gives rise to the mind,
so the Way of the world is fully expressed in this life.
If one guards it with compassion,
affairs are sure to be perfectly secure
and actions invariably appropriate,
then it is called a treasure.
Therefore, it is said:
"I have three treasures,
which I hold and cherish."
What the text calls the "Great Dào"
is the upright Dào.
What is called appearing "lavish"
is the crooked Dào.
What is referred to as a "broad path"
is elegance and beauty.
Elegance and beauty
are aspects of the crooked Dào.
"The court is very clean"
means litigation is frequent.
Frequent litigation
leads to fields lying waste,
fields lying waste
causes granaries to empty,
granaries emptying
results in state poverty,
state poverty
and the people's customs become decadent and extravagant,
decadent and extravagant customs
cut off the livelihood of food and clothing,
the livelihood being cut off
forces the people to engage in ornamentation, cunning, and deceit,
ornamentation, cunning, and deceit
lead to knowledge of flowery patterns,
knowing flowery patterns is called "wearing ornate colors."
With frequent litigation,
empty granaries,
and making extravagance a custom,
the harm to the state
is like piercing it with a sharp sword.
Hence it is said:
"Gird with a sharp sword."
All those who adorn themselves with cunning and artifice,
to the point of harming the state,
must have wealthy private households;
with wealthy private households,
it is said:
"Resources and goods are in excess."
When a state has such cases,
the ignorant people cannot help but imitate them by some means,
imitating them
gives rise to petty thieves.
From this perspective,
when great villains arise, petty thieves follow,
when great villains lead, petty thieves harmonize.
The yú,
being the chief of the five notes,
so when the yú leads, bells and sè all follow,
when the yú plays, all instruments harmonize.
Now, when great villains arise, the vulgar people lead,
when the vulgar people lead, petty thieves inevitably harmonize.
Therefore, "those who wear ornate colors,
gird with sharp swords,
satiate themselves with food and drink,
and have abundant resources and goods,
these are called the yú of thieves."
Be they foolish or wise,
all people have their inclinations and aversions.
In tranquility and peace,
none are unaware of the origins of fortune and misfortune.
But when swayed by likes and dislikes,
tempted by extravagant things,
they then become disordered and chaotic.
The reason for this
is being drawn by external things,
and confused by playthings and desires.
Tranquility involves the principle of inclinations and aversions,
peace understands the calculation of fortune and misfortune.
But now, playthings alter them,
external things draw them.
Drawn away, they go,
hence it is called "being led astray."
The ultimate sage is not so:
once he establishes his inclinations and aversions,
even upon seeing desirable things,
he cannot be drawn,
not being drawn is called "not being led astray."
When one is unified in their emotions,
even if there are categories of desirable things,
the spirit remains unmoved.
The state of the spirit not being moved is called "not being beguiled."
For descendants,
embodying this principle to guard the ancestral temple,
the ancestral temple not perishing
is called "the sacrifices not ceasing."
The body regards accumulating essence as its virtue,
the family regards wealth as its virtue,
the village, state, and the world all regard the people as their virtue.
Now, in governing the self,
external things cannot disturb one's spirit,
hence it is said:
"Cultivate it in the self,
and its virtue becomes genuine."
Genuineness means
being steadfast in caution.
In governing the family,
useless things cannot sway its plans,
then resources become abundant,
hence it is said:
"Cultivate it in the family,
and its virtue becomes abundant."
Those who govern the village
practice this discipline,
then the families with abundance increase in number,
hence it is said:
"Cultivate it in the village,
and its virtue becomes enduring."
Those who govern the state
practice this discipline,
then the villages with virtue increase in number,
hence it is said:
"Cultivate it in the state,
and its virtue becomes plentiful."
Those who rule the world
practice this discipline,
then the lives of the people all receive its benefits,
hence it is said:
"Cultivate it in the world,
and its virtue becomes universal."
Those who cultivate the self
use this to distinguish the noble from the petty;
those who govern villages, states, or the world,
each use this criterion
to observe gains and losses appropriately,
then not one in ten thousand will be mistaken.
Hence it is said:
"Observe the self through the self,
the family through the family,
the village through the village,
the state through the state,
the world through the world.
How do I know the world is so?
Through this."
When the world has the Way,
there are no urgent calamities,
then it is called tranquil,
and fast relays are not used.
Hence it is said:
"Horses are turned back to carry manure."
When the world lacks the Way,
attacks and conflicts do not cease,
holding out against each other for years without end,
armor breeds lice,
swallows and sparrows nest in the tents,
yet the soldiers do not return.
Hence it is said:
"Warhorses are born in the suburbs."
A man from Dí presented the pelts of a luxuriant fox
and a dark leopard to Duke Wén of Jìn.
Duke Wén received the guest's pelts and sighed, saying:
"These, because of the beauty of their fur, brought guilt upon themselves."
Now, those who govern states
incur guilt because of their titles and names—
such was King Xú Yǎn.
Because of their cities and lands—
such were Yú and Guó.
Hence it is said:
"No guilt is greater than that which invites desire."
Zhì Bó annexed Fàn and Zhōngháng
and attacked Zhào incessantly,
Hán and Wèi turned against him,
his army was defeated at Jìnyáng,
he died east of Gāoliáng,
and ultimately his territory was divided,
his head lacquered to make a urinal.
Hence it is said:
"No disaster is greater than not knowing contentment."
The lord of Yú desired the steeds of Qūchǎn
and the jade of Chuíjí,
and did not heed Gōng Zhīqí's advice,
hence his state perished and he died.
Hence it is said:
"No fault is more grievous than the desire to gain."
The state regards preservation as its constant norm,
then hegemony and kingship are possible;
the self regards life as its constant norm,
then wealth and honor are possible.
Not harming oneself with desires,
then the state does not perish,
and the self does not die.
Hence it is said:
"Knowing contentment is true contentment."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ, after his victory,
hunted at Héyōng,
returned and rewarded Sūn Shū'áo.
Sūn Shū'áo requested land in Hànjiān,
a place of sand and stones.
According to the laws of the state of Chǔ,
the lands of ministers were reclaimed after two generations,
yet only Sūn Shū'áo's land remained.
This was because his land was not reclaimed by the state,
being barren,
hence for nine generations his sacrifices did not cease.
Hence it is said:
"He who establishes well cannot be uprooted,
he who embraces well cannot be separated,
his descendants
generation after generation without cease in their sacrifices."
This refers to Sūn Shū'áo.
Control residing in oneself is called weightiness,
not departing from one's position is called stillness.
Weightiness
then can command the light,
stillness
then can command the restless.
Hence it is said:
"Weightiness is the root of lightness,
stillness is the master of restlessness."
Hence it is said:
"The nobleman travels all day,
without leaving his heavy baggage."
The state is
the ruler's heavy baggage.
Lord Fù bequeathed his state while alive,
this was leaving his heavy baggage;
hence, even with the pleasures of Dài and Yúnzhōng,
he had already transcendentally lost Zhào.
Lord Fù,
a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
made himself light in the world.
Lacking authority is called lightness,
departing from one's position is called restlessness,
thus he lived imprisoned and died.
Hence it is said:
"Lightness loses subjects,
restlessness loses the ruler."
This refers to Lord Fù.
Weighty authority
is the ruler's deep pool.
The ruler,
with authority weightier than that of his ministers,
if lost, cannot be regained.
Duke Jiǎn lost it to Tián Chéng,
the Duke of Jìn lost it to the six ministers,
and their states perished and they died.
Hence it is said:
"Fish cannot leave the deep pool."
Rewards and punishments
are the sharp tools of the state.
In the ruler's hands,
they control the ministers;
in the ministers' hands,
they overcome the ruler.
If the ruler displays rewards,
ministers reduce them to create virtue;
if the ruler displays punishments,
ministers augment them to create authority.
When the ruler displays rewards,
ministers use that authority;
when the ruler displays punishments,
ministers wield that power.
Hence it is said:
"The sharp tools of the state
cannot be shown to others."
The King of Yuè entered into servitude in Wú,
and observed their campaign against Qí to weaken Wú.
After Wú's army had defeated the Qí people at Àilíng,
they expanded along the Jiāng and Jì rivers,
and showed their strength at Huángchí,
thus becoming vulnerable to control at Wǔhú Lake.
Hence it is said:
"To contract something,
one must surely expand it first;
to weaken something,
one must surely strengthen it first."
When Duke Xiàn of Jìn planned to attack Yú,
he presented them with jade discs and horses;
when Zhì Bó planned to attack Qiúyóu,
he presented them with large chariots.
Hence it is said:
"To take something,
one must surely give it first."
To initiate affairs without visible form,
yet achieve great merit under heaven,
this is called subtle clarity.
To remain in a position of smallness and weakness while humbling oneself,
is how weakness overcomes strength.
For things with physical form,
the large must arise from the small;
for enduring things,
abundance must arise from scarcity.
Hence it is said:
"Under heaven, difficult matters must be handled where they are easy;
great matters must be handled where they are small."
Therefore, those who wish to control things must do so when they are minute.
Hence it is said:
"Plan for the difficult while it is still easy;
do the great while it is still small."
A thousand-zhàng dike can collapse from ant holes;
a hundred-chǐ house can burn from cracks in the chimney.
Hence it is said:
Bái Guī, in maintaining dikes, plugs their holes;
the careful old man, in fire prevention, seals chimney cracks.
Therefore Bái Guī faces no flood disasters,
and the old man has no fire calamities.
These are examples of being cautious with the easy
to avoid the difficult,
and attentive to the small
to keep away the great.
When Biǎn Què visited Duke Huán of Cài,
he stood for a while.
Biǎn Què said:
"You have an illness in the skin's texture,
if not treated, I fear it will deepen."
Duke Huán replied:
"I have none."
After Biǎn Què left,
Duke Huán said:
"Doctors enjoy treating the healthy
to claim merit."
After ten days,
Biǎn Què visited again and said:
"Your illness has reached the muscles,
if not treated, it will worsen."
Duke Huán did not respond.
Biǎn Què left.
Duke Huán was again displeased.
After another ten days,
Biǎn Què visited again and said:
"Your illness has reached the stomach and intestines,
if not treated, it will worsen further."
Duke Huán again did not respond.
Biǎn Què left.
Duke Huán was again displeased.
After another ten days,
Biǎn Què saw Duke Huán from a distance and turned to flee,
so Duke Huán sent someone to ask why.
Biǎn Què said:
"When the illness was in the skin,
hot compresses could reach it;
when in the muscles,
acupuncture and stone needles could reach it;
when in the stomach and intestines,
herbal decoctions could reach it;
but when in the bone marrow,
it becomes the domain of the Director of Fate,
and nothing can be done.
Now it is in the bone marrow,
therefore I make no more requests."
After five days,
Duke Huán experienced body pain,
sent someone to find Biǎn Què,
but he had already fled to Qín.
Duke Huán then died.
Thus, when a good doctor treats illness,
he attacks it while in the skin,
this exemplifies striving when matters are small.
Now, the fortune and misfortune of affairs
also have their stage like the skin's texture,
therefore the sage acts early.
Previously, when Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn was in exile,
he passed through Zhèng,
but the ruler of Zhèng showed him no courtesy.
Shū Zhān advised:
"This is a worthy prince,
if you treat him generously,
you can accumulate virtue."
The ruler of Zhèng did not listen.
Shū Zhān advised again:
"If not treating him generously,
better to kill him,
to avoid future troubles."
The ruler of Zhèng again did not listen.
When the prince returned to Jìn,
he raised troops to attack Zhèng,
greatly defeated them,
and captured eight cities.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn used the jade from Chuíjí
to borrow passage through Yú to attack Guó,
Minister Gōng Zhī Qí advised:
"This cannot be.
When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
Yú and Guó rescue each other,
not out of mutual virtue.
If today Jìn destroys Guó,
tomorrow Yú will surely follow in destruction."
The ruler of Yú did not listen,
accepted the jade and granted passage.
After Jìn had taken Guó,
on returning,
they turned and destroyed Yú.
These two ministers
both strove at the skin-texture stage,
but the two rulers did not employ them.
Thus, Shū Zhān and Gōng Zhī Qí
were also the Biǎn Què of Yú and Zhèng,
yet the two rulers did not listen,
so Zhèng was defeated,
and Yú perished.
Hence it is said:
"What is stable is easy to maintain;
what has not yet shown signs is easy to plan for."
Previously, when Zhòu had ivory chopsticks made,
Jīzǐ lamented,
thinking
ivory chopsticks would not be used with earthenware bowls,
but surely with rhino horn and jade cups;
ivory chopsticks and jade cups
would not be used for bean soup,
but for yak, elephant, and leopard fetus;
yak, elephant, and leopard fetus
would not be eaten while wearing coarse clothing
in a thatched hut,
but rather in nine layers of brocade,
in vast halls and high towers.
I fear the end,
so I lament the beginning."
After five years,
Zhòu built a forest of meat,
set up roasting pillars,
mounted a hill of distillers' grains,
and overlooked a lake of wine,
and Zhòu thus perished.
Therefore, Jīzǐ, seeing ivory chopsticks,
knew the disaster for all under heaven.
Hence it is said:
"To see the small is called clarity."
Gōu Jiàn entered servitude in Wú,
personally bearing shield and spear
to serve as the King of Wú's groom,
thus he could kill Fūchāi at Gūsū.
King Wén was insulted at the Yǒulǐ gate,
yet his countenance did not change,
and King Wǔ captured Zhòu at Mùyě.
Hence it is said:
"To maintain softness is called strength."
When the King of Yuè achieved hegemony,
he did not resent officials;
when King Wǔ ruled the kingdom,
he did not resent slander.
Hence it is said:
"The sage's freedom from affliction
lies in his not considering things afflictions,
therefore he has no afflictions."
A rustic man of Sòng obtained an uncut jade
and presented it to Zǐ Hǎn,
but Zǐ Hǎn declined to accept it.
The rustic said:
"This is a treasure,
fit to be a vessel for a noble man,
unsuitable for use by a common person."
Zǐ Hǎn replied:
"You consider the jade a treasure,
but I consider my refusal to accept your jade a treasure."
Thus the rustic desired the jade,
while Zǐ Hǎn did not desire it.
Hence it is said:
"Desire what is not desired,
and do not value goods hard to obtain."
Wáng Shòu carried books on his back as he traveled,
and met Xú Féng on the road of Zhōu.
Féng said:
"Affairs are actions,
actions arise from timeliness,
and the wise have no constant affairs.
Books are words,
words arise from knowledge,
and the knowledgeable do not store books.
Why then do you alone carry them on your back?"
Thereupon Wáng Shòu burned his books and danced.
Thus the wise do not teach through speech,
and the intelligent do not store books in boxes.
This is what the world considers mistaken,
yet Wáng Shòu returned to it,
which is learning what is not learned.
Hence it is said:
"Learn what is not learned,
and return to what the multitude passes by."
