All things have their constant forms,
so one should ride along and guide them accordingly.
By following the forms of things,
one remains tranquil to establish virtue,
and acts to follow the Dào.
A man of Sòng carved a mulberry leaf from ivory for his lord,
taking three years to complete it.
The thickness and thinness of stem and veins,
the fine tips and lush gloss,
made it indistinguishable
when mixed among real mulberry leaves.
This man thus earned an official salary in Sòng for his skill.
Lièzǐ heard of this and said:
"If Heaven and Earth took three years to produce a single leaf,
then things with leaves would be few indeed."
Thus, not relying on Heaven and Earth's resources
but burdening a single person's body,
not following the principles of the Dào
but studying a single person's wisdom—
these are all like the one-leaf endeavor.
Hence, crops planted in winter
could not be abundant even for Hòu Jì;
and lush grains in a bumper year
could not be ruined even by slaves.
Relying on one person's strength,
even Hòu Jì would be insufficient;
following nature,
even slaves would have surplus.
Therefore it is said:
"Rely on the natural course of all things
and dare not interfere."
The orifices are
the windows and doors of the spirit.
If ears and eyes are exhausted by sounds and sights,
and the essence-spirit is exhausted by external appearances,
then within there is no master.
When within there is no master,
then fortune and misfortune, though large as hills,
cannot be perceived.
Hence it is said:
"Without going out the door,
one can know the world;
without peeping through the window,
one can know the Way of Heaven."
This means the spirit does not leave its abode.
Lord Xiāng of Zhào learned charioteering from Wángzǐ Yúqī,
and soon raced against Yúqī,
changing horses three times yet falling behind three times.
Lord Xiāng said:
"Have you not taught me all your charioteering techniques?"
Yúqī replied:
"The techniques are exhausted;
it is their application that is at fault.
What is valued in charioteering
is that the horse's body is comfortable with the chariot,
and the driver's mind is harmonized with the horse;
only then can one advance swiftly and cover long distances.
Now when behind, you wish to catch up with me,
and when ahead, you fear I will catch up with you.
Whether leading or trailing in a long-distance race,
one is either ahead or behind;
but with your mind focused entirely on me,
how can you harmonize with the horse?
This is why you fall behind."
Báigōng Shèng was plotting rebellion;
after court, leaning on his staff,
he pierced his chin with the sharp tip,
blood flowing to the ground unnoticed.
A man of Zhèng heard of this and said:
"If he can forget his chin,
what would he not forget?"
Hence it is said:
"The farther one goes out,
the less wisdom one has."
This means when wisdom focuses on distant matters,
what is near is neglected.
Therefore, the sage has no constant actions.
Being able to simultaneously know,
he is said:
"To know without going."
Being able to simultaneously see,
he is said:
"To understand without seeing."
Acting according to the time,
achieving merit by relying on resources,
utilizing the capabilities of all things
to gain benefits from them—
hence it is said:
"To accomplish without acting."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had been on the throne for three years
without issuing decrees
or engaging in governance.
The Right Marshal, while attending him,
hinted to the king:
"A bird has perched on a southern hill,
for three years not stretching its wings,
not flying nor calling,
silent without a sound—
what name does this bear?"
The king replied:
"Not stretching wings for three years
is to grow feathers and wings;
not flying nor calling
is to observe the people's ways.
Though it does not fly now,
once it flies, it will soar to the sky;
though it does not call now,
once it calls, it will startle everyone.
Set your mind at ease,
for I understand."
After half a year,
he began to personally administer state affairs.
He abolished ten policies,
initiated nine reforms,
executed five senior ministers,
and promoted six reclusive scholars,
bringing great order to the state.
He raised armies to punish Qí,
defeating them at Xúzhōu;
triumphed over Jìn at Héyōng;
assembled the feudal lords in Sòng,
and thus achieved hegemony over the world.
King Zhuāng did not let small matters harm great goodness,
thus he gained great fame;
he did not reveal himself early,
thus he achieved great merit.
Hence it is said:
"The great vessel is late to complete;
the great sound is rarely heard."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ intended to attack Yuè,
when Dù Zǐ admonished him:
"Why does Your Majesty wish to attack Yuè?"
The king replied:
"Because their governance is chaotic and their military weak."
Dù Zǐ said:
"Your servant is foolish but worries about
wisdom. It is like the eyes,
which can see a hundred paces away
but cannot see their own eyelashes.
Your Majesty's forces were defeated by Qín and Jìn,
losing hundreds of lǐ of territory,
this shows the weakness of your military.
Zhuāng Qiāo Jué commits robbery within our borders
yet officials cannot stop him,
this shows the chaos in your governance.
Your weakness and chaos
are no less than Yuè's,
yet you wish to attack Yuè,
this is wisdom being like the eyes."
The king then desisted.
Thus the difficulty of knowledge
lies not in seeing others,
but in seeing oneself.
Hence it is said:
"To see oneself is called clarity."
Zǐ Xià visited Zēng Zǐ.
Zēng Zǐ asked:
"Why have you grown plump?"
Zǐ Xià replied:
"I have won a battle,
hence I am plump."
Zēng Zǐ asked:
"What do you mean?"
Zǐ Xià said:
"When I enter and contemplate the righteousness of former kings
I honor it,
but when I go out and see the pleasures of wealth and honor
I also honor them.
These two fought within my breast,
uncertain which would win,
so I grew thin.
Now the righteousness of former kings has prevailed,
hence I am plump."
Thus the difficulty of aspiration
lies not in overcoming others,
but in overcoming oneself.
Hence it is said:
"To overcome oneself is called strength."
Zhōu possessed a jade tablet,
King Zhòu ordered Jiāo Gé to demand it,
but King Wén refused;
when Fèi Zhòng came to request it,
he gave it to him.
This was because Jiāo Gé was virtuous
while Fèi Zhòng was unprincipled.
Zhōu disliked virtuous men achieving their aims,
so they gave it to Fèi Zhòng.
When King Wén elevated Tài Gōng by the Wèi river,
it was to honor him;
while providing Fèi Zhòng with the jade tablet
was to make use of him.
Hence it is said:
"Not honoring one's teacher,
not valuing one's resources,
though seemingly wise is greatly deluded,
this is called essential subtlety."
When Tāng was about to attack Jié,
he feared the world would call him greedy,
so he offered the empire to Wù Guāng.
But fearing Wù Guāng would accept it,
he sent someone to persuade Wù Guāng saying:
"Tāng killed his ruler and wishes to pass his bad reputation to you,
hence he offers you the empire."
Wù Guāng consequently threw himself into the river.
King Wǔ of Qín ordered Gān Mào to choose between being chamberlain
or minister of works.
Mèng Mǎo said:
"You'd better be chamberlain.
Your excellence lies in
diplomacy.
Even as chamberlain,
the king will still employ you for diplomacy.
You would wear the chamberlain's seal while performing ministerial duties,
thus holding dual offices."
Zǐ Yǔ introduced Confucius to the prime minister of Sòng.
After Confucius left,
Zǐ Yǔ entered
and inquired about the guest.
The prime minister said:
"Having met Confucius,
I now see you as insignificant as a flea or louse.
I shall now introduce him to the ruler."
Zǐ Yǔ feared Confucius would gain the ruler's favor,
so he told the prime minister:
"If the ruler meets Confucius,
he will also see you as a flea or louse."
The prime minister consequently did not introduce him.
King Huì of Wèi held the Jiùlǐ alliance,
intending to restore the Son of Heaven.
Péng Xǐ told the ruler of Zhèng:
"Do not listen, my lord.
Large states detest having a Son of Heaven,
while small states benefit from it.
If you and the large states refuse,
how can Wèi establish him with only small states?"
When the Jìn people attacked Xíng,
Duke Huán of Qí planned to rescue them.
Bào Shū said:
"Too early.
If Xíng doesn't perish,
Jìn won't be exhausted;
if Jìn isn't exhausted,
Qí won't gain weight.
Moreover, the merit of supporting the endangered
is not as great as the virtue of restoring the perished.
You'd better delay rescue to exhaust Jìn,
which truly benefits Qí.
Wait until Xíng falls then restore it,
your reputation will be truly glorious."
Duke Huán consequently did not rescue them.
When Wǔ Zǐ Xū fled,
the border guard caught him.
Zǐ Xū said:
"The reason they seek me
is because I possess precious pearls.
Now I have lost them.
I will say:
You took and swallowed them."
The guard consequently released him.
When Qìng Fēng caused turmoil in Qí and wanted to flee to Yuè,
his clansman said:
"Jìn is nearer,
why not go to Jìn?"
Qìng Fēng replied:
"Yuè is distant,
advantageous for avoiding trouble."
The clansman said:
"If you change this heart of yours,
dwelling in Jìn would suffice;
if you don't change this heart,
even distant Yuè,
could it bring you peace?"
When Zhì Bó demanded territory from Wèi Xuān Zǐ,
Wèi Xuān Zǐ refused.
Rén Zhāng asked:
"Why refuse?"
Xuān Zǐ said:
"He requested land without reason,
so I refused."
Rén Zhāng said:
"Demanding land without cause
will surely frighten neighboring states.
His heavy desires know no satiety,
the whole world will fear him.
If you give him land,
Zhì Bó will grow arrogant and underestimate enemies,
while neighbors will fear him and draw closer together.
Using united forces against an underestimating state,
then Zhì Bó's life won't be long.
The Zhōu Shū says:
'If you wish to defeat them,
you must first assist them;
if you wish to take from them,
you must first give to them.'
You'd better give to make Zhì Bō arrogant.
Moreover, why abandon having the world scheme against Zhì,
and alone make our state Zhì's target?"
Xuān Zǐ said:
"Good."
He then gave him a city of ten thousand households.
Zhì Bó was greatly pleased,
then demanded land from Zhào,
He did not give it;
consequently, they besieged Jìnyáng.
Hán and Wèi rebelled from outside,
while the Zhào clan responded from within,
and the Zhì clan was thereby destroyed.
Duke Kāng of Qín built a tower for three years.
The Chǔ people raised an army,
intending to attack Qí with their troops.
Rén Wàng said:
"Famine invites troops,
disease invites troops,
toil invites troops,
chaos invites troops.
You have built a tower for three years,
and now the Chǔ people are raising an army to attack Qí.
I fear that their attack on Qí is a pretense,
while the real intention is to surprise Qín.
It would be better to prepare for it."
They garrisoned the eastern border,
and the Chǔ people halted their advance.
Qí attacked Sòng,
and Sòng sent Zāng Sūnzǐ south to seek help from Chǔ.
Chǔ was greatly pleased,
promised to rescue them,
and was very encouraging.
Zāng Sūnzǐ returned worried.
His charioteer said:
"You sought help and obtained it,
yet now you wear a worried expression;
why is that?"
Zāng Sūnzǐ said:
"Sòng is small and Qí is large.
To rescue small Sòng and earn the enmity of large Qí
is what makes one worry;
yet the King of Chǔ is pleased,
surely to strengthen our resolve.
If we stand firm and Qí becomes exhausted,
that is to Chǔ's benefit."
Zāng Sūnzǐ then returned.
The Qí people captured five cities from Sòng,
yet Chǔ's rescue never arrived.
Marquis Wén of Wèi requested passage from Zhào
to attack Zhōngshān,
and Marquis Sù of Zhào was about to refuse.
Zhào Kè said:
"You are mistaken.
If Wèi attacks Zhōngshān and cannot take it,
then Wèi will surely be weakened.
Weakened, Wèi becomes light,
and if Wèi is light, then Zhào becomes heavy.
If Wèi captures Zhōngshān,
it certainly cannot cross Zhào to hold Zhōngshān.
Thus, the one using military force
is Wèi;
yet the one gaining territory
is Zhào.
You must grant it.
If you grant it with great enthusiasm,
they will realize you stand to benefit,
and will surely halt the campaign.
You would do better to grant them passage,
showing it is out of necessity."
Chīyí Zǐpí served Tián Chéngzǐ.
When Tián Chéngzǐ left Qí,
fleeing to Yān,
Chīyí Zǐpí carried the credentials and followed.
When they reached Wàngyì,
Zǐpí said:
"Have you not heard of the marsh snakes?
When the marsh dried up,
the snakes prepared to move.
A small snake said to a large snake:
'If you go and I follow you,
people will think we are just passing snakes,
and someone will surely kill you.
It would be better to carry me in your mouth as we go,
and people will regard us as divine lords.'
So they carried each other
across the public road.
Everyone avoided them,
saying:
'They are divine lords.'
Now you are handsome and I am ugly.
If you present me as your distinguished guest,
you appear as a lord of a thousand chariots;
if as your envoy,
as a minister of ten thousand chariots.
You would do better to have me as your retainer."
Tián Chéngzǐ then carried the credentials and followed him.
When they reached an inn,
the innkeeper treated them with great respect
and offered them wine and meat.
A man from Wēn went to Zhōu,
but Zhōu did not admit visitors.
He was asked:
"Are you a visitor?"
He replied:
"I am a host."
When asked about his alley neighbors and he did not know them,
the officials imprisoned him.
The ruler sent someone to ask him:
"You are not from Zhōu,
yet you claim not to be a visitor;
why is that?"
He replied:
"In my youth, I recited the Shī, which says:
'Under the vast heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's;
within the borders of the land,
there is no one who is not the king's subject.'
Now you, my lord,
are the Son of Heaven,
so I am a subject of the Son of Heaven.
How can one be a subject
and also be a visitor?
Therefore, I said:
I am a host."
The ruler had him released.
King Xuān of Hán said to Jiū Liú:
"I wish to employ both Gōng Zhòng and Gōng Shū;
is that feasible?"
He replied:
"It is not.
Jìn employed six ministers
and the state was divided;
Duke Jiǎn employed both Tián Chéng and Kǎn Zhǐ
and Duke Jiǎn was killed;
Wèi employed both Xī Shǒu and Zhāng Yí,
and lost the land west of the Yellow River.
If you now employ both,
the more powerful will build their factions,
the less powerful will borrow external influence.
If ministers build internal factions to domineer the ruler,
or form external alliances to divide the land,
then your state will be in danger."
Shào Jī Mèi got drunk, fell asleep, and lost his fur coat.
The ruler of Sòng asked:
"Is drunkenness enough to lose a fur coat?"
He replied:
"Jié lost the empire through drunkenness,
and the 'Kāng Gào' says
'Do not indulge in wine'—
indulging means constant drinking.
Constant drinking
causes the Son of Heaven to lose the empire,
and a commoner to lose his life."
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng accompanied Duke Huán
to attack Gūzhú,
setting out in spring and returning in winter,
but they lost their way.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The wisdom of an old horse can be used."
So they let an old horse lead and followed it,
and thus found the way.
Traveling in the mountains without water,
Xí Péng said:
"Ants dwell on the sunny side of the mountain in winter,
and on the shady side in summer.
Where there is an inch of ant soil, water is eight feet below."
So they dug the ground,
and thus found water.
With the sagacity of Guǎn Zhòng
and the wisdom of Xí Péng,
when they encountered what they did not know,
they did not hesitate to learn from an old horse and ants.
Yet people today, with their foolish minds,
do not learn from the wisdom of sages;
is that not a mistake?
Someone presented an elixir of immortality to the King of Chǔ,
and the court usher carried it in.
A palace guard asked:
"Is this edible?"
He said:
"Yes."
So he snatched it and ate it.
The king was furious,
and sent someone to kill the palace guard.
A palace guard had someone persuade the king, saying:
"I inquired of the herald,
who said, 'It is edible,'
so I ate it.
Thus, I am without fault,
and the blame lies with the herald.
Moreover, the visitor presented an elixir of immortality,
yet if you kill me after I consumed it,
it becomes a deadly poison instead,
proving that the visitor deceived you.
To execute an innocent subject
and thereby expose someone's deceit against you—
it would be better to release me."
The king then refrained from killing him.
Tián Sì deceived the lord of Zōu,
who then intended to have him killed.
Tián Sì, in fear,
informed Huìzǐ.
Huìzǐ went to see the lord of Zōu and said:
"If someone, upon seeing you,
winks with one eye,
what would you do?"
The lord replied:
"I would certainly have him killed."
Huìzǐ said:
"A blind man,
who winks with both eyes,
why do you not kill him?"
The lord said:
"He cannot help but wink."
Huìzǐ then said:
"Tián Sì has been disrespectful to the Marquis of Qí in the east,
and deceived the King of Jīng in the south;
when it comes to deceiving others,
Tián Sì is like a blind man—
why do you hold a grudge against him?"
The lord of Zōu then did not kill him.
Duke Mù of Lǔ sent his sons,
some to serve in Jìn,
others in Jīng.
Lí Chú said:
"To borrow help from Yuè to save a drowning child—
even if the Yuè people are good swimmers,
the child will surely not survive.
If a fire breaks out and you fetch water from the sea,
though the sea has plenty of water,
the fire will certainly not be extinguished,
for distant water cannot quench a nearby fire.
Now, though Jìn and Jīng are strong,
Qí is close by,
so how can Lǔ's troubles be relieved by them?"
Yán Suì was not on good terms with the ruler of Zhōu,
who worried about it.
Féng Jǔ said:
"Yán Suì is a minister,
and Hán Guī is esteemed by the ruler.
It would be better to assassinate Hán Guī,
then the ruler will surely blame the Yán family."
Zhāng Qiǎn was the chancellor of Hán
and fell gravely ill.
Gōngchéng Wúzhèng, carrying thirty pieces of gold,
went to inquire about his illness.
A day later,
the ruler asked Zhāng Qiǎn:
"If you were to die,
whom should I appoint to replace you?"
He replied:
"Wúzhèng values the law and fears his superiors.
Nevertheless,
he is not as popular among the people as the prince Shíwǒ."
After Zhāng Qiǎn died,
the ruler appointed Gōngchéng Wúzhèng as chancellor.
Yuè Yáng, a general of Wèi, attacked Zhōngshān,
while his son was in Zhōngshān.
The lord of Zhōngshān had his son boiled
and sent the broth to him.
Yuè Yáng sat under his tent and drank it,
finishing a full cup.
Marquis Wén said to Dǔshī Zàn:
"Yuè Yáng, for my sake, ate the flesh of his own son."
The reply was:
"If he could eat his own son,
then whose flesh would he not eat?"
When Yuè Yáng returned from Zhōngshān,
Marquis Wén rewarded his achievement but doubted his heart.
Mèngsūn captured a fawn while hunting,
and had Qín Xībā carry it back.
The mother deer followed, crying.
Qín Xībā, unable to bear it, gave the fawn back to her.
When Mèngsūn returned,
he asked for the fawn.
The reply was:
"I could not bear to and returned it to its mother."
Mèngsūn was furious,
and banished him.
Three months later,
he recalled him to be his son's tutor.
His carriage driver asked:
"Previously, you punished him,
yet now you summon him to be your son's tutor;
why is that?"
Mèngsūn said:
"He could not bear to harm a fawn,
how could he bear to harm my son?"
Hence it is said:
"Cunning deceit is inferior to simple honesty."
Yuè Yáng was doubted for his achievement,
while Qín Xībā was trusted more for his fault.
Zēng Cóngzǐ
was skilled at appraising swords.
The ruler of Wèi held a grudge against the King of Wú.
Zēng Cóngzǐ said:
"The King of Wú loves swords,
and I am a sword appraiser.
I request to appraise a sword for the King of Wú;
when I draw it to show him,
I will take the opportunity to assassinate him for you."
The ruler of Wèi said:
"Your intention to do this
is not out of righteousness,
but for profit.
Wú is strong and wealthy,
while Wèi is weak and poor.
If you must go,
I fear you will be used by the King of Wú against me."
So he banished him.
When Zhòu had ivory chopsticks made, Jīzǐ lamented,
believing that with ivory chopmakers
he would certainly not use earthenware for soup,
but must have cups of rhinoceros horn and jade;
with jade cups and ivory chopsticks
he would not be content with beans and野菜,
but must have the meat of yak, elephant, and leopard fetus;
and with such delicacies
he would not wear short coarse clothes
and live in a thatched hut,
but must have multiple layers of embroidered robes
and high towers with spacious halls.
Pursuing such extravagance,
the whole world would not suffice him.
A sage sees the subtle to know the sprouting,
sees the beginning to know the end.
Thus, upon seeing the ivory chopsticks, he lamented,
knowing the world would not be enough.
After the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, had defeated Yīn,
he planned to attack Shānggài.
Xīn Gōngjiǎ said:
"The great are hard to attack,
the small are easy to subdue.
It is better to subdue the many small to threaten the great."
So they attacked the Jiǔyí tribes, and Shānggài submitted.
Zhòu indulged in all-night drinking,
reveling to the point of losing track of days.
He asked his attendants,
but none knew.
Then he sent someone to ask Jīzǐ.
Jīzǐ said to his followers:
"To be the ruler of the world
and have the entire state lose track of days—
the world must be in peril.
If the whole state does not know
and I alone know,
I must be in danger."
So he claimed drunkenness and ignorance.
A man from Lǔ was skilled at weaving sandals,
his wife at weaving white silk,
and they wished to move to Yuè.
Someone told him:
"You will surely become impoverished."
The man from Lǔ asked:
"Why is that?"
It was said:
"Shoes are made for wearing,
yet the Yuè people go barefoot;
fine silk is for making hats,
yet the Yuè people wear their hair loose.
With your particular skills,
traveling to a country that has no use for them,
hoping to avoid poverty,
how could it be possible?"
Chén Zhěn was highly regarded by the King of Wèi,
and Huìzǐ said:
"You must diligently serve those around him.
Take the poplar tree—
plant it sideways and it will grow,
plant it upside down and it will grow,
break it and plant it, and it will still grow.
However, if ten people plant it
but one person uproots it,
then no poplar will survive.
Even with a crowd of ten people
planting such an easily grown thing,
they cannot overcome one person—
why is that?
Because planting is difficult
while removing it is easy.
Though you are skilled at planting yourself with the king,
if there are many who wish to remove you,
you will surely be in danger."
When Jì Sūn of Lǔ had newly assassinated his lord,
Wú Qǐ took office under him.
Someone said to Qǐ:
"When a person dies,
first there is blood at death,
after blood comes congealing,
after congealing comes decay to ash,
after ash comes earth.
Once it turns to earth,
nothing more can be done.
Now Jì Sūn is just at the stage of blood—
is it not that the outcome is still unknown?"
Wú Qǐ therefore left and went to Jìn.
Xí Sīmí went to see Tián Chéngzǐ,
and Tián Chéngzǐ ascended a tower with him to look out in all four directions.
Three sides were open and clear,
but looking south,
the trees of Xí's house blocked the view.
Tián Chéngzǐ said nothing.
Xí returned home,
and sent men to cut down the trees.
After the axe had made several cuts,
Xí stopped them.
His steward said:
"Why do you change your mind so often?"
Xí replied:
"There is an ancient saying:
'To know the fish in the deep is unlucky.'
Now Tiánzǐ is about to undertake great affairs,
and if I show him that I perceive his subtleties,
I will surely be in danger.
Not cutting the trees
is no crime;
but knowing what others do not speak of—
that crime is great."
So he did not cut them down.
Yángzǐ passed by an inn east of Sòng.
There were two concubines,
the ugly one was honored,
the beautiful one was despised.
Yángzǐ asked the reason.
The innkeeper replied:
"The beautiful one is aware of her beauty,
so I do not see her as beautiful;
the ugly one is aware of her ugliness,
so I do not see her as ugly."
Yángzǐ said to his disciples:
"Practice virtue
and rid yourself of the mind that thinks yourself virtuous—
then wherever you go, will you not be esteemed?"
A man of Wèi, marrying off his daughter, instructed her:
"Be sure to secretly accumulate wealth.
For a wife to be sent away
is common;
to succeed in staying
is fortunate."
The daughter thus secretly hoarded,
and her mother-in-law, considering her too selfish, sent her away.
The daughter returned home
with twice what she had when married,
yet the father did not blame himself for teaching her wrongly,
but instead took pride in his increased wealth.
Nowadays, officials in their posts
are all of this kind.
Lǔ Dān presented his advice three times to the ruler of Zhōngshān
but was not accepted,
so he distributed fifty pieces of gold to win over the attendants.
When he saw the ruler again,
before he had spoken,
the ruler feasted him.
Lǔ Dān left
and, without returning to his lodging,
immediately departed from Zhōngshān.
His driver said:
"On seeing you again,
he began to treat us well.
Why leave?"
Lǔ Dān replied:
"He who favors me because of others' words,
will surely condemn me because of others' words."
Before he had crossed the border,
a nobleman slandered him, saying:
"He came from Zhào to spy on Zhōngshān."
The ruler then pursued and punished him.
Tián Bódǐng loved scholars and thereby preserved his lord;
Báigōng loved scholars and thereby threw Jīng into chaos.
Their love for scholars was the same,
but their purposes in doing so differed.
Gōngsūn Yǒu cut off his own foot to elevate Bǎilǐ,
while Shù Diāo castrated himself to flatter Duke Huán.
Their self-mutilation was the same,
but their reasons for it differed.
Huìzǐ said:
"A madman runs east,
a pursuer also runs east.
Their running east is the same,
but their reasons for running east differ.
Hence it is said:
For those engaged in the same affair,
one must carefully examine their motives."
Bó Lè taught two men to identify kicking horses,
and they went together to Jiǎnzǐ's stable to observe the horses.
One picked out a kicking horse.
The other followed behind and stroked it,
patting its rump three times without it kicking.
The first thought he had misjudged.
The other said:
"You did not misjudge.
This horse,
has a wounded shoulder and swollen knees.
A horse that kicks
lifts its hind legs while bearing weight on the front,
but with swollen knees it cannot bear the weight,
so the hind legs do not lift.
You are skilled at spotting kicking horses
but unskilled in assessing the effect of swollen knees."
All events have their necessary causes,
and that swollen knees prevent bearing weight
is something only the wise perceive.
Huìzǐ said:
"Put a monkey in a cage,
and it is no different from a pig."
Thus, when circumstances are unfavorable,
it is not the time to display one's abilities.
General Wénzǐ of Wèi visited Zēngzǐ,
and Zēngzǐ did not rise but merely gestured to the mat,
sitting upright in the corner.
Wénzǐ said to his driver:
"Zēngzǐ—
what a fool!
If he takes me for a gentleman,
how can a gentleman not be respected?
If he takes me for a tyrant,
how can a tyrant be insulted?
That Zēngzǐ was not punished
was mere fate."
There is a bird called the zhōu zhōu,
with a heavy head and bent tail,
that when about to drink from the river,
is sure to tumble in.
So it holds its own feathers to drink—
similarly, those who have desires they cannot fulfill
must not fail to seek their own 'feathers.'
The eel resembles a snake,
and the silkworm resembles a caterpillar.
When people see a snake
they are startled and terrified,
and when they see a caterpillar
their hair stands on end.
Yet fishermen handle eels,
and women pick up silkworms—
where profit lies,
all become as brave as Mèng Běn and Zhuān Zhū.
Bó Lè taught those he disliked to recognize thousand-mile horses,
but taught those he loved to recognize nags.
Thousand-mile horses appear only once in a while,
so the profit is slow;
nags are sold daily,
so the profit is swift.
This is what the "Zhōu Shū" means by
"adopting words meant for lower purposes in higher matters
leads to confusion."
Huán Hè said:
"The principle of carving is that
the nose should better be too large,
and the eyes should better be too small.
A large nose can be reduced,
but a small one cannot be enlarged;
small eyes can be enlarged,
but large ones cannot be reduced."
The same applies in handling affairs:
if one allows for future adjustments,
then endeavors rarely fail.
Chóng Hóu and È Lái knew they would not be punished by Zhòu,
but did not foresee King Wǔ destroying him.
Bǐ Gān and Wǔ Zǐxū knew their rulers would surely perish,
but did not realize they themselves would die.
Hence it is said:
"Chóng Hóu and È Lái understood the ruler's heart but not the course of events,
while Bǐ Gān and Wǔ Zǐxū understood events but not the ruler's heart."
The sage is complete in both.
The prime minister of Sòng was powerful and decisive.
Jìzǐ was about to have an audience with the ruler of Sòng,
when Liángzǐ heard of it and said:
"Unless your words can be spoken before the prime minister in a triple assembly,
otherwise,
you will not escape harm."
Jìzǐ therefore spoke about valuing the ruler
and lightly regarding the state.
Yáng Zhū's younger brother Yáng Bù went out wearing white clothes.
It rained,
so he took off the white clothes,
and returned wearing black ones,
but his dog did not recognize him and barked at him.
Yáng Bù grew angry
and was about to beat the dog.
Yáng Zhū said:
"Do not beat it,
for you would be the same.
If earlier your dog had gone out white
and came back black,
would you not find it strange?"
Huìzǐ said:
"When Yì gripped his thumb-ring and held his guard,
drawing his bow and aiming the mechanism,
even the Yuè people vied to hold the target for him.
But when a clumsy child draws a bow,
even his loving mother rushes indoors and shuts the door."
Therefore it is said:
"If success is certain,
even a Yuè man does not doubt Yì;
if it is uncertain,
even a loving mother flees her own child."
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"Does wealth have a boundary?"
He replied:
"The boundary of water
is where there is no more water.
The boundary of wealth
is where one already has enough.
If a person cannot stop at sufficiency
and perishes,
is that not the boundary of his wealth?"
There was a rich merchant of Sòng named Jiān Zhǐzǐ
who competed with someone to buy a raw jade worth a hundred gold pieces.
He pretended to drop and damage it,
then compensated the owner a hundred gold,
and after repairing the damage,
gained a thousand yì from it.
There are endeavors that may fail when undertaken,
yet it is wiser not to undertake them
only when one would bear the loss.
A man wanted to gain an audience with the King of Jīng by demonstrating his driving skill,
but the royal grooms were jealous of him.
So he claimed:
"I can drive well enough to chase deer."
He was granted an audience.
When the king drove,
they could not catch up to the deer;
when the man drove himself,
they did.
The king praised his driving,
and then he mentioned the grooms' jealousy.
The state of Jīng ordered a nobleman to lead an attack on Chén.
An old man seeing him off said:
"Jìn is strong;
you must be cautious."
The nobleman replied:
"Why should you worry, old man?
I will defeat Jìn for you."
The old man said:
"Fine.
I shall build a hut outside the southern gate of Chén."
The nobleman asked:
"What do you mean by that?"
He replied:
"I am laughing at Gōu Jiàn.
If others find it so easy,
why did he alone toil arduously for ten difficult years?"
Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
but Xǔ Yóu fled from it
and stayed with a common family,
who hid their leather cap from him.
To reject the empire
yet have a family hide their leather cap
shows they did not understand Xǔ Yóu.
Three lice were arguing
when another lice passed by
and asked:
"What are you arguing about?"
The three lice said:
"We are competing for the fattest spots."
The lone lice said:
"Aren't you worried about the arrival of the year-end sacrifice
and the burning of the thatch?
Why worry about that instead?"
Thereupon, they all gathered to suck on their host sow
and feed.
The sow grew lean,
and so was not killed.
There is a worm called huì
with one body and two mouths,
which fight over food and bite each other.
They ended up killing each other,
and thus committed suicide.
Ministers who contend for power and cause their state's destruction
are all of the huì kind.
If a palace is whitewashed
and utensils are scrubbed,
they become clean.
So it is with personal conduct:
if there is no place needing cleansing or whitewashing,
then faults are few.
When Gōngzǐ Jiū was about to rebel,
Duke Huán sent an envoy to observe him.
The envoy reported:
"He laughs without joy,
and looks without seeing—
he will surely rebel."
Thereupon, he had the men of Lǔ kill him.
Gōngsūn Hóng cut his hair and became a cavalryman for the King of Yuè,
so Gōngsūn Xǐ sent someone to disown him, saying:
"I will no longer be your brother."
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"I cut my hair,
but you risk your neck leading troops for others;
what should I say about you?"
At the battle of Zhōunán,
Gōngsūn Xǐ died there.
A man had a violent neighbor
and wanted to sell his house to avoid him.
Someone told him:
"His string of offenses is about full."
He replied:
"Indeed, I shall wait a while."
The reply was:
"I fear he will use me to fill his quota."
So he left him.
Hence it is said:
"Things on the brink,
should not be toyed with."
Confucius said to his disciples:
"Who can guide Zǐxī in his fishing for fame?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Cì can."
So he guided him,
and there was no more doubt.
Confucius said:
"How broad-minded!
Not ensnared by profit.
How pure!
The nature of the people is constant.
Crooked is crooked,
straight is straight."
Confucius said:
"Zǐxī will not escape calamity."
During the rebellion of Báigōng,
Zǐxī died there.
Therefore it is said:
"Straight in action but crooked in desire."
When Jìn's Zhōngháng Wénzǐ was fleeing into exile,
he passed through a district town.
His follower said:
"The local official here,
is an old acquaintance of yours.
Why not rest here,
and wait for the following carriages?"
Wénzǐ said:
"I once favored music,
and this man gave me a chiming qín;
I favored adornments,
and this man gave me a jade ring:
he is one who encouraged my faults.
One who seeks to ingratiate himself with me,
I fear he will use me to ingratiate himself with others."
So he left.
Indeed, the official seized two of Wénzǐ's following carriages
and presented them to his lord.
Zhōu Zào said to Gōng Tuō:
"For me, tell the King of Qí:
'If Qí supports me in Wèi,
I will make Wèi serve Your Majesty.'"
Gōng Tuō said:
"That won't do.
This would show him you lack Wèi,
and the King of Qí certainly will not support one who lacks Wèi,
and will resent one who has Wèi.
You'd better say:
'According to Your Majesty's wishes,
your servant requests to make Wèi heed Your Majesty.'
The King of Qí will certainly think you have Wèi,
and will rely on you.
Then you will have Qí,
and thereby have both Qí
and Wèi."
Báiguī said to the Sòng Grand Administrator:
"If the ruler grows up and administers governance himself,
you will have no position.
Now the ruler is young and strives for reputation,
so it's better to have Jīng congratulate him on his filial piety.
Then the ruler will not seize your position,
but will greatly respect you,
and you will long hold power in Sòng."
Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū said to each other:
"The lord is exceedingly disorderly,
and will surely lose the state.
Among the various princes of Qí, those worth supporting
are either Prince Jiǔ
or Xiǎobái.
Let us each serve one of them,
and the one who achieves power first will take in the other."
So Guǎn Zhòng followed Prince Jiǔ,
and Bào Shū followed Xiǎobái.
The people of the state indeed assassinated the ruler.
Xiǎobái entered first and became ruler,
the people of Lǔ detained Guǎn Zhòng and sent him over,
and Bào Shū spoke for him and made him chancellor.
Hence the proverb says:
"Though Wūxián was skilled at invocations,
he could not bless himself.
Though the Qín physician was skilled at removing ailments,
he could not needle himself."
With Guǎn Zhòng's sageliness
he still needed Bào Shū's help—
this is what the common saying calls
"a captive selling his own fur robe but finding no buyer,
a scholar praising his own eloquence but gaining no trust."
The King of Jīng attacked Wú,
and Wú sent Jū Wèi and Jué Róng to present gifts to the Jīng army.
The general said:
"Bind them,
and kill them to anoint the drums."
He asked them:
"Did you come
after divining?"
They replied:
"We divined."
"Was the divination auspicious?"
They said:
"Auspicious."
The men of Jīng said:
"Now Jīng is about to use you to anoint the drums—
what does that mean?"
They replied:
"That is precisely why it is auspicious.
Wú sent us here
precisely to gauge the general's anger.
If the general is angry,
they will dig deep moats and build high ramparts;
if the general is not angry,
they will be lax.
Now
if the general kills us,
then Wú will certainly be alert in defense.
Moreover, the state's divination
was not for one minister's sake.
To kill one minister and preserve a state—
if that is not called auspicious,
then what is?
Besides, if the dead have no consciousness,
then using us to anoint the drums is of no benefit;
if the dead have consciousness,
we will, at the moment of battle,
make the drums not sound."
So the men of Jīng did not kill them.
When Zhì Bó was about to attack Qiúyóu,
but the road was difficult and impassable,
he cast a large bell and presented it to the lord of Qiúyóu.
The lord of Qiúyóu was greatly pleased,
and cleared the road to bring it in.
Chìzhāng Mànzhī said:
"This must not be.
This is how a small state serves a large one,
but now the large state has sent it,
and troops are sure to follow—
it cannot be brought in."
The lord of Qiúyóu did not listen,
and brought it in.
Chìzhāng Mànzhī then cut his axle and fled,
reaching Qí,
and in seven months Qiúyóu perished.
After Yuè had defeated Wú,
it further demanded troops from Jīng to attack Jìn.
The Grand Historian Yǐ Xiàng said to the King of Jīng:
"Now that Yuè has crushed Wú,
its brave men are dead,
its crack troops exhausted,
and its armor damaged.
Now it demands troops to attack Jìn—
this shows us it is not weak.
It would be better to raise an army and share in Wú's territory."
The King of Jīng said:
"Good."
So he raised an army and followed Yuè.
The King of Yuè was enraged,
and prepared to attack them.
Minister Wén Zhǒng said:
"We cannot.
Our brave men are exhausted,
our armor damaged.
If we fight them,
we surely will not prevail—
it is better to bribe them."
So they ceded five hundred lǐ north of Lùshān
as a bribe.
When Jīng attacked Chén,
Wú came to its aid,
and the armies were thirty lǐ apart.
It rained for ten days,
and at night the stars appeared.
Zuǒshǐ Yǐ Xiāng said to Zǐ Qī:
"It has rained for ten days,
our armor is gathered and weapons assembled,
the Wú people will surely come,
we'd better prepare for them."
So they formed battle lines.
Before the formation was complete, the Wú people arrived,
saw Jīng's battle formation and turned back.
Zuǒshǐ said:
"Wú has marched sixty lǐ back and forth,
their nobles must be resting,
common soldiers must be eating.
If we march thirty lǐ and attack them,
we can certainly defeat them."
They followed his advice,
and subsequently defeated the Wú army.
Hán and Zhào were in conflict with each other.
The ruler of Hán requested troops from Wèi, saying:
"I wish to borrow your army to attack Zhào."
Marquis Wén of Wèi said:
"I am like a brother to Zhào,
I cannot comply."
Zhào then also requested troops to attack Hán.
Marquis Wén said:
"I am like a brother to Hán,
I dare not comply."
When both states failed to obtain troops,
they angrily returned.
Later they realized Marquis Wén had reconciled them through this,
and both came to pay homage to Wèi.
Qí attacked Lǔ,
demanding the Slander Tripod,
Lǔ sent a imitation instead.
The Qí people said:
"This is fake."
The Lǔ people said:
"It's genuine."
Qí said:
"Send Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn here,
then I will believe you."
The ruler of Lǔ requested this of Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn,
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said:
"Why not send the genuine one?"
The ruler said:
"I cherish it."
He replied:
"I too cherish my credibility."
Hán Jiū's establishment as ruler was not yet settled.
His younger brother was in Zhōu,
Zhōu wanted to support him,
but feared Hán Jiū wouldn't be established.
Qímǔ Huī said:
"Better to send him with a hundred chariots.
If he becomes ruler,
say it was for protection;
if not,
say we're delivering a traitor."
Jìngguō Jūn was about to fortify Xuē,
many guests advised against it.
Jìngguō Jūn told his receptionist:
"Don't admit any guests."
A man from Qí requested audience, saying:
"I ask to speak just three words.
If I exceed three words,
I ask to be boiled."
Jìngguō Jūn therefore received him.
The guest hurried forward and said:
"Sea big fish."
Then turned to leave.
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"Please explain."
The guest said:
"I dare not treat death as a game."
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"I wish you to explain to me."
He replied:
"Have you heard of the big fish?
Nets cannot stop it,
arrows cannot hook it,
but if it washes ashore and loses water,
ants can enjoy it.
Now Qí is your sea.
While you rule Qí,
what need is there for Xuē?
If you lose Qí,
even if you raise Xuē's walls to heaven,
it would still be useless."
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"Good."
Then stopped,
and did not fortify Xuē.
The King of Jīng's brother was in Qín,
Qín wouldn't release him.
A palace guard said:
"Provide me with a hundred gold pieces,
I can get him out."
So he took a hundred gold to Jìn,
met Shū Xiàng,
and said:
"The King of Jīng's brother is in Qín,
Qín won't release him.
I entrust this hundred gold to you, Shū Xiàng."
Shū Xiàng accepted the gold,
and went to see Duke Píng of Jìn, saying:
"We can fortify Hǔqiū now."
Duke Píng said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"The King of Jīng's brother is in Qín,
Qín won't release him,
this means Qín dislikes Jīng,
so they certainly won't stop us fortifying Hǔqiū.
If they prohibit it,
we can say:
'Release the King of Jīng's brother for us,
and we won't fortify it.'
If they release him,
we can ingratiate Jīng;
if they don't release him,
this proves their lasting dislike,
and they certainly won't dare stop us fortifying Hǔqiū."
The Duke said:
"Good."
So they fortified Hǔqiū.
They told the Duke of Qín:
"Release the King of Jīng's brother for us,
and we won't fortify it."
Qín therefore released him.
The King of Jīng was greatly pleased,
and sent a hundred yì of refined gold to Jìn.
Hélǚ attacked Yǐng,
won three battles,
and asked Wǔ Zǐxū:
"Can we withdraw now?"
Wǔ Zǐxū replied:
"If someone drowning drinks once and stops,
none would ultimately drown,
but since they rest,
better take advantage to sink them completely."
A man of Zhèng had a son,
about to take office,
who told his family:
"We must repair the broken wall,
this insecurity
may invite thieves."
His neighbor said the same.
They didn't repair it in time,
and someone indeed stole from them.
They considered their son wise,
but the neighbor who warned them a thief.
People of old
had eyes too short to see themselves,
so used mirrors to view their faces;
wisdom too short to know themselves,
so used principles to correct themselves.
Thus the mirror bears no blame for showing flaws,
principles incur no resentment for revealing faults.
Eyes without mirror
cannot adjust beard and eyebrows,
self without principles
cannot recognize confusion.
Xīmén Bào had an impatient nature,
so wore leather to remind himself to slow;
Dǒng Ānyú had a sluggish mind,
so wore bowstring to urge himself faster.
Thus using surplus to supplement deficiency,
lengthening the short
characterizes enlightened rulers.
Under heaven are three certain truths:
First, wisdom cannot accomplish everything;
Second, strength cannot lift everything;
Third, might cannot overcome everything.
Therefore, even with the wisdom of Yáo,
without the assistance of the multitude,
great achievements cannot be established;
even with the strength of Wū Huò,
without others' help,
one cannot lift oneself;
even with the might of Bēn and Yù,
without methods and techniques,
one cannot achieve lasting victory.
Thus, there are circumstances one cannot obtain,
and endeavors one cannot accomplish.
Hence, Wū Huò would consider a thousand jun light
but his own body heavy,
not because his body is heavier than a thousand jun,
but because the situation is unfavorable.
Lí Zhū could easily see at a hundred paces
yet struggle with his own eyebrows and eyelashes,
not because a hundred paces is near and eyebrows and eyelashes are far,
but because the way is impossible.
Thus, an enlightened ruler does not push Wū Huò to the limit
for his inability to lift himself;
nor does he distress Lí Zhū
for his inability to see himself.
By relying on feasible circumstances,
and seeking accessible ways,
he achieves great merit and fame with little effort.
Times have fullness and emptiness,
affairs have advantage and harm,
things have life and death.
If the ruler displays joy and anger over these three,
then even steadfast individuals will become disheartened.
The simplicity of sages and worthies runs deep.
Hence, an enlightened ruler observes others,
but does not allow others to observe him.
Understanding that Yáo could not succeed alone,
Wū Huò could not lift himself,
and Bēn and Yù could not overcome themselves,
by employing methods and techniques,
the way of observing conduct is fully realized.
There are seven ways to safety,
and six paths to peril.
The ways to safety:
First,
rewards and punishments follow right and wrong;
second,
fortune and misfortune follow good and evil;
third,
life and death follow laws and measures;
fourth,
there are the worthy and unworthy without personal likes or dislikes;
fifth,
there are the foolish and wise without censure or praise;
sixth,
there are standards of measurement without arbitrary conjectures;
seventh,
there is trustworthiness without deceit.
The paths to peril:
First,
carving within the line (arbitrary decisions within rules);
second,
cutting outside the law (acting beyond legal boundaries);
third,
benefiting from others' harm;
fourth,
delighting in others' misfortune;
fifth,
endangering others in their safety;
sixth,
not being close to those one loves,
and not distancing those one dislikes.
If so,
then people lose their reason to enjoy life,
and forget their reason to value death.
If people do not enjoy life,
then the ruler is not respected;
if they do not value death,
then orders are not carried out.
If all under heaven exert their utmost intelligence on standards,
and devote their efforts to measures,
then in action they prevail,
and in stillness they are secure.
In a well-governed age, people find joy in life through doing right,
and cherish their lives by avoiding wrong,
so that the petty are few and the noble are many.
Thus, the altars of soil and grain stand long,
and the state remains secure for ages.
On a speeding chariot, there is no Confucius;
beneath a capsized boat, there is no Bó Yí.
Hence, commands and orders
are the boat and chariot of the state.
In safety, wisdom and integrity arise;
in peril, strife and baseness emerge.
Therefore, the way to secure the state
is like eating when hungry,
or clothing when cold,
occurring naturally without being ordered.
The ancient kings entrusted principles to bamboo and silk,
their ways being accordant,
so later generations submitted.
Now, if people are made to abandon hunger and cold,
even Bēn and Yù could not do it;
if the natural is discarded,
even accordant ways cannot stand.
If what the strong and brave cannot accomplish is enforced,
then the ruler cannot be secure.
If the ruler, with insatiable demands, blames them for exhaustion,
then the subordinates respond with "there is nothing,"
and having nothing,
they轻视 the law.
The law is what sustains the state,
and if it is轻视ed,
then achievements are not established,
and fame is not attained.
It is said that in ancient times, when Biǎn Què treated illnesses,
he pierced bones with a knife;
when sages saved states in peril,
they offered loyal words that grated on the ears.
Piercing the bone,
thus a small pain is in the body
but a lasting benefit is in the person;
grating on the ears,
thus a small discomfort is in the heart
but lasting fortune is in the state.
Therefore, for a severely ill person,
the benefit lies in enduring pain;
for a fierce and resolute ruler,
fortune comes from words that grate on the ears.
Enduring pain,
thus Biǎn Què could fully apply his skill;
heeding grating words,
then figures like Zǐ Xū are not lost.
This is the way to longevity and safety.
If ill but unable to endure pain,
one loses Biǎn Què's skill;
if in peril but not heeding grating words,
one loses the sages' intent.
Thus,
long-term benefits will not long endure,
and merit and fame will not long stand.
If the ruler does not measure himself against Yáo,
but demands his ministers be like Zǐ Xū,
this is like hoping all people of Yīn were like Bǐ Gān.
If all were like Bǐ Gān,
then the ruler would not err,
and the subordinates would not perish.
Without weighing one's strength
and having a Tián Chéng,
yet hoping all would be like Bǐ Gān,
the state cannot achieve a moment's safety.
If Yáo and Shùn are abandoned and Jié and Zhòu are established,
then people cannot enjoy their strengths
but worry about their weaknesses.
Losing their strengths,
the state achieves no merit;
clinging to their weaknesses,
the people find no joy in life.
With no merit to rule over those who find no joy in life,
this cannot be implemented among the common people.
Thus,
the ruler has no means to command the subordinates,
and the subordinates have no means to serve the ruler.
Safety and peril lie in right and wrong,
not in strength and weakness;
survival and destruction lie in emptiness and fullness,
not in multitude and fewness.
Thus, the state of Qí,
though a myriad-chariot power,
had name and reality mismatched,
the court empty within the state,
internally not filled with name and reality,
so ministers could seize power from the ruler.
Jié, the Son of Heaven,
yet lacked judgment of right and wrong:
he rewarded the undeserving,
causing slanderers and flatterers who practiced deceit to be esteemed;
he punished the innocent,
making the hunchbacked have their backs split open despite their natural condition.
Considering deceit as right,
and natural conditions as wrong,
the minor prevailed over the major.
An enlightened ruler strengthens the internal,
thus avoiding external losses,
for there has never been one who suffered losses nearby
yet did not perish in the long run.
Thus, when the Zhōu took over from the Yīn,
they picked up what was left in the court.
Had the Yīn not left anything behind in their court,
the Zhōu would not have dared to covet even the slightest hair within their borders,
let alone dare to change their positions?
The way of an enlightened ruler is loyal to the law,
and his law is loyal to the people's hearts,
so when he governs, there is order,
and when he leaves, he is remembered.
Yáo made no firm bonds in his time
yet his way was practiced,
Shùn had not even a place to stick an awl in later ages
yet his virtue endured.
One who can establish the Way from ancient times
and leave virtue for ten thousand generations is called an enlightened ruler.
When a sage king establishes laws,
his rewards are sufficient to encourage goodness,
his authority enough to overcome violence,
and his preparations enough to ensure the laws' completeness.
In a well-governed age, ministers
with numerous achievements hold high positions,
those who exert utmost effort receive generous rewards,
and those who fully devote their sentiments earn fame.
Goodness flourishes like spring,
evil perishes like autumn,
thus the people are encouraged to exert their strength
and are willing to give their all,
this is called mutual satisfaction between ruler and subject.
With mutual satisfaction between ruler and subject,
those who use their strength will naturally exert themselves within the balance of the law,
and strive to become like Rén Bǐ;
warriors will face death in battle,
and aspire to be like Bēn and Yù;
those upholding the Way will all harbor hearts as firm as metal or stone,
and die with the integrity of Zǐxū.
When the strong become like Rén Bǐ,
fight like Bēn and Yù,
and remain as steadfast as metal or stone,
then the ruler can rest easy
and his rule is secure.
In ancient times, those skilled in governance
used what people valued to prohibit what they轻视,
and used what was difficult to stop what was easy.
Thus both gentlemen and petty men were corrected,
and both Dào Zhí and Zēng Shēn were honest.
How do we know this?
A greedy thief would not go into a stream to pick up gold,
for going into the stream to pick up gold
would endanger his life.
Bēn and Yù, if they did not assess the enemy,
would not gain a reputation for bravery,
and Dào Zhí, if he did not calculate feasibility,
would not succeed in his gains.
When an enlightened ruler sets prohibitions,
Bēn and Yù would be restrained from attempting what they cannot overcome,
and Dào Zhí would be harmed in what he cannot obtain.
Thus, being able to prohibit what even Bēn and Yù cannot challenge,
and guard what even Dào Zhí cannot take,
then the violent become cautious,
and the wicked turn to righteousness.
With the greatly brave being cautious,
and the great thieves upright,
the world becomes just,
and the sentiments of the common people are rectified.
If a ruler deviates from the law
and loses the people,
he is in danger even with Bó Yí who would not take unjustly,
and cannot avoid the calamities of Tián Chéng and Dào Zhí.
Why?
Now, there is not a single Bó Yí in the world,
yet wicked men never cease to exist,
hence the establishment of laws and standards.
With trustworthy standards,
Bó Yí would not lose what is right,
and Dào Zhí would not gain what is wrong.
With clear laws,
the worthy cannot seize from the unworthy,
the strong cannot invade the weak,
and the many cannot oppress the few.
Entrusting the world to Yáo's laws,
the upright would not lose their share,
and the wicked would not have luck.
Placing a thousand pieces of gold in Yì's arrow's path,
Bó Yí could not lose it,
and Dào Zhí would not dare take it.
Yáo was discerning in not overlooking the wicked,
thus the world had no evil;
Yì was skillful in never missing his shot,
thus the thousand pieces of gold were not lost.
The wicked do not live long, and Dào Zhí's activities cease.
In this way,
pictures would not depict Zǎi Yú,
nor list the six ministers;
documents would not record Zǐxū,
nor mention Fūchāi.
The strategies of Sūn and Wú would be abandoned,
and Dào Zhí's heart would be subdued.
The ruler enjoys ease in his jade hall,
without the worry of glaring eyes, gnashing teeth, or overthrow;
ministers govern effortlessly within the golden city,
without the disaster of wringing wrists, gathering lips, or sighing in frustration. 〓#
To subdue a tiger without a cage,
restrain the wicked without laws,
or prevent deceit without tallies,
this is what troubles even Bēn and Yù,
and what Yáo and Shùn found difficult.
Thus, setting up a cage
is not to guard against mice,
but to enable the timid and weak to subdue a tiger;
establishing laws
is not to guard against Zēng Shēn,
but to enable an average ruler to stop Dào Zhí;
creating tallies
is not to prepare for Wěi Shēng,
but to prevent people from deceiving each other.
Do not rely solely on Bǐ Gān's martyrdom,
nor hope that treacherous ministers are without deceit;
rely on what the timid can subdue,
and grasp what an average ruler can easily maintain.
In the present age,
for those who loyally plan for the ruler
and cultivate virtue for the world,
no benefit is greater than this.
Thus, the ruler has no scenario of a fallen state,
and loyal ministers have no plan of losing their lives.
Understanding that high positions must be rewarded,
he can make people exert their strength within the law's balance,
and die with integrity in their official duties.
Comprehending the sentiments of Bēn and Yù,
they do not exchange life for death;
aware of Dào Zhí's greed,
they do not trade their lives for wealth.
Then the way to preserve the state is fully prepared.
It is said that in ancient times, those skilled in employing people
necessarily followed heaven and complied with human nature
and clearly practiced rewards and punishments.
Following heaven,
they used little effort yet achieved merit;
complying with human nature,
they reduced penalties yet orders were carried out;
with clear rewards and punishments,
Bó Yí and Dào Zhí would not cause chaos.
In this way,
black and white are distinguished.
Ministers in a well-governed state
prove their merit to the country to secure their positions,
demonstrate their ability in office to receive their duties,
and exert their strength within the law's balance
to undertake affairs.
All ministers suit their abilities,
excel in their offices,
handle their tasks with ease,
holding no extra strength in their hearts,
and bearing no additional responsibilities for the ruler.
Thus, internally, there is no turmoil from hidden resentment,
and externally, no threat like Mǎ Fú.
An enlightened ruler ensures that duties do not interfere with each other,
thus eliminating disputes;
he assigns officials to single posts,
so their skills are honed;
he prevents people from sharing achievements,
thus averting contention.
When disputes cease
and skills are perfected,
the strong and weak do not vie for power,
ice and fire do not coexist,
and none in the world can harm one another—
this is the pinnacle of governance.
Abandon laws and rule by personal whim,
and even Yáo could not govern a state.
Discard compass and square to guess measurements,
and Xī Zhòng could not craft a single wheel.
Reject rulers to judge length,
and Wáng Ěr would miss half his marks.
But let an average ruler uphold laws
or a clumsy artisan use tools properly,
and nothing will go amiss.
A sovereign who rejects what even the wise cannot achieve
and embraces what the average never fail at
will harness all human effort
and establish merit and renown.
Enlightened rulers set attainable rewards
and design avoidable punishments.
Thus the virtuous strive for rewards
without suffering Wǔ Zǐxū’s fate,
and the unworthy avoid grave penalties
without being hacked like the hunchback.
The blind walk on level ground
and avoid deep gorges;
fools stay inactive
and escape peril.
This forges bonds
between ruler and subject.
The ancients said:
"Hearts are hard to know,
joys and rages hard to predict."
Hence use markers for the eyes,
drums for the ears,
and laws to instruct the heart.
A sovereign who abandons these three easy tools
to rely on his inscrutable heart
accumulates wrath above
and resentment below.
Ruling with pent-up rage over collective grievance
spells disaster for both.
An enlightened ruler’s markers are clear,
so standards stand firm;
his teachings are comprehensible,
so words are heeded;
his laws are practicable,
so orders are obeyed.
With these three established
and the ruler free of bias,
subjects follow laws to order,
moving as markers guide,
cutting by the ink line,
sewing with the awl’s aid.
Thus the ruler wields no toxic authority,
and subjects face no foolish punishments.
The ruler governs wisely with less anger,
subjects serve faithfully with fewer crimes.
It is said:
"To act without worry,
not even Yáo could achieve."
Yet the world is never without events.
A sovereign who prizes rank and wealth
cannot save a failing state.
Thus enlightened rulers promote integrity
and uphold benevolence.
Once, Jièzǐtuī without rank
followed Duke Wén of Jìn out of duty,
starved yet shared his flesh out of kindness.
Thus the ruler cherished his virtue,
and records immortalized his name.
Rulers delight in public service
but resent private power grabs.
Ministers accept posts by merit
but suffer double duties.
Thus enlightened rulers eliminate ministers’ woes
and secure their own joys.
No benefit greater
unites high and low.
Overlooking private misconduct,
acting rashly on grave matters,
harshly punishing minor faults,
nursing grudges over trifles,
indulging contempt for fleeting joy,
often using kindness to atone for wrongs—
is like reattaching a hand with jade:
thus arises the peril of overthrown rulers.
Setting impossible tasks
and punishing failure
breeds private resentment;
forcing ministers to neglect their strengths
for unbearable demands
stores hidden grievances.
Ignoring laborers’ hardships,
unmoved by their sorrows;
praising villains in joy,
rewarding both worthy and unworthy;
slandering nobles in rage,
humiliating Bó Yí with robbers—
thus ministers betray their lord.
Had King of Yān despised his people
but loved the Lǔ folk,
Yān would be useless and Lǔ unallegiant.
Hated subjects withhold effort;
favored outsiders won’t die for alien lords.
Then ministers become loopholes,
and the ruler stands alone.
Loophole-serving ministers
with an isolated ruler
spell extreme danger.
Shoot without a target,
and even a hit is unskilled;
rage without laws,
and even killings won’t frighten the wicked.
When A’s crime
brings B’s punishment,
resentment festers.
Thus in well-governed states,
reward and punishment replace joy and anger.
Sages establish strict penalties
without venomous intent,
so the wicked submit.
Hitting the mark in archery,
matching rewards to deeds—
then Yáo is reborn,
and Yì reigns again.
Thus rulers avoid the fates of Shāng and Xià,
ministers escape Bǐ Gān’s tragedy,
sovereigns rest easy
and officials serve contentedly,
the Way enveloping heaven and earth,
virtue reaching all ages.
A ruler who ignores cracks in the wall
to paint over them
invites stormy collapse.
Neglecting imminent danger
to admire Mèng Běn and Xià Yǔ’s deaths,
overlooking internal threats
to fortify distant borders,
rejecting nearby wise counsel
to seek alliances afar—
once sudden storms arise,
even Mèng Běn and Xià Yǔ cannot save,
and distant allies cannot arrive.
No disaster greater than this.
In our age,
those loyal to rulers
must not have them please outsiders like the King of Yān did,
admire ancient sages over modern ones,
nor expect Yuè divers
to save central plains’ drowners.
Thus, ruler and subject bond,
internal achievements rise,
and external fame blooms.
The enlightened ruler establishes merit
and achieves fame through four factors:
first, celestial timing;
second, popular sentiment;
third, technical skill;
fourth, positional authority.
Without celestial timing,
even ten Yáos could not make a single ear of grain grow in winter;
opposing popular sentiment,
even Bēn and Yù could not exhaust human effort.
Thus, with celestial timing,
one need not labor yet growth occurs naturally;
with popular sentiment,
one need not urge yet people encourage themselves;
leveraging technical skill,
one need not rush yet things proceed swiftly;
with positional authority,
one need not push forward yet fame is achieved.
Like water flowing,
like a boat floating.
Preserving the way of spontaneity,
implementing inexhaustible decrees,
thus is called an enlightened ruler.
Having talent but no authority,
even the virtuous cannot control the unworthy.
Thus, placing a short timber atop a high mountain,
it overlooks a thousand-ren chasm,
not because the timber is tall,
but because its position is high.
When Jié was the Son of Heaven,
he could control the world,
not because he was virtuous,
but because his authority was weighty.
When Yáo was a commoner,
he could not govern three households,
not because he was unworthy,
but because his position was lowly.
A thousand jūn floats with a boat,
but a zīzhū sinks without one,
not because the thousand jūn is light or the zīzhū heavy,
but because one has support and the other does not.
Thus, the short overlooks the high through position,
the unworthy controls the virtuous through authority.
The ruler of men
is jointly upheld by the unified strength of the world,
hence he is secure;
unanimously established by the masses,
hence he is honored.
Ministers preserve their strengths,
exhaust their capabilities,
hence they are loyal.
With an honored ruler directing loyal ministers,
lasting joy arises
and merit and fame are achieved.
Name and substance support each other to form,
form and shadow respond to each other to stand,
thus ruler and minister share desires but differ in function.
The ruler's worry lies in having no response,
hence it is said:
one hand clapping alone,
however swift, produces no sound.
The minister's anxiety lies in lacking singularity,
hence it is said:
the right hand drawing circles,
the left hand drawing squares,
cannot accomplish both.
Thus it is said:
in a perfectly governed state,
the ruler is like the drumstick,
ministers like the drum,
skills like the chariot,
affairs like the horse.
Thus, when people have surplus energy, response is easy;
when skills have surplus dexterity, handling affairs is convenient.
Those who establish merit lack not in strength,
those who are intimate lack not in trust,
those who achieve fame lack not in authority.
If the close are not intimate,
and the distant are not bonded,
then name does match substance.
Even if a sage has virtue like Yáo and Shùn,
conduct like Bó Yí,
but holds no position in the world,
then merit is not established,
fame not realized.
Thus, those in antiquity who could attain merit and fame
were aided in strength by the masses,
bonded in success by the close,
praised in name by the distant,
upheld in authority by the honored.
In this way,
the merit of Tài Shān
stands long within the state,
and the fame of sun and moon
endures brightly between heaven and earth.
This is how Yáo faced south and preserved his name,
how Shùn faced north and rendered his merit.
Those in antiquity who comprehended the grand scheme:
observed heaven and earth,
watched rivers and seas,
followed valleys and mountains,
where the sun and moon shine,
where the four seasons proceed,
where clouds spread and winds move;
they did not burden their minds with cleverness,
nor burden themselves with selfishness;
entrusted order and chaos to laws and methods,
placed right and wrong in rewards and punishments,
assigned lightness and heaviness to scales and balances;
did not oppose heavenly principles,
did not harm human nature;
did not blow on hair seeking tiny flaws,
did not wash off dirt examining the hard-to-know;
did not pull beyond the plumb line,
did not push within the plumb line;
did not rush beyond the law,
did not delay within the law;
preserved established order,
followed spontaneity;
fortune and misfortune arose from the Way and laws,
not from personal likes and dislikes;
the responsibility for honor and disgrace lay with oneself,
not with others.
Thus, in the most tranquil age,
laws were like morning dew,
pure and simple, undispersed,
hearts bore no accumulated grudges,
mouths uttered no vexatious words.
Thus, chariots and horses were not exhausted on long roads,
banners and flags were not disordered in great marshes,
the myriad people did not lose their lives to invaders,
heroic steeds were not cut down by battle standards;
outstanding figures did not have their names recorded in books,
their merits not inscribed on vessels,
the chronicles of years remained empty.
Hence it is said:
no benefit is longer than simplicity,
no blessing more enduring than peace.
Were Shí the craftsman to take hook and line with a thousand-year lifespan,
observe compass and square,
wield the ink line,
and try to correct Tài Shān;
were Bēn and
Yù to wield Gānjiàng swords
and try to uniform the myriad people;
though exhausting their skill in dexterity,
reaching the zenith of longevity,
Tài Shān would not be corrected,
the people could not be uniformed.
Thus it is said:
those in antiquity who governed the world
did not make Shí the craftsman exhaust his skill
to ruin the form of Tài Shān,
nor make Bēn and Yù use their full might
to harm the nature of the myriad people,
but followed the Way to perfect the law,
so the noble rejoiced and great villains ceased.
Serenely calm and still,
they followed heaven's decree,
upheld the grand scheme.
Thus, people had no crime of breaking the law,
fish no calamity of losing water.
In this way,
the world had little that was amiss.
If the top is not like heaven, it cannot cover all below;
if the heart is not like earth, it cannot bear all things.
Tài Shān does not establish likes and dislikes,
hence it can achieve its height;
rivers and seas do not select minor contributions,
hence they can achieve their abundance.
Thus, when the great man entrusts his form to heaven and earth,
all things are complete;
when he applies his mind across mountains and seas,
the state and its families prosper.
Above, there is no poison of wrath,
below, no calamity of hidden grievances.
Superiors and subordinates alike are simple,
taking the Way as their dwelling.
Hence, long-term benefits accumulate,
great achievements are established,
fame is accomplished in the present,
and virtue is bequeathed to the future—
this is the pinnacle of governance.
The methods employed by the ruler are seven,
and the subtleties he examines are six.
The seven methods:
first, comparing perspectives from multiple sources;
second, enforcing punishment to make authority clear;
third, bestowing rewards faithfully to exhaust capabilities;
fourth, listening individually to hold subordinates accountable;
fifth, issuing ambiguous orders to test loyalty;
sixth, questioning while holding knowledge;
seventh, speaking inversely and acting contrarily.
These seven are what the ruler employs.
Canon One: Comparing Perspectives.
If observation and listening are not compared,
then truth remains unheard;
if listening has a single gateway,
then ministers will block it.
This is illustrated by the dwarf dreaming of a stove,
and Duke Āi's statement, "Without the multitude, one is confused."
Hence, the man of Qí seeing the River Earl,
and Huìzǐ's words about "losing half."
The peril lies in Shù Niú starving Shūsūn,
and Jiāng Yǐ discussing the customs of Chǔ.
Sì Gōng desired order but lacked understanding,
so he created rivals.
Thus, the enlightened ruler infers from examples like accumulating iron,
and perceives the dangers of an entire market.
Canon Two: Enforcing Punishment. 〓#
Where affection is excessive,
laws cannot be established;
where authority is scant,
subordinates encroach upon superiors.
Thus, if penalties are not inevitable,
prohibitions will not be enforced.
This is illustrated by Dǒngzǐ's journey to Shíyì,
and Zǐchǎn instructing Yóu Jí.
Hence, Confucius spoke of frostfall,
and the Yīn law punished ash discarders;
Jiāng Xíng left Yuè Chí,
while Gōngsūn Yāng加重 light offenses.
Thus, the gold of Lìshuǐ could not be guarded,
and the fire in Jīzé could not be extinguished.
Chéng Huān weakened the state of Qí with excessive benevolence,
Bǔ Pí caused the king of Wèi's downfall with kindness and favor.
Guǎn Zhòng understood this,
hence he adjudicated on the dead.
Sì Gōng understood it, hence he purchased convicts.
Canon Three: Rewards and Praise. 〓#
If rewards and praise are meager and deceptive,
subordinates will not be used;
if rewards and praise are generous and trustworthy,
subordinates will lightly face death.
This is illustrated by Wénzǐ's remark
"like deer."
Hence, the King of Yuè burned his palace,
Wú Qǐ leaned against a chariot shaft,
Lǐ Kuī decided lawsuits with archery,
and Sòng's Chóngmén died from grief.
Gōu Jiàn understood this,
hence he bowed to an angry frog.
Marquis Zhāo understood it,
hence he stored worn trousers.
Generous rewards make men become like Bēn and Zhū;
women gathering silkworms,
fishermen gripping eels—
these exemplify it.
Canon Four: Individual Listening. 〓#
Listening individually prevents confusion between foolish and wise;
holding subordinates accountable prevents ministerial interference.
This is illustrated by searching for Zhèng and blowing the yu.
The peril lies in Shēnzǐ using Zhào Shào and Hán Tà as tests.
Hence, Prince Fàn debated ceding Hédōng,
and Marquis Yīng谋划 relaxing Shàngdǎng.
Canon Five: Deceptive Employment. 〓#
Frequent audiences and long waits without appointment,
then villains scatter like deer.
Sending others to inquire
prevents selling private influence.
Thus, Páng Jìng recalled the senior official,
and Dài Huàn ordered inspection of the covered carriage;
the ruler of Zhōu lost a jade hairpin,
the Shāng Grand Steward discussed ox dung.
Canon Six: Holding Knowledge. 〓#
Holding knowledge to question,
makes the unknowing wise;
deeply understanding one thing,
all hidden matters change.
This is illustrated by Marquis Zhāo holding a claw.
Hence, inspecting the south gate revealed three districts.
The ruler of Zhōu sought a crooked staff, and ministers feared;
Bǔ Pí employed a lesser son,
Xīmén Bào pretended to lose a linchpin.
Canon Seven: Inverted Speech. 〓#
Inverted speech and contrary actions
to test suspicions,
then treacherous circumstances are revealed.
Hence, Yángshān deceived Jiāo Shù,
Nào Chǐ acted as Qín's envoy,
a man of Qí planned rebellion,
Zǐzhī used a white horse,
Zǐchǎn separated litigants,
Sì Gōng passed through the border market.
Explanation One: 〓#
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Mí Zǐxiá enjoyed favor,
dominating Wèi.
A dwarf who saw the duke said:
"My dream has come true."
The duke asked:
"What dream?"
He replied:
"I dreamed of a stove,
for seeing you."
The duke angrily said:
"I hear that those who see the ruler dream of the sun;
why did you dream of a stove upon seeing me?"
He replied:
"The sun illuminates all under heaven,
no single thing can block it;
a ruler illuminates all people of the state,
no one person can obscure him.
Thus, those about to see the ruler dream of the sun.
As for a stove,
if one person is warming at it,
then others cannot see it.
Now, perhaps there is one person warming at you, my lord?
Then even if I dreamed of a stove,
is it not fitting!"
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"A rustic saying goes:
'Without the multitude, one is confused.'
Now, when I undertake affairs,
and deliberate with my ministers,
the state becomes more chaotic;
what is the reason?"
Confucius replied:
"When an enlightened ruler questions ministers,
one may know,
another may not.
In such cases,
with the enlightened ruler above,
ministers debate candidly below.
Now, all your ministers unanimously echo Jìsūn,
the entire state of Lǔ has become one;
even if you inquire among all within the borders,
you still cannot avoid chaos."
Another account:
Yànzǐ visited Lǔ,
Duke Āi asked him:
"The saying goes:
'Without three men, one is confused.'
Now I deliberate with the whole state,
yet Lǔ cannot avoid chaos;
why?"
Yànzǐ said:
"What ancients called 'without three men, one is confused'
means if one errs,
two correct it,
three suffice as a multitude,
hence it is said
'without three men, one is confused.'
Now, the ministers of Lǔ number in hundreds and thousands,
but all speak for the private interest of the Jì family;
the number is not small,
yet the speaker is effectively one—
how can there be three?"
A man of Qí said to the King of Qí:
"Hé Bó
is a great deity.
Why does Your Majesty not try to meet with him?
I beg to arrange for you to encounter him."
Thereupon, he built an altar by the great river,
and stood there with the king.
After a while,
a large fish moved,
and he declared:
"This is Hé Bó."
Zhāng Yí wanted to use the forces of Qín, Hán, and Wèi
to attack Qí and Jīng,
while Huì Shī sought to halt hostilities with Qí and Jīng.
The two debated the matter,
and all the ministers and courtiers spoke for Zhāng Yí,
considering it advantageous to attack Qí and Jīng,
with none speaking for Huì Shī.
The king indeed listened to Zhāng Yí,
deeming Huì Shī's counsel unacceptable.
When the plan to attack Qí and Jīng was settled,
Huì Shī entered for an audience.
The king declared:
"Sir, say no more!
The attack on Qí and Jīng is indeed advantageous,
and the entire state agrees."
Huì Shī then argued:
"This must be examined carefully.
If the matter of Qí and Jīng is truly advantageous,
and the whole state considers it so,
how can there be so many wise men?
If the attack on Qí and Jīng is truly not advantageous,
yet the whole state considers it so,
how can there be so many fools?
In all deliberations,
there is doubt.
Doubt means
genuine uncertainty:
half believe it feasible,
half believe it not.
Now the entire state considers it feasible,
which means you, King, have lost half.
Those who hijack their ruler
are precisely those who eliminate the opposing half."
Shūsūn served as minister of Lǔ,
esteemed and authoritarian.
His favorite was named Shù Niú,
who also arbitrarily wielded Shūsūn's authority.
Shūsūn had a son named Rén,
whom Shù Niú envied and sought to kill.
He thus took Rén to visit the Lord of Lǔ.
The Lord of Lǔ bestowed a jade ring upon Rén,
who bowed and received it but dared not wear it,
sending Shù Niú to ask Shūsūn for permission.
Shù Niú deceived him, saying:
"I have already asked for you,
and you are to wear it."
Rén thus wore it.
Shù Niú then said to Shūsūn:
"Why not present Rén to the lord?"
Shūsūn said:
"Why should a child be presented?"
Shù Niú replied:
"Rén has already been received by the lord several times.
The lord gave him a jade ring,
and Rén is already wearing it."
Shūsūn summoned Rén and saw
that he indeed wore the ring.
Enraged, Shūsūn killed Rén.
Rén's elder brother was named Bǐng,
whom Shù Niú also envied and sought to kill.
Shūsūn had a bell cast for Bǐng.
When the bell was finished,
Bǐng dared not strike it,
sending Shù Niú to ask Shūsūn.
Shù Niú did not ask,
but deceived him again:
"I have already asked for you,
and you are to strike it."
Bǐng thus struck it.
Shūsūn heard of this and said:
"Bǐng struck the bell without permission."
Furious, he banished him.
Bǐng fled to Qí.
After a year,
Shù Niú pretended to apologize to Shūsūn for Bǐng,
and Shūsūn sent Shù Niú to recall him.
Again, without summoning him, he reported:
"I have summoned him,
but Bǐng is very angry
and refuses to come."
Shūsūn, greatly enraged,
sent someone to kill him.
After both sons died,
Shūsūn fell ill.
Shù Niú then tended him alone,
dismissing his attendants,
and allowing no one in,
saying:
"Shūsūn does not wish to hear human voices."
He starved him to death by withholding food.
After Shūsūn died,
Shù Niú did not announce the death,
but plundered the treasury of its heavy treasures,
emptied it, and fled to Qí.
Thus, by trusting the words of a confidant,
father and sons were brought to ruin—
this is the calamity of not verifying.
Jiāng Yǐ, on a mission from the King of Wèi to Jīng,
said to the King of Jīng:
"Entering your realm,
I heard your state's custom is:
'A gentleman does not conceal others' virtues,
nor speak of others' faults.'
Is this truly so?"
The king said:
"It is."
"Then in cases like Bái Gōng's rebellion,
would that not be perilous?
If it truly is so,
I am spared the death penalty."
Lord Sì of Wèi esteemed Rú Ěr
and loved Shì Jī,
but feared they might use his favor to manipulate him.
So he elevated Bó Yí to rival Rú Ěr,
and honored Wèi Jī to pair with Shì Jī,
saying:
"This is to balance them."
Lord Sì knew he wanted no manipulation,
but had not found the method.
For not allowing the lowly to critique the noble,
nor subordinates to challenge superiors,
but insisting on equal status
before daring to critique each other—
this only plants more manipulative ministers.
Thus, Lord Sì's manipulation began.
If arrows come from one direction,
pile iron to shield that side;
if arrows come from all directions,
forge an iron room for full protection.
With protection, the body is unharmed.
So, as full protection prevents injury,
full opposition prevents treachery.
Páng Gōng accompanied the crown prince as a hostage in Hándān,
and said to the King of Wèi:
"If one person says there's a tiger in the market,
would you believe it?"
He said:
"No."
