"If two say there's a tiger in the market,
would you believe it?"
He said:
"No."
"If three say there's a tiger in the market,
would you believe it?"
The king said:
"I would believe it."
Páng Gōng said:
"That there is no tiger in the market is clear,
yet three speakers create a tiger.
Now Hándān is farther from Wèi than the market,
and those discussing me exceed three.
I beg you to scrutinize this."
When Páng Gōng returned from Hándān,
he ultimately could not gain an audience.
A second argument:
Dǒng Yūyú was governor of Shàngdì for Zhào.
Traveling through the Shíyì mountains,
he saw a gorge so deep,
its cliffs like walls,
a hundred ren deep.
He asked the local villagers:
"Has anyone ever entered this place?"
He replied:
"None."
The lord asked:
"Have infants,
the deaf and insane,
ever entered this place?"
He replied:
"None."
"Have oxen, horses, dogs, or pigs
ever entered this place?"
He replied:
"None."
Dǒng Èyú sighed deeply and said:
"Now I know how to govern.
If I enforce laws without pardon,
just as anyone falling into this ravine would surely die,
then no one would dare to violate them.
Why worry about disorder?"
When Zǐchǎn was prime minister of Zhèng,
he fell gravely ill
and said to Yóu Jí:
"After my death,
you will surely lead Zhèng.
You must govern with severity.
Fire is fierce in form,
so few get burned;
water is gentle in form,
so many drown.
You must maintain severe authority,
don't let people drown in your gentleness."
After Zǐchǎn died,
Yóu Jí refused to exercise severe authority,
and young men in Zhèng formed robber bands,
occuping Huánzé marshland,
threatening to plunge Zhèng into disaster.
Yóu Jí led chariots and cavalry against them,
fighting for a full day and night
before barely defeating them.
Yóu Jí sighed and lamented:
"Had I followed my master's teaching earlier,
I would not have regrets like this!"
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals record:
'In winter, the twelfth month, frost fell but did not kill beans.'
Why record this?"
Zhòngní replied:
"This means it should have killed but did not.
When what should be killed is spared,
peach and plum trees bear fruit in winter.
When Heaven loses its way,
even plants and trees will violate its order,
how much more would a ruler of men!"
Under Yīn law,
those who dumped ashes in the street were punished.
Zǐgòng considered this too severe
and asked Zhòngní about it.
Zhòngní said:
"This shows understanding of governance.
Dumping ashes in the street would surely blow into people's faces,
which would make people angry,
anger would lead to fights,
and fights would cause whole clans to kill each other.
This is the way to destroy clans,
so punishment is justified.
Moreover, severe punishment
is what people fear;
while not dumping ashes
is easy for people.
Making people do what is easy
while avoiding what they fear
—this is the way of governance."
Another account says:
Under Yīn law,
those who dumped ashes on public roads had their hands cut off.
Zǐgòng said:
"The crime of dumping ashes is minor,
while the punishment of hand-cutting is severe.
Why were the ancients so cruel?"
The reply was:
"Not dumping ashes
is easy;
losing hands
is dreaded.
Doing what is easy
without involving what is dreaded
—the ancients considered this practicable,
hence they implemented it."
Yuè Chí, chancellor of Zhōngshān,
led a hundred chariots on a mission to Zhào,
selecting among his retainers one of wisdom and ability
to serve as procession commander.
Yet the procession fell into disorder midway.
Yuè Chí said:
"I thought you were wise,
and made you procession commander.
Now we have disorder midway—
why?"
The retainer thereupon took leave and departed,
saying:
"You do not understand governance.
One needs authority to make people obey,
and rewards to encourage them,
then order can be maintained.
Now I am
but a junior among your retainers.
To have the young lead the elder,
the lowly govern the noble,
without holding power over their advantages and disadvantages
to control them—
this is why disorder arose.
If you had empowered me:
to make the good among them ministers,
and behead the bad among them,
what reason would there be for disorder!"
Gōngsūn Yāng's laws punished minor offenses severely.
Serious crimes
are what people find hard to commit;
while minor faults
are what people can easily avoid.
Making people avoid what is easy
and stay away from what is difficult
—this is the way of governance.
When minor faults don't occur,
major crimes don't arise.
Thus people remain faultless and disorder doesn't breed.
Another account says:
Gōngsūn Yāng stated:
"In administering punishments, make light offenses serious.
If light offenses don't occur,
serious ones won't come.
This is called using punishment to eliminate punishment."
In the southern Chǔ region,
gold grew in the Lì River,
and many people secretly mined it.
The prohibition against gold mining
mandated immediate execution and dismemberment in the market upon capture.
So many were executed
that bodies clogged the river,
yet people kept stealing gold.
No crime is heavier than public dismemberment,
yet it continues because
capture is not certain.
Suppose someone said here:
"I'll give you the whole world but kill you afterward."
No ordinary person would accept.
To possess the world
is the greatest benefit,
yet people refuse because
they know they would certainly die.
Thus when capture is uncertain,
even dismemberment won't stop gold theft;
when death is certain,
even the world cannot tempt them.
Some people of Lǔ set fire to accumulated marshes.
The north wind blew,
pushing the flames southward,
threatening to burn the capital.
Duke Āi grew fearful,
personally leading the crowd to fight the fire.
But none around him remained—
all had gone to chase animals,
and the fire went unchecked.
He then summoned Zhòngní for advice.
Zhòngní said:
"Those chasing animals enjoy it
without punishment,
while fire-fighters suffer
without reward.
This is why the fire goes unchecked."
Duke Āi said:
"Good."
Zhòngní said:
"The situation is urgent,
there's no time for rewards.
If all who help put out the fire were rewarded,
the state wouldn't have enough to reward everyone,
I request we only implement punishments."
Duke Āi said:
"Good."
Thereupon Zhòngní issued an order:
"Those who don't help fight the fire
will be treated as guilty of desertion in battle;
those who chase animals
will be treated as guilty of trespassing into forbidden areas."
Before the order had been fully circulated,
the fire was already extinguished.
Chéng Huān said to the King of Qí:
"Your Majesty is too benevolent,
too compassionate towards people."
The King said:
"Being too benevolent,
too compassionate towards people—
are these not good reputations?"
He replied:
"These are virtues for ministers,
not conduct for rulers.
Ministers must be benevolent
before one can consult with them,
compassionate towards people
before one can keep them close;
if not benevolent, one cannot consult with them,
if cruel to people, one cannot keep them close."
The King said:
"Then in what ways am I too benevolent,
too compassionate?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty is too benevolent towards Lord Xuē,
and too compassionate towards the Tián clan.
Being too benevolent towards Lord Xuē
means ministers lack authority;
being too compassionate towards the Tián clan
means relatives violate the law.
When ministers lack authority,
the military is weak externally;
when relatives violate the law,
the government is chaotic internally.
With a weak military externally
and chaotic government internally,
this is the foundation of a state's downfall."
King Huì of Wèi said to Bǔ Pí:
"What have you heard
about my reputation?"
He replied:
"I've heard of Your Majesty's kindness and generosity."
The King joyfully said:
"Then what achievements will this bring?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty's achievement will be downfall."
The King said:
"Kindness and generosity
are virtuous conduct.
Practicing them leads to downfall—
why?"
Bǔ Pí replied:
"Kindness means being unable to bear suffering,
and generosity means liking to give.
Being unable to bear suffering
means not punishing the guilty,
liking to give
means rewarding without waiting for merit.
The guilty go unpunished,
the unrewarded receive rewards—
even if the state falls,
isn't it appropriate?"
The state of Qí favored lavish burials,
using all cloth and silk for shrouds,
and all timber for coffins.
Duke Huán was troubled by this,
and told Guǎn Zhòng:
"If cloth and silk are exhausted, we'll have nothing for clothing,
if timber is exhausted, we'll have nothing for defense,
yet people won't stop lavish burials—
how can we prohibit this?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Whenever people act,
it's either for fame
or for profit."
Thereupon he issued an order:
"Those whose coffins exceed limits
will have their corpses desecrated,
and the mourners will be punished."
Desecrating the dead
brings no fame,
punishing mourners
brings no profit—
why would anyone do it then?
During the time of Lord Sì of Wèi,
a convict escaped to Wèi,
and treated the Queen of King Xiāng.
Lord Sì of Wèi heard of this,
sent someone to offer fifty jīn to buy him back,
but after five attempts King of Wèi wouldn't give him up,
so he exchanged Zuǒshì for him.
His ministers and attendants remonstrated:
"Trading a city for a convict—
is this acceptable?"
The Lord said:
"This is beyond your understanding.
In governance, nothing is too small
and in chaos, nothing is too big;
if laws aren't established and punishments not enforced,
even ten Zuǒshì would be useless;
if laws are established and punishments enforced,
losing ten Zuǒshì does no harm."
The King of Wèi heard this and said:
"If a ruler desires order but we don't comply,
it's inauspicious."
So he transported him back,
and presented him freely.
Argument Three: 〓#
The King of Qí asked Wénzǐ:
"How should a state be governed?"
He replied:
"Rewards and punishments as methods
are sharp tools.
The ruler must firmly grasp them,
and cannot show them to others.
As for ministers like me,
we're like deer,
only going where there's good grass."
The King of Yuè asked Minister Wén Zhǒng:
"I wish to attack Wú—
is it feasible?"
He replied:
"It is feasible.
Our rewards are generous and trustworthy,
our punishments strict and certain.
If you wish to verify this,
why not try burning the palace?"
So they burned the palace,
and no one tried to extinguish it.
Then he issued an order:
"Those who die fighting the fire
will receive the reward for dying in battle;
those who fight the fire and survive
will receive the reward for victory in battle;
those who don't fight the fire
will be punished as deserters."
People coated their bodies,
soaked their clothes and rushed into the fire—
three thousand on the left,
three thousand on the right.
This shows the certainty of victory.
Wú Qǐ was commandant of Xīhé for Marquis Wǔ of Wèi.
Qín had a small outpost near the border,
and Wú Qǐ wanted to attack it.
Not removing it
would greatly harm farmers,
but removing it
wouldn't justify mobilizing troops.
So he leaned a chariot shaft outside the north gate
and ordered:
"Whoever can move this outside the south gate
will be granted superior land and residence."
No one moved it.
When someone finally did,
he rewarded them as ordered.
Soon he placed a dàn of red beans outside the east gate
and ordered:
"Whoever can move this outside the west gate
will be rewarded as before."
People competed to move it.
Then he issued an order:
"Tomorrow we shall attack the watchtower;
whoever is first to scale it
shall be appointed as a senior official of the state,
and granted the finest fields and residences."
People vied to volunteer,
so they assaulted the watchtower,
and captured it in a single morning.
Lǐ Kuī, as governor of Shàngdì under Marquis Wén of Wèi,
wishing to make people skilled in archery,
issued an order:
"In doubtful legal disputes,
have the parties shoot at a target;
he who hits it wins his case,
he who misses loses."
Once the order was given, everyone diligently practiced archery,
ceaselessly day and night.
When they battled the Qín forces,
they routed them thoroughly,
due to the people's proficiency in combat archery.
A commoner from the Chóngmén district in Sòng, while in mourning,
grieved so severely he became emaciated.
The ruler deemed this filial devotion to his parent,
and promoted him to an official post.
The following year,
those who died from excessive grieving
numbered over ten annually.
A child's mourning for a parent
stems from love,
yet it can still be encouraged by rewards;
how much more so the people by their ruler!
The King of Yuè, contemplating an attack on Wú,
desiring people to disregard death,
went out and saw an angry frog, bowing to it from his carriage.
An attendant asked:
"Why honor this?"
The king replied:
"Because it has spirit."
The next year, those offering their heads to the king
numbered over ten annually.
From this we see
that praise alone can suffice to make men die.
Another account says:
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè saw an angry frog and bowed to it.
His charioteer asked:
"Why bow?"
The king said:
"The frog has such spirit,
how could I not bow?"
The warriors heard this and said:
"If the frog has spirit,
and the king bows to it,
how much more for warriors with courage!"
That year,
there were men who cut off their own heads to present them.
Thus, when the King of Yuè planned to retaliate against Wú
and tested his training,
he set a tower ablaze and drummed,
making people rush into the fire,
for the reward was in the fire;
facing a river and drumming,
he made people plunge into the water,
for the reward was in the water;
in battle, he made men sever heads
and rip open bellies without a backward thought,
for the reward was in the weapons.
How much more, then,
when advancing the worthy according to law, is the encouragement greater than this!
Hán Zhāo Hóu had someone store away worn trousers.
An attendant said:
"My lord, this is unkind;
not giving the worn trousers to your attendants
but storing them away."
Zhāo Hóu replied:
"This is beyond your understanding.
I have heard that a wise ruler values every frown and smile.
A frown has its purpose,
and a smile has its purpose.
Now these trousers,
are they not more significant than a frown or a smile?
Trousers are far more important than frowns or smiles;
I must reserve them for those who achieve merit,
hence I store them and have not given them away."
The eel resembles a snake,
the silkworm resembles a caterpillar.
People startle at the sight of a snake,
and bristle at the sight of a caterpillar.
Yet women pick up silkworms,
and fishermen handle eels,
for where profit lies,
they forget their aversion,
and all become like Mèng Bēn.
Persuasion Four: #
The King of Wèi said to the King of Zhèng:
"Initially, Zhèng and Liáng were one state,
later separated,
and now I wish to regain Zhèng and reunite it with Liáng."
The Lord of Zhèng was troubled,
summoned his ministers,
and sought their counsel on how to respond to Wèi.
A nobleman said to the Lord of Zhèng:
"This is very easy to answer.
Your Lordship should reply to Wèi:
'If considering Zhèng as part of the former Wèi justifies reuniting it,
then our humble state also wishes to obtain Liáng
and reunite it with Zhèng.'"
The King of Wèi then desisted.
King Xuān of Qí had people play the yu,
always requiring three hundred musicians.
Nánguō, a retired scholar, requested to play for the king,
and King Xuān was pleased,
providing state provisions for hundreds.
When King Xuān died,
King Mǐn ascended,
preferring to listen to them one by one,
the scholar fled.
Another account says:
Hán Zhāo Hóu said:
"With so many yu players,
I cannot tell the skilled ones."
Tián Yán replied:
"Listen to them one by one."
Zhào had someone approach Shēn Zǐ in Hán to request troops,
intending to attack Wèi.
Shēn Zǐ wanted to mention it to the lord,
but feared the lord would suspect him of colluding externally,
yet not doing so might offend Zhào,
so he had Zhào Shào and Hán Tà
first test the lord's disposition
before speaking of it.
Internally, he learned Zhāo Hóu's intent,
externally, he achieved merit with Zhào.
When the armies of three states reached Hán,
the King of Qín said to Lóu Huǎn:
"The three states' troops are deep in our territory!
I consider ceding Hédōng to negotiate peace,
what do you think?"
He replied:
"To cede Hédōng
is a great cost;
but to save the state from peril
is a great achievement.
This is a matter for the elders and nobles,
why does Your Majesty not summon Prince Fàn
and ask him?"
The king summoned Prince Fàn and informed him,
who replied:
"To negotiate peace will bring regret,
not to negotiate will also bring regret.
If Your Majesty now cedes Hédōng and negotiates,
and the three states withdraw,
you will surely say:
'The three states would have left anyway,
I merely gave them three cities.'
If you do not negotiate,
and the three states penetrate Hán,
then the state will face a major assault,
and you will deeply regret it.
You will say:
'It was for not offering the three cities.'
Therefore, I say:
'Your Majesty will regret negotiating,
and regret not negotiating.'"
The king said:
"If I must regret,
I would rather regret losing three cities
than regret facing peril; #
I decide to negotiate peace."
Marquis Yìng said to the King of Qín:
"Your Majesty has obtained Yuān, Yè, Lántián, and Yángxià,
cut off Hénèi,
and pressured Liáng and Zhèng,
yet the reason you have not become king
is that Zhào remains unsubdued.
Relaxing over Shàngdǎng is but a minor matter;
advancing to Dōngyáng,
then Hándān will be like a louse in one's mouth."
The king, holding a ceremonial tablet, faced his court and the realm,
but his successor seized power through military force.
However, the peace and comfort of Shàngdǎng
are in a critical situation,
and I fear that if we relax our efforts, it will not be heeded.
What can be done?"
The king said:
"We must indeed relax and change our approach."
Illustration Five: 〓#
Páng Jìng,
a county magistrate,
sent market inspectors on their rounds,
then summoned the senior officials and had them return.
After standing for a while,
without giving any orders,
he finally sent them off.
The market inspectors thought the magistrate and the senior officials had discussed something,
leading to distrust among them,
thereby preventing any misconduct.
Dài Huān,
the Grand Steward of Sòng,
sent a man at night, saying:
"I have heard that for several nights, a covered carriage has been arriving at Lǐ Shǐ's door.
Carefully observe this for me."
The man reported back:
"I did not see a covered carriage,
but I saw someone holding a bamboo box speaking with Lǐ Shǐ.
After a while,
Lǐ Shǐ accepted the box."
The ruler of Zhōu lost a jade hairpin,
ordered his officials to search for it,
but they could not find it in three days.
The ruler then had others search,
and it was found in a servant's room.
The ruler of Zhōu said:
"My officials are not attending to their duties.
They searched for the hairpin
and could not find it in three days;
I had others search,
and it was found within a day."
Thereupon, the officials were all frightened,
considering their ruler to be divine.
The Grand Steward of Shāng sent a young attendant to the market,
and upon his return, asked him:
"What did you see at the market?"
He replied:
"I saw nothing."
The Grand Steward said:
"Even so,
what did you see?"
He replied:
"Outside the south gate, there were many ox carts,
barely allowing passage."
The Grand Steward then warned the messenger:
"Do not dare tell anyone what I asked you."
He then summoned the market official and rebuked him:
"Why is there so much ox dung outside the market gate?"
The market official was very surprised that the Grand Steward knew so quickly,
and became fearful in his duties.
Illustration Six: 〓#
Hán Zhāohóu clenched his hand,
pretending to have lost a fingernail,
and searched for it urgently.
His attendants then cut their own nails and presented them.
Zhāohóu used this to test his attendants' honesty.
Hán Zhāohóu sent a rider to the county.
The messenger reported back,
and Zhāohóu asked:
"What did you see?"
He replied:
"I saw nothing."
Zhāohóu said:
"Even so,
what did you see?"
He said:
"Outside the south gate,
there was a yellow calf eating seedlings on the left side of the road."
Zhāohóu told the messenger:
"Do not dare reveal what I asked you."
He then issued an order:
"During the seedling season,
there is an existing ban on cattle and horses entering people's fields,
but the officials have not taken it seriously,
and many cattle and horses have entered the fields.
Quickly report the numbers;
if you fail,
the penalty will be severe."
Thereupon, three districts reported their counts.
Zhāohóu said:
"It is not complete."
They went back to check,
and found the yellow calf outside the south gate.
The officials considered Zhāohóu to be perceptive,
all became fearful in their duties
and dared not do wrong.
The ruler of Zhōu ordered a search for a curved staff,
but the officials searched for several days
and could not find it.
The ruler privately had others search,
and it was found within a day.
He then said to the officials:
"I know you officials are not doing your jobs.
The curved staff is very easy to find,
yet you could not get it;
I had others search,
and it was found within a day.
How can this be called loyal?"
The officials were all frightened in their duties,
considering their ruler divine.
Bǔ Pí served as a county magistrate,
and his investigating official was corrupt and had a beloved concubine.
Bǔ Pí then had a young attendant pretend to love her,
to uncover the official's hidden affairs.
Xīmén Bào served as magistrate of Yè,
pretending to lose a linchpin from his carriage,
ordered officials to search but they could not find it,
then had others search
and found it in a servant's room.
Illustration Seven: 〓#
Yángshān Jūn was chancellor of Wèi,
and upon hearing that the king suspected him,
he falsely slandered Jiāo Shù to find out.
Nào Chǐ heard that the king of Qí disliked him,
so he pretended to be a Qín envoy to discover it.
A man of Qí wanted to start a rebellion,
but feared the king would know,
so he falsely banished his beloved,
having him flee to the king to reveal it.
Zǐ Zhī was chancellor of Yān,
sat and falsely said:
"What is that running out the gate,
a white horse?"
His attendants all said they saw nothing.
One person ran out to chase it,
and reported:
"There is."
Zǐ Zhī thus knew his attendants were not honest.
When there were people disputing,
Zǐ Chǎn separated them
so they could not communicate,
then reversed their statements when telling each other
to uncover the truth.
Wèi Sìgōng had a traveler pass through a border market,
where the market officials harassed him,
so he bribed them with gold,
and the officials let him go.
Sìgōng said to the officials:
"At a certain time, a traveler passed your post,
gave you gold,
and you let him go."
The market officials were greatly afraid,
and considered Sìgōng to be perceptive.
Six Subtleties:
First, power lent to inferiors;
second, differing interests leading to external alliances;
third, reliance on semblances;
fourth, conflicting gains and losses;
fifth, suspicion and internal strife;
sixth, enemy states' appointments and removals.
These six,
are what the ruler must scrutinize.
Canon One: 〓#
Lending Power.
Authority and power must not be lent to others.
If the ruler loses one unit,
ministers will make it a hundred.
Thus, if ministers can borrow power,
their strength grows,
and with greater strength,
both internal and external forces serve them,
and with such service,
the ruler is blinded.
The argument is illustrated by Lǎo Dān's saying about losing fish.
Thus, when a ruler speaks at length,
his attendants sell favors by offering trivial gifts.
The peril lies in Xú Tóng's remonstrance with Duke Lì of Jìn,
the uniformity of response regarding Zhōu Hóu,
and the Yān man bathing in dog feces.
Canon II: 〓#
Divergent Interests.
The interests of ruler and minister differ,
hence no minister is wholly loyal,
so when ministers' interests are established,
the ruler's interests are destroyed.
Thus, treacherous ministers
summon enemy troops to eliminate internal foes,
initiate foreign ventures to dazzle the ruler,
seeking only their private gain,
with no regard for the state's calamities.
The argument is illustrated by the couple from Wèi praying at the shrine.
Hence, Dài Xiē discussed the sons and brothers,
and the Sān Huán attacked Duke Zhāo;
Gōng Shū introduced Qí's army,
while Dí Huáng summoned Hán's troops;
Grand Steward Pǐ persuaded Wén Zhǒng,
Dà Chéng Niú instructed Shēn Bù Hài;
Sīmǎ Xǐ reported to the King of Zhào,
Lǚ Cāng advised Qín and Chǔ;
Sòng Shí sent a letter to the Lord of Wèi,
Bái Guī instructed Bào Qiǎn.
Canon III: 〓#
Resemblance and Similarity.
Matters of resemblance and similarity
are why rulers fail in punishment,
and how ministers achieve private ends.
Thus, the gatekeeper dumped water and Yí Shè was executed,
Jì Yáng forged orders and two men were blamed,
Sīmǎ Xǐ killed Yuán Qiān and Jì Xīn was put to death,
Zhèng Xiù spoke of a foul odor and the new consort had her nose cut off,
Fèi Wú Jí instructed Xì Wǎn and the Lingyǐn was executed,
Chén Xū killed Zhāng Shòu and Xī Shǒu fled.
Hence, burning the fodder store led to punishment in Zhōngshān,
and killing the old Confucian brought reward in Jì Yáng.
Canon IV: 〓#
Reversal.
When an event occurs and benefits someone,
that person is its master;
if it causes harm,
one must examine the reverse.
Thus, in the deliberations of an enlightened ruler,
if the state is harmed, he investigates who benefits;
if a minister is harmed, he examines the opposing side.
The argument is illustrated by Chǔ troops arriving and Chén Xū becoming chancellor,
and millet seeds being expensive while the granary official was examined.
Hence, Zhāo Xī Xù arrested the straw vendor,
and Duke Xī reprimanded his attendant,
Duke Wén found hair on his roast,
while Ráng Hóu requested the establishment of an emperor.
Canon V: 〓#
Rivalry and Suspicion.
Situations of rivalry and suspicion
are the source of chaos,
so an enlightened ruler is cautious of them.
Thus, Lí Jī of Jìn killed Crown Prince Shēn Shēng,
and the Lady of Zhèng used poison,
Zhōu Xū of Wèi killed his ruler Wán,
Prince Gēn seized Eastern Zhōu,
Prince Zhí was highly favored
and Shāng Chén indeed rebelled,
Yán Suì and Hán Guǐ contended
and Duke Āi indeed met with assassins,
Tián Cháng, Kǎn Zhǐ, Dài Huān, and Huáng Xǐ were rivals
and the rulers of Sòng and Duke Jiǎn were killed.
The argument is illustrated by Hú Tū's mention of the two favorites,
and Zhèng Zhāo's reply about the unborn.
Canon VI: 〓#
Appointment and Removal. 〓#
What enemies strive for
is to confuse investigations and lead to decay;
if the ruler does not discern this,
the enemy will control appointments and removals.
Hence, King Wén supported Fèi Zhòng,
and the King of Qín worried about Chǔ's envoy,
Lí Qiǔ removed Zhòngní,
and Gàn Xiǎng thwarted Gān Mào.
Thus, Wǔ Zǐ Xū spread rumors and Zǐ Cháng was employed,
introducing beauties led to the fall of Yú and Guó,
feigning a lost letter caused Cháng Hóng's death,
using chickens and pigs wiped out Kuài's heroes.
Temple Attacks. 〓#
Matters of rivalry, suspicion, appointment, and removal,
the enlightened ruler stops internally
but employs them externally.
Support the frivolous,
assist the weak,
this is called a temple attack.
When correlation and verification are used internally,
and observation and listening are applied externally,
then the enemy's deceptions are uncovered.
The argument is illustrated by the Qín dwarf's report to Lord Huì Wén.
Hence, Xiāng Cī spoke of attacking Yè,
and Duke Sì granted a mat to the magistrate.
Explanation I: 〓#
Power and authority
are the ruler's deep pool;
ministers
are the fish in that pool.
If a fish is lost from the pool,
it cannot be recovered;
if a ruler loses his power and authority to ministers,
it cannot be regained.
The ancients found it hard to speak directly,
so they used fish as a metaphor.
Rewards and punishments
are sharp tools,
which the ruler wields to control ministers,
but ministers can use them to overpower the ruler.
Thus, if the ruler foreshadows rewards,
ministers will sell them as favors;
if the ruler foreshadows punishments,
ministers will sell them as threats.
Hence it is said:
"The sharp tools of the state
should not be shown to others."
Jìng Guō Jūn served as chancellor of Qí;
if he spoke long with an old acquaintance,
that acquaintance would grow rich;
if he bestowed trivial gifts on attendants,
the attendants would gain influence.
Long conversations and small gifts
are minor aids,
yet they could lead to wealth;
how much more so with official power?
In the time of Duke Lì of Jìn,
the six ministers were powerful.
Xú Tóng and Cháng Yú Jiǎo remonstrated, saying:
"When great ministers are noble and powerful,
they contend with the ruler over affairs,
form cliques through external dealings,
disrupt state laws below,
and coerce the ruler above.
That the state would not be endangered
has never happened."
The duke said:
"Well said."
He then executed three ministers.
Xú Tóng and Cháng Yú Jiǎo remonstrated again:
"Those who share the same crime
are partially punished but not all,
which leaves resentment and provides an opportunity."
The duke said:
"I wiped out three ministers in one morning;
I cannot bear to finish them all."
Cháng Yú Jiǎo replied:
"If you cannot bear it,
they will bear to act against you."
The duke did not listen.
After three months,
the remaining ministers rebelled,
killed Duke Lì, and divided his land.
Zhōu Hóu was chancellor of Chǔ,
noble and decisive in authority.
The King of Chǔ grew suspicious of him
and asked his attendants,
who replied:
"There is nothing."
As if from one mouth.
The Yān man was not deluded,
hence he bathed in dog feces.
A man of Yān
whose wife was having an affair with a scholar—
the husband returned early from outside,
just as the scholar was leaving.
The husband said:
"Who is this guest?"
His wife said:
"There is no guest."
He asked his attendants,
and they all said, "There was no one,"
as if speaking with one voice.
His wife said:
"You are bewildered and changed."
So she bathed him with dog feces.
Another version says:
A man from Yān named Lǐ Jì was fond of traveling far away,
and his wife privately had an affair with a scholar.
Jì suddenly arrived,
while the scholar was inside,
and his wife was troubled by it.
Her maid said:
"Have the gentleman strip naked and loosen his hair,
then go straight out the door,
and we will pretend not to see him."
Thereupon, the gentleman followed her plan,
and rushed out the door.
Jì said:
"Who was that?"
All the household said:
"There was no one."
Jì said:
"Did I see a ghost?"
The women said:
"Yes."
"What should I do about it?"
They said:
"Take the feces of the five sacrificial animals and bathe in them."
Jì said:
"Alright."
So he bathed with feces.
Another version says he bathed in an orchid-scented bath.
Second Argument: 〓#
A man from Wèi and his wife were praying,
and she wished:
"Let me have no mishaps,
and obtain a hundred bolts of cloth."
Her husband said:
"Why so little?"
She replied:
"If it's more than that,
you will use it to buy a concubine."
The King of Jīng wanted to appoint his sons to official posts in the neighboring states,
but Dài Xiē said:
"It cannot be done."
"Appointing the princes to the neighboring states,
the neighbors will surely value them."
He said:
"The sons sent out will be valued,
and being valued,
they will inevitably become partisans of the states that value them,
which is teaching our sons to trade with outsiders,
and is not beneficial."
In Lǔ, Mèngsūn, Shūsūn, and Jìsūn
joined forces to coerce Duke Zhāo,
eventually seizing his state and monopolizing its governance.
The three Huán families of Lǔ pressured the duke,
and Duke Zhāo attacked the Jìsūn family.
The Mèngsūn and Shūsūn families consulted each other, saying:
"Shall we rescue them?"
The charioteer of the Shūsūn family said:
"I
am a household servant;
how should I know state affairs?
But consider whether having Jìsūn or not having Jìsūn
is more beneficial to us?"
All said:
"Without Jìsūn, there will be no Shūsūn."
"Then we must rescue them."
Thereupon, they breached the northwest corner and entered.
When Mèngsūn saw Shūsūn's banner entering,
he also came to the rescue.
The three Huán families united,
and Duke Zhāo was defeated.
He was driven out
and died at Gānhóu.
Gōngshū served as minister of Hán and had achievements against Qí,
while Gōngzhòng was highly regarded by the king.
Gōngshū feared the king would appoint Gōngzhòng as minister,
so he had Qí and Hán form an alliance to attack Wèi.
Gōngshū then brought the Qí army into Zhèng,
to coerce his ruler,
secure his own position,
and affirm the alliance between the two states.
Dí Huáng,
a minister of the King of Wèi,
was on good terms with Hán.
He summoned Hán troops to attack Wèi,
then requested to mediate for the King of Wèi,
thereby enhancing his own importance.
The King of Yuè attacked the King of Wú,
and the King of Wú apologized and declared submission.
The King of Yuè intended to accept it,
but Fàn Lǐ and Minister Wén Zhǒng said:
"It cannot be.
In the past, Heaven gave Yuè to Wú,
but Wú did not accept it.
Now Heaven turns against Fūchāi,
which is also Heaven's curse.
Giving Wú to Yuè,
we should bow twice and accept it;
we cannot agree."
Grand Steward Pǐ sent a letter to Wén Zhǒng, saying:
"When the cunning hares are gone, the good hounds are cooked;
when the enemy state is destroyed, the strategists perish.
Minister, why not spare Wú and let it trouble Yuè?"
Wén Zhǒng received the letter and read it,
then sighed deeply and said:
"Killing me,
Yuè and Wú would share the same fate."
Dàchéng Niú from Zhào said to Shēn Bùhài in Hán:
"If you use Hán to enhance my status in Zhào,
I will use Zhào to enhance yours in Hán.
Thus, you will have two Háns,
and I will have two Zhàos."
Sīmǎ Xǐ,
a minister of the Lord of Zhōngshān,
was on good terms with Zhào,
and once secretly informed the King of Zhào of Zhōngshān's plans.
Lǚ Cāng,
a minister of the King of Wèi,
was friendly with Qín and Jīng.
He subtly urged Qín and Jīng
to attack Wèi,
then requested to negotiate peace to enhance his own status.
Sòng Shí
was a general of Wèi;
Wèi Jūn
was a general of Jīng.
The two states were at war,
and both were commanding.
Sòng Shí sent a letter to Wèi Jūn, saying:
"Our two armies face each other,
our banners in sight,
and unless we avoid battle,
fighting will surely mean mutual destruction.
This is a matter for our two rulers,
and between you and me, there is no personal grudge.
Let the wise find a way to avoid it."
Bái Guī served as minister of Wèi,
and Bào Qiǎn served as minister of Hán.
Bái Guī said to Bào Qiǎn:
"You use Hán to assist me in Wèi,
and I will use Wèi to support you in Hán.
Thus, I will long hold power in Wèi,
and you will long hold power in Hán."
Third Argument: 〓#
In Qí, there was a middle-grade official named Yí Shè,
who drank with the king,
and left very drunk,
leaning against the palace gate.
A gatekeeper who had suffered foot amputation pleaded:
"Would you mind bestowing some leftover drops upon me?"
Yí Shè scolded him:
"Away!
A punished cripple,
how dare you beg drink from your betters!"
The amputee retreated hastily.
After Yí Shè had left,
the amputee poured water under the eaves of the gate,
making it look like someone had urinated there.
The next day,
the king came out and angrily asked,
saying:
"Who urinated here?"
The amputee replied:
"I did not see.
However, yesterday the middle-grade official Yí Shè stood here."
The king then condemned Yí Shè and had him executed.
The King of Wèi had two ministers who were on bad terms with Jìyáng Jūn.
Jìyáng Jūn then falsely had someone
forge the king's order to plot an attack against himself.
The king sent someone to ask Jìyáng Jūn:
"Who holds a grudge against you?"
He replied:
"No one dares to hold a grudge.
However,
I have been on bad terms with two men,
but it shouldn't have come to this."
The king inquired of his attendants,
and they said:
"Indeed it is so."
The king then executed the two men.
Jì Xīn and Yuán Qiān held a mutual grudge.
Sīmǎ Xǐ, who had recently become hostile toward Jì Xīn,
secretly had someone kill Yuán Qiān.
The ruler of Zhōngshān believed it was Jì Xīn,
and thus executed him.
King of Chǔ had a favorite concubine named Zhèng Xiù.
When the king recently acquired a beautiful woman,
Zhèng Xiù instructed her, saying:
"The king greatly appreciates when people cover their mouths.
When you approach the king,
you must cover your mouth."
When the beautiful woman entered for an audience,
approached the king,
she covered her mouth.
The king asked the reason,
and Zhèng Xiù said:
"She has said she dislikes the king's odor."
When the king, Zhèng Xiù, and the beautiful woman were sitting together,
Xiù first warned the attendants, saying:
"If the king says anything,
you must immediately obey his command."
The beautiful woman came very close to the king,
frequently covering her mouth.
The king flew into a rage and said:
"Cut off her nose!"
The attendants then drew their knives and mutilated the beauty.
Another account says:
The King of Wèi sent a beauty to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ was very pleased with her.
His wife, Zhèng Xiù, knowing the king's affection for her,
also showed her affection,
even more than the king did.
Clothing and playthings,
she chose whatever the beauty desired to give her.
The king said:
"My wife knows I love the new lady,
and she shows even more affection for her than I do;
this is how a filial son serves his parents,
and a loyal minister serves his lord."
Knowing the king did not suspect her of jealousy,
she then said to the new lady:
"The king is very fond of you,
but he dislikes your nose.
When you see the king, always cover your nose,
then the king will favor you long."
So the new lady followed this advice,
and every time she saw the king,
she always covered her nose.
The king said to his wife:
"The new lady always covers her nose when she sees me;
why is that?"
She replied:
"I do not know."
The king pressed her,
and she answered:
"She recently said she dislikes the smell of the king."
The king angrily said:
"Cut off her nose!"
The wife had previously warned the attendants:
"If the king says anything,
you must comply with his order."
The attendants then drew their knives and mutilated the beauty.
Fèi Wújí
was a close associate of the Ling Yǐn of Chǔ.
Xì Yuǎn had recently begun serving the Ling Yǐn,
and the Ling Yǐn was very fond of him.
Wújí then said to the Ling Yǐn:
"Since you are so fond of Yuǎn,
why not have a drink at his home?"
The Ling Yǐn said:
"Good."
He then ordered a banquet to be prepared at Xì Yuǎn's home.
Wújí instructed Yuǎn, saying:
"The Ling Yǐn is very proud and fond of weapons;
you must be respectful and careful,
first quickly display weapons in the hall and courtyard."
Yuǎn accordingly did so.
When the Ling Yǐn arrived, he was greatly alarmed,
and said:
"What is this?"
Wújí said:
"You are in danger,
leave quickly!
The situation is unpredictable."
The Ling Yǐn was furious,
raised troops, and executed Xì Yuǎn,
thus killing him.
Xī Shǒu and Zhāng Shòu were enemies.
Chén Xū, who had recently arrived,
was on bad terms with Xī Shǒu,
so he secretly had someone kill Zhāng Shòu.
The King of Wèi believed it was Xī Shǒu,
and thus executed him.
In Zhōngshān, there was a low-ranking prince
whose horses were very thin,
and his carriage very shabby.
A courtier who privately disliked him
then made a request to the king on his behalf, saying:
"The prince is very poor,
his horses are very thin;
why does the king not increase their feed?"
The king did not consent.
The courtier then secretly had someone
burn the fodder barn at night.
The king thought it was the low-ranking prince,
and thus executed him.
In Wèi, there was an old scholar
who was on bad terms with Jìyáng Jūn.
A visitor who had a private grudge against the old scholar
attacked and killed him,
then sought favor with Jìyáng Jūn,
saying:
"I killed him because he was against you,
thus I have killed him for you."
Jìyáng Jūn, without investigation, rewarded him.
Another account says:
Jìyáng Jūn had a young steward
who was not well-known
and wished to gain the lord's favor.
Qǐ sent an old scholar
to dig for herbs on Mǎlí Mountain.
The young steward of Jìyáng wanted to make this a merit,
so he went to see the lord, saying:
"Qǐ has sent an old scholar
to dig for herbs on Mǎlí Mountain,
nominally to dig herbs,
but actually to spy on your state.
If you do not kill him,
he will use Jìyáng Jūn
to bear the blame with Qǐ.
I request to assassinate him."
The lord said:
"You may."
So the next day, they found him in the northern part of the city
and assassinated him,
and Jìyáng Jūn thereafter grew closer to him.
Persuasion Four: #
Chén Xū,
a minister of the King of Wèi,
was on good terms with the King of Chǔ,
and had Chǔ attack Wèi.
When Chǔ attacked Wèi,
Chén Xū then requested to act as mediator for the King of Wèi,
and thus used the influence of Chǔ to become prime minister of Wèi.
During the time of Hán Zhāo Hóu,
millet seed was once very expensive.
Zhāo Hóu ordered an inspection of the granaries,
and the officials were indeed stealing millet seed
and selling large quantities of it.
When Zhāo Xīxù was in power in Chǔ,
someone burned the granaries and storehouses,
but the perpetrator was unknown.
Zhāo Xīxù ordered the arrest of a straw seller
and interrogated him,
and indeed, he was the arsonist.
During the time of Zhāo Xī Hóu,
when the cook presented the meal,
there was raw liver in the soup.
Zhāo Hóu summoned the cook's assistant
and rebuked him, saying:
"Why did you put raw liver in my soup?"
The cook kowtowed, admitting his fault worthy of death,
and said:
"I secretly wished to remove the head cook."
First account:
When Marquis Xī was bathing,
there was a pebble in the hot water.
Marquis Xī said:
"If the Chief Bath Attendant were dismissed,
would there be someone to replace him?"
His attendants replied:
"Yes."
Marquis Xī said:
"Summon him here."
He reprimanded him, saying:
"Why did you put a pebble in the hot water?"
The man replied:
"If the Chief Bath Attendant were dismissed,
then I could take his place,
so I put a pebble in the hot water."
During Duke Wén's time,
the chef presented roasted meat with a hair wrapped around it.
Duke Wén summoned the chef and reprimanded him, saying:
"Do you want me to choke?
Why did you wrap a hair around the roast?"
The chef kowtowed twice and pleaded:
"I have three capital offenses:
I whetted my knife on a grindstone,
making it as sharp as Gānjiàng's sword,
yet when cutting meat, the meat severed but the hair did not—
this is my first offense.
I skewered the meat slices on a stick
but did not see the hair—
this is my second offense.
I held the blazing stove,
with charcoal fire glowing entirely red,
and the roast cooked through
yet the hair did not burn—
this is my third offense.
Might there be someone in the court who dislikes me?"
The duke said:
"Well said."
He then summoned the court attendants and questioned them,
and indeed it was so,
so he executed the culprit.
Another account:
When Duke Píng of Jìn was feasting guests,
a minor official presented roasted meat with a hair wrapped around it.
Duke Píng urgently ordered the cook killed,
with no chance for appeal.
The cook cried out to heaven:
"Alas!
I have three crimes,
and I die without knowing them myself!"
Duke Píng said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"My knife is so sharp
that it cuts through bone like wind yet the hair remains unsevered—
this is my first capital offense.
Roasting it over mulberry charcoal,
the meat turns red and white but the hair does not scorch—
this is my second capital offense.
When the roast was done,
I scrutinized it closely with focused eyes,
yet failed to see the hair wrapped around the roast—
this is my third capital offense.
I suspect there might be someone in the court who secretly hates me!
Is it not too hasty to kill me?"
When the Marquis of Ráng was chancellor of Qín, Qí was strong.
The Marquis of Ráng wanted to establish Qín as emperor
but Qí would not consent,
so he requested that Qí be established as Eastern Emperor,
yet this too failed to materialize.
Persuasion Five: 〓#
During the time of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
Lí Jī was highly favored,
comparable to the principal wife,
and wanted her son Xī Qí to replace the crown prince Shēn Shēng.
She thus slandered Shēn Shēng to the ruler and had him killed,
then established Xī Qí as crown prince.
The ruler of Zhèng had already established a crown prince,
but had a beloved beautiful woman
who wanted her son to be the heir.
The consort, fearing this,
used poison to assassinate the ruler.
Zhōu Xū of Wèi held great power in Wèi,
rivaling the ruler,
and all officials and commoners feared his influence.
Zhōu Xū indeed killed the ruler and seized the government.
Cháo, the crown prince of Zhōu,
had a younger brother, Gēn,
who was greatly favored by the ruler.
When the ruler died,
Gēn rebelled in Eastern Zhōu,
dividing the state into two.
King Chéng of Chǔ appointed Shāng Chén as crown prince,
but later wanted to install Prince Zhí instead.
Shāng Chén started a rebellion,
attacked and killed King Chéng.
Another account:
King Chéng of Chǔ appointed Shāng Chén as crown prince,
then intended to install Prince Zhí.
Shāng Chén heard of this,
but it was unconfirmed,
so he asked his tutor Pān Chóng:
"How can I confirm it?"
Pān Chóng said:
"Feast Jiāng Mǐ but show her disrespect."
The crown prince followed his advice.
Jiāng Mǐ said:
"Ugh, you menial!
No wonder the king wants to depose you
and install Zhí."
Shāng Chén said:
"It's true."
Pān Chóng asked:
"Can you serve him?"
He said: "No."
"Can you become a feudal lord under him?"
He said: "No."
"Can you undertake a great endeavor?"
He said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, he mobilized the palace guards and attacked King Chéng.
King Chéng requested to eat bear's paw before dying,
but was refused,
so he committed suicide.
When Hán Wěi was chancellor under Marquis Āi of Hán,
Yán Suì was highly favored by the ruler,
and the two greatly harmed each other.
Yán Suì then had someone assassinate Hán Wěi at court,
Hán Wěi fled to the ruler and embraced him,
so they stabbed Hán Wěi and also killed Marquis Āi.
Tián Héng served as chancellor of Qí,
while Kǎn Zhǐ was favored by Duke Jiǎn,
and the two hated and sought to harm each other.
Tián Héng thus used private favors
to win over the state,
then killed Duke Jiǎn and seized the government.
Dài Huān was the Grand Steward of Sòng,
Huáng Xǐ was favored by the ruler,
and the two contended for influence
and harmed each other.
Huáng Xǐ then killed the ruler of Sòng
and seized the government.
Hú Tū said:
"If the ruler favors inner court consorts,
the crown prince is in danger;
if he favors outer court ministers,
the chancellor is in danger."
The ruler of Zhèng asked Zhèng Zhāo:
"What about the crown prince?"
He replied:
"The crown prince has not yet been born."
The ruler said:
"The crown prince has already been appointed,
yet you say 'not yet born'—
why is that?"
He replied:
"Although the crown prince is appointed,
if the ruler's fondness for women does not cease,
and a favored consort bears a son,
the ruler will surely love him,
and loving him, will want to make him heir.
Therefore, I say 'the crown prince has not yet been born.'"
Persuasion Six: 〓#
King Wén supported Fèi Zhòng to move about beside King Zhòu,
instructing him to advise King Zhòu and扰乱 his mind.
The king of Jīng sent an envoy to Qín,
and the king of Qín treated him with great respect.
The king said:
"If a rival state has a worthy man,
it is a worry for our state.
Now the envoy from the king of Jīng is very worthy,
and I am concerned about it."
The ministers remonstrated, saying:
"Given Your Majesty's wisdom and sagacity and the state's abundant resources,
and wishing for the virtuous men of the King of Jīng,
why does Your Majesty not deeply befriend them
and secretly win them over?
If Jīng considers them to be serving external interests,
they will surely be executed."
When Zhòngní was administering governance in Lǔ,
property left on the road was not picked up,
and Duke Jǐng of Qí became troubled by this.
Lí Qiě said to Duke Jǐng:
"To remove Zhòngní is as easy as blowing off a feather.
Why not invite him with generous emoluments and high office,
and send Duke Āi female musicians to inflate his pride and delight his mind.
Once Duke Āi becomes newly enamored with them,
he will surely neglect governance,
and Zhòngní will certainly remonstrate.
When he remonstrates, he will inevitably be lightly dismissed by Lǔ."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he ordered Lí Qiě to send six female musicians to Duke Āi.
Duke Āi delighted in them,
and indeed neglected governance.
Zhòngní remonstrated but was not heeded,
so he left and went to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ said to Gàn Xiàng:
"I wish to use Chǔ to support Gān Mào
and have him become chancellor in Qín.
Is this feasible?"
Gàn Xiàng replied:
"It is not feasible."
The King said:
"Why?"
He said:
"Gān Mào in his youth served Master Shǐ Jǔ.
Shǐ Jǔ
was a gatekeeper in Shàngcài,
who in major matters did not serve his ruler,
and in minor matters did not manage his household,
and was known throughout the world for his harshness.
Gān Mào served him
and was obedient to him.
With King Huì's discernment
and Zhāng Yí's eloquence,
Gān Mào served them,
obtained ten offices, and yet avoided punishment—
this shows Gān Mào's capability."
The King said:
"To appoint a chancellor for a rival state
who is capable—
why is that not feasible?"
Gàn Xiàng said:
"Previously, Your Majesty sent Shào Huá to Yuè,
and within five years, he was able to cause Yuè's downfall.
The reason for this
was that Yuè was in disorder while Chǔ was well-governed.
In the past, we knew how to use this in Yuè,
but now to lose it to Qín—
is that not too quick a loss?"
The King said:
"Then what should be done about it?"
Gàn Xiàng replied:
"It would be better to make Gòng Lì chancellor."
The King said:
"Why can Gòng Lì be made chancellor?"
He replied:
"Gòng Lì was favored and beloved in his youth,
became a high minister when grown,
wears the king's robes,
holds Dùruò in his mouth,
grasps jade rings,
and listens at court—
and moreover, he can be used to bring disorder to Qín."
When Wú attacked Jīng,
Zǐxū had someone proclaim in Jīng:
"If Zǐqī is employed,
we will attack;
if Zǐcháng is employed,
we will withdraw."
The people of Jīng heard this,
and consequently employed Zǐcháng and dismissed Zǐqī.
The men of Wú attacked them,
and thus defeated them.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn, when attacking Yú and Guó,
sent them the steeds of Qūchǎn,
the jade of Chuíjí,
and six female musicians,
to inflate their pride and disrupt their governance.
When Shūxiàng slandered Cháng Hóng,
he wrote a letter saying:
"Cháng Hóng told Shūxiàng:
'You tell the ruler of Jìn for me
that the time we agreed upon with your lord
is now opportune.
Why not quickly bring troops here?'"
Thereupon, he pretended to drop the letter in the court of the Zhōu ruler
and hurried away.
Zhōu believed Cháng Hóng was betraying Zhōu,
and thus executed Cháng Hóng and put him to death.
When Duke Huán of Zhèng was about to attack Kuài,
he first inquired about Kuài's heroes, good ministers, eloquent and wise, resolute and daring men,
recorded all their names,
selected Kuài's fine fields to bribe them,
and wrote down official titles and ranks for them.
Then he set up an altar outside the outer city gate
and buried the list,
sprinkling it with the blood of a chicken and a boar,
as if making a covenant.
The ruler of Kuài thought it was an internal revolt
and executed all his good ministers.
Duke Huán attacked Kuài,
and thus captured it.
The magistrate of Yè, Xiāng Cī,
secretly befriended the King of Zhào's attendants.
When the King of Zhào plotted to attack Yè,
Xiāng Cī would always hear of it
and inform the King of Wèi beforehand.
The King of Wèi prepared for it,
and Zhào then halted the campaign.
Explanation Seven:
A dwarf of Qín was on good terms with the King of Jīng,
and secretly befriended the King of Jīng's attendants,
while being trusted internally by Lord Huìwén.
Whenever Jīng had a plan,
the dwarf would always hear of it first
and report it to Lord Huìwén.
During the time of Lord Sì of Wèi,
he had a man near the county magistrate.
The magistrate uncovered his mat,
and the mat was very worn.
Lord Sì then sent someone to give him a mat,
saying:
"I heard that you recently uncovered your mat
and it was very worn,
so I bestow upon you a mat."
The magistrate was greatly astonished,
and thought the lord was divine.
Canon One:
The way of an enlightened ruler
is like Yǒuruò's response to Mìzǐ.
When a ruler listens to speeches,
he admires their eloquence;
when he observes actions,
he values their loftiness.
Hence, the speeches of ministers, scholars, and commoners
are grandiose,
and their personal conduct
detaches from the world.
This argument is illustrated in Tián Jiū's reply to the King of Jīng.
Thus, Mòzǐ made the wooden kite,
and Ōu Guǐ built the Wǔ palace.
Medicinal wine and loyal words—
these are what enlightened rulers and sage monarchs alone understand.
Canon Two:
If a ruler, when listening to speeches,
does not take utility as the aim,
then speakers
will mostly offer theories of thorns and white horses;
if he does not use a target as the standard,
then all archers will be like Yì.
A ruler's approach to persuasion
is like the King of Yān learning immortality;
and those skilled in persuasion
are like the men of Zhèng arguing about age.
Thus, there are speeches that are subtle, discerning, and abstruse,
yet not practical—
hence, Jì, Huì, Sòng, and Mò all drew plans in sand;
there are discussions that are lofty, profound, and grand,
yet not useful—
hence, Wèi, Cháng, Zhān, Chén, and Zhuāng were all like ghosts;
there are actions that are arduous, difficult, and firm,
yet without merit—
hence, Wù, Biàn, Bāo, Jiè, and Tián Zhòng were all like hard gourds.
Moreover, Yú Qìng refuted the craftsman, yet the house collapsed;
Fán Qié exhausted the artisan, yet the bow broke.
Therefore, to seek sincerity,
one must rely on returning provisions.
Canon III: 〓#
When relying on mutual assistance, expectations arise;
when acting for oneself, affairs get done.
Thus, fathers and sons may complain and blame each other,
while hired laborers strive to prepare fine soups.
This is illustrated by Duke Wén's preemptive declaration,
and Gōu Jiàn's praise of the Rúhuáng platform.
Hence, Duke Huán concealed his anger at Cài to attack Chǔ,
while Wǔ Qǐ, hoping for recovery, sucked the pus from a wound.
Moreover, the odes and eulogies of the former kings,
the inscriptions on bells and tripods,
are all like the giant footprints at Bōwú
or the chess game on Huàshān.
Yet what the former kings sought was benefit,
and what they employed was effort.
The proverb about building the altar
explains this in its own words.
To allow scholars
to practice the vague and expansive ways of the former kings
—is it not unsuitable for the present?
If so,
it cannot be changed.
This is like the person from Zhèng county who found a broken yoke,
the Wèi man who assisted an archer,
the wife of Bǔ Zǐ who patched worn-out trousers,
or the young serving the elder at a drink.
The words of the former kings
include those intended as minor
but interpreted as major by the world,
and those intended as major
but interpreted as minor by the world;
this cannot be known for certain.
This is illustrated by the Sòng man's interpretation of the Documents,
and the Liáng man's reading of the Records.
Thus, the former kings had the Yǐng letter,
but later ages abound in Yān interpretations.
Those who do not adapt to state affairs but seek the former kings
are all like the man who went home to fetch a measurement.
Canon IV: 〓#
Where profit lies, the people gather;
where fame is glorified, scholars die for it.
Thus, if rewards are given for achievements outside the law,
the ruler cannot derive benefit from his subordinates;
if praise is given for fame outside the law,
scholars will be encouraged by fame but not store it with the ruler.
Hence, when Zhōng Zhāng and Xū Jǐ took office,
half the people of Zhōngmóu abandoned their fields to follow literary studies;
when Duke Píng's thighs ached and feet went numb,
he dared not sit improperly,
and those in Jìn who declined office and patronage were as numerous as hammers in the state.
These three scholars
spoke in accordance with the law
as if reciting government records,
acted in line with affairs
like people following orders,
yet the two rulers treated them with excessive courtesy.
If their words deviated from the law and their actions strayed from merit,
they would be people outside the bounds,
so why would the two rulers treat them with courtesy?
Such courtesy deserves to perish.
Moreover, reclusive scholars
do not exert strength when the state has no troubles,
and do not don armor when there is danger.
To treat them with courtesy
weakens the efforts in farming and warfare;
not to treat them with courtesy
harms the ruler's laws.
When the state is secure, they are honored and prominent;
when it is in peril, they wield the authority of Qū Gōng.
What can the ruler gain from reclusive scholars?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler considers Lǐ Cī's observation of Zhōngshān.
Canon V: 〓#
The Book of Songs says:
"If you do not act personally,
the common people will not believe."
Fù Yuè illustrated this with
"not wearing purple,"
citing Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng and Duke Xiāng of Sòng,
and urging respect for farming and warfare.
If roles are not clarified,
sincerity not demanded,
yet the ruler personally occupies a lower position,
even to the point of running about or sleeping below,
or disguising himself in humble clothes,
then even Kǒng Qiū did not understand this,
hence spoke of it as like a bowl;
Lord Zōu did not understand,
so first brought shame upon himself.
The way of an enlightened ruler
is like Shū Xiàng assigning the hunt,
or Lord Zhāo's question of what to listen to.
Canon VI: 〓#
When small trust is established,
great trust is built;
thus, an enlightened ruler accumulates trust.
If rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
then prohibitions and orders will not be carried out.
This is illustrated by Duke Wén's attack on Yuán,
and Jī Zhèng's relief of famine.
Thus, Wǔ Qǐ waited for an old acquaintance to eat,
and Lord Wén kept a appointment with a gamekeeper to hunt.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler demonstrates trust,
as in Zēng Zǐ killing the pig.
The danger lies in King Lì beating the alarm drum,
and Lǐ Kuī deceiving the two armies.
Explanation I: 〓#
Fú Zǐjiàn governed Dānfù.
Yǒu Ruò saw him and said:
"Why have you grown so thin?"
Fú Zǐjiàn replied:
"The lord, unaware of my incompetence,
appointed me to govern Dānfù.
Official duties are pressing,
and I worry about them,
hence I have grown thin."
Yǒu Ruò said:
"In the past, Shǔn played the five-stringed lute,
sang the poem of the 'South Wind,'
and the world was well-governed.
Now, with Dānfù being so small,
you worry about governing it;
how would you govern the world?
Thus, with method to control it,
one can sit in the hall of the temple,
with the complexion of a maiden,
and it does not hinder governance;
without method to control it,
even if one wears oneself thin,
it still brings no benefit."
The King of Chǔ said to Tián Jiū:
"Mòzǐ
is a prominent scholar.
His personal conduct is commendable,
but his words are numerous yet not eloquent;
why is that?"
Tián Jiū replied:
"In the past, the Earl of Qín married his daughter to the Prince of Jìn,
ordering Jìn to prepare her trousseau,
with seventy maids in embroidered robes accompanying her.
When they arrived in Jìn,
the Jìn people loved the maids and scorned the princess.
This can be called skill in marrying off maids,
but not skill in marrying off a daughter.
A man of Chǔ who was selling his pearl in Zhèng
made a casket of magnolia wood,
scented it with cinnamon and pepper,
adorned it with pearls and jade,
decorated it with rose-colored gems,
and lined it with kingfisher feathers.
A man of Zhèng bought the casket and returned the pearl.
This can be called skill in selling caskets,
but not skill in selling pearls.
Nowadays, in discussions,
all speak with eloquent and ornate words,
and the ruler admires the elegance but forgets the utility.
Mòzǐ's teachings
convey the way of the former kings,
discuss the words of the sages,
to proclaim to people.
If he made his words eloquent,
he feared people would cherish the elegance
and forget the straightforward meaning,
letting elegance harm utility.
This is similar to the Chǔ man selling pearls
and the Qín earl marrying off his daughter;
therefore, his words are mostly unadorned."
Mòzǐ made a wooden kite,
which took three years to complete,
but it flew for only one day before breaking.
His disciples said:
"Master, your skill
is such that you can make a wooden kite fly."
Mòzǐ said:
"I am not as skilled as those who make carriage yokes.
Using a piece of wood only a foot long,
without expending a single morning's effort,
it can pull a load of thirty shi,
traveling far with great strength,
lasting for many years.
Now I made a kite,
which took three years to complete,
yet it broke after flying for just one day."
Huìzǐ heard this and said:
"Mòzǐ is greatly skillful,
skillful in making the nì (collar for a yoke),
but clumsy in making kites."
The King of Sòng harbored enmity against Qí,
and built a Wǔ palace.
When Guǐ sang,
passersby stopped to watch,
and the builders did not tire.
The king heard of this,
summoned him, and rewarded him.
He replied:
"My teacher Shè Jī's singing
is even more excellent than Guǐ's."
The king summoned Shè Jī and had him sing,
but passersby did not stop,
and the builders felt tired.
The king said:
"Passersby do not stop,
the builders feel tired,
his singing is not as beautiful as Guǐ's,
why is that?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty, please measure their accomplishments."
Guǐ achieved four boards,
Shè Jī eight boards;
testing their firmness,
Guǐ's penetrated five inches,
Shè Jī's two inches.
Good medicine is bitter to the taste,
yet the wise urge to drink it,
knowing it enters and cures their illness.
Loyal words grate on the ears,
but an enlightened ruler listens to them,
knowing they can lead to achievement.
Second argument: #
A man of Sòng requested
to carve a mother monkey on the tip of a thorn for the King of Yān,
insisting on three months of fasting,
after which it could be viewed.
The King of Yān thus supported him with the salary of three chariots.
The right-side attendant and metalworker said to the king:
"I have heard that a ruler does not fast for ten days without feasting.
Now, knowing the king cannot fast long
to view a useless object,
he thus sets the period at three months.
All carvers
use tools that must be smaller than what they carve.
Now I am a metalworker,
and have no means to make such a small tool;
this is an impossible thing,
Your Majesty must investigate it."
The king then detained and questioned him,
and indeed it was false,
so he killed him.
The metalworker said to the king:
"Plans without measure,
talkative scholars often speak of thorn-tip carvings."
Another account: #
The King of Yān loved delicate craftsmanship.
A man of Wèi said:
"I can carve a mother monkey on the tip of a thorn."
The King of Yān was pleased,
and supported him with the salary of five chariots.
The king said:
"I wish to observe
the guest carving the thorn-tip mother monkey."
The guest said:
"If the ruler wishes to view it,
he must not enter the palace for half a year,
nor drink wine or eat meat.
When the rain clears and the sun shines,
view it in the shade between light and dark,
then the thorn-tip mother monkey can be seen."
The King of Yān thus supported the man of Wèi,
but could not see his mother monkey.
A metalworker from below the terrace in Zhèng
said to the King of Yān:
"I
am a carver.
All tiny objects must be carved with a carving tool,
and what is carved must be larger than the tool.
Now the tip of a thorn cannot accommodate the edge of a carving tool,
making it difficult to work on the thorn's tip.
Your Majesty, try to see the guest's carving tool,
and whether he can or cannot will be known."
The king said:
"Good."
He said to the man of Wèi:
"Guest, for carving the thorn-tip mother monkey,
what do you use to work it?"
He said:
"With a carving tool."
The king said:
"I wish to see it."
The guest said:
"I request to go to my lodgings to fetch it."
And thus he fled.
Ér Shuō,
a man of Sòng,
was skilled in debate,
holding
"a white horse is not a horse"
and convincing the debaters at Qí's Jìxià.
But riding a white horse through a pass,
he still had to pay the tax for white horses.
Thus, relying on empty rhetoric
he could overcome a whole state,
yet when tested against reality and form,
he could not deceive even one person.
Newly sharpened arrowheads,
shot from a drawn crossbow,
even if blindly and recklessly released,
may still hit autumn down without fail,
yet none can repeat the exact spot,
and cannot be called good shooting,
for there is no constant target.
Setting a five-inch target,
pulling from ten paces away,
none but Yì or Péng Méng could surely hit it entirely,
for there is a constant target.
Having a standard makes it difficult,
while having no standard makes it easy.
With a constant target,
then Yì and Péng Méng are considered skillful for hitting five inches;
without a constant target,
then hitting autumn down with a reckless shot
is deemed clumsy.
Thus, responding without standards,
leads to debaters' verbose arguments;
setting standards and upholding them,
even the wise fear to err,
daring not to speak recklessly.
Now when rulers listen to persuasions,
they do not respond with standards but delight in their rhetoric;
not measuring by results,
praising actions without passing through the gate.
This is why rulers are long deceived,
and persuaders are long nurtured.
A guest taught the King of Yān the way to immortality,
the king sent someone to learn it,
but the sent learner had not yet learned
when the guest died.
The king was greatly angered,
and executed him.
The king did not realize the guest had deceived him,
but punished the learner for being late.
Believing in impossible things
and executing innocent ministers,
is the calamity of lack of scrutiny.
Moreover, what people care about most
is nothing like their own person,
if one cannot cause oneself to avoid death,
how can one make the king live forever?
Some men of Zhèng were disputing about their age,
one said:
"I am the same age as Yáo."
The other said:
"I am the same age as Huángdì's elder brother."
They argued without resolution,
simply considering the last to speak as the winner.
A guest was crafting a painted bamboo slip for Lord Zhōu,
which took three years to complete.
When the lord examined it,
it appeared no different from a lacquered slip,
and Lord Zhōu grew furious.
The painter explained:
"Build a wall ten boards high,
cut an eight-foot window in it,
and at the moment the sun first rises,
place the slip against it to observe."
Lord Zhōu did so,
and gazing upon its form,
he saw it entirely transform into dragons, snakes, birds, beasts, chariots, and horses,
with every conceivable thing depicted in full,
leaving Lord Zhōu immensely pleased.
The craftsmanship of this slip was not unrefined or difficult,
yet its utility was the same as a plain lacquered slip.
A guest was painting for the King of Qí,
who asked him:
"What is the most challenging to paint?"
He replied:
"Dogs and horses are difficult."
"What is the easiest?"
He answered:
"Ghosts and spirits are the easiest."
For dogs and horses,
are known to everyone,
appearing constantly before our eyes from dawn to dusk,
making it hard to render them accurately,
hence the difficulty.
Ghosts and spirits,
being formless,
never appear before us,
so they are easy to depict.
In Qí, there was a recluse named Tián Zhòng,
whom a man from Sòng, Qū Gǔ, visited, saying:
"I have heard of your righteousness, sir,
that you do not rely on others for sustenance.
Now I possess a giant gourd,
hard as stone,
thick and without a hollow,
which I offer to you."
Zhòng said:
"What makes a gourd valuable
is its capacity to hold things.
Now, being thick and hollow-less,
it cannot be split to contain objects;
and bearing weight like solid stone,
it cannot be cut for use as a dipper.
I have no use for such a gourd."
Qū Gǔ replied:
"Indeed,
I shall discard it."
Now, Tián Zhòng, who does not rely on others for food,
also brings no benefit to others' states,
is much like this solid gourd.
Yú Qìng, while building a house,
told the carpenter:
"The roof is too steep."
The carpenter responded:
"This is a new house;
the plaster is wet, and the rafters are green."
Yú Qìng said:
"Not so.
Wet plaster is heavy, and green rafters warp;
using warped rafters to bear heavy plaster
should make it lower."
After more time passes,
the plaster dries and the rafters season.
Dry plaster becomes light,
seasoned rafters straighten,
and straight rafters bearing light plaster
will make it steeper.
The carpenter was at a loss,
built it as instructed, and the house collapsed.
Another account says: #
Yú Qìng was about to build a house,
and the carpenter said:
"The wood is green and the plaster wet.
Green wood warps,
wet plaster is heavy;
using warped wood to bear heavy weight,
though it may stand now,
will surely collapse in time."
Yú Qìng retorted:
"Dry wood straightens,
dry plaster lightens.
If indeed they dry,
becoming lighter and straighter daily,
even over time,
it will not collapse."
The carpenter was confounded,
built it, and upon completion,
after a while, the house indeed collapsed.
Fán Qiě said:
"A bow breaks
necessarily at the end of its use,
not at the beginning.
When craftsmen string a bow,
they press it on a former for thirty days before setting the string,
then release the trigger in one day,
thus easing it at the start
but straining it at the end,
how can it not break?
I, however, string a bow differently.
Press it on a former for one day and set the string,
then release the trigger after thirty days,
thus straining it at the start
and easing it at the end."
The craftsman was cornered,
followed the method,
and the bow broke.
The words of Fán Qiě and Yú Qìng,
though eloquent and persuasive,
contradicted the nature of things.
If rulers delight in such talk without restraint,
this is why failures occur.
Not striving for the achievements of order and strength,
but indulging in the allure of clever rhetoric
and ornate speech,
is to reject men of skill
and employ those who ruin houses and break bows.
Thus, rulers in matters of state
often fail to grasp the principles of craftsmen
building houses or stringing bows.
Yet men like Fán Qiě and Yú Qìng prevail,
using empty words
that are useless but winning;
while practical matters,
being unalterable, lead to impasse.
Rulers favor much useless debate,
and value little unchangeable truth,
which is the cause of chaos.
In this age, those like Fán Qiě and Yú Qìng never cease,
and rulers never stop delighting in them,
thus esteeming the types that lead to ruin and breakage,
and treating the knowledgeable as mere laborers.
Craftsmen cannot apply their skills,
so houses collapse and bows break;
those who understand governance cannot implement their methods,
so the state falls into disorder and the ruler into peril.
When children play together,
using dust as rice,
mud as soup,
and wood as meat,
yet by evening they must return for real food,
for dust-rice and mud-soup are fit for play
but not for eating.
Similarly, praising ancient legends,
eloquent but insubstantial,
or advocating the benevolence and righteousness of former kings
yet failing to rectify the state,
this too is fit for play
but not for achieving order.
Those who admire benevolence and righteousness yet are weak and chaotic
are the three states of Jìn.
Those who do not admire them but are orderly and strong
are Qín,
yet it has not become emperor,
because its governance is not yet complete.
Persuasion three: #
When a person is an infant,
if their parents raise them neglectfully,
the child grows up resentful.
When the child becomes a strong adult,
if they provide meager support,
the parents grow angry and reproach them.
Child and parent,
being closest kin,
may yet scold or resent each other,
all due to expecting mutual care
while failing to fulfill their own roles.
As for hiring laborers to plow and sow,
the master spends household resources on good food,
and pays wages seeking efficient service,
It is not that they love the hired laborers,
but they say:
"If we do this,
the plowers will till deeply,
and the weeders will diligently hoe."
The hired laborers exert their strength
and swiftly plow and hoe,
employing all their skill to straighten the ridges and paths,
not because they love their master,
but they say:
"If we do this,
the soup will be delicious,
and the money will be easily obtained."
This is how they nurture their efforts,
with a bond as close as that between father and son,
yet their hearts are attuned to utility,
all driven by self-interest.
Thus, when people act or give,
if their intention is to benefit others,
even strangers can harmonize easily;
if their intention is to harm,
even father and son may drift apart and resent each other.
When Duke Wén attacked Sòng,
he first proclaimed:
"I have heard that the ruler of Sòng is unprincipled,
disrespecting the elders,
distributing wealth unfairly,
and issuing deceitful decrees;
I have come to execute him for the people."
When Yuè attacked Wú,
they first proclaimed:
"I have heard that the King of Wú built the Rúhuáng Terrace,
dug deep pools,
exhausting and tormenting the people,
squeezing their wealth and goods,
draining their strength;
I have come to execute him for the people."
The daughter of Cài became Duke Huán's wife;
when Duke Huán rode in a boat with her,
the lady rocked the boat,
and Duke Huán was greatly frightened.
He forbade her, but she did not stop,
so in anger, he sent her away.
Later, when he was about to summon her back,
she had already been remarried to another.
Duke Huán was furious
and prepared to attack Cài.
Minister Zhòngfǔ admonished him:
"A jest in the bedchamber
is not sufficient reason to attack another state;
no achievement can be hoped for from this.
I beg you not to let this be a pretext."
Duke Huán did not listen.
Zhòngfǔ said:
"If it must be done,
Chǔ has failed to tribute菁茅 to the Son of Heaven
for three years now.
You might as well raise an army to attack Chǔ on behalf of the Son of Heaven.
Once Chǔ submits,
then turn and attack Cài,
saying:
'I attacked Chǔ for the Son of Heaven,
yet Cài did not send troops in support.'"
Thus, they destroyed Cài.
This was righteous in name
and beneficial in reality,
so there must be the pretext of punishing for the Son of Heaven,
while achieving the reality of revenge."
Wú Qǐ, as a general of Wèi, attacked Zhōngshān.
A soldier had a festering sore,
and Wú Qǐ knelt and personally sucked out the pus.
The soldier's mother stood weeping,
and someone asked her:
"The general treats your son like this;
why are you still weeping?"
She replied:
"Wú Qǐ sucked the wound of this boy's father, and the father died;
now this son will also die,
that is why I weep."
Lord Fù of Zhào ordered craftsmen to set up hook ladders
to climb Bōwú Mountain,
carving a footprint on it,
three feet wide,
five feet long,
and inscribed it:
"Lord Fù often roamed here."
King Zhāo of Qín ordered craftsmen to set up hook ladders
to ascend Huà Mountain,
using pine and cypress hearts to make a board,
with arrows eight feet long,
and pieces eight inches long,
inscribing it:
"King Zhāo once played a game here with a celestial god."
When Duke Wén returned to his state,
upon reaching the river,
he ordered the discarding of ritual vessels,
the discarding of mats and bedding,
and those with calloused hands and feet, dark and haggard faces
to be placed behind.
Jiù Fǎn heard this and wept at night.
The duke said:
"I have been in exile for twenty years,
and only now have I returned to the state.
Jiù Fǎn hears of this and weeps instead of rejoicing;
does he not wish for my return?"
Fǎn replied:
"Ritual vessels
are for eating,
mats and bedding for sleeping,
yet you discard them.
Those with calloused hands and feet,
dark and haggard faces,
are the ones who labored with merit,
yet you place them behind.
Now that I am among those placed behind,
my heart cannot bear the sorrow,
hence I weep.
Moreover, I have employed deceit and falsehoods many times to help you return to the state.
I myself detest such acts,
how much more should you?"
He bowed twice and prepared to leave.
Duke Wén stopped him, saying:
"As the proverb goes:
'Those who build the altar
handle it with bare hands and set it up,
then don ceremonial caps and robes to sacrifice to it.'
Now you helped me gain the state,
but will not help me govern it;
you helped me set it up,
but will not help me sacrifice to it;
how can that be?"
He untied the left trace horse
and made a covenant by the river.
A man from Zhèng County, Bǔ Zǐ, asked his wife to make trousers,
and his wife asked:
"What should the trousers be like?"
The husband said:
"Like my old trousers."
The wife thus ruined the new ones,
making them like the old trousers.
A man from Zhèng County found a chariot yoke,
but did not know its name,
so he asked someone:
"What is this thing?"
The reply was:
"This is a chariot yoke."
Soon he found another one
and asked someone:
"What is this thing?"
The reply was:
"This is a chariot yoke."
The questioner became furious and said:
"Earlier you said it was a chariot yoke,
now you say it's a chariot yoke again;
how can there be so many?
This woman is deceiving me!"
Thus, he fought with her.
A man from Wèi who assisted in archery,
when a bird arrived,
first waved his turban at it,
frightening the bird away instead of shooting it.
The wife of Bǔ Zǐ from Zhèng County went to the market
and bought a turtle to bring home.
Passing by the Yǐng River,
she thought it was thirsty,
so she released it to let it drink,
thus losing her turtle.
A young person serving an elder to drink,
when the elder drinks,
also drinks themselves.
Another account:
A man from Lǔ who prided himself on mimicry,
seeing an elder unable to finish his drink in one go,
spat,
and he imitated the spitting.
First:
In the state of Sòng, there was a young man who also wished to emulate virtuous behavior.
Seeing an elder drink without leaving any remainder,
though unable to handle much alcohol, he wanted to finish his drink completely.
The classic says:
"Bind it with a sash."
A man of Sòng who studied this,
accordingly used a double sash to bind himself.
Someone asked:
"What is this for?"
He replied:
"The classic says so,
and thus it should be."
The classic says:
"Once carved and polished,
return to simplicity."
A man of Liáng who studied this,
in his actions and speech imitated learning,
and conducted affairs with elaborate refinement,
saying:
"This is difficult."
Yet he lost the true essence.
Someone asked:
"What is this for?"
He replied:
"The classic says so,
and thus it should be."
A man of Yǐng was writing a letter to the chancellor of Yān.
Writing at night,
the light was dim,
so he said to the candle holder:
"Raise the candle."
And he mistakenly wrote "raise the candle" in the letter.
"Raise the candle"
was not the intended meaning of the letter.
The chancellor of Yān received the letter and interpreted it,
saying: "'Raise the candle'
means esteem brightness;
esteeming brightness
means promoting the worthy and appointing them."
The chancellor reported this to the king,
who was greatly pleased,
and the state was thereby well-governed.
Though it was well-governed,
this was not the letter's intended meaning.
Many scholars of today are like this.
A man of Zhèng was about to buy shoes.
