He first measured his foot and placed the measurement on his seat,
but upon going to the market, forgot to bring it.
Having found the shoes,
he then said:
"I forgot to bring the measurement."
He returned home to fetch it.
By the time he returned,
the market had closed,
and he could not get the shoes.
Someone asked:
"Why didn't you try them on with your foot?"
He said:
"I'd rather trust the measurement,
than trust myself."
Argument Four:
Wáng Dēng was magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
He reported to Lord Xiāng, saying:
"In Zhōngmóu, there are scholars named Zhōng Zhāng and Xū Jǐ.
Their conduct is very cultivated,
and their learning is very broad.
Why does my lord not promote them?"
The lord said:
"You bring them to see me,
and I will make them high officials."
His steward admonished him:
"High official is an important position in Jìn.
Now they receive it without merit,
which is not in line with the intentions of Jìn's ministers.
Has my lord only heard of them but not seen them?"
Lord Xiāng said:
"When I selected Wáng Dēng,
I both heard and saw him;
if for those Wáng Dēng selects,
I again have to hear and see them,
then this process of hearing and seeing others would never end."
Wáng Dēng presented two high officials in one day,
and granted them fields and residences.
The people of Zhōngmóu abandoned their plowing,
sold their homes and gardens to follow literary studies,
amounting to half the city.
Shū Xiàng was in attendance.
Duke Píng asked about affairs,
and though the duke's thighs ached, his feet were numb, and cramps twisted his muscles,
he dared not break proper posture.
When the state of Jìn heard of this, all said:
"Shū Xiàng is a worthy man,
and Duke Píng treats him with such respect
that he endured cramps without daring to break posture."
Those in Jìn who sought office or admired Shū Xiàng
were as numerous as grains in a measure.
In Zhèng county, there was a man named Qū Gōng.
Hearing the enemy,
he was terrified,
and feigned death;
when the fear passed,
he came back to life.
Lord Fù of Zhào sent Lǐ Cī to observe
whether Zhōngshān could be attacked or not.
Returning, he reported:
"Zhōngshān can be attacked.
If my lord does not attack soon,
he will fall behind Qí and Yān."
Lord Fù said:
"Why can it be attacked?"
Lǐ Cī replied:
"Its ruler shows favor to recluses,
tilting his carriage canopy
to visit scholars in poor alleys and narrow lanes,
doing so for tens of them,
and treating common scholars as equals
for hundreds of them."
The lord said:
"By your account,
this is a worthy ruler;
how can he be attacked?"
Cī said: "Not so.
If he favors prominent recluses
and gives them audience,
then warriors become negligent in battle formations;
if the ruler honors scholars
and places commoners at court,
then farmers become lazy in the fields.
If warriors are negligent in formations,
the army is weakened;
if farmers are lazy in the fields,
the state becomes poor.
With an army weaker than the enemy's,
and the state impoverished within,
yet not perishing—
such a thing has never happened.
Would it not be fitting to attack them?"
Lord Fù said:
"Well said."
He raised troops and attacked Zhōngshān,
and thus destroyed it.
Argument Five:
Duke Huán of Qí loved wearing purple,
and the whole state followed suit in wearing purple.
At that time,
five pieces of plain cloth were not worth one purple cloth.
Duke Huán was troubled by this
and said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I love wearing purple,
and purple has become extremely expensive.
The people of the whole state incessantly love wearing purple;
what am I to do?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"If my lord wishes to stop this,
why not try not wearing purple yourself?"
Then he said to his attendants:
"I detest the smell of purple."
Thereupon, whenever an attendant in purple approached,
the duke would surely say:
"Step back a little;
I detest the smell of purple."
The duke said:
"Agreed."
On that day,
no court officials wore purple;
the next day,
no one in the capital wore purple;
within three days,
no one within the borders wore purple.
First Account:
The King of Qí had a fondness for wearing purple,
and all the people of Qí followed suit.
In the state of Qí, five white garments could not buy one purple one.
The king was troubled by the high cost of purple,
and his tutor advised him, saying:
"The Book of Songs says:
'If you do not act personally and with sincerity,
the common people will not believe you.'
Now, if you wish for the people to stop wearing purple,
I beg Your Majesty to remove your own purple robe when holding court.
When any courtier approaches in purple attire,
say to them:
'Step back!
I detest the foul odor.'"
On that very day,
no court official wore purple;
within that month,
no one in the capital wore purple;
by the end of the year,
no one within the borders wore purple.
Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng said to Zǐchǎn:
"Our state is small,
sandwiched between Chǔ and Jìn.
Now our city walls are incomplete,
our weapons and armor are unprepared,
and we cannot handle unforeseen events."
Zǐchǎn replied:
"I have long sealed off our external threats,
and our internal defenses are already secure.
Although the state is small,
it is not yet in danger.
My lord, have no worry."
Thus, Duke Jiǎn lived out his life without calamity.
Another Account:
Zǐchǎn served as minister of Zhèng,
and Duke Jiǎn said to Zǐchǎn:
"I find no joy in drinking.
The ritual vessels are not grand,
the bells, drums, pipes, and lutes do not sound,
my affairs are not unified;
the state is unstable,
the people are ungoverned,
farming and warfare are not harmonized,
this too is your fault.
You have your duties,
and I have mine,
let each keep to their responsibilities."
Zǐchǎn withdrew and administered the government for five years,
until there were no thieves in the state,
no lost items were picked up on the roads,
no one would pluck peaches or dates shading the streets,
and a dropped awl or knife would be returned within three days.
For three years without change,
the people knew no hunger.
Duke Xiāng of Sòng battled the men of Chǔ
at Zhuō Valley.
The Sòng army had already formed ranks,
while the Chǔ troops had not yet crossed the river.
The Right Marshal Gòu Qiáng hurried forth to advise, saying:
"The Chǔ are many, and we of Sòng are few.
I beg to let the Chǔ cross halfway, before they form ranks, and strike them,
they will surely be defeated."
Duke Xiāng said:
"I have heard the gentleman say:
'Do not wound the already injured,
do not capture the gray-haired,
do not push others into danger,
do not press others in distress,
do not drum against those not in formation.'
Now to strike Chǔ before they have crossed
harms righteousness.
Let the Chǔ finish crossing and form their battle array
before we drum and advance our troops."
The Right Marshal said:
"My lord does not love the people of Sòng,
whose very hearts are not preserved,
but only insists on righteousness."
The Duke said:
"Return to your ranks, or face military law."
The Right Marshal returned to his position,
and the Chǔ had already formed ranks and arrayed themselves,
then the Duke drummed the advance.
The Sòng army was greatly defeated,
the Duke was wounded in the thigh,
and died after three days.
This was the calamity of admiring personal benevolence and righteousness.
If one must rely on the ruler's personal involvement
for the people to obey,
then this would require the ruler
to plow for his own food,
and to serve in battle in the front lines,
before the people would farm and fight;
wouldn't that make the ruler too endangered?
And wouldn't that make the ministers too secure?
Duke Jǐng of Qí was touring the Shǎo Sea,
when a courier came from the capital to report:
"Yàn is gravely ill,
and near death,
fearing you may arrive too late."
Duke Jǐng rose abruptly,
and another courier arrived.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Hurry and harness the team of Fán Qiě,
with Zōu Zǐ and Hán Shū as drivers."
After a few hundred paces,
thinking Zōu Zǐ was not fast enough,
he seized the reins and drove himself;
after a few hundred more paces,
thinking the horses were not advancing,
he abandoned the chariot entirely and ran.
With the excellence of Fán Qiě
and the skill of Zōu Zǐ and Hán Shū,
he still thought it inferior to running on foot.
King Zhāo of Wèi wished
to involve himself in official matters,
and said to Mèngcháng Jūn:
"I wish to participate in governance."
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"If you wish to involve yourself in official matters,
why not try studying the laws?"
King Zhāo read a dozen or so bamboo strips of the legal code and fell asleep.
The King said:
"I cannot read these laws."
As for not personally wielding power,
yet wanting to do what should be done by ministers,
isn't falling asleep quite fitting?
Confucius said:
"The ruler
is like a vessel;
the people
are like water.
If the vessel is square, the water is square;
if the vessel is round, the water is round."
The Lord of Zōu liked to wear long tassels,
and all his attendants wore long tassels too,
making tassels very expensive.
The Lord was troubled by this,
and asked his attendants,
who replied:
"My lord favors them,
so the common people wear them often,
hence the high cost."
The Lord then cut off his own tassels before going out,
and no one in the state wore long tassels thereafter.
The Lord could not issue orders
setting clothing standards for the people to prohibit it,
but cut his tassels to set an example for the people first,
which is like leading them by self-punishment.
Shū Xiàng distributed game from a hunt,
giving more to those with greater achievements,
and less to those with lesser achievements.
Hán Zhāo Hóu said to Shēn Zǐ:
"Laws and regulations are very hard to implement."
Shēn Zǐ replied:
"The law
grants rewards based on merit,
and appoints offices according to ability.
Now you establish laws
but heed the requests of your attendants,
this is why it is difficult to implement."
Zhāo Hóu said:
"From now on, I know how to enforce the law,
and whom I should listen to."
One day,
Shēn Zǐ requested an official post for his cousin.
Zhāo Hóu said:
"This is not what I learned from you.
Should I grant your request,
and ruin your principles?
Or should I refuse your request?"
Shēn Zǐ withdrew to his quarters and asked for punishment.
Persuasion Six: 〓#
Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Yuán,
carrying ten days' rations,
and set a deadline of ten days with his ministers.
After ten days at Yuán, it had not fallen,
so he sounded the gong to retreat,
withdrew the troops, and left.
A man emerging from Yuán reported:
"Yuán will surrender in three days."
The ministers and attendants advised:
"The supplies in Yuán are exhausted and their strength spent,
you should simply wait."
The lord said:
"I set ten days as the deadline with my troops,
if I don't withdraw,
this would mean abandoning my credibility.
To gain Yuán at the cost of breaking trust,
I will not do."
Thereupon he withdrew his troops and left.
The people of Yuán heard this and said:
"With a ruler so trustworthy,
how can we not submit to him?"
Then they surrendered to the lord.
The people of Wèi heard and said:
"With a ruler so trustworthy,
how can we not follow him?"
Then they surrendered to the lord.
Confucius heard of it and recorded:
"The means by which he attacked Yuán and gained Wèi was trustworthiness."
Lord Wén asked Jī Zhèng:
"How to relieve famine?"
He replied:
"Trustworthiness."
The lord asked:
"What kind of trustworthiness?"
He said:
"Trust in titles, trust in duties, and trust in principles.
Trust in titles
ensures officials adhere to their responsibilities,
good and evil do not transgress,
and all affairs proceed without negligence;
trust in duties
ensures not missing the opportune time,
and the common people do not overstep;
trust in principles
encourages close relatives to exert themselves,
and those afar will submit."
Wú Qǐ went out,
met an old acquaintance and invited him to dine.
The old acquaintance said:
"Alright,
I'll return to dine presently."
Wú Qǐ said:
"I'll wait for you to eat."
The old acquaintance did not come by evening,
yet Wú Qǐ waited without eating.
Early the next morning,
he sent someone to find the old acquaintance.
When the old acquaintance arrived,
only then did he eat with him.
Marquis Wén of Wèi scheduled a hunt with the gamekeeper.
The next day,
there happened to be strong winds,
his attendants tried to stop Marquis Wén,
but he would not listen,
saying:
"No. To break my word
because of strong winds
is something I won't do."
So he drove the carriage himself,
braved the wind, and dismissed the gamekeeper.
Zēngzǐ's wife went to the market,
their child followed her crying.
His mother said:
"You go back,
when I return I'll slaughter the pig for you."
Upon returning from the market,
Zēngzǐ prepared to catch and kill the pig,
his wife stopped him, saying:
"I was only joking with the child."
Zēngzǐ said:
"One shouldn't joke with a child.
A child lacks knowledge,
it learns from its parents,
heeding their teachings.
Now if you deceive him,
you're teaching him to deceive.
If a mother deceives her child,
the child will not trust his mother,
this is not the way to teach properly."
So he cooked the pig.
King Lì of Chǔ had an alarm system,
made a drum,
to use with the people for defense.
Once, drunk from wine,
he mistakenly struck it,
causing great alarm among the people.
He sent someone to stop them,
saying:
"I was drunk and joking with my attendants,
and struck it by mistake."
The people all dispersed.
After several months,
when there was a real alarm,
he beat the drum but the people did not respond,
so he had to change the order and clarify the signal
before the people trusted it again.
Lǐ Kuī warned his two flanks,
saying:
"Be vigilant against the enemy,
they may attack you at any time."
After repeating this several times with no enemy appearing,
the two flanks grew slack,
and no longer believed Lǐ Kuī.
Several months later,
the Qín people launched a surprise attack,
nearly capturing his army.
This was the disaster of not being trusted.
Another account says:
Lǐ Kuī was fighting the Qín people,
he said to the left flank:
"Charge quickly!
The right flank has already advanced."
Then he galloped to the right flank and said:
"The left flank has already advanced."
Both flanks said:
"They've advanced."
Thereupon they all rushed forward.
The following year,
in a battle with the Qín people,
when the Qín launched a surprise attack,
they nearly captured his army.
This was the disaster of not being trusted.
#There were people disputing with each other.
Zǐ Chǎn separated them and prevented them from communicating,
then inverted their statements to inform and thus understand the truth.
Duke Sì of Wèi sent someone to pretend at the customs market,
the market officer interrogated him harshly,
whereupon the man offered the officer money,
and the officer let him go.
Duke Sì then said to the market officer:
"Once a passerby gave you money,
and you reprimanded him for it."
The market officer was greatly alarmed,
considering Duke Sì to be perceptive.
Canon One: #
Being punished for a crime,
one bears no grudge against the superior,
as with Yuè Wēi sitting before Zǐ Gāo.
Being rewarded for merit,
the minister feels no gratitude toward the ruler,
as with Dí Huáng holding the right tally and riding in a carriage.
If King Xiāng had understood,
Zhāo Mǎo wouldn't have had five carriages yet worn straw sandals.
If the superior does not err in appointments,
and ministers do not falsely claim ability,
then ministers will be like Fū Shǎoshì Zhōu.
Canon Two: #
Rely on authority, not on trust,
hence Dōngguō Yá criticized Guǎn Zhòng.
Rely on methods, not on trust,
hence Hún Xuān faulted Lord Wén.
Thus, a ruler with methods
honors rewards to fully utilize abilities,
and enforces punishments to prohibit evil.
Even with flawed conduct,
he surely gains benefits.
As when Lord Jiǎn employed Yáng Hǔ,
and Lord Āi asked about "one foot."
Canon Three: #
If the principles between ruler and minister are lost,
then even King Wén would tie his own shoes and boast.
Not distinguishing between court and leisure,
then Jì Sūn remained solemn for life yet met with assassination.
Canon Four: #
Benefiting what should be prohibited,
prohibiting what should be benefited,
even a deity couldn't manage.
Praising the guilty,
condemning the rewarded,
even Yáo couldn't govern.
To make a gate yet not let people enter,
to offer profit yet not let them advance,
this is how chaos arises.
The Marquis of Qí did not heed his courtiers,
and the Lord of Wèi did not listen to flatterers,
but with keen insight illuminated all his ministers,
so Jù did not waste gold and coins,
nor did Chán use jade discs.
When Xīmén Bào requested to govern Yè again,
it was sufficient to understand this.
It is like a thief being proud of an infant's fur coat,
or a punished cripple glorifying in his garment.
Zǐ Chuò drew to the left and right,
removing ants and driving away flies.
How could there not be Duke Huán's worry over seeking office,
and King Xuān's concern about emaciated horses?
Canon Five: 〓#
If ministers conduct themselves with humility and frugality,
then ranks are insufficient to demonstrate rewards;
if favor and glory are without restraint,
then ministers will encroach and oppress.
The explanation lies in Miáo Bēnhuáng criticizing Xiàn Bó,
and Confucius discussing Yàn Yīng.
Hence Confucius judged Guǎn Zhòng and Sūnshū Áo.
And the demeanor of coming and going changed,
Yáng Hǔ's words revealed his ministers.
But Lord Jiǎn's response to his ministers lost the ruler's method.
When factions harmonize with each other,
and ministers achieve their desires,
then the ruler becomes isolated;
when all ministers recommend publicly,
and subordinates do not harmonize,
then the ruler is enlightened.
Yáng Hǔ would have been as worthy as Zhào Wǔ,
and as impartial as Xiè Hú,
yet Lord Jiǎn considered him thorny brambles,
which is not the way to govern the state.
Canon Six: 〓#
When the ducal house is weak,
it fears straightforward speech;
when private conduct prevails,
public achievements diminish.
The explanation lies in Wénzǐ's direct words,
and Wǔzǐ's use of the cane;
Zǐchǎn's loyal admonitions,
angered Zǐguó with reprimands;
Liáng Chē applied the law,
yet Marquis Chéng confiscated his seal;
Guǎn Zhòng acted impartially,
yet the people of the state complained and resented him.
Explanation One: 〓#
When Confucius served as minister in Wèi,
his disciple Zǐgāo was a prison officer,
who amputated people's feet,
and one of the amputated guarded the gate.
Someone spoke ill of Confucius to the Lord of Wèi,
saying:
"Ní intends to start a rebellion."
The Lord of Wèi wanted to arrest Confucius.
Confucius fled,
his disciples all escaped,
Zǐgāo followed going out the gate,
the cripple guided him
and hid him in a room under the gate,
so the officers could not catch him.
At midnight,
Zǐgāo asked the cripple:
"I could not violate the ruler's laws
and personally amputated your foot,
this is the time for you to take revenge,
so why were you willing to help me escape?
How have I deserved this from you?"
The cripple said:
"My foot was cut off,
rightly because my crime deserved it,
there was nothing to be done.
But when you, sir, tried my case,
you tilted the laws,
speaking for me in order,
greatly desiring my exemption,
and I knew it.
When the case was decided and guilt fixed,
you looked distressed and unhappy,
showing it in your face,
I saw and knew it again.
It was not due to personal favor towards me,
but your innate benevolence
and heart's nature made it so.
This is why I am pleased
and grateful to you, sir."
Confucius said:
"Those skilled in benefiting others
plant virtue,
those unable to benefit others
plant resentment.
The leveler
is for evening measures,
the officer
is for balancing laws,
those who govern the state
must not lose balance."
Tián Zǐfāng went from Qí to Wèi,
and saw Zhái Huáng riding in a carriage with outriders.
Fāng thought it was Marquis Wén,
so he moved his chariot to another road to avoid him,
but it was only Zhái Huáng.
Fāng asked:
"Why do you ride in this carriage?"
He said:
"The ruler planned to attack Zhōngshān,
I recommended Zhái Jiǎo
and the plan succeeded;
and when about to attack,
I recommended Yuè Yáng and Zhōngshān was taken;
having obtained Zhōngshān,
he worried about governing it,
I recommended Lǐ Kè and Zhōngshān was well-governed:
therefore the ruler bestowed this carriage."
Fāng said:
"The favor given for your merit is still meager."
When Qín and Hán attacked Wèi,
Zhāo Mǎo persuaded in the west and Qín and Hán withdrew;
when Qí and Jīng attacked Wèi,
Mǎo persuaded in the east and Qí and Jīng withdrew.
King Xiāng of Wèi supported him with five chariot teams.
Mǎo said:
"Bóyí was buried with the rank of general at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
and all under heaven said:
'With Bóyí's worth
and his praised benevolence,
to bury him as a general,
is like not covering his hands and feet.'
Now I have stopped the armies of four states,
yet the king gives me only five chariot teams,
this recognition of merit
is like being loaded with victory yet wearing straw sandals."
"Shǎoshì Zhōu was
an ancient man of integrity, purity, and honesty,
serving as a strongman for Lord Xiāng of Zhào.
When he wrestled with Xúzǐ of Zhōngmóu,
he was not as strong,
so he went in and told Lord Xiāng
to recommend him as his replacement.
Lord Xiāng said:
"Your position
is what others desire,
why do you recommend Xúzǐ to replace yourself?"
He said:
"I serve my lord with my strength.
Now Xúzǐ is stronger than I,
if I do not recommend him as my replacement,
I fear others will speak of it
and I will be at fault."
Another account:
Shǎoshì Zhōu was the attendant rider for Lord Xiāng,
when they reached Jìnyáng,
there was a strongman, Niú Zǐgēng,
and wrestling with him, he could not win.
Zhōu said to his lord:
"The reason my lord employs me as attendant rider
is because of my great strength.
Now there is one stronger than I,
I wish to recommend him."
Explanation Two: 〓#
Duke Huán of Qí was about to establish Guǎn Zhòng,
and ordered his ministers:
"I will establish Guǎn Zhòng as Zhòngfù.
Those in favor enter the gate and go left,
those against enter and go right."
Dōngguō Yá stood in the middle of the gate.
The lord said:
"I have appointed Guǎn Zhòng as 'Zhòng Fù',
and issued the order:
'Those who approve go to the left,
those who disapprove go to the right.'
Now why do you stand in the middle gate?"
Yá said:
"With Guǎn Zhòng's wisdom,
is he capable of planning for the empire?"
The lord said:
"He is capable."
"With his decisiveness,
would he dare undertake great affairs?"
The lord said:
"He would dare."
Yá said:
"If his wisdom can plan for the empire,
and his decisiveness dares undertake great affairs,
you would then entrust him with the state's authority entirely.
With Guǎn Zhòng's ability,
leveraging your power to govern Qí State,
wouldn't this be perilous?"
The lord said:
"Well said."
He then ordered Xí Péng to handle internal affairs,
and Guǎn Zhòng to handle external affairs, making them check each other.
When Duke Wén of Jìn was fleeing exile,
Jī Zhèng carried a pot of food
and followed him.
They lost their way while wandering,
and got separated from the duke.
Though hungry and crying on the road,
he endured starvation and dared not eat from it.
When Duke Wén returned to his state,
he raised troops to attack Yuán,
conquering and capturing it.
Duke Wén said:
"One who lightly endures the suffering of hunger
and preserves the pot of food intact
will surely not betray Yuán."
He then appointed him as governor of Yuán.
Minister Hún Xuān heard of this and criticized it,
saying:
"To trust that he won't betray Yuán
merely because he didn't touch the pot of food
—isn't this lacking in method?"
Therefore, an enlightened ruler
does not rely on others not betraying him,
but relies on making himself unbetrayable;
does not rely on others not deceiving him,
but relies on making himself undeceivable.
Yáng Hǔ declared:
"If the ruler is worthy and wise,
then serve him with all one's heart;
if unworthy,
then conceal treachery and test him."
Expelled from Lǔ,
suspected in Qí,
he fled to Zhào,
where Lord Jiǎn of Zhào welcomed him and made him minister.
His attendants said:
"Hǔ is adept at usurping state power from others,
why make him minister?"
Lord Jiǎn said:
"Yáng Hǔ is bent on seizing power,
I am bent on preserving it."
He then applied methods to control him.
Yáng Hǔ dared not do wrong,
serving Lord Jiǎn well,
strengthening his lord's state,
nearly achieving hegemony.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"I've heard that in ancient times Kuí had one foot—
is it really true he had only one foot?"
Confucius replied:
"No,
Kuí did not have one foot.
Kuí was ill-tempered and malicious,
so people generally disliked him.
Nevertheless,
the reason he avoided harm from others
was his trustworthiness.
People all said:
'This one quality alone,
is sufficient.'
Kuí did not have one foot,
but one quality was enough."
Duke Āi said:
"If this is indeed so,
then it certainly is sufficient."
Another account says:
Duke Āi asked Confucius:
"I've heard Kuí had one foot—
is it true?"
He replied:
"Kuí
was a man;
why would he have one foot?
He had no other extraordinary traits,
but uniquely understood music.
Yáo said:
'One Kuí is enough.'
He appointed him as Music Master.
Therefore, gentlemen say:
'Kuí has one,
enough'
—not one foot."
Persuasion Three:
When King Wén attacked Chóng,
he reached Fèng Huáng Xū,
where his shoelace came untied,
so he tied it himself.
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Why do this yourself?"
The king said:
"A superior
ruler's companions
are all his teachers;
a middling
ruler's companions
are all his friends;
an inferior ruler's companions
are all his servants.
Now these are all my former lord's ministers,
so there is no one I can order."
Another account says:
When Duke Wén of Jín battled Chǔ,
he reached Huáng Fèng Ridge,
where his shoelace came untied,
so he tied it himself.
His attendants said:
"Couldn't you have someone else do it?"
The duke said:
"I have heard:
a superior ruler's companions
are all those he respects;
a middling
ruler's companions
are all those he loves;
an inferior
ruler's companions
are all those he despises.
Though I am unworthy,
my former lord's men are all here,
therefore I find it difficult to order them."
Jìsūn favored scholars,
remaining dignified his whole life,
his residence and clothing always like at court.
But when Jìsūn happened to relax,
making a fault,
he couldn't maintain it long.
So the guests thought he disliked and slighted them,
conspired to resent him,
and eventually killed Jìsūn.
Therefore, gentlemen avoid excess and extremity.
Another account says:
Nángōng Jìngzǐ asked Yán Zhuōjù:
"Jìsūn supported Confucius' disciples,
those in court robes sitting with him numbered tens,
yet he met with assassination—
why?"
He said:
"Formerly, King Chéng of Zhōu
kept entertainers and dwarves close
to satisfy his whims,
but consulted gentlemen on affairs—
thus he could fulfill his desires in the empire.
Now Jìsūn supported Confucius' disciples,
those in court robes sitting with him numbered tens,
but consulted entertainers and dwarves on affairs—
thus he met with assassination.
Therefore it is said:
What matters is not whom you live with,
but whom you consult."
Confucius was seated in attendance with Duke Āi of Lǔ,
who presented him with peaches and millet.
The Duke said:
"Please partake."
Zhòngní first ate the millet and then tasted the peaches,
whereupon all the attendants covered their mouths and laughed.
Duke Āi said:
"The millet
is not for eating,
but for cleansing the peaches."
Zhòngní replied:
"Qiū knows this.
However, millet
is the foremost of the five grains,
and is used as the principal offering in sacrifices to former kings.
Among the six categories of fruits,
the peach is the lowliest,
and cannot enter the temple in sacrifices to former kings.
I have heard
that a gentleman uses the humble to cleanse the noble,
but never the noble to cleanse the humble.
Now to use the foremost of the five grains
to cleanse the lowliest of fruits
is to use the superior to cleanse the inferior.
I consider this contrary to righteousness,
and therefore dare not place it before
the temple offerings."
Lord Jiǎn said to his attendants:
"The carriage mat is too luxurious.
Though a cap may be humble,
it must be worn on the head;
though shoes may be noble,
they must be trodden underfoot.
Now this carriage mat
is so excessively fine,
what shoes should I wear to tread upon it?
To lavish care on what is below while exhausting what is above
undermines the foundation of righteousness."
Fèi Zhòng advised Zhòu:
"Lord Xībó Chāng is virtuous,
the common people admire him,
and the feudal lords rally to him.
He must be executed;
if not,
he will surely become a calamity for Yīn."
Zhòu said:
"You speak of a righteous lord,
how can he be executed?"
Fèi Zhòng said:
"Though a cap may be worn and torn,
it must be worn on the head;
though shoes may be richly colored,
they must be trodden on the ground.
Now Xībō Chāng,
though a minister,
cultivates righteousness and attracts followers.
In the end, he will become the world's scourge.
Is he not destined to flourish?
When a minister does not use his virtue for his lord's benefit,
he must be executed.
Moreover, when a lord executes his minister,
how can there be fault?"
Zhòu said:
"Benevolence and righteousness
are what the superior uses to encourage the inferior.
Now Chāng values benevolence and righteousness,
he cannot be executed."
After three attempts went unheeded,
the state was lost.
King Xuān of Qí asked Kuāng Qiàn:
"Do Confucians play board games?"
He replied:
"They do not."
The King asked:
"Why not?"
Kuāng Qiàn answered:
"In board games, the 'owl' piece is valued,
yet the winner must remove it.
Removing the 'owl'
means destroying what is valued.
Confucians consider this harmful to righteousness,
hence they do not play."
He asked further:
"Do Confucians practice archery?"
The reply:
"They do not.
Archery
involves harming from below what is above,
which is like subordinates injuring their lord.
Confucians consider this harmful to righteousness,
hence they do not practice archery."
He asked again:
"Do Confucians play the sè?"
The reply:
"They do not.
The sè uses small strings for loud sounds
and large strings for soft sounds,
thus reversing the order of large and small,
exchanging the positions of noble and base.
Confucians consider this harmful to righteousness,
hence they do not play it."
King Xuān said:
"Well said."
Zhòngní said:
"Rather than having the people flatter their inferiors,
it is better to have them flatter their superiors."
Persuasion Four:
Jù was a recluse of Qí;
Chán was a recluse of Wèi.
The rulers of Qí and Wèi lacked discernment,
unable to personally oversee their domains,
they heeded their attendants' words.
Thus these two men spent gold and jade
to seek official posts.
Xīmén Bào served as magistrate of Yè,
upright, restrained, pure, and sincere,
not seeking the slightest personal gain.
But he was very curt with the attendants.
The attendants therefore conspired together
to slander him.
After one year,
during the annual report,
the lord confiscated his seal.
Bào requested:
"Formerly, I did not know how to govern Yè,
but now I have learned.
I beg to receive the seal
and govern Yè again.
If I fail,
I will accept execution by axe."
Marquess Wén relented
and returned it to him.
Bào then heavily taxed the people
and diligently served the attendants.
After one year,
during the annual report,
Marquess Wén welcomed him with a bow.
Bào replied:
"In previous years I governed Yè for you,
and you took away my seal;
now I govern Yè for your attendants,
and you bow to me.
I cannot govern any longer."
Thereupon he tendered his seal and left.
Marquess Wén would not accept it,
saying:
"I formerly did not understand you,
but now I do.
I hope you will strive to govern for me."
Still, he did not accept it.
In Qí, the son of a dog-skin thief
and the son of a foot-amputee were playing and boasting.
The thief's son said:
"Only my father's robe has a tail."
The amputee's son said:
"Only my father never lacks trousers in winter."
Zǐ Chuò said:
"No one can draw a square with the left hand
and a circle with the right simultaneously.
Using meat to rid ants
only attracts more ants;
using fish to drive away flies
only brings more flies."
Duke Huán said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"Offices are few but seekers are many,
I am troubled by this."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"If my lord does not heed the requests of attendants,
but assigns stipends according to ability,
and grants offices based on merit,
then none will dare seek office improperly.
What concern would my lord have?"
Hán Xuānzǐ said:
"My horses have plenty of beans and grain,
yet they are very lean,
why is this?
I am troubled by it."
Zhōu Shì replied:
"If you have the grooms feed them all the grain,
even if you don't want them fat,
it would be impossible.
If you claim to give them much,
but actually give little;
even if you don't want them lean,
it would also be impossible.
If my lord does not examine the actual situation,
but just sits and worries about it,
the horses will still not get fat."
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng about appointing officials,
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In discerning speech,
and integrity with goods,
and understanding human nature,
I am not as good as Xián Shāng,
I ask to appoint him as Chief Justice.
In dignified etiquette,
and treating guests with proper rites,
I am not as good as Xí Péng,
I ask to appoint him as Master of Ceremonies.
In reclaiming wasteland and building towns,
opening up land and producing grain,
I am not as good as Nìng Qì,
I ask to appoint him as Minister of Agriculture.
When the three armies are arrayed for battle,
making soldiers look upon death as going home,
I am not as good as Gōngzǐ Chéngfù,
I ask to appoint him as Grand Marshal.
In offending the ruler's countenance with extreme remonstrance,
I am not as good as Dōngguō Yá,
I ask to appoint him as Remonstrance Minister.
To govern Qí,
these five men are sufficient;
but to achieve hegemony and kingship,
I, Yíwú, am here."
Story Five:
When Mèng Xiànbó was minister of Jìn,
weeds grew in his courtyard,
thorns grew outside his gate,
he ate only one kind of food,
sat on single mats,
had no concubines wearing silk in Jìn,
did not feed grain to his horses at home,
and did not take a carriage when going out.
Shū Xiàng heard of this,
and told Miáo Bēnhuáng about it.
Bēnhuáng criticized it, saying:
"This is distributing the ruler's ranks and emoluments
to curry favor with subordinates."
Another account:
When Mèng Xiànbó was appointed Chief Minister,
Shū Xiàng went to congratulate him,
noticed no carriage at the gate,
and horses not eating grain.
Xiàng said:
"You don't have two carriages and teams,
why is this?"
Xiànbó said:
"I observe that the people of our state
still have hungry looks,
therefore I don't feed grain to my horses;
and many gray-haired elders walk on foot,
so I don't have two carriages."
Xiàng said:
"I came first to congratulate your appointment as minister,
now I congratulate your frugality."
As Xiàng left,
he said to Miáo Bēnhuáng:
"Help me congratulate Xiànbó on his frugality."
Miáozi said:
"What is there to congratulate?
Ranks, emoluments, banners and insignia
are meant to distinguish merit,
and separate the worthy from the unworthy.
Thus according to Jìn's laws,
upper grand masters have two carriages with teams,
middle grand masters have two carriages with one team,
lower grand masters have one carriage with team,
this makes clear the hierarchy.
Moreover, a minister must have military affairs,
therefore he maintains chariots and horses,
trains soldiers and charioteers,
to prepare for warfare.
If there is trouble,
they provide for unexpected needs;
in peacetime,
they serve court functions.
Now he disrupts Jìn's governance,
lacks preparation for emergencies,
to achieve personal integrity,
and purify his private reputation -
can Xiànbó's frugality be approved?
What is there to congratulate?"
When Guǎn Zhòng was minister of Qí,
he said:
"I am noble,
but I am poor."
Duke Huán said:
"I will give you the income of three collections."
He said:
"I am rich,
but I am lowly."
Duke Huán placed him above the Gāo and Guó families.
He said:
"I am respected,
but I am distant."
Then he was established as Zhòngfù.
Confucius heard of this and criticized it, saying:
"Extravagant and oppressive to superiors."
Another account:
When Guǎn Zhòngfù went out,
he had vermilion canopies and black robes,
returned with drums set up,
had displayed tripods in his courtyard,
and the income of three collections at home.
Confucius said:
"He is a good minister,
but his extravagance oppresses superiors."
When Sūnshū Áo was minister of Chǔ,
he rode in plain carriages with mares,
ate coarse rice with vegetable soup,
dried fish for meals,
wore lamb fur in winter,
and hemp clothes in summer,
with a hungry look on his face -
he was indeed a good minister,
but his frugality oppressed subordinates.
When Yáng Hǔ left Qí and fled to Zhào,
Lord Jiǎn asked:
"I hear you are good at cultivating men."
Hǔ said:
"When I lived in Lǔ,
I cultivated three men,
all became high officials;
when I was convicted in Lǔ,
they all searched for me.
When I lived in Qí,
I recommended three men,
one gained access to the king,
one became county magistrate,
one became border guard;
when I was convicted,
the one close to the king would not see me,
the magistrate came to arrest and bind me,
the border guard pursued me to the border,
stopping only when he couldn't catch up.
Hǔ is not good at cultivating men."
The lord bowed his head and laughed, saying:
"Those who plant oranges and pomelos
eat sweet fruit,
smell fragrant blossoms;
those who plant trifoliate oranges and thorns
get pricked when they mature.
Therefore the gentleman is careful about what he plants."
When Zhōngmóu had no magistrate,
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Zhào Wǔ:
"Zhōngmóu,
the thigh and arm of our state,
the shoulder and hip of Hándān,
I want to get a good magistrate for it,
whom should I send?"
Wǔ said:
"Xíng Bózi would do."
The duke said:
"Isn't he your enemy?"
It was said:
"Personal grudges should not enter the court."
The duke then asked:
"Who should be appointed as the minister of the central treasury?"
The reply was:
"Your servant's son is suitable."
Hence the saying:
"When recommending outsiders, do not avoid enemies;
when recommending insiders, do not avoid sons."
Zhào Wǔ recommended forty-six people,
and when Wǔ died,
each took their place as guests,
such was his lack of personal favoritism.
Píng Gōng asked Shū Xiàng:
"Which among the ministers is virtuous?"
He replied: "Zhào Wǔ."
The duke said:
"You are partial to your mentor."
Xiàng said:
"Wǔ stood as if unable to bear his clothes,
spoke as if words couldn't leave his mouth,
yet the scholars he recommended numbered in the tens,
all meeting expectations,
and the state greatly relied on them.
During Wǔ's lifetime,
he brought no profit to his own family,
and upon his death, he entrusted no orphans to others,
so I dare consider him virtuous."
Xiè Hú recommended his enemy to Lord Jiǎn for the position of chancellor.
His enemy, thinking he was fortunately pardoned,
went to offer thanks.
Hú then drew his bow and shot at him,
saying:
"Recommending you
was for the public good,
because you are capable.
My enmity toward you
is a private grudge;
I will not use my private grudge against you
to block you from our lord."
Thus, personal grudges do not enter the court.
Another account:
Xiè Hú recommended Xíng Bó Liǔ as governor of Shàngdǎng,
Liǔ went to thank him, saying:
"You have forgiven my offense,
dare I not bow again?"
Hú said: "Recommending you
is for the public;
my resentment toward you
is private.
Go now,
my resentment remains as before."
A man from Zhèng County was selling a pig,
someone asked its price.
He said:
"The road is long, the day is late,
how can I spare time to tell you?"
Argument Six: 〓#
Fán Wénzǐ delighted in straightforward speech,
Wǔzǐ struck him with a staff:
"Those who speak bluntly
are not tolerated by others;
being without tolerance,
endangers oneself.
Not only endangering oneself,
but also endangering one's father."
Zǐ Chǎn was
the son of Zǐ Guó.
Zǐ Chǎn was loyal to the lord of Zhèng,
Zǐ Guó angrily scolded him:
"To stand out among ministers
and be solely loyal to the ruler—
if the ruler is wise,
he may listen to you;
if not,
he will not heed you.
Whether he listens or not is uncertain,
yet you have already alienated yourself from the other ministers.
Being alienated from them,
will surely endanger you.
Not only endangering yourself,
but also endangering your father."
Liáng Chē was newly appointed magistrate of Yè,
his elder sister went to visit him,
arriving after dusk,
the gate was closed,
so she climbed over the wall to enter.
Chē then had her feet amputated.
Marquis Chéng of Zhào deemed him unkind,
took his seal and dismissed him from office.
Guǎn Zhòng was bound captive,
traveling from Lǔ to Qí,
on the way hungry and thirsty,
he passed by the border guard of Qǐwū and begged for food.
The guard knelt and fed him,
showing great respect.
The guard then secretly said to Zhòng:
"If by chance,
you reach Qí alive and are employed there,
how will you repay me?"
Zhòng replied:
"If it turns out as you say,
I will employ the virtuous,
utilize the capable,
and reward the diligent.
What should I use to repay you?"
The guard resented him.
There are three ways a ruler governs ministers.
Canon One: 〓#
If authority cannot transform them, then remove them.
Shī Kuàng's response,
Yànzǐ's discourse,
both abandoned the ease of using authority
and advocated the difficulty of virtuous conduct,
this is like racing with beasts,
not understanding how to eliminate dangers.
That dangers can be eliminated
is shown in Zǐxià's explanation of the Spring and Autumn Annals:
"Those skilled at maintaining authority cut off treacherous sprouts early."
Thus Jì Sūn reproached Confucius for encountering authority,
how much more so when applied to a ruler?
Therefore, Tàigōng Wàng killed Kuáng Yù,
and slaves do not ride thoroughbreds.
Lord Sì understood this,
hence did not drive deer.
Xuē Gōng understood this,
thus gambled with the two Luáns.
These all knew the principle of opposite outcomes.
Thus, the enlightened ruler's way of governing ministers
is illustrated by the analogy of keeping birds.
Canon Two: 〓#
The ruler is
the hub of profit and harm;
many take aim at it,
so the ruler is shared.
Thus, if likes and dislikes appear,
subordinates will exploit them,
and the ruler becomes confused.
If speech is unrestricted,
ministers find it hard to speak,
and the ruler loses his divinity.
Illustrated by Shēnzǐ's discourse on "six cautions",
and Táng Yì's words on archery.
The danger lies in Guó Yáng's request for change,
and King Xuān's deep sighs.
Made clear by Jìng Guō's offering of ten earrings,
and Xī Shǒu
and Gān Mào's eavesdropping through a hole.
Táng Xī Gōng understood statecraft,
hence asked about the jade vessel;
Zhāo Hóu mastered statecraft,
therefore listened and slept alone.
The way of the enlightened ruler
lies in Shēnzǐ's exhortation to decide alone.
Canon Three: 〓#
Statecraft fails to be implemented
for a reason.
If one doesn't kill his dog,
the wine turns sour.
The state also has its dogs,
and those close to the ruler are like shrine rats.
If the ruler lacks Yáo's repeated executions,
or King Zhuāng's response to the crown prince,
but all have decisions like Bó Ǎo's judgment by the Cai woman.
To know worthiness and incompetence,
first gauge them by the method of teaching singing.
Wú Qǐ's dismissal of his beloved wife,
and Duke Wén's execution of Diān Jié,
all went against their personal feelings.
Thus, those who can make others lance their boils
must be able to endure pain themselves.
Explanation One: When rewards and praise fail to motivate,
and punishments and slander do not instill fear,
and these four methods applied bring no change,
then such individuals should be removed.
Duke Jǐng of Qí went to Jìn,
attended a banquet with Duke Píng,
with Shī Kuàng seated in attendance.
Duke Jǐng asked Shī Kuàng about governance, saying:
"What will the Grand Master teach me?"
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Your Lordship must simply benefit the people."
Midway through the banquet,
as the wine flowed freely,
and they were about to depart,
he again asked Shī Kuàng about governance:
"What does the Grand Master teach me?"
The reply was:
"Your Lordship must simply benefit the people."
When Duke Jǐng went to his lodings,
Shī Kuàng saw him off,
and he once more inquired about governance from Shī Kuàng.
Shī Kuàng said:
"Your Lordship must simply benefit the people."
Duke Jǐng returned,
pondered,
and before sobering up,
grasped what Shī Kuàng meant:
Lords Wěi and Xià,
Duke Jǐng's two younger brothers,
were greatly favored by the people of Qí,
their households wealthy and esteemed, and the people delighted in them,
rivaling the ducal house,
posing a threat to his position.
Now, advising me to benefit the people—
is it to make me compete with my two brothers for the people's allegiance?
Thereupon, upon returning to his state,
he opened the granaries to distribute grain to the impoverished masses,
dispersed the treasury's surplus wealth to bestow upon orphans and widows,
until the granaries had no old grain,
the treasury no extra wealth,
and he married off palace women not in his service,
granting stipends of rice to those over seventy.
Thus, by selling virtue and bestowing kindness upon the people,
he competed with his two brothers.
After two years,
the two brothers fled,
Lord Xià escaping to Chǔ,
and Lord Wěi fleeing to Jìn.
Duke Jǐng and Yànzǐ were traveling by Shǎo Hǎi,
ascended the Bǎiqǐn Tower and looked back at his state,
saying:
"How magnificent!
Vast and boundless,
grand and imposing!
Who in future generations will possess this?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Perhaps it will be Tián Chéngshì!"
Duke Jǐng said:
"I possess this state,
yet you say Tián Chéngshì will have it—
why?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Tián Chéngshì is greatly favored by the people of Qí.
In his dealings with the people,
above, he requests titles and stipends for the great ministers,
below, he privately uses large dǒu, hú, qū, and fǔ measures to lend out grain,
and small ones to collect it back.
When he slaughters an ox,
he takes one dòu of meat for himself,
and the rest is fed to his scholars.
Throughout the year,
he takes two lengths of cloth and silk for himself,
and the rest is used to clothe his scholars.
Thus, the price of wood in the market
is no higher than in the mountains;
fish, salt, turtles, clams, snails, and mussels from the marshes
are no more expensive than from the sea.
Your Lordship imposes heavy taxes,
while Tián Chéngshì gives generously.
Once, Qí suffered a great famine,
and those who starved to death by the roadsides were countless,
yet fathers and sons leading each other to Tián Chéngshì
were never heard to perish.
Therefore, the people of Qínzhōu sang together:
'Sing aloud,
is it over?
Bundle up,
and go join Tián Chéngzǐ!'
The Book of Songs says:
'Though I have no virtue to give you,
yet you sing and dance.'
Now, with Tián Chéngshì's virtue, the people sing and dance,
their allegiance returns to him.
Hence it is said:
'Perhaps it will be Tián Chéngshì!'"
The duke wept, shedding tears, and said:
"Is it not sorrowful!
I possess the state,
yet Tián Chéngshì has it.
What can be done now?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Why should Your Lordship worry?
If you wish to seize it back,
then draw near to the worthy and distance the unworthy,
bring order to the chaos,
relax the penalties and punishments,
relieve poverty and care for orphans and widows,
bestow kindness and provide for the needy,
and the people will return to you.
Then, even if there were ten Tián Chéngshì,
what could they do to you?"
Some say:
Duke Jǐng did not know how to use power,
and Shī Kuàng and Yànzǐ
did not know how to eliminate threats.
A hunter
relies on the safety of the chariot,
uses the speed of six horses,
and with Wáng Liáng holding the reins,
his body is not wearied
and he easily catches swift animals.
Now, if one abandons the advantage of the chariot,
discards the speed of six horses
and Wáng Liáng's driving,
and instead runs on foot chasing animals,
then even with Lóu Jì's legs, one would never catch them in time.
Relying on fine horses and sturdy chariots,
even a Zānghuò would have ability to spare.
The state is the ruler's chariot;
power is the ruler's horse.
Not using power
to restrain and punish ministers who monopolize favor,
but instead competing for the people's allegiance
by vying in generosity with all under heaven,
is like not riding in the ruler's chariot,
not utilizing the horse's advantage,
abandoning the chariot and running on foot.
Hence it is said:
"Duke Jǐng was a ruler who did not know how to use power,
and Shī Kuàng
and Yànzǐ
were ministers who did not know how to eliminate threats."
Zǐxià said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals record instances of ministers killing rulers
and sons killing fathers,
numbering in the tens.
None accumulated in a single day,
but gradually reached that point."
All treacherous individuals,
through long conduct, accumulate influence,
and with accumulated influence comes strength,
and with strength comes the ability to kill;
thus, an enlightened ruler cuts them off early.
Now, Tián Cháng's rebellion
had shown gradual signs,
yet the ruler did not punish him.
Yànzǐ did not have his ruler restrain the encroaching ministers,
but had his lord practice benevolence,
hence Duke Jiǎn suffered the disaster.
Therefore, Zǐxià said:
"Those skilled at maintaining power
cut off the sprouts of treachery early."
Jìsūn was chancellor of Lǔ,
and Zǐlù was magistrate of Hòu.
Lǔ mobilized the people in May to dig a long canal,
and during this project,
Zǐlù used his private grain stores to make porridge,
and invited the canal workers at the crossroads of Wǔfù
to dine.
Confucius heard about this,
sent Zǐgòng to dump out the rice,
smash the containers,
and said:
"The ruler of Lǔ owns the people,
why are you feeding them?"
Zǐlù became furiously angry,
rolled up his sleeves and entered,
asking:
"Does the Master disapprove of Yóu practicing benevolence and righteousness?
What I learned from you, Master,
is benevolence and righteousness;
benevolence and righteousness mean
sharing all one has with the world and benefiting others together.
Now that I use my official grain to feed the people,
why is this not acceptable?"
Confucius said:
"How crude you are, Yóu!
I thought you understood,
but you haven't reached that level yet.
You are so ignorant of ritual!
Your feeding them
is out of love for them.
Now according to ritual,
the Son of Heaven loves all under heaven,
feudal lords love within their territories,
high officials love their offices,
scholars love their families,
exceeding what one should love is called encroachment.
Now the ruler of Lǔ owns the people
yet you presume to love them,
this is your encroachment,
isn't this transgression!"
Before he finished speaking,
a messenger from Jìsūn arrived,
reproaching:
"I, Féi, mobilized the people to employ them,
yet you, sir, ordered your disciples
to feed them,
are you going to steal my people?"
Confucius harnessed his carriage and left Lǔ.
With Confucius' virtue,
and Jìsūn not being the ruler of Lǔ,
yet with the status of a minister,
borrowing the methods of a ruler,
preventing problems before they materialized,
so Zǐlù couldn't carry out his private charity,
and harm couldn't occur,
how much more should a true ruler!
If Duke Jǐng had used his power to prevent Tiáncháng's encroachment,
then certainly the disaster of regicide wouldn't have occurred.
Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí to the east,
off the eastern sea of Qí there were recluses
named Kuángyù and Huáshì, two brothers who declared:
"We won't serve the Son of Heaven,
won't befriend feudal lords,
we'll farm for our food,
dig wells for our drink,
we have no demands on others.
We seek no high titles,
no ruler's salaries,
we won't serve in office but work with our strength."
When Tàigōng Wàng reached Yíngqiū,
he had officials arrest and execute them
as the first punishment.
Zhōu Gōng Dǎn heard about this from Lǔ,
sent an urgent message asking:
"These two men
were worthies.
Now you enjoy a state yet kill worthies,
why?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"These two brothers declared:
'We won't serve the Son of Heaven,
won't befriend feudal lords,
we'll farm for our food,
dig wells for our drink,
we have no demands on others.
We seek no high titles,
no ruler's salaries,
we won't serve in office but work with our strength.'
Those who won't serve the Son of Heaven
cannot be made my servants;
those who won't befriend feudal lords
cannot be employed by me;
farming for their food,
digging wells for their drink,
having no demands on others
cannot be encouraged or restrained by my rewards and punishments.
Moreover, without seeking high titles,
even if wise,
they won't be used by me;
not relying on ruler's salaries,
even if worthy,
they won't achieve merit for me.
Not taking office
means not governing,
not accepting appointment
means not being loyal.
Moreover, how the former kings employed their ministers and people
was either through ranks and salaries or punishments.
Now if these four methods cannot employ them,
then who should I be as ruler?
Not wearing armor yet becoming prominent,
not farming personally yet gaining fame,
this is not what should be taught in a state.
Suppose there's a horse here
that looks like a fine steed,
the finest under heaven.
Yet if driving it doesn't make it go forward,
stopping it doesn't make it halt,
pulling left it doesn't go left,
pulling right it doesn't go right,
then even the lowliest servant
wouldn't rely on its feet.
The reason servants wish to rely on a fine steed's feet
is because it can pursue benefit and avoid harm.
Now if it cannot be used by people,
even the lowliest servant
wouldn't rely on its feet.
If they consider themselves worthy men of the age
yet won't be used by their ruler,
behaving extremely worthy yet not employed by the ruler,
such men are not those an enlightened ruler keeps as servants,
just like a steed that cannot be directed left or right,
therefore I executed them."
Another version:
Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí to the east.
There was a worthy named Kuángyù off the coast,
Tàigōng Wàng heard about him and went to visit,
three times he retreated his horse from the gate
yet Kuángyù didn't come out to receive him,
so Tàigōng Wàng executed him.
At that time,
Zhōu Gōng Dǎn was in Lǔ,
and rushed to stop it;
by the time he arrived,
Kuángyù had already been executed.
Zhōu Gōng Dǎn said:
"Kuángyù
was a worthy of the age,
why did you execute him, sir?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Kuángyù declared he wouldn't serve the Son of Heaven,
wouldn't befriend feudal lords,
I feared he would disrupt laws and change teachings,
therefore I made him the first execution.
Suppose there's a horse here
that resembles a fine steed,
yet driving it doesn't make it go,
leading it doesn't make it advance,
even the lowliest servant wouldn't rely on its carriage."
When Rú'ěr persuaded Duke Sì of Wèi,
Duke Sì was pleased yet sighed.
His attendants asked:
"Why don't you make him chancellor?"
The Duke said:
"A horse that resembles a deer
may be priced at a thousand gold.
Yet there are horses worth a thousand gold
but no deer worth a thousand gold,
because horses can be used by people
while deer cannot be used by people.
Now Rú'ěr
has the talent to be chancellor of a great state,
but his intentions lie with other great states,
his heart isn't in Wèi,
though eloquent and wise,
he won't be used by me,
therefore I won't make him chancellor."
When Xuēgōng was chancellor to Marquis Zhāo of Wèi,
among the attendants were two brothers
named Yánghú and Pānqí,
who were highly valued by the king,
but didn't serve Xuēgōng.
Xuēgōng worried about this,
so he summoned them to gamble,
gave them a hundred pieces of gold each,
and had the brothers gamble;
soon he gave them another two hundred pieces each.
Lord Fāng Bó was at leisure,
when the usher announced that the son of guest Zhāng Jì was at the gate.
The lord flared up in anger,
grasped his weapon, and handed it to the usher, saying:
"Kill him!
I have heard that Jì does not serve Lord Wén."
After a moment,
with Jì's supporter Yǔ at his side,
he said:
"Not so.
I have privately heard that Jì serves you diligently,
but his efforts have been discreet and thus unheard."
Thereupon, he halted the order to kill the guest,
treated him with great courtesy,
and said:
"Earlier, I heard that Jì did not serve Lord Wén,
so I intended to kill him;
now that he truly does serve,
how could I forget Jì!"
He ordered the granary to present a thousand shi of grain,
the treasury to offer five hundred in gold,
and the stablemaster of his private stables to provide two fine horses and sturdy carriages,
then commanded a eunuch to lead twenty beautiful concubines from the palace ladies and present them to Jì.
The followers then said among themselves:
"Those who serve the lord will surely benefit,
while those who do not will certainly face harm.
Why should we hold back from serving the lord?"
Thus, they privately vied to encourage each other
and proceeded to do so.
Lord Xuē, with the power of a minister,
borrowed the methods of a sovereign,
and thus harm could not arise;
how much more so for one who errs as a sovereign!
Those who tame birds clip their lower wing feathers.
Once their lower feathers are clipped,
they must rely on humans for food;
how can they not be tamed?
Similarly, an enlightened ruler nurtures ministers thus,
making it so that ministers cannot but benefit from the ruler's stipends,
and cannot avoid submitting to the ruler's authority.
Benefiting from the ruler's stipends,
and submitting to the ruler's authority,
how can they not be submissive?
Persuasion Two: 〓#
Shěn Zǐ said:
"If the superior's insights are clear,
people will prepare for them;
if they are unclear,
people will be perplexed by them.
If his knowledge is apparent,
people will embellish for him;
if it is not apparent,
people will conceal from him.
If he shows no desires,
people will spy on him;
if he shows desires,
people will bait him.
Therefore, it is said:
'I have no way to know them,
only through non-action can I observe them.'"
Another account:
Shěn Zǐ said:
"Be cautious in speech,
for others will come to know you;
be cautious in action,
for others will follow you.
If you show knowledge,
others will hide from you;
if you show no knowledge,
others will speculate about you.
If you are knowledgeable,
others will store you away;
if you are ignorant,
others will act upon you.
Therefore, it is said:
'Only non-action allows for observation.'"
Tián Zǐfāng asked Táng Yìjū:
"What must an archer be cautious of?"
He replied:
"The bird watches you with hundreds of eyes,
while you manage it with only two;
you must carefully guard your blind."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"Good.
You apply this to archery,
I will apply it to the state."
Zhèng Zhǎngzhě heard this and said:
"Tián Zǐfāng knew he needed a blind,
but did not grasp how to create one.
For emptiness and non-action, without revealing oneself,
that is the blind."
Another account:
King Xuān of Qí asked Táng Yìzǐ about archery:
"What does an archer value most?"
Táng Yìzǐ said:
"It lies in carefully maintaining the blind."
The king said:
"What do you mean by carefully maintaining the blind?"
He replied:
"The bird watches humans with dozens of eyes,
while humans watch the bird with only two;
how can one not carefully guard the blind? 〓#
Thus it is said 〓#
'It lies in carefully maintaining the blind.'"
The king said:
"Then for ruling the world,
how can one use such a blind?
Now, the sovereign watches the state with two eyes,
while the state watches the sovereign with ten thousand eyes;
how can one create a blind for oneself?"
He replied:
"Zhèng Zhǎngzhě once said:
'Through emptiness, stillness, non-action, and non-revelation.'
That can serve as this blind!"
Guó Yáng was influential with the Lord of Zhèng,
and upon hearing that the lord disliked him,
while attending a drink,
he preemptively said to the lord:
"If I unfortunately err,
I hope you will kindly inform me.
I will then change my ways,
and thus avoid the death penalty."
A persuader pleased King Xuān of Hán,
and the king, pleased, sighed deeply.
His attendants, capitalizing on the king's pleasure,
informed the persuader first to curry favor.
When Jìngguō Jūn was chancellor of Qí,
the queen died,
and it was unknown who would be appointed next,
so he presented jade earrings to find out.
Another account:
Lord Xuē was chancellor of Qí,
and the wife of King Wēi of Qí had died.
Among the palace were ten maidens all favored by the king,
and Lord Xuē wanted to know whom the king wished to establish,
so he requested to appoint one as queen.
If the king agreed,
it would mean his advice was heeded,
and he would gain influence in appointing the queen;
if the king refused,
his advice would be rejected,
and he would lose sway in the appointment.
Wishing to know in advance whom the king wanted to appoint
to encourage the king accordingly,
he made ten jade earrings,
beautifying one of them,
and presented them.
The king distributed them among the ten maidens.
The next day, during an audience,
he observed where the beautiful earring was
and urged the king to make that one queen.
Gān Mào served as chancellor to King Huì of Qín,
and the king favored Gōngsūn Yǎn,
once confiding in him,
saying:
"I intend to make you chancellor."
Gān Mào's official overheard this through a hidden passage,
and reported it to Gān Mào.
Gān Mào entered to see the king,
and said:
"Your Majesty has found a worthy chancellor,
I dare to bow twice in congratulations."
The king said:
"I have entrusted the state to you;
how could I have another worthy chancellor?"
He replied:
"You are to make Xīshǒu chancellor."
The king said:
"How did you hear of this?"
He replied:
"Xīshǒu told me."
The king was angry that Xīshǒu had leaked the secret,
and thus expelled him.
First account:
Xī Shǒu was the finest commander in the world,
and a minister of the King of Liáng.
The King of Qín wished to secure his services to govern the world,
but Xī Shǒu said:
"Yǎn (referring to himself) is a mere subject,
and dare not leave his lord's state."
After a year had passed,
Xī Shǒu incurred punishment from the King of Liáng,
fled, and entered Qín,
where the King of Qín treated him very well.
Chūlǐ Jí, a general of Qín,
fearing that Xī Shǒu would replace him as general,
dug a tunnel to where the king often held confidential conversations.
Soon enough, the king indeed consulted with Xī Shǒu,
saying:
"I wish to attack Hán,
what do you think?"
Xī Shǒu replied:
"It can be done in the autumn."
The king said:
"I intend to burden you with state affairs,
you must not leak this."
Xī Shǒu stepped back, bowed twice, and said:
"I accept your command."
Thereupon, Chūlǐ Jí listened through the tunnel.
The court officials all said:
"Troops will rise in autumn to attack Hán,
with Xī Shǒu as general."
On that very day,
all the court officials knew of it;
within that month,
the entire state knew of it.
The king summoned Chūlǐ Jí and said:
"Why is there such a clamor,
and how did the news get out?"
Chūlǐ Jí replied:
"It seems to be Xī Shǒu."
The king said:
"I haven't spoken with Xī Shǒu,
so how could it be him?"
Chūlǐ Jí said:
"Xī Shǒu is a traveler,
newly arrived after incurring punishment,
his heart is lonely,
so he spreads such words to win over the crowd."
The king said:
"Indeed."
He sent someone to summon Xī Shǒu,
but he had already fled to another state.
Tángxī Gōng said to Zhāo Hóu:
"Suppose there is a jade goblet worth a thousand pieces of gold,
hollow but without a bottom,
can it hold water?"
Zhāo Hóu said:
"No."
"Suppose there is an earthenware vessel that does not leak,
can it hold wine?"
Zhāo Hóu said:
"Yes."
Tángxī Gōng replied:
"The earthenware vessel
is of the lowest value,
but being leak-proof,
it can hold wine.
Even if there is a jade goblet worth a thousand pieces of gold,
of the highest value but without a bottom,
leaking,
unable to hold water,
then who would pour drink into it?
Now, if a ruler
leaks the words of his ministers,
he is like a jade goblet without a bottom.
Even with sagely wisdom,
none can fully employ their methods,
because of the leakage."
Zhāo Hóu said:
"Indeed."
After hearing Tángxī Gōng's words,
from then on,
whenever Zhāo Hóu intended to initiate major affairs of the world,
he never failed to sleep alone,
fearing that talking in his sleep
might let others know his plans.
Another account:
Tángxī Gōng appeared before Zhāo Hóu and said:
"Suppose there is a white jade goblet without a bottom,
and an earthenware goblet with a bottom.
If you are thirsty,
which will you use to drink?"
The lord said:
"The earthenware goblet."
Tángxī Gōng said:
"The white jade goblet is beautiful,
yet you do not use it to drink,
is it because it has no bottom?"
The lord said:
"Yes."
Tángxī Gōng said:
"A ruler
who leaks and divulges the words of his ministers
is comparable to a jade goblet without a bottom."
Every time Tángxī Gōng visited and left,
Zhāo Hóu would always sleep alone,
fearing that talking in his sleep
might leak secrets to his wives and concubines.
Shēn Zǐ said:
"He who sees alone is called clear-sighted,
he who hears alone is called acute.
He who can decide alone,
therefore can be the ruler of the world."
Third argument: 〓#
There was a man of Sòng who sold wine,
his measures were very fair,
he treated customers very respectfully,
he made very good wine,
he hung his sign very high and prominently,
yet he did not sell any,
and the wine turned sour.
Puzzled by the reason,
he asked someone he knew,
inquiring of the elder Yáng Qiàn.
Qiàn said:
"Is your dog fierce?"
He replied:
"The dog is fierce,
but why should that prevent the wine from selling?"
Qiàn said:
"People are afraid of it.
If someone sends a child
carrying money and a pot to buy wine,
and the dog rushes out to bite him,
that is why the wine turns sour and does not sell."
Now, the state also has its dogs:
men of the Way, carrying their methods,
wish to enlighten the lord of ten thousand chariots,
but the great ministers act as fierce dogs, rushing to bite them.
This is why the lord is obscured and coerced,
and why men of the Way are not employed.
Thus, Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"In governing the state, what is the greatest worry?"
He replied:
"The greatest worry is the altar rats."
The duke said:
"Why worry about altar rats?"
He replied:
"Have you seen those who build altars?
They set up wood and plaster it,
rats burrow through the gaps,
digging holes to dwell within.
If you smoke them, you fear burning the wood;
if you flood them, you fear washing away the plaster.
This is why the altar rats cannot be caught.
Now, the attendants of a ruler,
when outside, use their powerful positions
to extract profits from the people,
and when inside, they collude to conceal their evils from the ruler.
They spy on the ruler's intentions to report outside,
forming a powerful alliance inside and out,
and all the officials and clerks enrich themselves thereby.
If the officials are not punished, the law is disrupted;
if they are punished, the ruler feels insecure.
They entrench themselves and hold sway,
these are the altar rats of the state."
Thus, when ministers hold power and monopolize control,
clearly, those who serve them gain benefits,
while those who do not inevitably suffer harm.
These are also the fierce dogs.
The great ministers act as fierce dogs
biting men of the Way,
and the attendants act as altar rats spying on the ruler's intentions,
yet the ruler remains unaware.
In such a situation,
how can the ruler avoid being blocked,
and how can the state avoid perishing?
One version says:
In Sòng, there was a wine seller named Zhuāng,
whose wine was always excellent.
Someone sent a servant to buy Zhuāng's wine,
but his dog bit people,
so the messenger dared not go,
and instead bought wine from another house.
When asked:
"Why didn't you buy Zhuāng's wine?"
He replied: "Today Zhuāng's wine is sour."
Hence it is said: "If you don't kill the dog, the wine turns sour."
Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What is the greatest worry in governing a state?"
He replied:
"The most troublesome are the altar mice.
The altar,
made of wood and plastered with clay,
is where mice take refuge.
Smoking them out would burn the wood,
flooding them would wash away the clay,
this is why altar mice are so troublesome.
Now, the ruler's attendants,
when outside, use their authority to exploit the people for profit,
and when inside, collude to deceive and cover up misdeeds
to cheat the ruler.
Not punishing them disrupts the law,
punishing them endangers the sovereign.
To hold and possess them,
these are also altar mice."
Thus, when ministers hold power and control decrees,
clearly rewarding those who serve them
and harming those who do not,
they are also fierce dogs.
So if attendants are altar mice,
and officials in power are fierce dogs,
then governance cannot be implemented.
Yáo wished to pass the throne to Shùn,
Gǔn admonished him:
"This is inauspicious!
Who would give the realm to a commoner?"
Yáo did not listen,
and raised an army to execute Gǔn in the outskirts of Yǔshān.
Gònggōng also admonished:
"Who would give the realm to a commoner?"
Yáo did not listen,
and again raised an army
to execute Gònggōng in the capital of Yōuzhōu.
Thereafter, no one in the realm dared speak
against passing the throne to Shùn.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"For Yáo to know Shùn's worthiness
was not the difficult part.
But to execute those who admonished in order to pass it to Shùn,
that was the true difficulty."
Another version says:
"Not letting doubts undermine one's discernment
is the difficulty."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a law for the Máo Gate, stating:
"Any minister, official, or prince entering court
whose horse's hoof steps on the eaves' drip line,
the court magistrate shall break his carriage shaft,
and execute his driver."
Once, the crown prince entered court,
his horse's hoof stepped on the drip line,
the magistrate broke his shaft,
and executed his driver.
The prince was furious,
entered and wept to the king:
"Punish the magistrate for me."
The king said:
"The law
serves to honor the ancestral temple,
and respect the state.
Thus, those who uphold the law and follow orders,
showing respect for the state,
are loyal ministers of the state;
how can they be punished?
Those who violate the law and disregard orders,
showing no respect for the state,
are ministers overriding the ruler and subordinates challenging superiors.
If ministers override the ruler,
the sovereign loses authority;
if subordinates challenge
superiors, the throne is endangered.
Authority lost and position endangered,
the state cannot be preserved—
what would I leave for my descendants?"
Thereupon, the prince retreated hastily,
left his residence to sleep outdoors for three days,
faced north and bowed twice to plead for his death penalty.
Another version:
The King of Chǔ urgently summoned the crown prince.
By Chǔ law,
carriages were not allowed up to the Máo Gate.
It was raining,
and the courtyard was flooded,
so the prince drove his carriage to the Máo Gate.
The magistrate said:
"Carriages may not reach the Máo Gate.
To do so
is unlawful."
The prince said:
"The king's summons is urgent,
I cannot wait for the flood to recede."
And drove on.
The magistrate raised his staff and struck the horse,
ruining the carriage.
The prince entered and wept to the king:
"The courtyard was flooded,
so I drove to the Máo Gate.
The magistrate said:
'This is unlawful.'
He raised his staff and struck my horse,
ruining my carriage.
Your Majesty must punish him."
The king said:
"He did not exceed his duty before the old ruler,
nor fawn on the future heir—
admirable!
This is truly my law-abiding minister."
So he promoted him two ranks,
and had the prince leave through the back gate,
saying, "Do not err again."
Lord Sì of Wèi said to Bó Yí:
"You think my state too small
and not worth serving,
but I have the means to employ you;
let me grant you rank and make you a high minister."
And bestowed ten thousand qǐng of land.
Bó Yí said:
"My mother trusts me,
believing I am capable of governing a large state
without inadequacy.
Yet, there is a shamaness, old woman Cài, in my household,
whom my mother deeply trusts and loves,
entrusting her with family affairs.
My wisdom is sufficient to handle family matters credibly,
and my mother fully listens to me.
However, after discussing matters with me,
she always consults old woman Cài again.
Thus, judging by my wisdom and ability,
she deems me fit to govern a large state without inadequacy;
considering our closeness,
we are mother and son;
yet she still cannot avoid consulting old woman Cài.
Now, my relationship with the ruler
is not as close as mother and son,
and every ruler has his 'old woman Cài.'
The ruler's 'old woman Cài'
is surely a powerful figure.
Powerful figures
are those who can act for personal gain.
Those acting for personal gain
operate outside the plumb line;
while what I propose
is within the law.
Outside the plumb line and within the law
are opposed,
and cannot coexist."
Another version:
The Lord of Wèi went to Jìn,
and said to Bó Yí:
"I wish for you to accompany me."
Bó Yí said:
"My mother is at home;
allow me to return and discuss it with her."
The Lord of Wèi personally requested from Bó's mother.
Bó's mother said:
"Yí is your servant;
if you wish to take him along,
that is very well."
The Lord of Wèi said:
"I have requested it of you, mother,
and you have agreed."
Bó Yí returned,
and spoke to his mother,
saying:
"How does the Lord of Wèi's love for me compare to yours?"
The old woman said:
"Not as much as I love my son."
"How does the virtue of the Lord of Wèi compare to yours, mother?"
She replied:
"Not as virtuous as my son."
"When you and your son decide family matters,
having already settled them,
you still seek final judgment from the fortune-teller Granny Cài.
Now the Lord of Wèi follows your son's advice,
yet though he decides with your son,
he will inevitably consult another Granny Cài to overturn it.
In this way,
your son cannot long remain a minister."
Those who teach singing
first have students vocalize to test their range,
and only those whose voices can reach the pure zhǐ note are taught.
Another account says:
When teaching singing,
first apply the method:
rapid tones should hit the gōng note,
slow tones should hit the zhǐ note.
If rapid tones miss gōng,
slow tones miss zhǐ,
it cannot be called teaching.
Wú Qǐ,
a man from Zuǒshì in Wèi,
had his wife weave a belt
whose width fell short of the standard.
Master Wú ordered her to redo it.
His wife said:
"Alright."
When completed,
he measured it again,
and indeed it didn't meet the standard,
so Master Wú grew furious.
His wife replied:
"I began the warp and it couldn't be changed."
Master Wú divorced her,
whereupon his wife asked her brother to seek reconciliation.
Her brother said:
"Master Wú
is a man of law.
In establishing his laws,
he aims to achieve merit with a state of ten thousand chariots,
so he must first implement them with his wife and concubines,
before extending them to others.
You should not hope for reconciliation."
His wife's younger brother held influence with the Lord of Wèi,
and thus used this connection to appeal to Master Wú.
Master Wú would not listen,
so he left Wèi and entered Chǔ.
Another account says:
Wú Qǐ showed his wife a belt, saying:
"Weave a belt for me
exactly like this."
When the belt was finished and compared,
it was exceptionally fine.
Qǐ said:
"I told you to weave a belt
exactly like this,
yet now it's exceptionally fine,
why?"
His wife said:
"The materials used are the same,
I just put extra care into making it better."
Wú Qǐ said:
"That's not what I instructed."
He made her wear it back to her family.
Her father came to plead for her,
but Wú Qǐ said:
"In my household, words are never spoken in vain."
Duke Wén of Jìn asked Hú Yǎn:
"I have sweet and rich foods distributed throughout the court,
cups of wine and plates of meat gathered in the palace,
no wine is left undrunk,
no fresh meat uneaten,
when I slaughter an ox
it's shared throughout the state,
a year's labor
is entirely used to clothe my soldiers,
is this enough to make the people fight?"
Master Hú said:
"It is not enough."
The Duke said:
"I have relaxed market taxes
and eased punishments,
is this enough to make the people fight?"
Master Hú said:
"It is not enough."
The Duke said:
"When my people suffer losses,
I personally send court officials to handle matters,
pardon the guilty,
and give to the poor and needy,
is this enough to make the people fight?"
Master Hú replied:
"It is not enough.
These are all means to secure livelihood;
but to make them fight
is to kill them.
The people follow you
for the security of their livelihood,
if you then turn around and get them killed,
you lose the reason for their following you."
The Duke asked:
"Then what would be enough to make the people fight?"
Master Hú replied:
"Make it so they have no choice but to fight."
The Duke said:
"How to make it so they have no choice?"
Master Hú replied:
"Reward faithfully and punish inevitably,
that would be enough to make them fight."
The Duke asked:
"To what extreme should punishments reach?"
He replied:
"Do not avoid the close and noble,
let the law reach those you love."
Duke Wén said:
"Good."
The next day he ordered a hunt at Pǔlù,
setting noon as the deadline,
with military law applied to those late.
There was a man dear to the Duke named Diān Jié
who arrived late,
the officer requested his punishment,
and Duke Wén shed tears in sorrow.
The officer said:
"I request to carry out the sentence."
So they broke Diān Jié's spine,
and displayed him to the common people,
to demonstrate the credibility of the law.
Thereafter the people all feared, saying:
"The Lord valued Diān Jié so highly,
yet still applied the law to him,
what chance do we have?"
Seeing the people were ready to fight,
Duke Wén then raised troops to attack Yuán,
and conquered it.
He attacked Wèi,
aligned its fields eastward, and took Wǔlù.
He attacked Yáng. Defeated Guó.
Attacked Cáo.
Surrounded Zhèng from the south,
and overturned its battlements.
Lifted the siege of Sòng.
Returned to fight the Chǔ people at Chéngpú,
greatly defeating them,
returned to form the Jiāntǔ alliance,
and thus established the Héngyōng covenant.
In one move he achieved eight merits.
The reason for this
was no other cause or strange thing,
but following Hú Yǎn's strategy,
and using Diān Jié's spine.
The pain of a boil,
unless it stings to the marrow,
is an unbearable vexation to the heart;
if not so,
one cannot make people use a half-inch stone lancet to lance it.
Now rulers in governance are the same:
not that they don't know peace comes through hardship;
to want to govern their state,
unless like this
they cannot heed the wise and punish rebellious ministers.
Rebellious ministers are inevitably powerful men;
powerful men are inevitably those the ruler holds very dear.
Those the ruler holds very dear
are like the unity of hardness and whiteness.
For a commoner,
to try to separate the ruler from his beloved unity
is like explaining the left thigh to the right thigh,
ensuring his own death
and the failure of his counsel.
Canon I: 〓#
When rewards and punishments are shared,
prohibitions and orders cannot be implemented.
How is this clarified?
It is clarified by the examples of Zàofù and Wūqī.
Zǐhǎn acted as the released pig,
Tián Héng acted as the garden pond,
hence the sovereigns of Sòng and Duke Jiǎn were assassinated.
The peril lies in Wáng Liáng and Zàofù sharing a carriage,
and Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào sharing a qín.
Canon II: 〓#
Order and strength arise from law,
weakness and chaos arise from favoritism.
If the ruler understands this,
he will rectify rewards and punishments
and not be benevolent to his subordinates.
Ranks and emoluments arise from merit,
