punishments and penalties arise from crime.
If the minister understands this,
he will exhaust his efforts unto death
and not out of loyalty to the ruler.
When the ruler comprehends the absence of benevolence,
and the minister comprehends the absence of loyalty,
then one can become a true king.
King Zhāoxiāng understood the ruler's essence and thus did not distribute the five gardens;
Tián Wěi understood the minister's essence, hence he instructed Tián Zhāng,
and Gōngyí declined the fish.
Canon III: 〓#
An enlightened ruler
takes warning from external affairs,
and thus external matters cannot but succeed.
Therefore, Sū Dài criticized the King of Qí.
A ruler takes warning from those above,
and recluses are not suitable if not illustrious.
Hence, Pān Shòu spoke of Yǔ's true nature.
If a ruler has no awareness or enlightenment,
Fāng Wú knew this,
thus he feared those sharing clothes and clan,
let alone relying on authority!
Wú Zhāng understood it, 〓#
therefore he advised through pretense, 〓#
and even more so by relying on sincerity! 〓#
The King of Zhào disliked tiger-like eyes and was blocked. 〓#
The way of an enlightened ruler 〓#
is like the Zhōu official's refusal of the Marquis of Wèi. 〓#
Canon IV: 〓#
The ruler
upholds the law and demands results
to achieve merits.
It is heard that there may be corrupt officials
yet individually good people,
but not that there are chaotic people
with individually orderly officials.
Thus, the enlightened ruler governs officials, not the people.
This is illustrated by shaking the tree's root
and pulling the net's main cord.
Therefore, the minor official in charge of a fire
must be held accountable.
In firefighting,
if an official carries a pot to run to the fire,
it is the effort of one person.
If he wields a whip to direct others,
then ten thousand men are put to work.
Thus, the method encountered
is like Zàofù meeting a startled horse:
pulling the horse and pushing the carriage, it cannot advance;
but taking over the reins and whip,
the horses all gallop.
Hence, it is illustrated by hammering and forging to level,
and using straightening tools to correct.
Otherwise,
the failure lies in Nào Chǐ using Qí to kill King Mǐn,
and Lǐ Duì using Zhào to starve Lord Fù.
Canon V: 〓#
Following the principle of things,
one achieves without toil.
Thus, Zī Zhèng sat on the shaft and sang
to ascend the high bridge.
The peril lies in Jiǎn Zhǔ's tax official requesting light or heavy taxes;
Báo Yí's statement "the state is full,"
made Jiǎn Zhǔ happy while the treasury was empty,
and the people starved while corrupt officials grew rich.
Therefore, Duke Huán toured among the people
and Guǎn Zhòng inspected rotten wealth and resentful women.
Otherwise,
it would be like Yán Líng unable to advance on horseback,
and Zàofù passing by weeping for him.
Explanation I: 〓#
Zàofù drove four horses,
galloping and maneuvering
with full control over the horses.
Having full control over the horses
means mastering the reins and whip.
Yet when the horse was startled by a released pig,
and Zàofù could not restrain it,
it was not due to lack of strictness in the reins and whip,
but because his authority was divided by the pig.
Wángzǐ Wūqī, as an assistant driver,
did not use reins or whip
but controlled the horses through selection,
mastering the benefits of fodder and water.
Yet when the horse passed by a garden pond
and the carriage failed,
it was not due to insufficient benefit from fodder and water,
but because his virtue was divided by the pond.
Thus, Wáng Liáng and Zàofù,
the world's best drivers,
if Wáng Liáng held the left rein and shouted,
and Zàofù held the right rein and whipped,
the horses could not travel ten lǐ,
due to shared control.
Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào,
the world's best qín players,
if Tián Lián played the upper strings
and Chéng Qiào plucked the lower ones,
they could not produce a melody,
also due to shared control.
With the skill of Wáng Liáng and Zàofù,
sharing reins to drive could not move the horses;
how can a ruler
share power with his ministers to govern?
With the skill of Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào,
sharing a qín could not complete a tune;
how can a ruler
share authority with his ministers to achieve success?
Another account:
Zàofù served as assistant driver for the King of Qí,
training thirsty horses to completion,
and tested the carriage in the garden.
The thirsty horses saw the garden pond,
left the carriage and ran to the pond,
and the carriage failed.
Wángzǐ Wūqī, for Jiǎn Zhǔ of Zhào, took the road
competing for a thousand-lǐ standard,
at the start of the journey,
a pig lay hidden in a ditch.
Wángzǐ Wūqī adjusted the reins and whip to advance,
the pig suddenly emerged from the ditch,
the horses startled and the carriage failed.
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said to the sovereign of Sòng:
"Rewards, gifts, and bestowals
are what the people delight in;
you, my lord, should administer them.
Killings, executions, and punishments
are what the people detest;
I request to take charge of them."
The sovereign of Sòng said:
"Agreed."
Thereafter, he issued威严 commands,
executed great ministers,
and the sovereign would say:
"Consult Zǐhǎn."
Thus, the great ministers feared him,
and the common people turned to him.
After a year,
Zǐhǎn killed the sovereign of Sòng and seized the government.
Thus, Zǐhǎn acted as the released pig
to usurp his sovereign's state.
Duke Jiǎn was in the high position,
with heavy penalties and strict punishments,
imposing heavy taxes
and killing the people.
Tián Chéng Héng displayed kindness and affection,
demonstrating generosity and tolerance.
Duke Jiǎn treated the Qí people as thirsty horses,
not bestowing grace upon them;
while Tián Chéng Héng used benevolence and tolerance as the garden pond.
Another account:
Zàofù served as assistant driver for the King of Qí,
training horses by making them thirsty,
and in a hundred days, the training was complete.
Once trained,
he requested to test the carriage for the King of Qí.
The king said:
"Test it in the garden."
Zàofù drove the carriage into the garden,
the horses saw the garden pond and ran,
Zàofù could not restrain them.
Zàofù had long trained his horses by thirst,
but now the horses saw a pond,
bolted and ran,
and even Zàofù could not control them.
Now, Jiǎn Gōng had long used laws to restrain his people,
yet Tián Chéng Héng took advantage of it,
which is like Tián Chéng Héng opening a garden pond
to show thirsty people.
Another saying:
Wángzǐ Yúqī prepared a thousand-mile chase for the ruler of Sòng.
The carriage was already harnessed,
and he rubbed his hands and checked the reins.
Just as they were about to set off,
he drove the horses forward,
and the wheels ran true;
he pulled them back,
and the horses covered their tracks.
But when he tapped to start,
a pig dashed out from a hole.
The horses retreated and backed away,
and the whip could not make them advance;
the horses bolted and ran,
and the reins could not steer them straight.
Another saying:
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said to the ruler of Sòng:
"Rewards and bestowals
are what the people favor,
so you, my lord, should handle them;
punishments and executions
are what the people detest,
so I ask to take charge of them."
Thereupon, he punished commoners and executed ministers,
and the ruler would say:
"Discuss it with Zǐhǎn."
After a year,
the people knew that the power over life and death lay with Zǐhǎn,
so the whole state submitted to him.
Thus, Zǐhǎn seized the ruler of Sòng
and usurped his governance,
and the laws could not prevent it.
Hence it is said:
"Zǐhǎn acted as the emerging pig,
and Tián Chéng Héng served as the garden pond."
If Wáng Liáng
and Zàofù shared a carriage,
each holding one side of the reins
to pass through the gate,
the driving would surely fail
and the road would not be reached.
If Tián Lián
and Chéng Qiào shared a qin,
each plucking one string and strumming,
the music would surely be ruined,
and the melody would not be achieved.
Second Argument:
King Zhāo of Qín fell ill,
and the people bought oxen village by village
and prayed for the king at home.
Gōngsūn Shù went out and saw this,
then entered to congratulate the king, saying:
"The people have all bought oxen village by village
to pray for you."
The king sent someone to inquire,
and it was indeed true.
The king said:
"Fine them two suits of armor each.
For praying without orders
is showing love for me.
If they love me,
I might change the laws
and empathize with them,
which would undermine the law;
if the law is not upheld,
it leads to chaos and ruin.
It is better to fine them two suits of armor each
and then restore order with them."
Another saying:
King Xiāng of Qín was ill,
and the people prayed for him;
when he recovered,
they slaughtered oxen to fulfill their vows.
The court officials Yán È
and Gōngsūn Yǎn went out
and saw this,
saying:
"It is not the time for community or harvest sacrifices;
why slaughter oxen
and offer them at the altar?"
They wondered and asked about it.
The people said:
"The ruler was ill,
and we prayed for him;
now he has recovered,
so we slaughter oxen to fulfill our vows."
Yán È
and Gōngsūn Yǎn, pleased,
went to see the king,
bowed, and congratulated him:
"You surpass Yáo
and Shùn."
The king was startled and said:
"What do you mean?"
They replied:
"Yáo
and Shùn
never had people pray for them to this extent.
Now, you fell ill,
and the people prayed with oxen;
when you recovered,
they slaughtered oxen to fulfill their vows.
So we privately believe you surpass Yáo and Shùn."
The king then sent someone to inquire,
asking which villages had done this,
and fined their village heads and neighborhood elders two suits of armor each.
Yán È and Gōngsūn Yǎn were ashamed and dared not speak.
After several months,
the king was drinking merrily,
and Yán È
and Gōngsūn Yǎn said to the king:
"Earlier, we privately thought you surpassed Yáo
and Shùn,
not merely to flatter you.
When Yáo and Shùn were ill,
their people did not pray for them like this.
Yet you sent someone to inquire,
asking which villages had done it,
and now that you were ill and the people prayed with oxen,
and you recovered,
they slaughtered oxen to fulfill their vows.
But you fined their village heads and neighborhood elders two suits of armor each;
we find this puzzling."
The king said:
"Why do you not understand this?
The reason those people serve me
is not because I love them that they serve me,
but because of my authority that they serve me.
If I relinquish authority to bond with the people,
in that case,
if I happen not to love them,
they would not serve me,
so I must abandon the way of love."
There was a great famine in Qín,
and Yìnghóu requested:
"The plants in the five gardens—
vegetables,
acorns,
dates, and chestnuts—
could save the people;
I ask to distribute them."
King Zhāo Xiāng said:
"By the laws of our Qín,
the people are rewarded for achievements
and punished for crimes.
Now, to distribute the vegetables from the five gardens
would reward both the deserving and undeserving.
Rewarding both the deserving and undeserving
leads to chaos.
To distribute from the gardens and cause chaos,
it is better to discard the dates and vegetables and maintain order."
Another saying:
"To order the distribution of the melons,
vegetables, dates,
and chestnuts from the five gardens,
though it could save the people,
would make the deserving and undeserving compete for them.
To live in chaos
is worse than to die in order;
sir, please drop the matter."
Tián Wěi taught his son Tián Zhāng:
"If you wish to benefit yourself,
first benefit your ruler;
if you wish to enrich your family,
first enrich the state."
Another saying:
Tián Wěi taught his son Tián Zhāng:
"The ruler sells offices and ranks,
the minister sells his intellect and strength.
So rely on yourself, not on others."
Gōngyí Xiū served as prime minister of Lǔ and was fond of fish.
The entire state competed to buy fish and present them to him,
but Gōngyízǐ would not accept them.
His younger brother remonstrated with him, saying:
"You, sir, are fond of fish yet refuse them.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"Precisely because I am fond of fish,
that is why I do not accept them.
If I were to accept fish,
I would inevitably have the demeanor of one who is subordinate to others;
having the demeanor of one who is subordinate to others,
I would then pervert the law;
perverting the law,
I would be dismissed from the prime ministership.
Although fond of fish,
then I would certainly not be sent fish,
nor would I be able to supply myself with fish.
If I do not accept fish and thus avoid dismissal from the prime ministership,
although fond of fish,
I can long supply myself with fish."
This illustrates that relying on others is not as good as relying on oneself,
and that understanding how others act for you
is not as good as understanding how to act for yourself.
Persuasion Three:
Zǐzhī served as prime minister of Yān,
holding a noble position and wielding decisive authority.
Sū Dài was on a mission from Qí to Yān,
and the king asked him:
"What kind of ruler is the king of Qí?"
He replied:
"He certainly will not achieve hegemony."
The king of Yān said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"In the past, when Duke Huán achieved hegemony,
he entrusted internal affairs to Bào Shū,
and external affairs to Guǎn Zhòng.
Duke Huán would let down his hair and amuse himself with women,
daily roaming the markets.
Now the king of Qí does not trust his great ministers."
Thereupon, the king of Yān consequently placed even greater trust in Zǐzhī.
Zǐzhī heard of this,
sent someone to present Sū Dài with a hundred yì of gold,
and allowed himself to be used as Sū Dài saw fit.
Another account:
Sū Dài was on a mission from Qí to Yān,
and seeing that he could not benefit Zǐzhī,
he would certainly fail in his mission and have to return,
with no tribute or rewards forthcoming,
so he went to see the king of Yān,
and praised the king of Qí.
The king of Yān said:
"How can the king of Qí be so worthy?
Then surely he is destined to become king?"
Sū Dài said:
"He is too busy trying to save his state from ruin,
how could he become king?"
The king of Yān said:
"Why is that?"
He said:
"Because his appointments of those he favors are not equitable."
The king of Yān said:
"Why is his state facing ruin?"
He said:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí loved Guǎn Zhòng,
appointing him as his 'uncle',
entrusting him with internal affairs,
and giving him authority over external matters,
delegating the entire state to him.
Thus, he unified and corrected the world,
and nine times assembled the feudal lords.
Now the king of Qí's appointments of those he favors are not equitable,
therefore I know his state is facing ruin."
The king of Yān said:
"Now I have appointed Zǐzhī,
has the world not heard of it?"
Thereupon, the next day he held a grand court audience
and deferred to Zǐzhī.
Pān Shòu said to the king of Yān:
"Your Majesty should rather yield the state to Zǐzhī.
The reason people call Yáo worthy
is because he yielded the world to Xǔ Yóu,
and Xǔ Yóu certainly did not accept it.
Thus, Yáo gained the reputation of yielding to Xǔ Yóu,
while in reality not losing the world.
Now if Your Majesty yields the state to Zǐzhī,
and Zǐzhī certainly does not accept it,
then Your Majesty will have the reputation of yielding to Zǐzhī,
and will be acting in the same way as Yáo."
Thereupon, the king of Yān consequently entrusted the entire state to him,
Zǐzhī, and Zǐzhī became extremely powerful.
Another account:
Pān Shòu
was a recluse.
Yān sent someone to invite him.
Pān Shòu saw the king of Yān and said:
"I fear that Zǐzhī will suffer the same fate as Yì."
The king said:
"What about Yì?"
He replied:
"In ancient times, when Yǔ died,
he intended to pass the world to Yì,
but Qǐ's followers joined together to attack Yì and establish Qǐ.
Now Your Majesty trusts and favors Zǐzhī,
and intends to pass the state to Zǐzhī,
yet the crown prince's followers all hold official seals,
while among Zǐzhī's followers,
not a single one holds a position at court.
If Your Majesty unfortunately were to pass away,
then Zǐzhī would become another Yì."
The king consequently collected the officials' seals,
and from those with a salary of three hundred shí upwards, all submitted them to Zǐzhī,
and Zǐzhī became extremely powerful.
Now, the means by which a ruler mirrors himself
are the scholars and followers of the feudal lords,
but now the scholars and followers of the feudal lords
are all partisans of private factions.
The means by which a ruler brightens himself
are the scholars and followers from the cliffs
and caves,
but now the scholars and followers from the cliffs and caves
are all retainers of private factions.
Why is this?
Because the power to strip and confer is in the hands of Zǐzhī.
Therefore, Wú Zhāng said:
"A ruler should not pretend to hate or love someone.
If he pretends to love someone,
he cannot later hate him;
if he pretends to hate someone,
he cannot later love him."
Another account:
The king of Yān wished to pass the state to Zǐzhī,
and asked Pān Shòu about it.
He replied:
"Yǔ loved Yì and entrusted the world to Yì,
but then appointed Qǐ's followers as officials.
When he grew old,
and considered Qǐ inadequate to take on the world,
he passed the world to Yì,
yet the positions of power were all in Qǐ's hands.
Later, Qǐ and his partisans attacked Yì and seized the world from him.
Thus, Yǔ in name passed the world to Yì,
but in reality allowed Qǐ to take it for himself.
This makes it clear that Yǔ was not the equal of Yáo
and Shùn.
Now Your Majesty wishes to pass the state to Zǐzhī,
yet the officials are all the crown prince's men,
so this is to pass it in name while in reality allowing the crown prince to take it for himself."
The king of Yān then collected the seals,
and from those with a salary of three hundred shí upwards, all submitted them to Zǐzhī,
and Zǐzhī thus became powerful.
Fāngwúzǐ said:
"I have heard that according to ancient rites:
When traveling, one does not share a carriage with those wearing the same mourning garments,
nor share a household with those of the same clan,
so how much more should a ruler
lend his authority and externalize his power!"
Wú Zhāng said to King Xuān of Hán:
"A ruler should not pretend to love someone,
for then one day he cannot hate him;
he should not pretend to hate someone,
for then one day he cannot love him.
Therefore, if signs of pretended hatred or pretended love appear,
flatterers will use them as grounds to slander or praise.
Even an enlightened ruler
cannot then retrieve the situation,
so how much more when he genuinely lends his authority to others!"
King Zhào was strolling in the garden,
when his attendants offered a rabbit to a tiger but then withdrew it,
causing the tiger to glare fiercely with rounded eyes.
The King exclaimed:
"How detestable
are the tiger's eyes!"
His attendants replied:
"Lord Píngyáng's eyes are even more detestable than these.
Seeing this tiger poses no harm,
but whoever sees Lord Píngyáng's eyes like this
is certain to die."
The next day,
when Lord Píngyáng heard of this,
he sent someone to kill the speaker,
yet the King did not punish him.
The ruler of Wèi went to pay homage to Zhōu,
where the Zhōu official in charge of ceremonies asked for his name.
He replied:
"I am the feudal lord Pìjiàng."
The Zhōu official refused him, saying:
"A feudal lord cannot share the same name as the Son of Heaven."
The ruler of Wèi then changed it himself, saying:
"I am the feudal lord Huǐ."
Only then was he admitted.
Confucius heard of this and remarked:
"How far-reaching is the prohibition against presumption!
Not even an empty name is lent to others,
let alone matters of substance?"
Argument Four:
If one shakes a tree
by plucking each leaf individually,
it is laborious and not thorough;
but if one shakes it by patting the trunk from both sides,
all the leaves will tremble.
Shaking a tree near a deep pool,
birds will be startled and fly high,
and fish will be frightened and dive deep.
A skilled net-caster pulls the main rope;
if one had to handle each of the thousands of meshes to succeed,
it would be laborious and difficult;
but by pulling the main rope,
the fish are already ensnared.
Thus, officials are
the root of the people
and the guiding rope;
hence, the sage governs the officials, not the people directly.
In firefighting,
if the officer is ordered to carry pots and jars to the fire,
that is the use of one person;
but if he directs with a whip and commands to urge others on,
he can control ten thousand men.
Therefore, the sage does not attend to the common people personally,
and the enlightened ruler does not handle minor affairs himself.
When Zàofǔ was weeding,
a father and son passed by in a carriage,
but the horses were startled and would not move.
The son got down to pull the horses,
and the father pushed the carriage,
asking Zàofǔ to help them push the cart.
Zàofǔ then put away his tools,
stopped his work, and hitched a ride with them,
taking the reins from the son.
Only then did he gather the reins and take the whip,
before even using them,
the horses all galloped forward.
Had Zàofǔ been unable to drive,
even if he had exhausted his strength and worn himself out
helping them push the cart,
the horses would still not have budged.
Now, to keep oneself at ease
and even hitch a ride,
benefiting others,
one must have the method to control it.
Thus, the state is
the ruler's carriage;
power is
the ruler's horse.
Without the method to control them,
even if the ruler labors personally,
chaos is still unavoidable;
with the method to control them,
the ruler can reside in a place of ease and pleasure,
yet achieve the merits of an emperor or king.
The hammer and anvil are
used to level what is uneven;
the straightening frame is
used to correct what is not straight.
The sage's establishment of laws
is to level what is uneven
and correct what is not straight.
When Nàochǐ held power in Qí,
he pulled out King Mǐn's tendons;
when Lǐ Duì held power in Zhào,
he starved Lord Fù to death.
These two rulers
both failed to use their hammer, anvil, and straightening frame,
so they died violently,
becoming the laughingsstock of the world.
One version says:
Upon entering Qí,
one only hears of Nàochǐ and not the King of Qí;
upon entering Zhào,
one only hears of Lǐ Duì and not the King of Zhào.
Hence it is said:
If the ruler does not wield the method,
his authority and power become light,
and his ministers monopolize the fame.
Another version:
King Wǔlíng had King Huìwén assume the government,
with Lǐ Duì as chancellor.
King Wǔlíng did not personally hold the power of life and death,
so he was coerced by Lǐ Duì.
Yet another version:
Tián Yīng served as chancellor of Qí,
and someone advised the king, saying:
"The annual financial accounts,
if you do not take a few days to review them personally,
you will have no way to know the corruption, deceit, gains, and losses of your officials."
The king said:
"Good."
Tián Yīng heard of this,
and immediately requested the king to review the accounts.
As the king was about to do so,
Tián Yīng ordered the officials to prepare account documents in great detail down to pecks, bushels, and pints.
The king personally reviewed the accounts,
but the accounts were too numerous to finish.
After a meal break,
he resumed his seat,
not even eating his evening meal.
Tián Yīng then said to him:
"These are matters that your officials have worked on day and night all year, not daring to be negligent.
If you spend one night reviewing them,
it will encourage and motivate the officials."
The king said:
"Alright."
Soon, the king had fallen asleep,
and the officials all took out knives to alter the account documents with their detailed measures.
The king's personal review
only gave rise to chaos.
Argument Five:
Zī Zhèngzǐ was pulling a cart up a high bridge but could not manage it.
Zī Zhèng sat on the shaft and sang,
causing those ahead to stop,
and those behind to hurry forward,
and thus the cart went up.
Had Zī Zhèng no method to attract people,
even if he had exhausted his strength to death,
the cart would still not have gone up.
Now, without reaching the point of toil and hardship,
the cart ascended,
because he had a method to attract people.
When Jiǎn Zhǔ of Zhào sent out tax collectors,
an official asked about the tax rate's severity or leniency.
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"Not too heavy, not too light.
If too heavy,
the profits go to the ruler;
if too light,
the benefits go to the people.
With no private profit for the officials, it is just."
Bó Yí said to Jiǎn Zhǔ of Zhào:
"Your state is 'full' in the middle."
Jiǎn Zhǔ cheerfully asked:
"What do you mean?"
Bó Yí replied:
"The state treasury is empty above,
the common people are poor and hungry below,
yet the corrupt officials are wealthy."
Duke Huán of Qí traveled incognito to inspect the households of the common people.
There was an elderly man who was supporting himself,
and Duke Huán asked him the reason.
The man replied:
"I have three sons,
but my family is too poor to get them wives,
so they are away working as hired laborers and have not returned."
Duke Huán returned to the palace,
and reported this to Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"When stored grain rots and wealth is discarded,
the people will starve;
when there are pining women in the palace,
then men among the populace will lack wives."
Duke Huán said:
"Well said."
He then surveyed the palace and had the women married off.
He issued an order to the people stating:
"Men shall take a wife at twenty,
and women shall marry at fifteen."
Another account says:
Duke Huán traveled incognito among the common people,
and there was a man named Lùmén Jì,
who was seventy years old and had no wife.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"Are there commoners who are old and wifeless?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There is Lùmén Jì,
who is seventy years old and has no wife."
Duke Huán said:[34"How can we ensure that he gets a wife?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I have heard that:
if those above have accumulated wealth,
then the ministers and people below will surely be in want;
if there are pining women in the palace,
then there will be old men without wives."
Duke Huán said:
"Well said."
He ordered that in the palace,
"women who have not yet served the ruler be sent out to marry."
He then decreed that men should marry at twenty,
and women should marry at fifteen.
Thus, there were no pining women within,
and no unmarried men outside.
Yánlíng Zhuōzǐ rode in a carriage drawn by blue-dragon horses with patterned coats,
with hook-shaped ornaments in front,
and sharp goads behind.
When the horses wanted to advance, the hook ornaments restrained them,
and when they wanted to retreat, the sharp goads pierced them,
so the horses dodged sideways.
Zào Fǔ passed by and wept for them,
saying:
"The way of governing people in ancient times was also like this.
Rewards are meant to encourage, yet slander is present;
punishments are meant to restrain, yet praise is added.
The people stand in confusion, not knowing which way to turn,
this is also why a sage would weep."
Another account says:
Yánlíng Zhuōzǐ rode in a carriage drawn by blue-dragon horses with pheasant-patterned coats,
with ornate ornaments in front,
and sharp goads behind.
To advance, he pulled them,
to retreat, he whipped them.
The horses could neither advance forward,
nor retreat backward,
so they dodged and bolted,
whereupon he got down, drew a knife, and cut their legs.
Zào Fǔ saw this,
and wept,
Another account says:
Yánlíng Zhuōzǐ rode in a carriage drawn by blue-dragon horses with pheasant-patterned coats,
with ornate ornaments in front,
and sharp goads behind.
To advance, he pulled them,
to retreat, he whipped them.
The horses could neither advance forward,
nor retreat backward,
so they dodged and bolted,
whereupon he got down, drew a knife, and cut their legs.
Zào Fǔ saw this, and wept,
refusing to eat all day,
then looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"The whip,
is meant to make them advance,
yet ornate ornaments block the front;
the reins,
are meant to make them retreat,
yet sharp goads menace behind.
Now, the ruler promotes men for their purity,
but demotes them for not catering to his attendants;
he praises them for their fairness and integrity, 〓#
but dismisses them for not obeying. 〓#
The people are fearful, 〓#
and stand in confusion, not knowing which way to turn, 〓#
this is why a sage weeps." 〓#
Duke Wén of Jìn was about to battle the Chǔ army,
and summoned Jiùfàn to ask him,
saying:
"I am going to fight the Chǔ army,
they are many and we are few,
what should I do?"
Jiùfàn said:
"I have heard that:
a gentleman of elaborate rites,
never tires of loyalty and trustworthiness;
but in the midst of battle formations,
one never tires of deception and falsehood.
Your Majesty should simply use deceit."
Duke Wén dismissed Jiùfàn,
then summoned Yōng Jì and asked him,
saying:
"I am going to fight the Chǔ army,
they are many and we are few,
what should I do?"
Yōng Jì replied:
"Burning the forest to hunt,
may stealthily capture many beasts,
but in the future there will be none left;
using deceit to deal with the people,
may steal temporary gains,
but in the future there will be no repeat."
Duke Wén said:
"Well said."
He dismissed Yōng Jì,
and used Jiùfàn's strategy to battle and defeat the Chǔ army.
Upon returning, he distributed honors,
placing Yōng Jì first and Jiùfàn later.
The ministers said:
"Regarding the matter of Chéngpú,
it was Jiùfàn's plan.
To use his advice but rank him lower,
is that acceptable?"
Duke Wén said:
"This is not something you understand.
Jiùfàn's words
were a temporary expedient;
Yōng Jì's words
concerned the benefit for ten thousand generations."
Zhòngní heard of this,
and said:
"Duke Wén's rise to hegemony
was fitting indeed!
He knew both the temporary expedient,
and the benefit for ten thousand generations."
Some say:
Yōng Jì's reply
did not address Duke Wén's question.
In general, when responding to a question,
one should answer according to the question's scale, urgency, and importance.
If the question is lofty and grand,
but the answer is lowly and narrow,
an enlightened ruler will not accept it.
Now Duke Wén asked
"how to face many with few",
but the reply was
"in the future there will be no repeat",
this is not a proper response.
Moreover, Duke Wén neither understood the temporary expedient,
nor the benefit for ten thousand generations.
If the battle is won,
then the state is secure and the ruler's position firm,
the military strong and authority established,
even if there are future consequences,
none could be greater than this,
so why worry that the benefit for ten thousand generations
would not come?
If the battle is lost,
then the state perishes and the army weakens,
the ruler dies and his name fades,
escaping immediate death would be impossible,
how could there be leisure to await the benefit for ten thousand generations?
Awaiting the benefit for ten thousand generations
depends on victory today;
victory today
depends on deceiving the enemy.
Deceiving the enemy
is a benefit for all eternity.
Thus it is said:
Yōng Jì's response
did not address Duke Wén's question.
Moreover, Duke Wén did not understand Jiù Fàn's words.
What Jiù Fàn meant by
"not disdaining deception"
was
not deceiving one's own people,
but deceiving the enemy.
The enemy
is the state being attacked;
even if there are no subsequent gains,
what harm is there?
The reason Duke Wén prioritized Yōng Jì
—was it because of his merit?
Yet the strategy that defeated Chǔ and crushed their army
was Jiù Fàn's plan;
was it because of his wise words?
Then Yōng Jì merely spoke of
"no subsequent gains,"
which
was not wise counsel.
Jiù Fàn, however, combined both.
When Jiù Fàn said
"a gentleman of elaborate rites
does not disdain loyalty and good faith,"
loyalty
is how one cares for subordinates;
good faith
is how one avoids deceiving the people.
Since he already advocated care and non-deception,
what words could be wiser than this?
Yet he necessarily added "resorting to deception"
as a military strategy.
Jiù Fàn first offered wise counsel,
then achieved victory in battle.
Thus Jiù Fàn had dual accomplishments yet was evaluated later,
while Yōng Jì had none yet was rewarded first.
"Duke Wén's rise to hegemony—
was it not fitting?"
Yet Zhòngní failed to understand proper reward.
When farmers at Lìshān encroached on each other's fields,
Shùn went to plow there,
and after one year,
the field boundaries were straightened.
When fishermen by the river contested fishing spots,
Shùn went to fish there,
and after one year they yielded to elders.
When potters of the Eastern Yí made brittle vessels,
Shùn went to pot there,
and after one year the vessels became sturdy.
Zhòngní sighed:
"Plowing,
fishing and potting
were not Shùn's offices,
yet he went to practice them
to remedy corruption.
How truly benevolent was Shùn!
He personally labored in hardship
and the people followed him.
Thus it is said:
The virtue of sages transforms others!"
Someone asked a Confucian scholar:
"At this time,
where was Yáo?"
The man replied:
"Yáo was the Son of Heaven."
"Then
how could Zhòngní consider Yáo sage?
If a sage rules with clear-sightedness from above,
he would eliminate all corruption from the world.
Now if plowing and fishing caused no disputes,
and pottery vessels weren't brittle,
what virtue had Shùn to transform?
If Shùn remedied corruption,
then Yáo had failings.
To praise Shùn
negates Yáo's clear-sightedness;
to sage Yáo
negates Shùn's transformative virtue—
both cannot be upheld.
A man from Chǔ sold shields and spears,
praising them thus:
'My shields are so strong
nothing can pierce them.'
Then praising his spears:
'My spears are so sharp
they pierce everything.'
Someone said:
'Using your spear to pierce your shield—
what then?'
The man could not reply.
An impenetrable shield
and an all-piercing spear
cannot coexist in the world.
Now Yáo and
Shùn cannot both be praised—
this is the spears-and-shields argument.
Moreover, when Shùn remedied corruption,
one year corrected one fault,
three years three faults.
Shùn's life had an end,
his longevity had an end,
but the world's faults are endless;
to chase the endless with the finite
would remedy very little.
Rewards and punishments, if enforced universally,
with the decree:
'Those who meet standards are rewarded,
those who don't are punished.'
Would see changes by dusk if decreed at dawn,
changes by dawn if decreed at dusk—
the whole realm could be transformed in ten days.
Why wait a full year?
If Shùn didn't advise Yáo to enforce such decrees
but labored personally instead,
wasn't that lacking in method?
Furthermore, transforming people through personal hardship
was difficult even for Yáo and Shùn;
while correcting subordinates through authority
is easy even for mediocre rulers.
To govern the world,
abandoning what mediocre rulers find easy
for what Yáo and
Shùn found difficult—
such approach cannot administer governance."
When Guǎn Zhòng fell ill,
Duke Huán visited him,
saying:
"Father Zhòng, if your illness
unfortunately proves fatal,
what would you advise me?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Even without your asking,
I intended to memorialize.
I urge you to dismiss Shù Diāo,
remove Yì Yá,
and distance yourself from Wèi's Prince Kāifāng.
Yì Yá managed your meals—
you had never tasted human flesh,
so he steamed his son's head and served it.
Human nature loves one's children;
if he doesn't love his own child,
how can he love you?
You are jealous and fond of inner court affairs,
so Shù Diāo castrated himself to manage them.
Human nature loves one's own body;
if he doesn't love his own body,
how can he love you?
Kāifāng served you fifteen years;
between Qí and Wèi it's but few days' journey,
yet he abandoned his mother,
serving long without returning.
If he doesn't love his mother,
how can he love you?
I have heard:
Feigned integrity cannot last,
covered falsehood cannot endure.
I urge you to remove these three men."
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
Duke Huán did not act.
When Duke Huán died,
maggots crawled out the door, his body unburied.
Some say:
What Guǎn Zhòng advised Duke Huán
was not the words of one with principles.
His reason for removing Shù Diāo and
Yì Yá
was that they didn't love their own persons,
merely catering to the ruler's desires.
Saying
"if they don't love their own persons,
how can they love the ruler?"
Then should subjects who exhaust their strength and die for their lord
be rejected by Guǎn Zhòng?
It is said,
"If one does not cherish his own life and strength,
how can he cherish his sovereign?"
This implies that the sovereign should dismiss loyal ministers.
Moreover, to assume that one who does not love himself
will not love his sovereign,
is akin to judging Guǎn Zhòng's failure to die for Prince Jiū
as proof that he would not die for Duke Huán,
thus placing Guǎn Zhòng in the category of those to be dismissed.
The way of an enlightened ruler is not so;
he establishes what the people desire to encourage their achievements,
hence creating ranks and emoluments to motivate them;
he establishes what the people detest to prohibit their wickedness,
hence instituting punishments to intimidate them.
Rewards are trustworthy and punishments are certain,
so the sovereign promotes ministers based on merit,
and the wicked are not employed by the ruler.
Even if there were a Shù Diāo,
what could he do to the sovereign?
Moreover, ministers exhaust their life and strength
to trade with the sovereign,
while the sovereign bestows ranks and emoluments
to trade with the ministers.
The relationship between sovereign and minister
is not like the intimacy of father and son,
but arises from calculations.
If the sovereign follows the right way,
then ministers exert their efforts and wickedness does not arise;
if he does not follow the way,
then ministers obstruct the sovereign's clarity above
and pursue private interests below.
Guǎn Zhòng did not clarify this principle
to Duke Huán,
urging him only to dismiss Shù Diāo;
but once one Shù Diāo is gone, another arrives,
which is not the way to eradicate wickedness.
Moreover, the reason Duke Huán died
with maggots flowing out his door unburied
was due to the overpowering ministers.
The reality of overpowering ministers
is the usurpation of the sovereign's authority.
With ministers who usurp authority,
the sovereign's commands do not reach below,
and the ministers' sentiments do not reach above.
The power of one man can separate sovereign and minister,
causing good and bad to go unheard,
and calamity and fortune to be uncommunicated,
hence the disaster of going unburied.
The way of an enlightened ruler is this:
one person does not hold multiple offices,
one office does not handle multiple affairs;
the lowly do not wait for the noble to advance,
high ministers do not rely on court attendants to be seen;
all officials are well-connected,
and the multitude of ministers converge like spokes;
those to be rewarded are seen by the sovereign for their merits,
those to be punished are known by the sovereign for their crimes.
With perception and knowledge not contradictory beforehand,
and rewards and punishments not obstructed afterward,
how could there be the disaster of going unburied?
Guǎn Zhòng did not clarify this to Duke Huán,
only urging him to dismiss the three men,
hence it is said:
"Guǎn Zhòng lacked principle."
When Lord Xiāng was besieged in Jìnyáng,
and emerged from the siege,
he rewarded five men who had merit,
with Gāo Hè as the first to be rewarded.
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"In the affair of Jìnyáng,
Hè had no great merit,
yet now he is the first rewarded,
why?"
Lord Xiāng said:
"During the Jìnyáng affair,
my state was in peril,
and the altars of land and grain were endangered.
Among my ministers, none were without arrogant or disrespectful intentions,
only Hè did not lose the propriety between sovereign and minister,
therefore I rewarded him first."
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"What excellent rewarding,
Lord Xiāng!
Rewarding one man ensures that no minister in the world dares to neglect propriety."
Some say:
Zhòngní did not understand excellent rewarding.
He who excels at rewards and punishments
ensures that officials dare not encroach on duties,
and ministers dare not neglect propriety.
The sovereign establishes laws above,
and below there are no deceitful hearts.
Thus,
one may be called excellent at rewards and punishments.
If Lord Xiāng in Jìnyáng
had commands unheeded,
and prohibitions unenforced,
then Lord Xiāng would have no state,
and Jìnyáng no sovereign;
with whom then could he defend it?
Now, Lord Xiāng in Jìnyáng,
with the Zhì clan flooding the city,
mortars and stoves breeding turtles,
yet the people had no thought of rebellion,
shows the closeness between sovereign and minister.
Lord Xiāng, having the closeness between sovereign and minister,
and wielding the method of enforcing commands and prohibitions,
still had arrogant and disrespectful ministers,
which was Lord Xiāng's failure in punishment.
As for ministers,
they should be rewarded when they accomplish tasks with merit.
Now Hè merely avoided arrogance and disrespect,
yet Lord Xiāng rewarded him,
which was a failure in rewarding.
An enlightened ruler does not reward the meritless,
nor punish the innocent.
Now Lord Xiāng did not punish the arrogant and disrespectful ministers,
but rewarded the meritless Hè,
wherein lies Lord Xiāng's excellence in rewarding?
Hence it is said
"Zhòngní did not understand excellent rewarding."
Duke Píng of Jìn was drinking with his ministers,
and in his intoxication,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Nothing is more joyful than being a sovereign,
for no one disobeys my words."
Shī Kuàng, seated in attendance before him,
took his lute and struck him.
The duke dodged by spreading his lapels,
and the lute broke against the wall.
The duke said:
"Grand Master, whom did you strike?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Just now, there was a petty man speaking at your side,
so I struck him."
The duke said:
"It was I."
Shī Kuàng said:
"Alas!
These are not the words of a ruler."
The attendants requested to punish him.
The duke said:
"Release him,
let this be a warning to me."
Some say:
Duke Píng failed in the way of a sovereign,
and Shī Kuàng failed in the propriety of a minister.
To condemn one's actions and punish one's person
is the sovereign's role toward the minister;
if one's actions are wrong,
then one should remonstrate with words,
and if good advice is not heeded,
then one should distance oneself;
this is the minister's role toward the sovereign.
Now Shī Kuàng, condemning Duke Píng's actions,
did not present a minister's remonstrance,
but carried out a sovereign's punishment,
raising the lute to strike his person,
which inverted the positions of superior and inferior,
and violated the propriety of a minister.
As for a minister,
if the sovereign has faults, he should remonstrate;
if remonstrance is unheeded,
he should lightly regard rank and emolument and await his fate;
this is the propriety of a minister.
Now Shī Kuàng, condemning Duke Píng's fault,
raised the lute to strike his person;
even a stern father would not do this to his son,
yet Shī Kuàng did it to his sovereign,
which is the method of great treason.
A minister committing great treason,
and Duke Píng delighting in and accepting it,
shows his failure in the way of a sovereign.
Thus, Duke Píng's actions should not be praised,
lest it cause sovereigns to err in listening
without realizing their fault;
Shī Kuàng's actions should not be praised either,
lest it allow treacherous ministers to imitate extreme remonstrance
and disguise the way of regicide.
cannot be said to have both sides enlightened,
this constitutes dual faults.
Therefore it is said:
Píng Gōng failed in the way of a ruler,
and Shī Kuàng also failed in the propriety of a minister.
During the time of Qí Huán Gōng,
there was a recluse named Xiǎo Chén Jì,
whom Huán Gōng visited three times without managing to see.
Huán Gōng said:
"I have heard that commoner scholars,
if they do not disdain titles and emoluments,
have no means to influence the lord of ten thousand chariots;
the lord of ten thousand chariots,
if he does not love benevolence and righteousness,
also has no means to humble himself before commoner scholars."
Thereupon, after five visits, he finally managed to see him.
Some say:
Huán Gōng did not understand benevolence and righteousness.
Now benevolence and righteousness mean:
to worry about the harms of the world,
to address the troubles of a state,
without avoiding lowliness or humiliation—
this is called benevolence and righteousness.
Thus, Yī Yǐn, because the central states were in disorder,
served as a cook to Tāng;
Bǎi Lǐ Xī, because Qín was in disorder,
served as a captive to Mù Gōng.
Both worried about the harms of the world,
addressed the troubles of a state,
and did not refuse lowliness or humiliation,
therefore they are called benevolent and righteous.
Now Huán Gōng, with the power of ten thousand chariots,
humbled himself before a commoner scholar,
intending to care for the state of Qí,
yet Xiǎo Chén did not act accordingly,
showing that Xiǎo Chén neglected the people.
Neglecting the people cannot be called benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness mean:
not losing the propriety of a minister,
not undermining the positions of ruler and minister.
Therefore, within the four borders,
those who hold offerings and attend court are called ministers;
ministers and officials divided in duties and undertaking tasks are called the common people.
Now Xiǎo Chén, being among the multitude of common people,
yet opposing the desires of his ruler,
therefore cannot be called benevolent and righteous.
With benevolence and righteousness absent,
Huán Gōng further proceeded to treat him with respect.
If Xiǎo Chén had wisdom and ability yet avoided Huán Gōng,
this is concealment,
deserving punishment;
if he had no wisdom or ability
yet arrogantly slighted Huán Gōng,
this is deception,
deserving execution.
Xiǎo Chén's conduct
merits either punishment or execution.
Huán Gōng failed to understand the principles of ruler and minister,
and respected a person deserving punishment or execution.
This means Huán Gōng taught the state of Qí a custom of disrespecting superiors and insulting the ruler,
which is not the way to achieve order.
Therefore it is said:
Huán Gōng did not understand benevolence and righteousness.
In the battle of Mí Jī,
Hán Xiàn Zǐ was about to execute a man.
Xì Xiàn Zǐ heard of it,
and rode swiftly to save him.
By the time he arrived,
the man had already been executed.
Xì Zǐ then said:
"Why not expose the body?"
His attendant said:
"Did you not intend to save him earlier?"
Xì Zǐ said:
"How dare I not share the blame?"
Some say:
Xì Zǐ's words
must be carefully examined,
for they do not share the blame.
If the person Hán Zǐ executed
was guilty,
then he should not have been saved;
saving a guilty person
is what undermines the law,
and if the law is undermined, the state falls into disorder.
If he was not guilty,
then one should not advise exposing the body,
advising exposure
is to doubly wrong the innocent,
and doubly wronging the innocent
is what stirs resentment among the people,
and if the people resent, the state is endangered.
Xì Zǐ's words
either endanger the state or cause disorder,
and must be carefully examined.
Moreover, if the person Hán Zǐ executed was guilty,
what blame was there for Xì Zǐ to share?
If the executed was not guilty,
then he had already been executed,
and Xì Zǐ arrived only afterward,
meaning Hán Zǐ's blame was already incurred,
and Xì Zǐ arrived late.
Now Xì Zǐ said
"expose the body,"
which not only fails to share the blame for the execution,
but also generates blame for the exposure.
Is this what you call sharing the blame?
In the past, when Zhòu had the roasting pillar,
Chóng Hóu
and È Lái also said
to cut the shins of those crossing the river—
how did that share Zhòu's blame?
Moreover, the people's expectations of their superiors are great;
Hán Zǐ failed to meet them,
and they hoped Xì Zǐ would;
now Xì Zǐ also failed to meet them,
then the people lost all hope in their superiors.
Therefore it is said:
Xì Zǐ's words did not share the blame,
but increased it.
Furthermore, Xì Zǐ went to save the guilty,
implying that Hán Zǐ was wrong,
yet he did not explain why it was wrong,
but advised him
"to expose the body,"
this made Hán Zǐ unaware of his fault.
Thus, below, he made the people lose hope in their superiors,
and above, he made Hán Zǐ unaware of his error—
I do not see how Xì Zǐ shared the blame.
Huán Gōng loosened Guǎn Zhòng's bonds and made him chancellor.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am favored,
yet I am of low rank."
The Duke said:
"I will place you above Gāo
and Guó."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am honored,
yet I am poor."
The Duke said:
"I will grant you the revenue of three collections."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I am wealthy,
yet I am distant."
Thereupon, he was established as Zhòng Fù.
Xiāo Lüè said:
"Guǎn Zhòng, because low rank cannot govern the noble,
requested to be above Gāo
and Guó;
because poverty cannot govern the wealthy,
requested the three collections;
because distance cannot govern the intimate,
was placed as Zhòng Fù.
Guǎn Zhòng was not greedy,
but acted to facilitate governance."
Some say:
If now a slave were to convey the ruler's order to a minister,
none would dare disobey—
not because the minister is lowly and the slave honored,
but because the ruler's command is imposed,
and none dare not comply.
Now if Guǎn Zhòng's governance
did not rely on Huán Gōng,
that would be to have no ruler.
A state without a ruler
cannot be governed.
If he relied on Huán Gōng's authority,
and issued Huán Gōng's orders,
that is how even a slave gains trust—
why wait for the honor of Gāo,
Guó, or Zhòng Fù
to act?
In current affairs,
even low-ranking officials conveying orders
do not avoid the noble,
nor do they approach the lowly.
Therefore, when actions are lawful,
even a eunuch can be trusted by ministers and chancellors;
when actions are unlawful,
even high officials are disrespected by the common people.
Now Guǎn Zhòng did not strive to honor the ruler and clarify laws,
but engaged in increasing favor and ranks,
this is either due to Guǎn Zhòng's greed for wealth and honor,
or he must be ignorant and unaware of statecraft.
Hence it is said:
Guǎn Zhòng had faults in conduct,
and Xiāo Luè received excessive praise.
King Xuān of Hán asked Jiū Liú:
"I wish to employ both Gōng Zhòng and
Gōng Shū,
would that be acceptable?"
Jiū Liú replied:
"In the past, Wèi employed both Lóu and
Dí
and lost the Western Hé region,
Chǔ employed both Zhāo and
Jǐng
and lost Yān and
Yǐng.
Now if you employ both Gōng Zhòng and
Gōng Shū,
they will surely contend over affairs and seek external alliances,
then the state will inevitably face troubles."
Some say:
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí employed both Guǎn Zhòng and
Bào Shū,
and Chéng Tāng employed both Yī Yǐn and
Zhòng Huǐ.
If employing two ministers is a state's worry,
then Duke Huán would not have achieved hegemony,
nor would Chéng Tāng have become king.
King Mǐn employed only Nào Chǐ
and met his death at the Eastern Temple,
Lord Fù employed only Lǐ Duì,
and died from reduced food.
If the ruler has statecraft,
employing two is not a problem;
without statecraft,
employing two leads to contention and external alliances,
while employing one leads to autocracy
and regicide.
Now Jiū Liú lacked statecraft to advise his superior,
making his ruler abandon two for one,
this would either bring the worries of losing Western Hé,
Yān, and Yǐng,
or the peril of personal death and reduced food,
thus Jiū Liú did not have good insight in his words.
Duke Jǐng visited Yàn Zǐ,
saying:
"Your residence is small,
close to the market,
please move your home to the gardens of Yùzhāng."
Yàn Zǐ bowed twice and declined:
"Moreover, my family is poor,
we rely on market food,
and go there morning and evening,
so we cannot live far away."
Duke Jǐng laughed and said:
"Since your family is familiar with the market,
do you know what's expensive and cheap?"
At that time, Duke Jǐng had excessive punishments,
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Prosthetic feet are expensive, while shoes are cheap."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"Because there are many punishments."
Duke Jǐng suddenly changed expression and said:
"Am I being tyrannical!"
Thereupon he reduced five punishments.
Some say:
Yàn Zǐ's claim about expensive prosthetic feet,
was not sincere,
but intended as a convenient excuse
to stop the numerous punishments.
This is the problem of not examining governance properly.
Punishments should be appropriate, not numerous,
if inappropriate, even few are not enough.
Not hearing about inappropriateness,
but complaining about too many,
is the problem of lacking statecraft.
In a defeated army, executions number in hundreds and thousands,
yet retreats do not stop;
if punishments for order and chaos
are feared to be insufficient,
and villains still are not fully eliminated.
Now Yàn Zǐ did not examine their appropriateness,
but complained about too many,
isn't that absurd?
Sparing weeds depletes grain crops,
favoring thieves harms good people.
Now to slow punishments,
practice leniency and kindness,
is to benefit villains and harm good people,
this is not the way to govern.
Duke Huán of Qí got drunk,
lost his cap,
felt ashamed,
and did not hold court for three days.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This is a shame for the state,
why not cleanse it through governance?"
The Duke said:
"Well said!"
Then he opened granaries,
gave to the poor,
reviewed prisons,
and released minor offenders.
After three days, people sang:
"Why doesn't the Duke lose his cap again!"
Some say:
Guǎn Zhòng cleansed the Duke's shame among commoners,
but created shame for the Duke among gentlemen.
If Duke Huán opened granaries
and gave to the poor,
reviewed prisons
and released minor offenders,
unjustly,
it cannot cleanse shame;
if done justly,
yet Duke Huán delayed righteousness,
waiting to lose his cap before acting,
then was the Duke acting righteously
not because of the lost cap?
Thus, while cleansing the shame of losing the cap among commoners,
he also created the shame of neglecting righteousness among gentlemen.
Moreover, opening granaries for the poor
is to reward the undeserving;
reviewing prisons to release minor offenders
is to not punish faults.
Rewarding the undeserving,
makes people opportunistic towards superiors;
not punishing faults,
makes people unafraid to do wrong.
This is the root of chaos,
how can it cleanse shame?
In the past, King Wén invaded Méng,
conquered Jǔ,
and took Fēng,
three actions that angered King Zhòu.
King Wén then feared,
offered the land west of Luò,
and the state of Chìrǎng
spanning a thousand lǐ,
to request abolishing the pào-luò punishment.
All under heaven rejoiced.
Confucius heard this,
saying:
"How benevolent,
King Wén!
Lightly regarding a thousand-lǐ state
to request abolishing the pào-luò punishment.
How wise,
King Wén!
Giving up a thousand-lǐ land
and winning the hearts of all under heaven."
Some say:
For Confucius to consider King Wén wise,
isn't that mistaken?
The wise
know where calamities lie and avoid them,
thus keeping themselves from harm.
If King Wén incurred Zhòu's hatred
because he failed to win people's hearts?
Then seeking people's hearts
to resolve hatred might work.
If Zhòu hated him for greatly winning people's hearts,
Moreover, he then lightly treated his territory to win over people's hearts,
which further aroused suspicion,
and that was precisely why he was shackled and imprisoned in Yǒulǐ.
Zhèng Chángzhě once said:
"To embody the Dào,
one must neither act nor show."
This principle was most suitable for King Wén,
as it prevented others from suspecting him.
Although Confucius considered King Wén wise,
he did not reach this conclusion.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shū Xiàng:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí nine times assembled the feudal lords,
and once rectified the world.
Was this due to the strength of his ministers,
or the strength of the ruler?"
Shū Xiàng replied:
"Guǎn Zhòng excelled at cutting the cloth,
Bīn Xūwú excelled at tailoring the seams,
Xí Péng excelled at finishing the edges.
When the garment was completed,
the ruler raised it and wore it.
Thus, it was the strength of the ministers.
What strength did the ruler have?"
Shī Kuàng leaned over his qín and laughed.
The Duke asked:
"Why does the Grand Musician laugh?"
Shī Kuàng replied:
"I laugh at Shū Xiàng's response to the ruler.
All who serve as ministers are like cooks blending the five flavors to present to the ruler.
If the ruler does not eat,
who dares to force him?
Allow me to use an analogy:
The ruler is like the soil;
the ministers are like the plants and trees.
Only when the soil is fertile
can the plants and trees grow large and strong.
Thus, it was the strength of the ruler.
What strength did the ministers have?"
Some say:
Both Shū Xiàng's and
Shī Kuàng's responses
are one-sided arguments.
To rectify the world once
and assemble the feudal lords nine times
is a great achievement.
It is not solely due to the ruler's strength,
nor solely due to the ministers' strength.
In the past, Gōng Zhīqí was in Yú,
and Xī Fùjī was in Cáo.
Both ministers were wise,
their words hit the mark in affairs,
and their actions achieved success.
Yet both Yú and Cáo perished.
Why?
Because they had such ministers but not such rulers.
Moreover, Jiǎn Shū stayed in Gān and Gān perished,
but when he was in Qín, Qín became hegemonic.
This was not because Jiǎn Shū was foolish in Gān
and wise in Qín,
but because in one case there was a capable ruler and in the other there was not.
Shū Xiàng's claim that
"it was the strength of the ministers"
is incorrect.
In the past, Duke Huán had two markets in his palace,
two hundred women's quarters,
and he let his hair down to consort with women.
With Guǎn Zhòng,
he became the foremost of the Five Hegemons;
without Guǎn Zhòng
and with Shù Diāo,
he died,
with maggots flowing out the door and no burial.
If it were not due to the ministers' strength,
then Guǎn Zhòng should not be credited with the hegemony;
if it were due to the ruler's strength,
then Shù Diāo should not be blamed for the chaos.
In the past,
Duke Wén of Jìn became infatuated with a woman of Qí
and forgot to return home.
Jiù Fǎn remonstrated strenuously,
thus causing him to return to Jìn.
Therefore, Duke Huán achieved assembly through Guǎn Zhòng,
and Duke Wén achieved hegemony through Jiù Fǎn.
Yet Shī Kuàng said
"it was the strength of the ruler,"
which is also incorrect.
All Five Hegemons who achieved success and fame under heaven
necessarily had both ruler and ministers contributing their strength.
Therefore it is said:
Both Shū Xiàng's and
Shī Kuàng's responses
are one-sided arguments.
During the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
when a guest from Jìn arrived,
the officer in charge requested the proper rites.
Duke Huán said
"report to Zhòngfù"
three times.
A court jester laughed and said:
"How easy it is
to be a ruler!
One moment it's Zhòngfù,
the next it's Zhòngfù."
Duke Huán said:
"I have heard that
'a ruler labors in seeking men,
but is at ease in employing them.'
I found it difficult to obtain Zhòngfù,
but after obtaining him,
why should it not be easy?"
Some say:
Duke Huán's response to the jester
was not the words of a true ruler.
Duke Huán considered it laborious for a ruler to seek men,
but why should seeking men be laborious?
Yī Yǐn offered himself as a cook to Tāng,
Bǎilǐ Xī offered himself as a captive to Duke Mù.
Being a captive is humiliating;
being a cook is shameful.
To endure humiliation and shame to approach a ruler
shows the urgency with which the worthy worry about the world.
Thus, a ruler need only not reject the worthy;
seeking the worthy is not difficult for a ruler.
Moreover, official positions
are for appointing the worthy;
ranks and emoluments
are for rewarding merit.
Establish official positions,
set forth ranks and emoluments,
and the scholars will come of their own accord.
How could a ruler labor in this?
Employing men is not a matter of ease either.
Although a ruler employs men,
he must measure them with standards,
and assess them with performance and titles;
if affairs accord with the law, they proceed,
if not, they stop;
if achievements match their words, reward them,
if not, punish them.
To control ministers with performance and titles,
and to measure subordinates with standards—
this cannot be relinquished.
How could a ruler be at ease?
Seeking men is not laborious,
employing men is not ease,
yet Duke Huán said
"labors in seeking men,
is at ease in employing them,"
which is incorrect.
Moreover, it was not difficult for Duke Huán to obtain Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng did not die for his lord and instead submitted to Duke Huán,
Bào Shū lightly regarded his own office, yielded to the capable,
and entrusted him with responsibility.
Clearly,
it was not difficult for Duke Huán to obtain Guǎn Zhòng.
After obtaining Guǎn Zhòng,
why would it suddenly become easy?
Guǎn Zhòng was not Zhōu Gōng Dàn.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn acted as regent for the Son of Heaven for seven years;
when King Chéng came of age,
he handed over the government to him.
This was not for the sake of the world's plans,
but was his duty.
One who would not seize power from a son to rule the world
would certainly not betray a dead lord to serve his enemy;
one who betrays a dead lord to serve his enemy
would certainly not find it difficult to seize power from a son to rule the world;
one who does not find it difficult to seize power from a son to rule the world
would certainly not find it difficult to seize his ruler's state.
Guǎn Zhòng
was a minister of Prince Jiǔ
and plotted to kill Duke Huán but failed.
When his lord died, he became a minister to Duke Huán.
It is evident that Guǎn Zhòng's choices were not those of Zhōu Gōng Dàn.
If Guǎn Zhòng were a great worthy,
he would be comparable to Tāng
and Wǔ.
Tāng
and Wǔ were ministers to Jié
and Zhòu;
when Jié and Zhòu created chaos,
Tāng and Wǔ seized power from them.
Now, Duke Huán easily held a position above him,
thus acting like Jié
and Zhòu,
while placing himself above Tāng
and Wǔ,
putting Duke Huán in peril.
If Guǎn Zhòng were an unworthy man,
he would be like Tián Cháng.
Tián Cháng
was a minister to Duke Jiǎn,
yet he assassinated his lord.
Now, Duke Huán easily held a position above him,
thus resembling Duke Jiǎn's ease,
placing himself above Tián Cháng,
and Duke Huán was again in peril.
That Guǎn Zhòng was not like Zhōu Gōng Dàn is clear,
but whether he would act as Tāng
and Wǔ or as Tián Cháng
was uncertain.
To be like Tāng
and Wǔ
would entail the dangers posed by Jié
and Zhòu;
to be like Tián Cháng
would bring the turmoil of Duke Jiǎn.
After having obtained the allegiance of Zhòng Fù,
why did Duke Huán so easily lower his guard?
If Duke Huán's appointment of Guǎn Zhòng
was based on knowing he would not deceive him,
then he recognized him as a minister who would not betray his lord.
Yet, even though he knew he had a minister who would not deceive him,
Duke Huán, in his exclusive reliance on Guǎn Zhòng,
also employed Shù Diāo
and Yì Yá,
leading to maggots flowing out the door and his body left unburied.
That Duke Huán could not discern whether his ministers were deceiving him
or not is evident,
and his exclusive trust in ministers to that extent
leads to the saying: Duke Huán was a benighted ruler.
Lǐ Kè governed Zhōngshān,
and the magistrate of Kǔxíng reported increased revenues in his financial accounts.
Lǐ Kè said:
"Eloquent speech,
pleasing to the ear but not measured by righteousness,
is called frivolous talk.
Increased revenues without the benefits of mountains, forests, marshes, or valleys
are called frivolous goods.
A nobleman does not listen to frivolous talk,
nor does he accept frivolous goods.
You are hereby dismissed."
Someone remarked:
Lǐ Zǐ set forth his argument saying:
"Speech that is eloquent,
pleasing to the ear,
and not measured by righteousness,
is called frivolous talk."
The eloquence lies with the speaker,
the pleasure with the listener,
and the speech is not the listener's doing.
What is called not measured by righteousness
does not refer to the listener,
but must refer to what is listened to.
The listener,
if not a petty person,
is a nobleman.
A petty person, lacking righteousness,
surely cannot measure it by righteousness;
a nobleman, measuring it by righteousness,
would not be pleased by it.
Thus, to say
"speech is eloquent,
pleasing to the ear,
and not measured by righteousness"
must be an insincere statement.
To call increased revenues frivolous goods
is not a far-reaching principle.
Lǐ Zǐ's deceit was not stopped early,
allowing it to reach the accounting stage,
which is to perpetuate error.
Without a method to understand why revenues increased,
and increased revenues
signify abundance,
even if they double,
what can be done?
If undertakings are careful with the harmony of yin and yang,
planting is timed to the suitability of the four seasons,
without errors in timing
or disasters of cold and heat,
then revenues increase.
If minor tasks do not hinder major duties,
personal desires do not harm human affairs,
men devote themselves to farming,
women exert effort in weaving,
then revenues increase.
If attentive to the principles of animal husbandry,
observant of the suitability of the land,
so that the six domestic animals thrive,
and the five grains are cultivated,
then revenues increase.
If skilled in strategic planning,
meticulous about the advantages of terrain,
boats and carts,
and machinery,
with little effort
achieving great results,
then revenues increase.
If facilitating trade at markets, passes, and bridges,
able to exchange what one has for what one lacks,
so that traveling merchants gather,
foreign goods remain,
frugal in expenditures,
economical in food and clothing,
with buildings and tools adequate for practical use,
and no indulgence in curiosities,
then revenues increase.
Increased revenues
are all due to human efforts.
As for natural events,
if winds and rains are timely,
cold and heat are moderate,
without an increase in land,
yet achieving the success of a bumper harvest,
then revenues increase.
Human efforts
and natural contributions,
both can lead to increased revenues,
not solely the benefits of mountains, forests, marshes, or valleys.
To call increased revenues without the benefits of mountains, forests, marshes, or valleys
frivolous goods
is a statement without method.
When Jiǎn Zǐ of Zhào besieged the outer walls of Wèi,
protected by rhinoceros-hide shields and shelters,
he stood where arrows and stones could not reach,
yet when he drummed, the soldiers did not advance.
Jiǎn Zǐ threw down his drumstick and said:
"Alas!
My soldiers are too exhausted."
The messenger Zhú Guò removed his helmet and replied:
"I have heard:
it is only that the ruler is incapable;
the soldiers are not exhausted.
In the past, our former lord Xiàn Gōng annexed seventeen states,
subdued thirty-eight states,
won twelve battles out of twelve fought,
and it was with these same people.
After Xiàn Gōng passed away,
Lord Huì ascended the throne,
given to excess and violence,
fond of beautiful women,
the Qín people invaded at will,
coming within seventeen lǐ of Jiàng,
yet it was with these same people.
After Lord Huì passed away, #
Lord Wén succeeded him, #
besieged Wèi, #
captured Yè, #
and at the battle of Chéng Pú, #
defeated the Jīng people five times, #
earning a revered name under heaven, #
all with these same people. #
So it is only that the ruler is incapable;
the soldiers are not exhausted."
Jiǎn Zǐ then discarded his shields and shelters,
stood where arrows and stones could reach,
drummed, and the soldiers charged forward,
achieving a great victory in battle.
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Rather than obtaining a thousand war chariots,
I would prefer to hear one word from the messenger Zhú Guò."
Some say:
The envoy had no means to persuade,
so he recounted how Duke Huì was defeated by such men,
while Duke Wén became hegemon through them,
but failed to reveal the true method of employing people.
Jiǎnzǐ should not hastily discard his shield
and large shield.
When one's parents are besieged,
braving arrows and stones without regard for oneself
is how a filial son cherishes his parents.
But filial sons who cherish their parents
are one in a hundred.
Now to assume that when oneself is in danger
others will still fight for you,
is to expect all clansmen under their lord
to be like filial sons cherishing their parents—
this is the envoy's deception.
Loving benefit and hating harm
is inherent in all people.
With generous and trustworthy rewards,
men will despise the enemy;
with severe and certain punishments,
none will flee from battle.
Those who would sacrifice themselves for their superior—
not one in hundreds;
those who delight in profit and fear punishment—
there are none otherwise.
To lead multitudes without relying on universal tendencies,
but expecting conduct found in none out of a hundred—
the envoy does not understand the way of commanding masses.
Duke Mù of Lǔ asked Zǐsī:
"I hear Páng Xì's son is unfilial—
what are his behaviors like?"
Zǐsī replied:
"A gentleman honors worthies to exalt virtue,
promotes the good to inspire the people.
As for faulty conduct,
that is what petty men notice—
I know not of it."
After Zǐsī left,
Zǐfú Lìbó entered for audience.
Asked about Páng Xì's son,
Zǐfú Lìbó replied:
"He has three faults,
all previously unheard by Your Majesty."
From then on,
the duke esteemed Zǐsī
and despised Zǐfú Lìbó.
Some say:
The ducal house of Lǔ
being thrice usurped by the Jì family—
was it not fitting?
An enlightened ruler seeks the good and rewards it,
seeks the wicked and punishes them—
both equally obtained.
Thus those who report goodness
align their praise of good with the ruler;
those who report wickedness
align their condemnation of evil with the ruler—
these deserve reward and honor.
Not reporting wickedness
means differing from the ruler and colluding with villains below—
these deserve disgrace and punishment.
Now Zǐsī not reporting faults was esteemed by Duke Mù,
while Lìbó reporting wickedness was despised.
Human nature favors honor
and despises disgrace,
so the Jì family's rebellions succeeded
without reaching the ruler's ears—
this caused the Duke of Lǔ's usurpation.
Moreover, these ruinous customs
that the people of Lǔ adopted as virtues,
and Duke Mù uniquely honored—
was this not upside down?
When Duke Wén fled exile,
Duke Xiàn sent the eunuch Pī to attack him at Púchéng—
Pī cut off his sleeve,
and Duke Wén fled to Dí.
When Duke Huì took the throne,
he again sent Pī to attack at Huìdǒu,
but failed.
When Duke Wén returned to his state,
Pī sought audience.
The duke said:
"At Púchéng campaign,
the lord ordered arrival in one night—
yet you came immediately;
at Huìdǒu crisis,
the lord ordered three nights—
yet you came in one night.
Why so swift?"
Pī replied:
"A lord's orders brook no second thoughts.
Eliminating the lord's enemies—I only feared inadequacy.
Whether men of Pú
or Dí—
what were they to me?
Now you've ascended the throne,
will there be no Pú or Dí enemies?
Moreover, Duke Huán overlooked the arrow-hook attempt
and made Guǎn Zhòng his minister."
Then the lord granted him audience.
Some say:
That Qí and Jìn lost their sacrifices—
was it not fitting?
Duke Huán could utilize Guǎn Zhòng's merits
while forgetting the arrow-hook grievance;
Duke Wén could heed the eunuch's words
while overlooking the severed-sleeve offense—
Duke Huán
and Duke Wén could tolerate these two men.
Later rulers
lacked these two dukes' discernment;
later ministers
were less worthy than these two.
When disloyal ministers serve undiscerning rulers,
if the ruler doesn't know,
then appear Yān Cāo,
Zǐ Hǎn,
and Tián Cháng's treasons;
if knowing,
they justify themselves using Guǎn Zhòng
and the eunuch as examples.
If the ruler doesn't punish them,
but considers himself possessing Duke Huán's
and Duke Wén's virtue,
then with ministers as enemies and insight too dim to illuminate,
granting them ample resources,
deeming himself worthy yet unvigilant—
even if without posterity,
is it not fitting?
Moreover, the eunuch's words
merely embellished unwavering obedience to orders—
this was touted as loyalty to the ruler.
But only if the dead ruler revived
and the minister felt no shame would it be true loyalty.
Now serving Duke Wén at dusk when Duke Huì died at dawn—
what kind of unwavering loyalty is this?
Someone posed a riddle to Duke Huán:
"First difficulty,
second difficulty,
third difficulty—
what are they?"
Duke Huán couldn't answer,
and told Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"First difficulty:
keeping entertainers close and scholars distant.
Second difficulty:
leaving the state frequently for the seas.
Third difficulty:
delaying heir appointment in old age."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent."
He immediately honored the heir in ancestral temple without choosing an auspicious day.
Some say:
Guǎn Zhòng's riddle-solving missed the mark.
Scholars' usefulness lies not in proximity or distance,
while actors and dwarves
are naturally the ruler's companions in leisure.
Thus keeping entertainers close and scholars distant
cannot be considered governance difficulty.
Holding power
yet unable to utilize what one has,
and foolishly refusing to leave the state—
this is trying to restrain the whole state with one man's strength.
Those who try to restrain the whole state with one man's strength
rarely prevail.
With discernment that illuminates distant treachery
and reveals hidden subtleties,
and commands that are surely implemented—
even far away at sea,
the state would remain unchanged.
Thus leaving the state for the seas
without suffering usurpation or murder—
this is not the difficulty.
King Chéng of Chǔ established Shāng Chén as crown prince,
then wished to install Prince Zhí instead,
whereupon Shāng Chén revolted
and assassinated King Chéng.
Prince Zǎi,
heir of Zhōu,
saw Prince Gēn favored,
who then rebelled in Dōngzhōu,
splitting the state in two.
These illustrate the perils of delaying the establishment of a crown prince.
When power is undivided,
secondary heirs remain humble,
favorites lack leverage,
even if they hold ministerial posts—
then delaying the heir's designation is permissible.
Thus, postponing the appointment
previts chaos among collateral lines,
which isn't the true difficulty.
The genuine challenges are these:
utilizing others' influence
while preventing harm to oneself—
this is the first challenge.
Preventing favored concubines from rivaling the queen—
the second.
Keeping beloved secundogenitures from endangering the legitimate heir,
heeding one minister exclusively
without his cornering the ruler—
this constitutes the third challenge.
When Lord Yè Zǐgāo inquired about governance from Zhòngní,
the master replied:
"Governance lies in delighting the near
and attracting the distant."
Duke Āi asked about governance,
and Zhòngní said:
"Governance lies in selecting the worthy."
Duke Jǐng of Qí posed the same question,
to which Zhòngní responded:
"Governance lies in economizing resources."
After the three rulers departed,
Zǐgòng asked:
"Though all three asked about governance,
your answers differed—
why?"
Zhòngní explained:
"Yè's capital is vast but its territory small,
with people tending to defect,
hence I said
'delight the near to attract the distant.'
Duke Āi of Lǔ has three ministers
who externally block relations with neighboring states
and their scholars,
while internally colluding to delude their lord,
causing ancestral temples to be neglected
and state sacrifices abandoned—
surely due to these three ministers,
thus I said
'governance lies in selecting the worthy.'
Duke Jǐng of Qí built Yōng Gate
and the main palace,
granting triple the estates of three hundred chariots in one morning—
therefore I said
'governance lies in economizing.'"
Some critique:
Zhòngní's responses
are words that ruin states.
If the people of Yè harbor rebellious intent,
advising
"delight the near to attract the distant"
teaches them to expect favors.
Governance through favoritism
rewards the meritless
and pardons the guilty,
which corrupts the law.
With law corrupted and governance chaotic,
using disordered rule to govern corrupted people—
this is untenable.
Moreover, rebellious sentiments arise
from the ruler's insufficient discernment.
Instead of urging Lord Yè to enhance his discernment,
advising him to delight the near and attract the distant
abandons the power he should wield
and pits him against inferiors in currying popular favor—
this fails to uphold authority.
Even Yáo's worthiness,
foremost among the Six Kings,
succumbed when Shùn's single relocation formed a city,
and Yáo lost the realm.
Rulers lacking methods to control subordinates,
relying on Shùn-like figures to retain the people—
is this not lacking method?
Enlightened rulers detect minor treachery in its infancy,
thus preventing major conspiracies;
they administer minor punishments for small offenses,
thus preventing great disorders.
This is called
"addressing difficulties while they are easy,
handling great matters while they are small."
Now, when the meritorious are rewarded,
the rewarded feel no debt to the ruler,
for it stems from their own efforts;
when the guilty are punished,
the punished bear no grudge against the superior,
for it arises from their own crimes.
People knowing that rewards and punishments originate from themselves
thus diligently pursue achievements in their work,
without expecting gifts from the ruler.
"The highest ruler, those below only know he exists."
This means under the highest ruler,
the people feel no attachment,
so how could they be favor-seeking?
The people of a superior ruler transcend considerations of profit and harm;
advising "delight the near to attract the distant"
becomes irrelevant.
Duke Āi had ministers blocking externally
and colluding internally
to delude him,
yet he was advised to "select the worthy"—
this isn't about evaluating merit,
but choosing those he subjectively deems worthy.
Had Duke Āi known these three ministers' external blocking and internal collusion,
they wouldn't have remained in power for a day.
Duke Āi didn't understand selecting the worthy;
choosing those he personally considered worthy
enabled these three to hold office.
Yān's King Kuài esteemed Zǐzhī
and rejected Xúnzǐ,
thus dying in disgrace;
Wú's Fūchāi trusted Grand Steward Pǐ
and ignored Wǔ Zǐxū,
leading to destruction by Yuè.
The ruler of Lǔ lacked discernment of worthiness,
yet was advised to select the worthy—
this risked subjecting Duke Āi
to the calamities of Fūchāi
and Yān Kuài.
Enlightened rulers don't personally promote ministers;
ministers advance each other.
They don't self-proclaim worthiness;
merit naturally manifests.
Evaluate them by their responsibilities,
test them through their actions,
assess them by their achievements—
thus ministers govern impartially without selfishness,
neither concealing the worthy
nor promoting the unworthy.
Then why should the ruler labor over selecting the worthy?
Duke Jǐng granted estates of hundred-chariot households,
yet was advised to
"economize resources"—
this left him without method
to recognize the extravagance of the wealthy,
merely practicing personal frugality,
unable to escape poverty.
If a ruler uses a thousand-lǐ domain to feed himself,
even Jié
and Zhòu weren't more extravagant.
Qí's territory spanned three thousand lǐ,
yet Duke Huán used half for his own sustenance—
more extravagant than Jié
and Zhòu;
yet he became chief of the Five Hegemons,
understanding the balance between extravagance and frugality.
Rulers who cannot restrain subordinates
but only themselves are being coerced;
those who cannot govern subordinates
but only themselves create chaos;
those who cannot regulate subordinates
but only themselves remain poor.
Enlightened rulers make people selfless,
prohibiting those who live by deceit.
Those who exhaust their strength in service
and attribute the benefits to their superiors will certainly be recognized,
