and those recognized will be rewarded;
those who engage in corrupt practices for private gain will certainly be discovered,
and those discovered will be punished.
Thus, loyal ministers devote themselves to public affairs,
the common people and scholars exert their utmost within their households,
and all officials serve their superiors with diligence and restraint.
Even if extravagance were twice that of Lord Jǐng,
it would not be a calamity for the state.
Therefore, advocating frugality in expenditures
is not the most urgent matter.
Now, a single statement to the Three Dukes
can ensure they have no troubles—
this refers to understanding those below.
Understanding those below clearly
enables prohibition at the subtle stage;
prohibiting at the subtle stage
prevents villainy from accumulating;
if villainy does not accumulate,
there will be no cliques;
if there are no cliques,
public and private interests will be distinguished;
if public and private interests are distinguished,
factions will dissolve;
if factions dissolve,
there will be no troubles of external obstructions and internal cliques.
Understanding those below clearly
leads to perceptive insight;
with perceptive insight,
punishments and rewards will be clear;
if punishments and rewards are clear,
the state will not be impoverished.
Hence it is said:
"A single response can free the Three Dukes from troubles"
refers to understanding those below.
When Zhǒng of Zhèng went out in the morning,
passing by the lane of the eastern artisans,
he heard a woman weeping.
He placed his hand on his driver's and listened.
After a while,
he sent an officer to arrest and question her,
and it turned out she had strangled her husband with her own hands.
Another day,
his driver asked him:
"How did you know, sir?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"Her voice was fearful.
Generally, when people are with their loved ones,
they worry when they first fall ill,
fear when near death,
and grieve after they have died.
Now she was weeping for one already dead,
but without grief and with fear—
therefore I knew there was foul play."
Some say:
Was Zǐchǎn's governance
not overly meddlesome?
If villainy must await what one's own ears and eyes perceive
before it can be known,
then few villains would be caught in Zhèng.
Not employing officials to handle completed cases,
not examining governance through multiple verifications,
not clarifying standards and measures,
but relying solely on one's own keen senses,
laboring one's wisdom and thoughts,
to detect villainy—
is that not lacking in method?
Moreover, affairs are numerous while wisdom is limited,
the limited cannot overcome the numerous;
wisdom alone cannot know all things completely,
so one must use things to govern things.
Those below are many while those above are few;
the few cannot overcome the many
means the ruler cannot know all ministers personally,
so one must use people to know people.
Thus, without physical toil, affairs are managed,
and without employing one's wisdom, villainy is uncovered.
Hence the saying among the Sòng people:
"If a single sparrow passed by Yì,
Yì would surely catch it,
but then Yì would be deceived.
If the whole world were his net,
then no sparrow would escape."
Detecting villainy also requires a great net,
so that not a single one is missed.
Not following this principle,
but using one's own mental deductions as bow and arrows,
then Zǐchǎn was deceived.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Governing the state with wisdom
is the state's curse."
This refers to Zǐchǎn.
King Zhāo of Qín asked his attendants:
"Compared to their beginning,
are Hán and Wèi stronger now?"
The attendants replied:
"They are weaker than at the start."
"How do current ministers like Rú'ěr
and Wèi Qí
compare to former ones like Mèngcháng
and Máng Mǎo?"
They replied:
"They are not as capable."
The king said:
"Even when Mèngcháng
and Máng Mǎo led strong Hán and Wèi,
they could do nothing against me."
The attendants responded:
"Indeed so."
Mid-period pushed aside his qín and replied:
"Your Majesty's assessment of the world is mistaken.
During the time of the six Jìn families,
the Zhì clan was the strongest,
destroyed Fàn
and Zhōngháng,
and followed with troops from Hán
and Wèi to attack Zhào,
flooding it with Jìn River waters,
until the city walls had only three planks left above water.
When Earl Zhì went out,
with Wèi Xuānzǐ driving his chariot,
and Hán Kāngzǐ as the attendant,
Earl Zhì said:
'I did not know before that water could destroy a state,
but now I know it.
Fén River can flood Ānyì,
and Jiàng River can flood Píngyáng.'
Wèi Xuānzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
and Kāngzǐ stepped on Xuānzǐ's foot;
elbow and foot met in the chariot,
and the Zhì clan was divided beneath Jìnyáng.
Now, although you are strong,
you are not like Earl Zhì;
although Hán and Wèi are weak,
they have not reached the state they were in beneath Jìnyáng.
This is a time when the world is apt for such elbow-and-foot signals;
I hope Your Majesty does not take it lightly."
Some say:
King Zhāo's question was flawed,
and the responses of his attendants and Mid-period were also mistaken.
Whenever an enlightened ruler governs the state,
he relies on his power.
If his power cannot be harmed,
then even the strongest in the world can do nothing against him,
let alone Mèngcháng,
Máng Mǎo,
Hán,
and Wèi—what could they do to me?
If his power can be harmed,
then even incompetents like Rú'ěr
and Wèi Qí,
along with Hán
and Wèi, could harm him.
Thus, whether one is harmed or not
depends on relying on oneself alone;
why ask others?
Relying on one's own inviolability,
what distinction is there between strong and weak?
The error lies in not relying on oneself
but asking what others can do—
if one is not invaded, it is mere luck.
Shēnzǐ said:
"To lose the method and seek trustworthiness
is dubious."
This refers to King Zhāo.
Earl Zhì had no restraint,
followed Hán Kāng
and Wèi Xuān
and plotted to flood and destroy their states with water.
This is why Earl Zhì lost his state and met his death,
with his skull made into a drinking vessel.
Now King Zhāo asks whether he is stronger than at the beginning,
fearing the calamity of water-dwellers.
Although he has attendants,
they are not like the two men of Hán
and Wèi,
so how could there be matters of elbows and feet?
Yet Zhōng Qī says
"Do not take it lightly,"
which is empty talk.
Moreover, what Zhōng Qī is in charge of
is the qín and sè.
If the strings are not tuned,
or the melodies unclear,
it is Zhōng Qī's responsibility,
this is how Zhōng Qī serves King Zhāo.
Zhōng Qī is good at fulfilling his duties,
not failing King Zhāo,
yet he speaks of what he does not know,
is that not absurd?
If the attendants had replied
"Weaker than at the beginning"
or
"Not as good"
it would have been acceptable,
but saying "Very much so" is flattery.
Shēn Zǐ said:
"In governance, do not overstep one's office,
even if one knows, do not speak."
Now Zhōng Qī does not know but still speaks of it.
Therefore it is said:
King Zhāo's question was flawed,
the replies of both the attendants and Zhōng Qī were at fault.
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"When you see something acceptable,
demonstrate your approval with evidence;
when you see something unacceptable,
show your disapproval tangibly.
If rewards and punishments are trustworthy based on what is seen,
even regarding the unseen,
how would anyone dare to act improperly?
If when seeing something acceptable,
one approves without evidence;
when seeing something unacceptable,
one disapproves without tangible form;
if rewards and punishments are not trustworthy based on what is seen,
yet one seeks to control beyond what is seen,
it cannot be achieved."
Some say:
In the grand court and solemn settings,
everyone is respectful.
In private rooms alone,
even Zēng and Shǐ would be remiss.
Observing people's respect in public
does not reveal their true conduct.
Moreover, the ruler
is what the ministers adorn themselves for.
If likes and dislikes are based only on what is seen,
then ministers will certainly conceal their deceitful acts to fool their ruler.
It is inevitable.
If the ruler's clarity cannot illuminate distant deceit,
or see the hidden and subtle,
and instead relies on observing adorned conduct
to determine rewards and punishments,
is that not flawed?
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Speaking in the chamber,
it fills the chamber;
speaking in the hall,
it fills the hall;
this is called the king of all under heaven."
Some say:
What Guǎn Zhòng meant by
"speaking in the chamber fills the chamber"
and "speaking in the hall fills the hall"
is not merely referring to words about games and food,
but surely to important matters.
The important matters of a ruler
are either laws or methods.
Laws
are compiled in documents,
established in government offices,
and promulgated to the common people.
Methods
are hidden in the heart,
used to comprehensively handle various matters
and secretly control the ministers.
Therefore, laws should be as open as possible,
while methods should not be revealed.
Thus, an enlightened ruler, when speaking of laws,
ensures that even the lowliest within the borders hear and know them,
not just filling the hall;
when using methods,
even the closest confidants cannot learn of them,
let alone filling the chamber.
Yet Guǎn Zǐ still said:
"Speaking in the chamber fills the chamber,
speaking in the hall fills the hall."
This is not about laws and methods.
When Sūn Wénzǐ of Wèi was on a mission to Lǔ,
the lord ascended and he ascended too.
Shūsūn Mùzǐ hurried forward and said:
"At meetings of the feudal lords,
our humble lord has never been behind the lord of Wèi.
Now you do not stay one step behind our humble lord,
and our humble lord does not know what fault he has committed,
please restrain yourself."
Sūnzǐ offered no apology,
nor did he show any sign of remorse.
Mùzǐ withdrew and told others:
"Sūnzǐ is sure to perish.
As a minister, he does not defer to his lord,
and when at fault, he does not repent,
this is the root of his downfall."
Some say:
When the Son of Heaven loses the Way,
the feudal lords attack him,
hence there were Tāng
and Wǔ.
When a feudal lord loses the Way,
his ministers attack him,
hence there were Qí
and Jìn.
If ministers who attack their lords must perish,
then Tāng
and Wǔ could not have become kings,
and Jìn and Qí could not have been established.
Sūnzǐ was a lord in Wèi,
yet later did not act as a minister in Lǔ,
he was a minister acting as a lord.
The lord had faults,
so the minister gained advantage.
To predict downfall not for the lord who has faults,
but for the minister who gains advantage,
is unperceptive.
Lǔ had no right to punish a minister of Wèi,
and the enlightened lord of Wèi
did not recognize the unrepentant minister.
Even if Sūnzǐ had these two faults,
would he necessarily perish?
The reason for his potential downfall
lies in his faults, which allowed him to gain the position of lord.
Some say:
The roles of minister and lord are distinct.
The reason a minister can usurp the lord
is that they gain an imbalance of power.
Therefore, taking what is not one's rightful share
is seized by the multitude;
relinquishing one's rightful share and then taking it
is given by the people.
Thus, when Jié sought the women of Mínshān,
and Zhòu demanded Bǐ Gān's heart,
all under heaven turned away;
when Tāng changed his personal name,
and Wǔ endured insults,
the realm submitted;
when Zhào Xuān fled to the mountains,
and the Tián clan acted as external servants,
then Qí
and Jìn followed.
Thus, the reason Tāng
and Wǔ became kings,
and Qí and Jìn were established,
was not necessarily due to their lords,
but because they gained the position and then acted as lords from it.
Now, without having gained the means to do so,
they act as if they have the position,
this is to invert righteousness and violate virtue.
Inverting righteousness
leads to the failure of affairs;
violating virtue
causes resentments to accumulate.
Why is the path to failure and downfall not understood?
In Lǔ, Yáng Hǔ wanted to attack the Sān Huán,
but failed and fled to Qí,
where Duke Jìng treated him with courtesy.
Bào Wénzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"This should not be done.
Yáng Hǔ was favored by the Jì family yet sought to attack Jì Sūn,
coveting his wealth.
Now, you are wealthier than Jì Sūn,
and Qí is larger than Lǔ,
so Yáng Hǔ will employ all his deceit here."
Duke Jìng then imprisoned Yáng Hǔ.
Some say:
In a household of a thousand gold,
the sons are not benevolent,
for people are extremely eager for profit.
Duke Huán,
foremost among the Five Hegemons,
fought for the state and killed his elder brother,
because the profit was great.
Between ruler and minister,
there is no kinship like that of brothers.
Through the achievement of usurpation and murder,
one can control a state of ten thousand chariots and enjoy great profit—
then which minister is not like Yáng Hǔ?
Affairs succeed through subtlety and skill,
and fail through negligence and clumsiness.
Before ministers rise in rebellion,
their preparations are not yet complete.
If all ministers harbor the heart of Yáng Hǔ,
yet the ruler remains unaware,
that is subtle and skillful.
Yáng Hǔ's greed
is known throughout the world,
and his desire to attack his superior
is negligent and clumsy.
Not making Duke Jìng punish the skillful ministers of Qí,
but having him punish the clumsy Hǔ,
means Bào Wénzǐ's argument is inverted.
The loyalty or deceit of ministers
lies in how the ruler acts.
If the ruler is perceptive and strict,
then the ministers will be loyal;
if the ruler is weak and dim,
then the ministers will be deceitful.
To recognize subtlety is called perceptiveness;
to allow no pardons is called strictness.
Not recognizing the skillful ministers of Qí
and punishing a completed disorder from Lǔ—
is that not misguided?
Some say:
Benevolence and greed differ in heart.
Thus, Prince Mùyí declined Sòng,
while Chǔ's Shāngchén murdered his father;
Zhèng's Qùjí yielded to his younger brother,
while Lǔ's Huán killed his elder brother.
The Five Hegemons engaged in annexations,
yet to measure others by Duke Huán's standard
would mean none were chaste and honest.
Moreover, if the ruler is perceptive and strict,
then the ministers will be loyal.
Yáng Hǔ caused disorder in Lǔ,
failed and fled,
entered Qí and was not punished—
that would be condoning disorder.
A perceptive ruler would punish him,
knowing Yáng Hǔ could perpetuate chaos;
this shows the insight into subtlety.
As the saying goes:
"The feudal lords consider the state as kin."
A strict ruler must not overlook Yáng Hǔ's crime,
which embodies the principle of no pardon;
thus, punishing Yáng Hǔ
serves to make the ministers loyal.
Not knowing the skillful ministers of Qí
and abandoning the punishment of evident disorder,
demanding accountability for what has not yet occurred,
while not punishing a clear crime—
that would be misguided.
Now, punishing the crime of disorder from Lǔ
to intimidate ministers with treacherous hearts,
and thereby gaining the kinship of the Jì,
Mèng, and Shūsūn families—
how can Bào Wénzǐ's argument
be considered inverted?
When the Earl of Zhèng intended to make Gāo Qúmí a minister,
Duke Zhāo detested him,
but remonstrance was firm and unheeded.
Upon Duke Zhāo's accession,
Gāo feared he would be killed;
on the day Xīnmǎo,
he murdered Duke Zhāo and set up Zǐ Dǎn.
A nobleman said:
"Duke Zhāo knew whom he detested."
Prince Yǔ said:
"Will Gāo Bó not be executed?
His retaliation for hatred is too severe."
Some say:
Regarding Prince Yǔ's words,
are they not inverted?
Duke Zhāo met his calamity
because he retaliated for hatred too late.
Then Gāo Bó's delayed death
was due to his excessive retaliation for hatred.
An enlightened ruler does not harbor suspended anger;
suspended anger
leads guilty ministers to act rashly in schemes,
endangering the ruler.
Thus, at the Língtái feast,
the Marquis of Wèi was angry but did not punish,
so Chǔ Shī launched a revolt.
Over the turtle soup,
the Lord of Zhèng was angry but did not punish,
so Zǐgōng killed his ruler.
The nobleman's remark
"knew whom he detested"
does not mean it was excessive,
but rather: his knowledge was so clear,
yet he did not carry out punishment,
leading to his death.
So "knew whom he detested"
reveals his lack of authority.
A ruler is not only insufficient in foreseeing danger,
but sometimes insufficient in decisive judgment.
Now Duke Zhāo recognized his detestation
but delayed punishment for the crime,
letting Qúmí harbor hatred and fear death to take a risk,
thus he could not avoid being killed;
this shows Duke Zhāo's retaliation for hatred was not severe enough.
Some say:
Severe retaliation for hatred
means great punishment for a minor offense.
Great punishment for a minor offense
is the extreme of judicial harshness.
The danger of such judgment
lies not in the punishment itself,
but in the multitude of enemies it creates.
Thus, Duke Lì of Jìn exterminated the three Xì families,
and Luán
and Zhōngháng rebelled;
Zǐdū of Zhèng killed Bó Xuǎn,
leading to the cauldron feast uprising;
the King of Wú executed Wǔ Zǐxū,
and Yuè's Gōujiàn achieved hegemony.
As for the Marquis of Wèi's expulsion
and Duke Líng of Zhèng's murder,
it was not because Chǔ Shī was not killed or Gōngfù not punished,
but because anger was shown when it should not have been,
and punishment was intended when it should not have been.
If anger is justified by the crime,
and punishment does not go against human sentiment,
then even if suspended, what harm is there?
If a crime was established before accession,
and after taking the throne,
an old offense is punished—
that is why Qí Hú was destroyed.
When a ruler acts against his ministers,
there can still be later troubles;
how much more if a minister acts against his ruler?
If punishment is already inappropriate,
and one intends to exterminate all,
that makes enemies of the whole world.
Then even if executed,
would it not be fitting?
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Mí Zǐxiá was favored,
wielding power exclusively in Wèi.
A dwarf who had an audience with the duke said:
"My dream has come true."
The duke asked:
"What dream?"
"I dreamed of a stove,
which means I saw you."
The duke angrily said:
"I have heard that one who is about to see his sovereign dreams of the sun.
Why then did you dream of a stove when about to see me?"
The dwarf said:
"The sun illuminates the whole world,
and nothing can block it.
A sovereign illuminates the entire state,
and no single person can obscure him.
Therefore, one dreams of the sun when about to see the sovereign.
As for the stove,
if one person is warming himself by it,
then those behind cannot see it.
Perhaps there is someone obscuring you, my lord?
Then although I dreamed of a stove,
is it not appropriate?"
The duke said:
"Well said."
Thereupon he dismissed Yōng Chú,
relegated Mí Zǐxiá,
and employed Sīkōng Gǒu.
Some say:
The dwarf skillfully used the dream
to illustrate the way of rulership,
yet Duke Líng did not understand the dwarf's words.
Dismissing Yōng Chú,
relegating Mí Zǐxiá,
and employing Sīkōng Gǒu
meant removing those he loved and employing those he deemed worthy.
Zhèng Zǐdū deemed Qìng Jiàn worthy but was obscured by him,
Yān Zǐkuài deemed Zǐzhī worthy but was obscured by him.
Thus, removing those one loves
and employing those one deems worthy
does not necessarily prevent someone from obscuring oneself.
If the unworthy obscure the ruler,
it is not enough to harm his clarity;
but if without discernment
one allows the worthy to obscure oneself,
then danger is inevitable.
Others say:
Qū Dào was fond of water caltrops,
King Wén was fond of pickled calamus,
which are not proper flavors,
yet these two worthies esteemed them—
what one relishes need not be delicious.
Jìn Líng Hóu delighted in Cān Wúxù,
Yān Kuài deemed Zǐzhī worthy,
who were not true gentlemen,
yet these two rulers honored them—
those deemed worthy need not be truly worthy.
To employ those not worthy but deemed so
is the same as employing those one loves.
If one is truly worthy and promoted,
it differs from employing those one loves.
Hence, King Zhuāng of Chǔ promoted Sūn Shū and achieved hegemony,
while King Zhòu of Shāng employed Fèi Zhòng and faced destruction—
both employed those they deemed worthy,
yet the outcomes were opposite.
Although Yān Kuài promoted those he deemed worthy,
it was akin to employing those he loved;
how could Wèi be the same?
Thus, the dwarf's insight was not yet evident.
If a ruler is obscured and unaware of it,
but after realizing it, understands the obscurity,
and then dismisses the obscuring ministers,
that is an increase in discernment.
To say
"without discernment,
allowing the worthy to obscure oneself
leads to danger,"
but now with increased discernment,
even if obscured,
there is no danger.
Shènzǐ said:
"The flying dragon rides the clouds,
the soaring serpent glides through the mist;
when the clouds disperse and the mist clears,
the dragon and serpent are no different from earthworms and ants—
they have lost what they rode.
If a worthy is subjugated by the unworthy,
it is due to light authority and low position;
if the unworthy can command the worthy,
it is due to heavy authority and high position.
When Yáo was a commoner,
he could not govern even three people;
but when Jié was the Son of Heaven,
he could throw the world into chaos.
From this, I know that power and position are reliable,
while worthiness and wisdom are not worthy of admiration.
When a weak crossbow shoots an arrow high,
it is propelled by the wind;
when one who is unworthy has his orders obeyed,
it is due to support from the masses.
When Yáo taught as a subordinate, the people did not listen;
but when he faced south and ruled the world,
his orders were executed,
his prohibitions heeded.
From this, it is clear
that worthiness and wisdom are insufficient to command the masses,
while power and position are enough to subdue the worthy."
In response to Shènzǐ:
The flying dragon rides the clouds,
the soaring serpent glides through the mist—
I do not deny that the dragon and serpent
rely on the force of clouds and mist.
However,
to abandon worthiness and rely solely on power—
is that sufficient for governance?
I have never seen it.
To be able to ride and glide with the force of clouds and mist
is due to the superior quality of the dragon and serpent.
Now, with abundant clouds, earthworms cannot ride them;
with thick mist, ants cannot glide through it.
To have the force of abundant clouds and thick mist
yet be unable to ride or glide—
is due to the inferior quality of earthworms and ants.
Now, Jié and Zhòu faced south and ruled the world,
using the majesty of the Son of Heaven
as their clouds and mist,
yet the world could not avoid great chaos—
because Jié and Zhòu were of inferior quality.
Moreover, if one uses Yáo's power
to govern the world,
how does that power differ from Jié's power,
which threw the world into chaos?
Power
does not necessarily ensure that the worthy use it
and the unworthy do not.
If the worthy use it, the world is well-governed;
if the unworthy use it, the world falls into chaos.
In human nature,
the worthy are few
and the unworthy are many.
To use the advantage of authority and power
to aid the unworthy in a chaotic age
means that many will use power to throw the world into chaos,
and few will use it to govern the world.
Power
facilitates both order and chaos.
Thus, the "Zhōu Shū" says:
"Do not add wings to a tiger,
lest it fly into the city
and choose people to devour."
To give power to the unworthy
is to add wings to a tiger.
Jié and Zhòu built high towers and deep pools
to exhaust the people's strength,
created the roasting torture
to harm the people's nature.
That Jié and Zhòu could act recklessly
was because the majesty of facing south served as their wings.
Had Jié
and Zhòu been commoners,
they would not have committed a single act
before facing execution.
Power
nurtures the hearts of tigers and wolves
and accomplishes violent and chaotic deeds—
this is the great calamity of the world.
As for power's relation to order and chaos,
it inherently has no fixed position,
yet to claim
that power alone is sufficient to govern the world
shows the shallow extent of one's wisdom.
With a fine horse and sturdy carriage,
if a Zāng Huó drives it,
people will laugh;
if Wáng Liáng drives it,
he can cover a thousand lǐ in a day.
The carriage and horse are no different,
yet one achieves a thousand lǐ,
while the other becomes a laughingstock—
so the difference in skill is vast.
Now, if the state's throne is the carriage,
power is the horse,
commands are the reins,
and punishments are the whip,
then if Yáo
or Shùn drives, the world is well-governed;
if Jié or Zhòu drives, the world falls into chaos—
so the difference between the worthy and unworthy is vast.
If one wishes to pursue speed and reach distant places,
but does not know to employ Wáng Liáng;
if one desires to promote benefits and eliminate harms,
but does not know to employ the worthy and capable,
this is the problem of not understanding categories.
Now, Yáo and
Shùn were also the Wáng Liángs in governing the people.
Again, it was responded:
That man believes power is sufficient to rely on for governing officials.
The guest said
"One must await the worthy to achieve order,"
but this is not so.
Now, power
has one name but countless variations.
If power is necessarily natural,
then there is no need to speak about power.
What I refer to as power
is that which is established by humans.
Now, Yáo and
Shùn were born into high positions;
even if there were ten Jiés or
Zhòus, they could not create chaos—
this is order through power.
Jié and Zhòu were also born into high positions;
even if there were ten Yáos and Shùns, they could not bring order—
this is chaos through power.
Therefore, it is said:
"What is ordered by power cannot be thrown into chaos,
and what is chaotic by power cannot be brought to order."
This is natural power,
not what humans can establish.
As for what I say,
it refers only to what humans can establish;
what has worthiness to do with it?
How to clarify that this is so?
The guest said:
"There was a man selling spears and shields,
who praised the sturdiness of his shield:
'Nothing can pierce it.'
Shortly after, he praised his spear, saying:
'My spear is so sharp,
there is nothing it cannot pierce.'
Someone responded to him:
'Using your spear
to pierce your shield,
how would that be?'
The man could not reply."
To consider an impenetrable shield
and an all-piercing spear
as claims that cannot both stand
—now, the way of worthiness cannot be restrained,
while the way of power restrains all;
to pit unrestrainable worthiness
against all-restraining power
is like the spear and shield argument.
That worthiness and power are incompatible is also clear.
Moreover, Yáo,
Shùn, Jié,
and Zhòu
appear once in a thousand generations,
which is like being born shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel.
Those who govern the world continuously are the average,
and the reason I speak of power
is for the average.
The average
are not as good as Yáo or
Shùn above,
nor are they as bad as Jié or
Zhòu below.
Upholding laws and wielding power
brings order,
while abandoning laws and discarding power
leads to chaos.
Now, to discard power and abandon laws
while awaiting Yáo or
Shùn,
so that only when Yáo or
Shùn arrive is there order,
means a thousand generations of chaos
and one of order.
Upholding laws and wielding power
while awaiting Jié or
Zhòu,
so that only when Jié or
Zhòu arrive is there chaos,
means a thousand generations of order
and one of chaos.
Moreover, order for a thousand and chaos for one,
versus order for one and chaos for a thousand,
is like riding a Jì or
Ěr horse and galloping in opposite directions—
the distance between them is vast.
Now, to discard the method of the carpenter's straightening tool,
and remove the measures of weights and scales,
even if Xī Zhòng were to make a cart,
he could not complete a single wheel.
Without the encouragement of rewards and commendations,
or the awe of punishments and penalties,
to relinquish power and abandon laws,
even if Yáo and Shùn went door to door persuading everyone,
they could not govern three families.
That power is sufficient is also clear,
yet to say "one must await the worthy"
is again not so.
Moreover, to go without food for a hundred days waiting for fine grain and meat,
the starving will not survive;
now, to await the worthiness of Yáo or
Shùn
to govern the people of the current age,
is like the argument of waiting for fine grain and meat to save the starving.
To say
"With a fine horse and sturdy carriage,
if a Zāng Huò drives it, people will laugh,
but if Wáng Liáng drives it,
he can cover a thousand li in a day,"
I do not consider this correct.
To rely on the skilled sea swimmers of Yuè
to save drowning people in the Central States,
the Yuè people may be good swimmers,
but the drowning will not be rescued.
To rely on the ancient Wáng Liáng
to handle today's horses
is also like the Yuè people saving the drowning argument,
its impossibility is also clear.
With a fine horse and sturdy carriage,
setting posts every fifty li,
and having a driver of average skill handle it,
pursuing speed and reaching distant places,
it can be achieved,
and a thousand li can be covered in a day;
why must one await the ancient Wáng Liáng?
Moreover, in driving,
if it is not done by Wáng Liáng,
then it must be done by a Zāng Huò who ruins it;
in governance, if it is not done by Yáo or
Shùn,
then it must be done by Jié or
Zhòu who chaos it.
This taste is not like malt sugar or honey,
but must be bitter herbs or
tínglì plant.
This is accumulating arguments and piling up words,
departing from reason and losing method,
an extreme and one-sided discussion;
how can it refute the speech of principle and reason?
The guest's argument does not reach this discussion.
Someone asked:
"How do disputations arise?"
The reply was:
"They arise from the superiors not being enlightened."
The questioner said:
"The superiors' lack of enlightenment gives rise to disputations;
why is that?"
The reply was:
"In the state of an enlightened ruler,
commands
are the most honored of words;
laws
are the most appropriate for affairs.
Words have no second honor,
laws have no dual appropriateness,
so words and actions
that do not conform to laws and commands
must be prohibited.
If there are no laws or commands
but one can engage in dealing with deceit,
responding to change,
producing benefits,
or assessing affairs,
the superior must adopt their words
and hold them accountable for the results.
If the words are appropriate,
there is great benefit;
if inappropriate,
there is heavy punishment.
Therefore, the foolish fear punishment
and dare not speak,
while the wise have no means to argue.
This is the reason why there is no debate.
In chaotic times, it is not so:
the ruler issues commands,
but the people use literary learning to criticize them;
the government has laws,
but the people use private conduct to distort them.
The ruler neglects to enforce his laws and decrees
and instead honors the wisdom and conduct of scholars,
which is why there is so much literary learning in the world.
Now, speech and action
should take practical effect as their target.
If one sharpens an arrow and shoots it randomly,
its point may still hit the autumn down,
yet one cannot be called a skilled archer,
for there is no constant target.
Set up a target five inches wide,
and shoot from a distance of ten paces:
neither Yì
nor Péng Méng could be sure to hit it,
but with a constant target.
Thus, with a constant target,
Yì
and Péng Méng are considered skilled for hitting the five-inch target;
without a constant target,
hitting the autumn down with a random shot is deemed clumsy.
Now, when listening to speeches and observing actions,
if one does not take practical effect as the target,
then no matter how insightful the speech or resolute the action,
it is like shooting randomly.
Thus, in chaotic times, when listening to speeches,
they consider obscurity as profundity,
and erudition as eloquence;
when observing actions,
they consider standing apart from the crowd as worthy,
and defying superiors as integrity.
The ruler delights in eloquent and profound speeches,
and honors worthy and defiant conduct,
so those who establish methods and techniques,
set standards for acceptance and rejection,
and distinguish between competing arguments,
find no one to uphold them.
Hence, there are many in scholarly robes
and carrying swords,
but few who till the land and fight battles;
sophistries like "hardness and whiteness" or "without thickness" flourish,
while the laws of statutes and decrees fade.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the ruler is unenlightened,
disputation arises." 」
Xú Qú asked Tián Jiū:
"I have heard that wise men do not rise from low ranks
to meet their lord,
and sages do not achieve merit before approaching their superior.
Now, Yángchéng Yìqú
is a brilliant general,
yet he was placed among the garrison chiefs;
Gōngsūn Dǎnhuí
is a sage minister,
yet he was confined to a local district.
Why is this?" 」
Tián Jiū replied:
"There is no other reason or extraordinary matter;
it is because the ruler has standards and employs methods.
Have you not heard
that the state of Chǔ employed Sòng Gū as a general and lost its good governance,
and the state of Wèi made Féng Lí its minister and brought about its ruin?
These two rulers were driven by reputation and rhetoric,
dazzled by sophistry,
without testing them in garrison duties,
or confining them to district administration,
hence they suffered the calamity of misgovernance and state collapse.
From this perspective,
to lack the test of garrison duties
or the confinement to district administration,
how could that be the preparation of an enlightened ruler!" 」
Tángxī Gōng said to Hánzǐ:
"I have heard that observing rites and practicing deference
is the way to preserve oneself;
cultivating conduct and renouncing cleverness
is the path to success.
Now, you, sir, establish methods and techniques,
set up regulations and measures,
I privately believe this endangers your life
and jeopardizes your person.
How can this be proven?
I have heard your methods say:
'Chǔ did not employ Wú Qǐ and thus declined into chaos,
while Qín implemented Shāng Jūn's policies and became wealthy and strong.
The words of these two gentlemen were indeed appropriate,
yet Wú Qǐ was torn apart
and Shāng Jūn was torn by chariots,
because they did not encounter the right era or the right ruler.'
Meeting the right opportunity is not guaranteed,
and calamities cannot be warded off.
To abandon the way of preservation and success
and indulge in perilous actions,
I privately believe you, sir, should not adopt this." 」
Hánzǐ replied:
"I understand your words, sir.
The handle to govern the world,
and the measures to regulate the people,
are extremely difficult to manage.
Yet the reason I abolish the teachings of former kings
and practice what I, a humble minister, deem acceptable,
is that I privately believe establishing methods and techniques,
setting up regulations and measures,
is the way to benefit the people
and convenience the masses.
Thus, to not fear the calamity of chaotic rulers and benighted superiors,
but insist on thinking of the resources and benefits for the people,
is the conduct of benevolence and wisdom.
To fear the calamity of chaotic rulers and benighted superiors,
and avoid the harm of death,
knowing only to preserve oneself
while ignoring the resources and benefits for the people,
is the behavior of greed and baseness.
I cannot bear to choose greedy and base behavior,
nor dare I harm benevolent and wise conduct.
You, sir, have the intention to care for me,
but in reality, you greatly harm me." 」
The questioner asked:
"Shēn Bùhài
and Gōngsūn Yāng—
which of these two schools' theories is more urgent for the state?" 」
The reply was:
"This cannot be measured.
A person without food
will die in ten days;
at the height of great cold,
without clothing, one will also die.
If asked which is more urgent for a person, food or clothing,
then one cannot lack either,
as both are essentials for sustaining life.
Now, Shēn Bùhài spoke of statecraft,
while Gōngsūn Yāng established laws.
Statecraft
involves appointing officials based on their responsibilities,
holding them accountable according to their titles,
wielding the power of life and death,
and examining the abilities of the ministers—
this is what the ruler holds.
Laws
are the statutes and decrees established in government offices,
ensuring penalties are firmly rooted in the people's minds,
rewards are given for careful adherence to the law,
and punishments are imposed for violating decrees—
this is what the ministers follow.
If the ruler lacks statecraft,
he will be misled from above;
if the ministers lack laws,
chaos will reign below.
These cannot lack even one,
as both are tools of the sovereign." 」
The questioner asked:
"If one has only statecraft but no laws,
or only laws but no statecraft,
why is that unacceptable?" 」
The reply was:
"Shēn Bùhài
was an assistant to Hán Zhāohóu.
The state of Hán
was a offshoot of Jìn.
The old laws of Jìn had not yet ceased,
while the new laws of Hán arose;
the decrees of the former ruler had not been withdrawn,
while the decrees of the later ruler were issued.
Shēn Bùhài did not unify the laws,
nor standardize the statutes and decrees,
so villainy multiplied.
Thus, if profit lay in the old laws or former decrees,
people followed them;
if profit lay in the new laws or later decrees,
they followed those instead.
When benefits lie in opposing the old and the new,
and priorities conflict with one another,
even if Shěn Bùhài had ten times urged Marquis Zhāo
to employ statecraft,
treacherous ministers would still find ways to manipulate their words.
Thus, despite entrusting the mighty state of Hán with ten thousand chariots for seventeen years,
it never achieved hegemony or kingship,
because although statecraft was applied from above,
the laws were not diligently enforced among the officials—this was the flaw.
When Gōngsūn Yāng governed Qín,
he established mutual denunciation and collective responsibility
to hold people accountable for reality,
organized households into groups of ten and five
to share punishment for crimes,
rewards were generous and trustworthy,
penalties were severe and inevitable.
Thus, the people labored tirelessly with effort,
pursued enemies dangerously without retreat,
so the state grew wealthy and its military strong;
yet without statecraft to detect treachery,
this wealth and strength
only served to enrich the ministers themselves.
After Duke Xiào
and Lord Shāng died,
King Huì ascended the throne,
and while Qín's laws had not yet decayed,
Zhāng Yí used Qín to sacrifice for Hán
and Wèi.
When King Huì died,
King Wǔ took the throne,
Gān Mào used Qín to sacrifice for Zhōu.
After King Wǔ's death,
King Zhāoxiāng assumed power,
the Marquis of Ráng crossed Hán
and Wèi to attack Qí in the east,
yet in five years, Qín gained not an inch of land,
instead he fortified his fief at Táoyì.
The Marquis of Yìng attacked Hán for eight years,
securing his fief in Rǔnán.
Since then,
all those who served Qín were of the same ilk as Yìng
and Ráng.
Thus, when battles were won,
high ministers were elevated,
and when territory expanded,
private fiefs were established,
because the ruler lacked statecraft
to detect treachery.
Even if Lord Shāng had ten times refined his laws,
the ministers would still turn them to their own advantage.
Therefore, despite leveraging the resources of a strong Qín for decades,
it never reached imperial status,
because although laws were diligently enforced among officials,
the ruler lacked statecraft from above—this was the flaw. "
Someone asked:
"If the ruler employs Shěnzǐ's statecraft,
and the officials implement Lord Shāng's laws,
would that work?"
The reply was:
"Shěnzǐ did not fully grasp statecraft,
and Lord Shāng did not perfect the laws.
Shěnzǐ said,
'Govern without overstepping one's office,
even if one knows, do not speak.'
Governing without overstepping one's office
may be called fulfilling one's duty;
but knowing and not speaking
is failing to report errors.
The ruler sees with the eyes of the whole state,
so his vision is unparalleled;
he hears with the ears of the whole state,
so his hearing is unmatched.
If those who know do not speak,
then what can the ruler rely on?
Lord Shāng's law stated:
'He who beheads one enemy is ennobled one rank,
and if he wishes to be an official, he becomes one of fifty dàn;
he who beheads two enemies is ennobled two ranks,
and if he wishes to be an official, he becomes one of a hundred dàn.'
Thus, promotions in office and rank corresponded to the merit of beheading enemies.
Now suppose there were a law saying:
'Those who behead enemies shall be made physicians
or craftsmen.'
Then houses would not be built, and illnesses would not be cured.
For craftsmen require manual skill,
and physicians need to mix medicines,
yet if they are appointed based on beheading merits,
it does not match their abilities.
Now, governing officials requires
wisdom and capability;
whereas beheading enemies
relies on courage and strength.
To use those who excel in courage and strength
to fill posts requiring wisdom and capability
is like making beheaders
serve as physicians or craftsmen.
Therefore, it is said:
Both gentlemen, in terms of law and statecraft,
were not entirely perfect. "
In general, the greater aspects of governance
do not merely lie in appropriate rewards and punishments.
Rewarding the undeserving,
punishing the innocent,
is not what is called enlightened.
Rewarding the meritorious,
punishing the guilty,
and not missing the right targets,
this depends on the individuals involved,
but it does not inherently generate merit or prevent errors.
Therefore, the method to prohibit treachery:
the highest is to forbid it in the heart,
next is to forbid it in speech,
and the lowest is to forbid it in action.
Nowadays, everyone says:
'To honor the ruler and secure the state,
one must use benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and capability,'
but they do not realize that those who debase the ruler and endanger the state
also necessarily use benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and capability.
Thus, a ruler who follows the Way
distances himself from benevolence and righteousness,
discards wisdom and capability,
and subdues people with laws.
Thereby, his praise spreads wide and his fame becomes awe-inspiring,
the people are governed and the state is secure,
for he knows the method of employing the people.
As for statecraft,
it is what the ruler holds;
as for laws,
they are what the officials follow.
Yet, having court officials daily hear of the Way outside the court gates,
so that the laws are seen daily throughout the land,
is not particularly difficult.
In the past, the Yǒuhù clan had Shīdù,
the Huāndōu clan had Gū'nán,
the Sānmiáo had Chéngjū,
Jié had Guīchǐ,
Zhòu had Chóng Hóuhǔ,
Jìn had Yōu Shī,
these six individuals
were all ministers who led to the downfall of states.
They called right wrong,
and wrong right,
inwardly treacherous and harmful,
outwardly appearing cautious,
to feign goodness;
they cited ancient times,
causing good deeds to be thwarted;
skillfully flattered their rulers,
gathering subtle influences,
confusing them with their preferences;
these are the types found among the ruler's court attendants.
Rulers of the past
some gained such men and enjoyed personal safety and state preservation,
others gained them
and faced personal danger and state ruin.
The name 'gaining men' is the same,
but the benefits and harms differ vastly,
so the ruler must be cautious in selecting his close aides.
If a ruler truly understands what his ministers say,
he can distinguish the worthy from the unworthy as clearly as black and white.
As for Xǔ Yóu,
Xù Yá,
Jìn Bóyáng,
Qín Diānxié,
Wèi Qiáorú,
Hú Bùjī,
Chóngmíng,
Dǒng Bùshí,
Biàn Suí,
Wù Guāng,
Bó Yí,
Shū Qí,
these twelve individuals
all, when faced with profit above, did not rejoice,
and when confronting danger below, did not fear,
some were offered the world and did not take it,
bearing the stigma of disgrace,
they found no pleasure in the benefits of official salary.
Those who show no joy at the sight of profit,
even if the ruler offers generous rewards,
cannot be encouraged;
those who show no fear in the face of danger,
even if the ruler imposes severe punishments,
cannot be intimidated:
these are called ungovernable people.
These twelve individuals,
some died hidden in caves,
some perished among the grass and trees,
some starved in mountain valleys,
some drowned in springs and rivers.
With people like these,
even the sage kings of antiquity could not subdue them—
in the present age,
how could they be of any use?
As for Guān Lóngpáng, Prince Bǐgān, Suí Jìliáng,
Chén Xièyě, Chǔ Shēnxū, and Wú Zǐxū,
these six men
all vehemently argued and forcefully remonstrated to overpower their rulers.
If their words were heeded and plans implemented,
they assumed the manner of mentors;
if a single word went unheeded
or one matter was not carried out,
they would verbally assault their sovereign,
staking their own lives—
even if it meant death and the destruction of their families,
their heads severed from their bodies,
limbs torn apart,
they did not consider it difficult.
Such ministers,
even the sage kings of antiquity could not tolerate—
in the present time,
how could they be of any use?
As for Qí's Tián Héng,
Sòng's Zǐhǎn,
Lǔ's Jìsūn Yìrú,
Jìn's Qiáorú,
Wèi's Zǐnán Jìng,
Zhèng's Grand Steward Xīn,
Chǔ's Báigōng,
Zhōu's Shāntú,
and Yān's Zǐzhī,
these nine men as ministers
all formed cliques and conspired together to serve their rulers,
concealing the right path to practice crooked schemes,
oppressing the sovereign above and disrupting governance below,
inviting external forces to disturb internal affairs,
befriending subordinates to plot against their superiors—
they did not consider it difficult.
Such ministers,
only sage kings and wise rulers can restrain—
as for benighted and chaotic rulers,
could they even recognize them?
As for Hòujì,
Gāoyáo,
Yīyǐn,
Zhōu Gōngdàn,
Tàigōng Wàng,
Guǎn Zhòng,
Xí Péng,
Bǎilǐ Xī,
Jiǎn Shū,
Jiùfàn,
Zhào Cuī,
Fàn Lǐ,
Grand Fū Zhǒng,
Páng Tóng,
and Huà Dēng,
these fifteen men as ministers
all rose early and retired late,
humbling their bodies and lowering their status,
with sincere hearts and pure intentions;
they clarified penal laws,
administered official duties
to serve their rulers,
presented wise counsel,
upheld the Dao and laws
yet never boasted of their goodness,
achieved merits and accomplished deeds
yet never flaunted their labors.
They did not hesitate to ruin their families to benefit the state,
sacrifice themselves to secure their lords,
regarding their sovereigns with the loftiness of high heaven and Mount Tài,
and themselves with the lowliness of ravines and cooking pots;
so their lords gained brilliant fame and widespread acclaim in the land,
while they themselves willingly accepted
the humility of ravines and cooking pots.
Such ministers,
even under benighted and chaotic rulers could still achieve merit—
how much more under illustrious and enlightened rulers?
These are called the supports of hegemons and kings.
As for Zhōu Huázhī,
Zhèng's Wángsūn Shēn,
Chén's Gōngsūn Níng,
Yí Xíngfù,
Jīng's Yùyǐn,
Shēn Hài,
Suí's Shàoshī,
Yuè's Zhǒng Gān,
Wú's Wángsūn É,
Jìn's Yángchéng Xiè,
Qí's Shù Diāo,
and Yì Yá,
these twelve men as ministers
all coveted petty gains while forgetting laws and righteousness,
in advancement they suppressed the worthy and virtuous
to darken their rulers' minds,
in retreat they confused and disrupted the百官
to create calamities;
they all aided their rulers
in indulging desires,
and if they could secure their lord's favor,
even if it meant ruining the state and slaughtering the people,
they did not consider it difficult.
With ministers like these,
even a sage king would fear being usurped—
how much more a benighted and chaotic ruler—
could they avoid failure?
Those who had such ministers
all met death and the destruction of their states,
becoming laughingstocks of the world.
Thus Duke Wēi of Zhōu was killed,
and his state divided in two;
Zǐyáng of Zhèng was killed,
and his state split in three;
Duke Líng of Chén died at the hands of Xià Zhēngshū;
King Líng of Jīng perished at Gānxī;
Suí was destroyed by Jīng;
Wú was annexed by Yuè;
Zhì Bó was vanquished beneath Jìnyáng;
Duke Huán's corpse lay unburied for seven days.
Therefore it is said:
Sycophantic and flattering ministers,
only sage kings recognize them,
while chaotic rulers keep them close—
hence they meet death and state destruction.
Sage kings and enlightened rulers are not so;
in internal appointments they do not avoid relatives,
in external selections they do not shun enemies.
Where there is merit,
they promote accordingly;
where there is fault,
they punish accordingly.
Thus the worthy and virtuous advance while the treacherous and wicked retreat,
so a single action can subdue the feudal lords.
The records state:
Yáo had Dānzhū,
Shùn had Shāngjūn,
Qǐ had Wǔguān,
Shāng had Tàijiǎ,
King Wǔ had Guǎn and Cài.
The ones these five kings executed
were all close kin—fathers, brothers, sons—
yet they had them killed, destroying their persons and families—why?
Because they harmed the state, injured the people, and corrupted the law.
Observe those they promoted:
some from mountain forests, marshes, and caves,
some from prisons and bound in ropes,
some from butchering, cooking, herding, or feeding oxen.
Yet enlightened rulers were not ashamed of their lowliness,
but for their abilities,
which could illuminate laws,
benefit the state and people,
they promoted them accordingly,
securing their own safety and noble reputation.
Chaotic rulers are not so;
they do not understand their ministers' intentions and conduct,
yet entrust them with the state—
so in minor cases their reputation is debased and territory diminished,
in major cases the state is lost and they themselves perish,
due to ignorance in employing ministers.
Those without methods to measure their ministers
inevitably judge them by the mouths of the multitude.
What the multitude praises,
they follow and delight in;
what the multitude condemns,
they follow and detest.
Thus, as ministers, they ruin families and deplete treasures,
forming cliques internally,
and connecting with local factions externally to gain praise,
secretly making pacts to solidify their alliances,
falsely bestowing ranks and emoluments to encourage each other.
They say:
"Those who side with me will be benefited,
those who do not side with me will be harmed."
The multitude covets their benefits,
and is coerced by their authority:
"If they are truly pleased,
they can benefit us;
if angered,
they can harm us."
Thus the masses adhere to them and the people remain loyal,
until their fame fills the state,
and reaches the ruler's ears.
The ruler cannot discern the truth of the matter,
and therefore considers them worthy.
They further employ deceitful strategists,
who outwardly pretend to be honored envoys from other feudal lords,
provided with carriages and horses,
authenticated by tallies and credentials,
persuasive in speech,
and supplied with valuables and silks,
sent to the feudal lords,
to mislead their rulers,
covertly carrying private agendas while publicly deliberating.
Those they are sent to
are rulers of other states;
those they converse with
are the close attendants.
The ruler is pleased with their words and convinced by their arguments,
believing such men to be the most worthy in the world.
Both internally and externally, among his attendants,
their insinuations are uniform and their words identical.
For major figures, he does not hesitate to humble himself
and lower his position to serve them;
for minor ones, he offers high ranks and generous emoluments to benefit them.
When treacherous men hold high ranks and emoluments
and their factions grow ever larger,
and they harbor wicked intentions,
then treacherous ministers increasingly turn to flatter them, saying:
"The so-called sage kings and enlightened rulers of antiquity
did not attain their positions through hereditary succession in order.
They formed cliques,
gathered local factions,
coerced their superiors and assassinated their rulers
to seek their own gain."
Someone asks:
"How do you know it was so?"
They then reply:
"Shùn coerced Yáo,
Yǔ coerced Shùn,
Tāng exiled Jié,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu.
These four kings
were all ministers who killed their rulers,
yet the world praises them.
Examining the motives of these four kings,
they were driven by greed for gain;
assessing their actions,
they employed violent and disorderly military force.
Yet these four kings expanded their own domains,
and the world acclaimed them as great;
they made their own names illustrious,
and the world hailed them as enlightened.
Thus their power was sufficient to command the world,
their benefits ample to overshadow the age,
and the world followed them."
They also say:
"From what we hear in recent times,
Tián Chéngzǐ seized Qí,
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn seized Sòng,
Grand Steward Xīn seized Zhèng,
the Shàn clan seized Zhōu,
Yì Yá seized Wèi,
and the three masters Hán, Wèi, and Zhào partitioned Jìn.
These eight individuals
were all ministers who killed their rulers."
Upon hearing this, treacherous ministers
perk up their ears eagerly, considering it true.
Thus they form cliques internally,
mobilize local factions externally,
watch for the right moment to act,
and in one move seize the state.
Moreover, internally they use their factions to coerce and assassinate their ruler,
externally they use the authority of feudal lords
to forcibly alter their state,
concealing the correct path,
upholding private crookedness,
restraining the ruler above,
and obstructing governance below—
such cases are too numerous to count.
Why is this so?
It is because they do not understand how to select ministers.
The records say:
"Since King Xuān of Zhōu,
dozens of states have perished,
and many were those where ministers killed their rulers and seized the state."
Thus, difficulties arising from within
and those arising from outside are about equal.
Those who could fully utilize their people's strength,
even if their state was destroyed and they themselves killed,
were still considered worthy rulers.
As for those who changed positions,
preserved the multitude, and handed over the state,
this is the worst fault.
For a ruler,
if he truly understands what his ministers say,
then even with hunting and racing,
striking bells and entertaining dancing girls,
the state will still survive;
if he does not understand what his ministers say,
even with frugality and diligence,
coarse clothing and poor food,
the state will still perish on its own.
The former lord of Zhào, Jìng Hóu,
did not cultivate virtuous conduct,
but indulged in his desires,
pursuing physical comfort
and pleasures for his ears and eyes,
hunting in winter,
reveling in summer,
holding all-night banquets,
not ceasing to drink for days on end,
forcing those who could not drink by pouring it down their throats with tubes,
and beheading before him
those who were not solemn in advancing or retreating, or disrespectful in response.
Thus, in his dwelling and diet he was so unrestrained,
in applying punishments and executions so immoderate,
yet Jìng Hóu reigned for several decades,
his troops were never defeated by enemy states,
his territory never diminished by neighboring states,
there was no disorder among the officials and百官 internally,
no troubles from feudal lords or neighboring states externally,
because he understood how to employ his ministers.
The ruler of Yān, Zǐ Kuài,
descendant of Shào Gōng Shì,
with a territory spanning thousands of miles,
and tens of thousands of halberd-bearing troops,
took no pleasure in the joys of women and children,
listened not to the sounds of bells and stones,
built no ponds, terraces, or pavilions internally,
engaged not in hunting or field sports externally,
and even personally handled the plow and hoe to tend the fields.
Zǐ Kuài tormented himself to worry for his people
to such an extreme extent
that even the so-called sage kings and enlightened rulers of antiquity
could not have surpassed his diligence and concern for the world.
Yet Zǐ Kuài died and his state perished,
usurped by Zǐ Zhī,
and the world laughed at him.
What is the reason for this?
He did not understand how to employ his ministers.
Therefore it is said:
Ministers have five forms of treachery,
yet the ruler may be unaware of them.
As ministers,
some extravagantly use wealth and bribes
to gain reputation,
some concentrate on rewards and gifts
to sway the multitude,
some form cliques, follow the wise, and honor scholars
to arrogate power for their own ends.
There are those who strive to pardon and absolve crimes and prisoners
to assert authority;
there are those who devote themselves to flattering subordinates, distorting right and wrong,
uttering strange words,
wearing extravagant attire,
and making grandiose claims
to dazzle the people's eyes and ears.
These five types of conduct
are what enlightened rulers view with suspicion,
and what sage sovereigns prohibit.
By eliminating these five,
then glib and deceitful individuals dare not stand facing north to speak;
those whose ornate words are many,
but actual deeds few,
and who do not conform to the law,
dare not distort the truth in their discourse.
Thus, ministers in their repose cultivate their character,
and in action exert their strength,
not daring to act arbitrarily, speak hastily, or falsify matters
without the sovereign's command.
This is how the sage king governs his subordinates.
Those sage sovereigns and enlightened rulers
do not entertain doubtful matters to spy on their ministers.
For those who encounter doubtful matters and do not reflect,
are rare in the world.
Therefore, it is said:
"When a concubine's son rivals the legitimate heir,
when a consort rivals the wife,
when a courtier rivals the prime minister,
when a minister rivals the sovereign's favor,
these four are the perils of the state."
Hence it is said:
"Favored consorts equal the queen,
external favorites divide the government,
branch sons match the legitimate heir,
great ministers rival the sovereign—
these are the ways to chaos."
Thus, the "Zhōu Jì" states:
"Do not honor the concubine and demean the wife,
do not elevate the legitimate heir's rival and honor the minor branch,
do not honor favored ministers to pair with high nobles,
do not honor great ministers to rival their sovereign."
If these four rivalries are broken,
then the sovereign has no worries,
and the people have no anomalies.
If the four rivalries are not broken,
then the ruler perishes and the state is destroyed.
The means by which the sages bring about orderly governance are three:
first, benefit;
second, authority;
third, reputation.
Now, benefit
is what wins the people;
authority
is what enforces commands;
reputation
is what aligns the high and low on the same path.
Without these three,
even if other things exist, they are not urgent.
Now, benefits are not absent,
yet the people are not transformed by the ruler;
authority is not lacking,
yet subordinates do not obey;
offices are not without laws,
yet governance does not match the reputation.
These three are not absent,
yet the world alternates between order and chaos—
why is this?
It is because what the ruler values
contradicts the means of achieving order.
Establishing titles and names
is for the purpose of respect;
yet now those who debase names and disregard reality
are called noble by the world.
Setting up ranks and positions
is to establish the basis of honor and humility;
yet those who neglect the sovereign and do not seek audience
are called worthy by the world.
Authority and benefit
are to enforce commands,
yet those who spurn benefit and belittle authority
are called steadfast by the world.
Laws and decrees
are for governance,
yet those who disobey laws and decrees
to perform private acts of kindness
are called loyal by the world.
Official ranks
are to encourage the people,
yet those who cherish fame and righteousness and do not advance in office
are called martyrs by the world.
Punishments
are to monopolize authority,
yet those who disregard the law and do not avoid penalties, execution, or death sentences
are called brave by the world.
The people's craving for fame
exceeds their pursuit of profit;
in such a case,
how can scholars who are starving and destitute
avoid dwelling in seclusion, suffering their bodies,
to contend for fame under heaven?
Thus, the reason the world is not well-governed
is not the fault of the subordinates,
but the sovereign's loss of the proper way.
Constantly valuing what leads to chaos,
and demeaning what leads to order,
therefore the desires of the subordinates
often contradict the means by which the sovereign seeks to govern.
Now, for subordinates to obey their sovereign
is what the sovereign urgently needs.
Yet those who are sincere, honest, pure, and trustworthy,
cautious in heart and speech,
are called base.
Those who firmly uphold the law,
and carefully heed commands,
are called foolish.
Those who respect the sovereign and fear punishment,
are called timid.
Those whose speech is timely,
and actions are moderate,
are called unworthy.
Those without divided loyalties, avoiding private studies,
and obeying officials by following teachings,
are called uncultured.
Those hard to summon
are called upright.
Those hard to bestow upon
are called incorrupt.
Those hard to restrain
are called disciplined.
Those who do not obey commands
are called courageous.
Those who bring no benefit to the sovereign
are called sincere.
Those with few desires,
broad kindness,
and virtuous conduct
are called benevolent.
Those dignified and self-respecting
are called elders.
Those with private studies forming groups
are called masters and disciples.
Those tranquil and settled in repose
are called thoughtful.
Those who abandon benevolence to chase profit
are called shrewd.
Those treacherous, impulsive, fickle, and contradictory
are called wise.
Those who act for others before themselves,
imitate titles and names,
and speak of universal love for all under heaven
are called sage.
Those who speak of great foundations,
are praised but unusable,
and act contrary to the world
are called great persons.
Those who disdain ranks and emoluments,
and do not yield to the sovereign
are called heroes.
When subordinates gradually behave thus,
at home they disrupt the people,
abroad they bring no convenience.
The sovereign ought to suppress their desires,
eradicate their traces,
yet not only does he not stop them;
he further honors them,
which is to teach subordinates to chaos against the sovereign in the name of governance.
Generally, what the sovereign uses to govern
is punishments and penalties;
yet now those who practice private righteousness are honored.
What establishes the altars of soil and grain
is tranquility;
yet those who are glib, treacherous, flattering, and sycophantic are employed.
What ensures obedience within the four borders
is trust and virtue;
yet those who are cunning, knowledge-twisting, and subversive are sent on missions.
The reason why decrees are carried out,
and authority is established,
is due to reverence, frugality, and obedience to superiors;
yet those who dwell in seclusion and criticize the world are prominent.
The reason why granaries are full,
is because farming is the fundamental occupation;
yet those engaged in embroidery,
brocade,
and carving—
the trivial crafts—become wealthy.
The reason why reputation is achieved,
and city walls and moats are expanded,
is because of warriors;
yet now the orphans of fallen soldiers starve and beg on the streets,
while entertainers and drunkards ride in carriages and wear silk.
Rewards and emoluments
are meant to exhaust the people's efforts and make them willing to die for their superiors;
yet now those who achieve victory in battle and conquer territories
toil without receiving rewards,
while diviners,
palm readers,
and flatterers
who utter pleasing words are daily bestowed with gifts.
The ruler holds the standards
to monopolize the power of life and death;
yet now those who uphold these standards and measures
seek to serve loyally
but are denied an audience,
while glib-tongued, cunning speakers
who practice deceit and opportunism
are frequently employed.
To speak directly according to the law,
align names with punishments,
follow the guidelines,
and punish the wicked—
these are means to govern for the ruler,
yet such persons are increasingly distanced,
while sycophants who cater to desires
and endanger the world are kept close.
Collecting taxes in full
and concentrating the people's labor
are meant to prepare for crises and fill storehouses;
yet soldiers and commoners evade duties and hide,
attaching themselves to powerful households
to avoid corvée and taxes,
numbering in the tens of thousands beyond the ruler's reach.
Offering fertile fields and fine residences
is intended to motivate soldiers;
yet those who are decapitated or dismembered,
their bones scattered on plains and fields,
have no homes to shelter them,
and upon death, their lands are seized;
while sisters and daughters with beauty,
or ministers and attendants without merit,
select mansions to receive
and choose fields to enjoy.
Rewards and benefits should emanate solely from the ruler,
to properly control subordinates;
yet armored warriors hold no office,
while recluses are honored and prominent.
If the ruler uses this as governance,
how can reputation not be debased,
and position not be endangered?
Those with a debased reputation and endangered position
must have subordinates who disobey laws and decrees,
harboring divided loyalties, pursuing private studies, and opposing the world;
yet if their actions are not prohibited,
their groups not broken up and their cliques dispersed,
but instead they are further honored,
then those in power are at fault.
The means by which the ruler establishes integrity and shame
are intended to discipline subordinates;
yet now officials feel no shame in corruption and disgrace
to secure positions,
and the doors of sisters and private favorites
obtain office without waiting their turn.
Rewards and gifts
are meant to convey importance;
yet warriors who fight with merit remain poor and lowly,
while flatterers and entertainers are promoted over ranks.
Titles and reputations, if sincere and trustworthy,
serve to communicate authority;
yet if the ruler is obscured,
with favorites and female intermediaries acting freely,
and officials controlling appointments and promotions,
then those in power are at fault.
When high officials appoint others,
conspiring with subordinates beforehand,
even if acting unlawfully,
authority and benefits lie below,
then the ruler is debased and the ministers powerful.
To establish laws and decrees
is to abolish private interests.
When laws and decrees are implemented,
private ways are eradicated.
Private interests
are what corrupt the law.
And when scholars have divided loyalties and private studies,
dwelling in caves or hidden paths,
concealing themselves in deep contemplation,
the greater ones criticize the world,
the lesser ones mislead the masses;
if the ruler does not prohibit this,
but instead honors them with reputation,
and transforms them with substance,
this enables the unmerited to be prominent,
and the idle to become wealthy.
In this way,
how can scholars with divided loyalties and private studies
avoid deep contemplation,
striving with cunning knowledge
and slandering the laws,
to seek what contradicts the world?
Generally, those who disrupt the ruler and oppose the world
are often scholars with divided loyalties
and private studies.
Hence, the "Běnyán" states:
"What brings order
is the law;
what brings chaos
is private interest.
When the law is established,
none can act for private gain."
Therefore, it is said:
Those who champion private interest bring chaos,
those who champion the law bring order.
If the ruler lacks this principle,
then the wise will have private rhetoric,
and the worthy will have private intentions.
If the ruler shows private favor,
the subordinates will have private desires.
The sagacious and intelligent form groups,
creating doctrines and arguments,
imposing unlawfulness upon the ruler;
if the ruler does not suppress and block this,
but instead honors them,
this teaches subordinates not to obey the ruler or follow the law.
Thus, the worthy dwell in prominence and clarity,
while the wicked rely on rewards to become rich.
The worthy dwell with illustrious names,
and the wicked rely on rewards to become rich—
this is why the ruler cannot overcome the subordinates.
Those who fear death and shun hardship
are people who surrender and flee,
yet the world honors them as "noble-life scholars."
Those who study doctrines and establish standards,
deviating from the law,
are honored by the world as "literary scholars."
Those who wander and live in luxury,
profiteering for food,
are honored by the world as "capable scholars."
Those who twist words and seek wisdom,
engaging in deceit and fraud,
are honored by the world
as "disputatious and wise scholars."
Those who wield swords and commit murder,
violent and fierce people,
are honored by the world
as "resolute and courageous scholars."
Those who harbor bandits and conceal the wicked,
deserving death,
are honored by the world as "reputation-bearing scholars."
These six types of people
are praised by the world.
Those who brave dangers and die with integrity,
sacrificing themselves for principles,
are disparaged by the world
as "imprudent people."
Those of little learning who follow orders,
upholding the law entirely,
are disparaged by the world
as "simple and crude people."
Those who toil and eat through their labor
are people who generate benefits,
yet the world disparages them as
"people of scant ability."
Those who are virtuous, sincere, and pure
are law-abiding people,
yet the world disparages them as
"foolish and simple-minded people."
Those who value life and handle affairs with caution, respecting their superiors,
are disparaged by the world as "timid and fearful people."
Those who suppress bandits and stop evildoers,
enlightening their superiors,
are disparaged by the world as
"flattering and slanderous people."
These six types of people
are denigrated by the world.
There are six types of deceitful and unbeneficial people,
yet the world praises them as such;
there are six types of farming and warfare beneficial people,
yet the world disparages them like this.
This is called the six contradictions.
Commoners follow selfish interests and praise them,
rulers heed empty reputations and honor them;
where honor is bestowed, benefits are sure to follow.
The common people follow personal harm and criticize them,
rulers are blinded by custom and belittle them;
where belittlement exists, harm is sure to be added.
Thus, fame and rewards go to those who privately deserve punishment for their crimes,
while slander and harm fall upon those who publicly merit reward for their goodness.
To seek a state's wealth and power
is unattainable this way.
An ancient proverb says:
"Governing is like washing hair;
though some hair is lost, it must be done."
To begrudge the loss of a few strands and forget the benefit of long hair
is to lack understanding of权衡轻重.
Lancing a boil is painful,
taking medicine is bitter;
if one avoids lancing the boil or taking medicine due to the pain and bitterness,
then life cannot be preserved, nor the illness cured.
Now in the interactions between superiors and subordinates,
there is no bond like that between father and son,
yet to try to restrain inferiors through righteousness
will inevitably lead to discord.
Moreover, when parents have children,
they congratulate each other for a boy,
but kill a girl.
Both come from the parents' embrace,
yet boys are congratulated and girls killed
because they consider future convenience and long-term benefits.
Thus, even parents towards their children
still use a calculating mindset
to treat each other,
let alone without the bond of father and son?
Now when scholars advise rulers,
they urge abandoning the pursuit of profit
and adopting the way of mutual love,
which is to expect rulers to surpass the affection of parents.
This shows ignorance in discussing kindness,
being deceitful and false;
thus, enlightened rulers do not accept it.
Sages in governance
are meticulous about laws and prohibitions;
when laws and prohibitions are clear and evident,
officials are well-governed.
They are firm in rewards and punishments;
when rewards and punishments are impartial,
the people are utilized.
When the people are utilized and officials well-governed,
the state becomes wealthy;
when the state is wealthy,
the military becomes strong,
and the hegemonic kingly enterprise is achieved.
Hegemonic kingship
is the great benefit of the ruler.
The ruler, holding this great benefit, governs accordingly,
thus appointing officials based on capability,
and administering rewards and punishments without favoritism.
Making scholars and common people understand this,
they will exert themselves to the death,
then achievements can be established and ranks with emoluments attained;
with ranks and emoluments, the enterprise of wealth and honor is achieved.
Wealth and honor
are the great benefit of ministers.
Ministers, holding this great benefit, engage in affairs,
thus they act courageously unto death,
exhausting their strength without resentment.
This means if the ruler is not benevolent,
and the ministers are not loyal,
then hegemony can be achieved.
Evil, if certain to be known, will be guarded against;
if certain to be punished, it will cease.
If not known, it will run rampant;
if not punished, it will persist.
Placing lightweight goods in a hidden spot,
even Zēng Shēn or Shǐ Qiū might be suspected;
hanging a hundred gold pieces in the market,
even a great thief would not take them.
If unknown,
then Zēng or Shǐ might be suspected in hidden places;
if certain to be known,
then even a great thief would not take the hanging gold in the market.
Thus, an enlightened ruler in governing the state
increases surveillance and加重 penalties,
making the people abide by legal prohibitions
rather than stopping out of integrity.
A mother's love for her child is twice that of the father,
yet a father's commands are heeded ten times more by the child;
officials have no love for the people,
yet their commands are heeded ten thousand times more than a father's.
A mother accumulates love but her commands are ineffective,
while officials use authority and the people obey;
the strategy of severity versus love can thus be decided.
Moreover, what parents seek from their children
in actions
is their safety and benefit,
in conduct
is their avoidance of crime.
The ruler towards the people,
in times of trouble uses their lives,
in peace
uses their labor to the fullest.
With deep affection, parents try to keep their children safe and benefited,
yet they are not heeded;
the ruler, without love or benefit,
demands the people's utmost labor and lives, and his commands are followed.
Enlightened rulers understand this,
thus they do not nurture affectionate hearts,
but enhance authoritative power.
Therefore, where maternal love is deep,
children often fail,
due to excessive affection.
Where paternal love is slight, with teaching and chastisement,
children often turn out well,
due to the use of severity.
Now, in managing a household's livelihood,
if they endure hunger and cold together,
and push each other through toil and hardship,
even facing the calamities of war
or the disasters of famine,
those who remain well-clothed and well-fed
will surely be this family.
If they pity each other with food and clothing,
and indulge each other with leisure and pleasure,
when famine and poor harvests strike,
those who must sell wives and children
will surely be this family.
Thus, the way of law
involves initial hardship but long-term benefit;
the way of benevolence
brings fleeting joy but eventual poverty.
Sages weigh the light and heavy,
choosing the greater benefit,
thus adopting the mutual endurance of law
and abandoning the mutual pity of the benevolent.
Scholars all say
"light punishments,"
but this is the way to chaos and ruin.
The certainty of rewards and punishments
serves to encourage and prohibit.
Generous rewards quickly obtain what is desired,
severe punishments urgently stop what is detested.
Those who desire benefit must detest harm,
for harm
is the opposite of benefit.
Being contrary to what is desired,
how can it not be detested?
Those who desire order must detest chaos,
for chaos
is the opposite of order.
Therefore, the more one desires order,
the more generous the rewards must be;
the more one detests chaos,
the heavier the punishments must be.
Now, those who advocate light punishments
do not detest chaos deeply enough,
nor desire order strongly enough.
This is not only lacking in method but also in integrity.
Thus, the measure of worthiness, unworthiness,
folly, and wisdom
lies in the severity of rewards and punishments.
Moreover, severe punishments are not
intended for the criminals themselves.
The laws of an enlightened ruler are a standard of measurement.
In dealing with bandits,
it is not about managing those who are already under control;
if it were about managing those under control,
that would be like managing dead people.
Punishing thieves
is not about handling those already punished;
if it were about handling those punished,
that would be like dealing with convicts in chains.
Therefore, it is said:
By making the penalty for one crime heavy
to stop all evil within the borders,
this is the means to achieve order.
Those who receive severe penalties
are thieves and bandits,
while those who are deterred and fearful
are the good citizens.
Why should those who desire order doubt severe punishments?
As for generous rewards,
they are not only to reward merit
but also to encourage the whole state.
Those who receive rewards enjoy the benefits,
while those not rewarded aspire to achieve,
thus rewarding one person's merit
motivates all within the borders.
Why should those who desire order doubt generous rewards?
Now, those who do not understand governance all say:
"Severe punishments harm the people;
light punishments can stop crimes,
why must they be severe?"
This shows a lack of insight into governance.
What is stopped by severity
may not necessarily be stopped by leniency;
what is stopped by leniency
will surely be stopped by severity.
Thus, when the ruler establishes severe punishments,
all crimes cease;
if all crimes cease,
how does this harm the people?
What is called severe punishment means
the gain from crime is small,
while the penalty imposed by the ruler is great.
People will not risk a great penalty for a small gain,
so crimes are sure to stop.
What is called light punishment means
the gain from crime is large,
while the penalty imposed by the ruler is small.
People covet the gain and disdain the penalty,
so crimes do not cease.
Hence, the ancient sages had a saying:
"One does not stumble on a mountain, but on a small mound."
Mountains are large,
so people are cautious of them;
mounds are small,
so people take them lightly.
Now, with light punishments,
the people are sure to take them lightly.
If offenses are not punished,
it is driving the state to ruin;
if offenses are punished,
it is setting traps for the people.
Therefore, light penalties for crimes
are the people's mounds.
Thus, using light penalties as a way to govern the people
either leads to a disordered state
or sets traps for them,
and this can truly be called harming the people.
Now, scholars all quote the praises from books and bamboo slips,
without examining the realities of the current age,
saying:
