"If the ruler does not love the people,
taxes are always heavy,
then resources become insufficient
and the people resent the ruler,
hence the world falls into great disorder."
They believe that by satisfying the people's wealth and showing more love,
even with light punishments,
order can be achieved.
This view is incorrect.
Generally, when people incur heavy penalties,
it is after they already have enough.
Even if wealth is sufficient
and love is generously given afterward,
if punishments are light,
disorder will still occur.
Consider a wealthy family that loves its child,
providing ample wealth and goods.
With ample wealth and goods,
the child uses them lightly,
and using them lightly
leads to extravagance.
Loving the child dearly,
the parents cannot bear to restrain him,
and not restraining him
leads to arrogance and willfulness.
Extravagance
impoverishes the family,
arrogance and willfulness
lead to violent behavior.
Even with sufficient wealth and deep love,
this is the harm of light punishments.
Generally, in human nature,
when wealth is sufficient, people slacken in their efforts;
if the ruler is weak,
they indulge in wrongdoing.
Those who work hard despite having enough are like Shénnóng;
those who cultivate themselves under weak governance are like Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiū.
But it is clear that the people are not equal to Shénnóng, Zēng Shēn, or Shǐ Qiū.
Lǎo Dān once said:
"He who knows contentment has no disgrace;
he who knows when to stop will not perish."
To refrain from seeking beyond sufficiency
for fear of disgrace and peril—
that is Lǎo Dān.
Now, to think that satisfying the people's desires
can bring order
is to assume that all people are like Lǎo Dān.
Thus, Jié, though honored as the Son of Heaven,
was not satisfied with his dignity;
though he possessed all within the four seas,
he was not satisfied with his treasures.
A ruler may satisfy the people's needs,
but he cannot make them feel as content as the Son of Heaven,
and Jié did not necessarily find that sufficient either.
So even if the people's needs are met,
how can that bring order?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler in governing the state
adjusts to the times to produce wealth and goods,
regulates taxes to balance rich and poor,
enriches ranks and emoluments to fully utilize the worthy and capable,
strengthens punishments to prohibit wickedness and evil,
enables the people to gain wealth through labor,
achieve honor through service,
receive penalties for faults,
and obtain rewards for merits,
without expecting kind and generous gifts—
this is the governance of emperors and kings.
If everyone is asleep,
the blind cannot be distinguished;
if all are silent,
the mute cannot be known.
But wake them and make them see,
ask them and make them answer,
then the mute and blind are exposed.
If we do not listen to their words,
the incompetent remain unknown;
if we do not employ them,
the unworthy remain undiscovered.
Listen to their words and demand appropriateness,
employ them and hold them accountable for results,
then the incompetent and unworthy are exposed.
If we want to find a strong man
and listen to his own claims,
even an ordinary person and Wū Huò
cannot be distinguished;
but give them a tripod to lift,
and the weak and strong are revealed.
Thus, official positions
are the tripods for capable men,
assign them tasks, and the foolish and wise are separated.
So the incompetent benefit from not being heard,
the unworthy benefit from not being employed.
Their words unused,
they adorn themselves as eloquent;
themselves unappointed,
they pretend to be lofty.
Rulers are dazzled by their eloquence,
misled by their false loftiness and honor them,
this is like determining eyesight without testing vision,
or judging eloquence without requiring a response—
then the mute and blind go undetected.
An enlightened ruler, hearing their words,
must demand their utility;
observing their actions,
must seek their achievements.
Then, empty and antiquated learning will not be discussed,
and boastful, deceptive conduct will not be embellished.
To do favors for old friends is called not abandoning them;
to distribute public wealth in largesse is called being benevolent;
to treat salary lightly and value oneself highly is called being a gentleman;
to bend the law for one's relatives is called having good conduct;
to abandon office and indulge in friendships is called being chivalrous;
to withdraw from the world and evade superiors is called being lofty;
to contend and defy orders is called being strong-willed;
to practice kindness to win the masses is called gaining the people's support.
Not abandoning old friends means officials are corrupt;
benevolence means public wealth is depleted;
being a gentleman means the people are hard to govern;
having good conduct means the legal system is destroyed;
being chivalrous means official posts are neglected;
being lofty means the people do not serve;
being strong-willed means orders are not carried out;
gaining the people's support means the ruler is isolated.
These eight are the private praises of commoners,
but great failures for the ruler.
Opposing these eight would be private condemnations by commoners,
but public benefits for the ruler.
If the ruler does not examine the interests and harms of the state,
but follows the private praises of commoners,
then to expect the state to be free from danger and disorder
is impossible.
Entrusting people with affairs
is the key to survival or destruction, order or chaos.
Without method in employing people,
no appointment will not end in failure.
What rulers look for in appointees
is either eloquence and wisdom or moral purity.
Appointing someone means giving them power.
Wise men are not necessarily trustworthy,
and because their wisdom is esteemed,
their trustworthiness is mistakenly assumed.
If a wise man, with his schemes
and the leverage of his position,
pursues his private urgent matters,
then the ruler is sure to be deceived.
Since the wise cannot be trusted,
moral purists are appointed
to make decisions on affairs.
But moral purists are not necessarily wise,
and because their personal integrity is esteemed,
their wisdom is mistakenly assumed.
With the confusion of a fool
in the position of managing affairs,
acting as they see fit,
affairs are sure to fall into disorder.
Thus, without method in employing people,
appointing the wise leads to deception of the ruler,
and appointing the pure leads to disorder in affairs—
this is the peril of lacking method.
The way of an enlightened ruler
is to allow the lowly to criticize the noble,
subordinates must implicate superiors,
decisions are verified through multiple checks,
and listening has no fixed channels,
so the wise cannot practice deceit.
Rewards are given according to achievements,
tasks assigned based on assessed ability,
examining beginnings to observe failures,
punishing the faulty,
rewarding the capable,
so fools are not entrusted with affairs.
When the wise dare not deceive,
and fools do not make decisions,
then affairs are without error.
Only the perceptive can understand certain things,
but they cannot be made into laws,
for not all people are perceptive.
Only the virtuous can practice certain things,
but they cannot be made into standards,
for not all people are virtuous.
Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí
were considered perceptive by the world,
yet they troubled the age and ultimately resolved nothing;
though perceptive,
they are unfit to set official laws.
Bào Jiāo and Huà Jué
were considered virtuous by the world,
but Bào Jiāo died of self-starvation by a tree,
and Huà Jué drowned himself in a river;
though virtuous,
they are unfit to be farmers or soldiers.
Thus, what the ruler perceives,
the wise exhaust their arguments on;
what the ruler honors,
the capable exhaust their efforts on.
If modern rulers value useless debates
and honor actions with remote benefits,
then to seek the state's wealth and strength
is impossible.
Even if as learned and eloquent as Confucius and Mò Dí,
if Confucius and Mò Dí do not plow the fields,
what does the state gain?
Even as filial and frugal as Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú,
if Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú do not fight in battles,
what benefit is it to the state?
Commoners have private conveniences,
the ruler has public benefits.
Not working yet having ample support,
not serving office yet having fame—
these are private conveniences.
Curbing literary pursuits and clarifying laws,
blocking private conveniences and unifying rewards for merit—
these are public benefits.
To establish laws to guide the people,
yet also value literary pursuits,
makes the people doubt what to emulate;
to reward merit to encourage the people,
yet also honor moral conduct,
makes the people lazy in productive endeavors.
Valuing literary pursuits to cast doubt on laws,
honoring moral conduct to divert from merit—
to seek the state's wealth and strength
is impossible.
Ceremonial scepters and ritual shields
are no match for spears and iron pikes;
courtly etiquette and formal steps
cannot compare to marching a hundred lǐ by noon;
archery rituals like "Lí Shǒu"
do not equal the rapid fire of strong crossbows;
defending walls and repelling assaults
are inferior to tunneling and smoke attacks.
The ancients competed in virtue,
the medieval era contended with wisdom,
the present age struggles with force.
In ancient times, affairs were few and preparations simple,
crude and incomplete,
so there were pottery plows and handcarts.
In ancient times, people were few and intimate,
goods were plentiful, and they lightly valued profit and yielded easily,
hence there was the yielding of the throne to pass on the world.
But to practice such yielding,
exalt kindness and generosity,
and advocate benevolence and magnanimity
are all outdated governance.
In an era of many affairs,
to use tools for few affairs
is not the preparation of the wise;
in a world of great struggle,
to follow the path of yielding
is not the rule of sages.
Therefore, the wise do not ride in handcarts,
and sages do not practice outdated governance.
Laws are what control affairs,
affairs are what demonstrate achievement.
If a law is established but difficult to implement,
weigh its difficulty; if the affair can be accomplished,
then establish it.
If an affair is accomplished but has harms,
weigh its harms; if the achievements are greater,
then proceed with it.
There is no such thing in the world
as a method without difficulties
or an achievement without harm.
Hence, when capturing a city of ten thousand feet,
defeating an army of a hundred thousand,
with casualties multiplying in the ranks,
armor and weapons broken and blunted,
soldiers wounded and dead,
yet celebrating the victory and gained territory—
it is because one weighs the minor harm against the great benefit.
Just as one washing their hair may shed some strands,
and removing a disease may injure flesh and blood.
If someone sees the difficulty
and thus abandons their task,
they are a person without strategy.
The ancient sages have said:
"The compass may have imperfections,
and water may have waves;
I wish to change this,
but there is nothing to be done!"
This is a statement about understanding expediency.
Therefore, some theories are firmly established
yet distant from reality,
while some words may be clumsily phrased
but urgently practical.
Thus, the sage does not seek flawless words,
but focuses on unalterable matters.
The reason people do not serve the measuring stone
is not because they are upright and indifferent to profit,
but because the stone cannot give more or less,
the scale cannot make things lighter or heavier;
seeking gains from it yields nothing,
so people do not serve it.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
officials dare not bend the law,
clerks dare not seek private gain,
bribery does not prevail,
so all affairs within the borders
are as fair as the measuring stone.
Thus, any treachery among ministers will be known,
and those known will be punished.
Therefore, a ruler with the Way
does not seek impeccably clean officials,
but strives for methods that ensure awareness.
A loving mother towards her young child
has unsurpassable affection.
Yet if the child has wayward behavior,
she sends him to a teacher;
if he has a severe illness,
she makes him see a doctor.
Not following the teacher leads to punishment,
not seeing the doctor risks death.
Though the mother loves him,
it does not help avoid punishment or save from death;
thus, preserving the child does not rely on love alone.
The nature between mother and child
is love;
the relationship between ruler and minister
is strategy.
If a mother cannot preserve the family with love,
how can a ruler hold the state with love?
An enlightened ruler understands wealth and power,
and thus can achieve his desires.
Therefore, diligent governance
is the method to wealth and power.
Make laws and prohibitions clear,
examine plans and schemes.
Clear laws prevent internal turmoil,
sound strategies avoid external disasters of death and capture.
Thus, preserving the state
does not depend on benevolence and righteousness.
A benevolent person
is kind and generous, belittling wealth;
a tyrannical person
is harsh in heart and quick to punish.
Kindness and generosity
lead to reluctance to punish,
belittling wealth
leads to frequent giving.
A harsh heart
makes hatred visible to subordinates,
quick punishment
results in reckless killings.
Reluctance to punish
means many offenses are pardoned,
frequent giving
means rewards go to the undeserving.
Hatred visible
makes subordinates resent their superiors,
reckless punishment makes the people rebel.
Thus, with a benevolent person in power,
subordinates become unrestrained
and lightly break laws,
idly hoping for favors from above;
with a tyrannical person in power,
laws are arbitrary and ruler-minister relations discordant,
people resent and thoughts of rebellion arise.
Therefore, it is said:
Both benevolence and tyranny
lead to the state's ruin.
Being unable to provide fine food yet urging the hungry to eat
does not save the starving;
being unable to clear land and grow grain
yet encouraging loans and rewards
does not enrich the people.
The words of today's scholars,
ignoring fundamentals and favoring trivialities,
using empty sagehood to persuade the people,
are like urging to eat.
Such urging
is not accepted
by an enlightened ruler.
Concise texts lead to disputes among disciples,
simple laws lead to increased litigation among the people;
thus, the sage's writings must elaborate theories,
the enlightened ruler's laws must detail affairs thoroughly.
Exhausting thought and consideration,
weighing gains and losses,
is difficult even for the wise;
without thought or consideration,
holding to former words and demanding later results,
is easy for the foolish.
The enlightened ruler considers what is easy for the foolish,
not demanding what is difficult for the wise,
thus without using intelligence or labor,
the state is well-governed.
If sour, sweet, salty, or bland
are not judged by the mouth
but decided by the steward,
then the cook slights the ruler
and honors the steward.
If high and low, clear and muddy notes
are not judged by the ear
but decided by the music master,
then the musicians slight the ruler
and honor the music master.
If right and wrong in governing the state
are not judged by method
but decided by a favorite,
then ministers slight the ruler
and honor the favorite.
If the ruler does not observe and listen personally,
but lets judgments be made below,
he is but a dependent in the state.
If people could go without clothing and food
yet not hunger or cold,
and not fear death,
they would have no intention to serve the superior.
If their will is not controlled by the ruler,
they cannot be commanded.
Now, if the power over life and death
lies with the ministers,
and the ruler's orders are carried out,
such a thing has never happened.
If tigers and leopards did not use their claws and teeth
they would have the same might as a small mouse;
if a wealthy family did not use its riches
they would have the same resources as a gatekeeper.
A ruler with land
who cannot benefit those he favors,
or harm those he dislikes,
yet expects others to fear and respect him,
cannot achieve it.
If a minister freely expresses desires
it is called chivalry;
if a ruler freely expresses desires
it is called chaos;
if a minister slights the superior it is called arrogance;
if a ruler slights the subordinates it is called tyranny.
The same action
brings praise to the subordinate,
blame to the superior.
The minister gains greatly,
the ruler loses greatly.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
there are esteemed ministers,
but no powerful ministers.
Esteemed ministers are those
with high rank and great office;
powerful ministers are those
whose words are heeded and whose influence is vast.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
promotions follow hierarchical steps,
offices and ranks are granted based on merit,
hence there are esteemed ministers.
If words do not align with actions and there is deceit,
they are inevitably punished,
hence there are no powerful ministers.
48.1 Acting According to Human Nature
Generally, to govern the world,
one must act according to human nature.
Human nature
involves likes and dislikes,
thus rewards and punishments can be applied;
when rewards and punishments can be applied,
prohibitions and orders can be established,
and the means of governance are complete.
The ruler holds the handle of authority and positions himself with power,
hence orders are carried out and prohibitions are observed.
The handle refers to the control over life and death;
power is the resource to overcome the masses.
If appointments and dismissals are without measure, authority is profaned;
if rewards and punishments are shared with subordinates, majesty is divided.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not listen out of affection,
nor does he plan based on personal pleasure.
Thus, if one listens to words without verification,
authority is shared with the treacherous;
if intelligence and strength are not utilized,
the ruler is impoverished by his ministers.
Hence, the enlightened ruler's execution of control is like heaven,
his employment of people is like a ghost.
Like heaven, he is beyond reproach;
like a ghost, he is free from困境.
With power in effect and teachings strict,
even opposition does not lead to defiance,
and criticism and praise are unified without dispute.
Thus, rewarding the worthy and punishing the violent
is the ultimate way of promoting good;
rewarding the violent and punishing the worthy
is the ultimate way of promoting evil:
this is called rewarding similarity and punishing difference.
Rewards should be as generous as possible,
to make the people benefit from them;
praise should be as splendid as possible,
to make the people glory in it;
punishments should be as severe as possible,
to make the people fear them;
criticism should be as harsh as possible,
to make the people ashamed of it.
Then, uniformly enforce the laws,
prohibit private executions,
without harming the assessment of merits and faults.
Rewards and punishments must be known,
and knowing them,
the Way is fully realized.
48.2 The Way of the Ruler
One's strength cannot match the multitude,
one's wisdom cannot exhaust all things.
Rather than employing one person,
it is better to employ the whole state,
thus with intelligence and strength matched,
all things are overcome.
If guessing correctly, it is due to personal effort;
if incorrect, one bears the blame.
A lower ruler exhausts his own abilities,
a middling ruler exhausts the strength of others,
a superior ruler exhausts the wisdom of others.
Therefore, when affairs arise, he gathers wisdom,
and after listening collectively, he makes a public decision.
If listening is not unified,
later views contradict earlier ones;
if later views contradict earlier ones,
the foolish and wise cannot be distinguished;
if not decided publicly,
there is hesitation and indecision,
and indecision causes affairs to linger.
By taking charge himself,
he avoids the risk of falling into a pit.
Thus, he has others propose,
and after proposals are settled, he expresses his decision.
Therefore, on the day words are presented,
there must be records.
Those who contribute wisdom are tested when events occur;
those who contribute ability
are assessed when achievements appear and plans succeed or fail.
Success and failure have evidence,
and rewards and punishments follow accordingly.
If affairs succeed, the ruler claims the merit;
if plans fail, the ministers bear the blame.
A ruler who aligns tallies does not personally intervene,
let alone rely on strength?
He does not personally engage in intellectual efforts,
let alone in distant matters?
Thus, in employing people, he does not choose those who agree with him,
for agreement provokes the ruler's anger.
Having people utilize each other makes the ruler divine,
and being divine, the subordinates exhaust their efforts.
When subordinates exhaust their efforts,
ministers do not manipulate the ruler from above,
and the way of the ruler is fully realized.
48.3 The Origins of Disorder
One who understands that the interests of ministers and rulers differ will become king;
one who assumes they are the same will be usurped;
one who shares affairs with ministers will be killed.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler examines the distinction between public and private,
scrutinizes the grounds of benefit and harm,
so that treachery has no opening.
There are six sources from which disorder arises:
the ruler's mother,
the queen and concubines,
sons and grandsons,
brothers,
high ministers,
and prominent worthies.
By appointing officials and holding ministers accountable,
the ruler's mother does not act arbitrarily;
by applying rituals in differentiated ranks,
the queen and concubines have no doubts;
by not dividing power ambiguously,
the legitimate and illegitimate sons do not contend;
by not losing authority and position,
brothers do not encroach;
by not allowing a single faction below,
high ministers do not amass power;
by enforcing prohibitions and rewards consistently,
prominent worthies do not cause disorder.
Ministers have two means of influence,
called external and internal.
External means fear,
internal means affection.
If what is feared is obtained through requests,
and what is loved is heeded in words,
this is how disorderly ministers find their opportunity.
If foreign states' appointed officials
are dealt with by punishing their close associates and seizing their wealth,
then external influence is not leveraged;
if ranks and emoluments follow merit,
and those who make requests share in guilt,
then internal influence is not used.
Without external leverage
or internal influence,
then treachery is blocked.
Officials advance by ascending through ranks,
until they reach great responsibilities,
which is wise.
For those whose positions are high and responsibilities great,
control them with three restraints:
called hostage,
called pacification,
called solidification.
Relatives, wives, and children
are hostages;
generous and certain ranks and emoluments
are pacification;
cross-examination and stern accountability
are solidification.
The worthy are restrained by hostages,
the greedy are transformed by pacification,
the treacherous are cornered by solidification.
If tolerance does not control, subordinates rise against superiors;
if small evils are not eliminated, great punishments follow;
and when name and reality match, act directly.
If alive, they harm affairs;
if dead, they damage reputation,
then use food and drink to eliminate them;
if not,
give them to their enemies,
this is called eliminating hidden treachery.
Deception is called guile,
guile is called change.
See merit and reward,
see crime and punish,
and guile will cease.
If right and wrong are not disclosed,
and remonstrances and advice do not reach the ruler,
then changes cannot be implemented.
When paternal uncles and worthy talents are sent away,
it is called inviting calamity,
with the danger that neighboring enemies gain many resources.
When disgraced individuals are kept close,
it is called befriending traitors,
with the danger
that feelings of resentment and suspicion arise.
Concealing anger and holding onto faults without acting
is called increasing chaos,
with the danger that reckless individuals who act on chance emerge.
When two high ministers hold equal power without imbalance
it is called rolling up disaster,
with the danger that the powerful families
instigate plots of seizure and murder.
Being casual and not maintaining an aura of divinity
is called diminishing authority,
with the danger that villains stir up chaos like poison.
If the ruler is unaware of these five dangers,
then incidents of seizure and murder will occur.
Matters of appointment and dismissal,
if originating from within, lead to order;
if from outside, lead to chaos.
Thus, an enlightened ruler assesses achievements internally,
and uses benefits to support external relations,
so his state is ordered while the enemy is in chaos.
The path to chaos:
if ministers are hated,
external threats arise like dizziness;
if ministers are favored,
internal troubles arise like poison.
48.4 Establishing Methods
The method of threes and fives:
use threes to strategize for abundance,
use fives to investigate faults.
Applying threes must involve analysis,
applying fives must involve severity.
Without analysis, there is disrespect toward superiors;
without severity, there is collusion.
The signs of analysis
suffice to know the extent,
and severity should precede involving the masses.
In observing and listening,
the sign is cliquishness,
so reward the different;
punish those who do not report,
and hold the same guilty.
Gather all aspects of statements,
must assess them by geography,
plan by heaven,
verify by objects,
and compare by people.
When these four verifications match,
then one can observe clearly.
Compare statements to know their sincerity,
change perspectives to alter their gloss,
hold to insights to grasp the extraordinary.
Unify applications to manage close associates,
emphasize words to intimidate distant envoys.
Review the past to understand their history,
approach the near to know their inner thoughts,
distance placements to know their external actions.
Use clarity to inquire into the obscure,
employ deceitful missions to stop leaks.
Reverse statements to test suspicions,
discuss opposites to uncover hidden treachery.
Set up spies to monitor solitary actions,
make moves to observe treacherous activities.
Speak clearly to lure out avoidance of faults,
humble approaches to see straightness or flattery.
Spread news to communicate the unseen,
stir conflicts to break up cliques.
Deepen one focus to alert all minds,
leak discrepancies to change their plans.
For similarities, combine and compare them,
expose faults to clarify their stubbornness.
Know crimes and punish them to establish authority,
secretly send periodic inspections
to examine
loyalty,
gradually change to separate and break collusions.
Lower levels conspire to encroach on superiors:
the chief minister
conspires with court officials,
court officials
with their subordinates,
military officers
with their soldiers,
envoys
with their attendants,
county magistrates
with their appointed officials,
palace guards
with their close aides,
queens and consorts
with their palace maids.
This is called the way of clear communication;
if words are leaked and affairs exposed,
then the method fails.
48.5 Comparing Statements
The enlightened ruler's
focus is on secrecy,
thus if joy is shown, favors are repaid;
if anger is shown, authority is divided.
Therefore, the words of an enlightened ruler
are blocked and do not pass through,
secret and not visible.
So, using one to get ten
is the inferior way,
using ten to get one
is the superior way.
The enlightened ruler employs both superior and inferior ways,
thus no villain escapes.
In groups of five, neighborhoods,
districts, and counties as neighbors,
report faults for reward,
fail to report faults for punishment.
From superior to subordinate,
subordinate to superior likewise.
Thus, high and low, noble and humble, fear each other by law,
and advise each other with benefits.
The nature of the people
has the substance of life,
and the reputation of life.
The ruler,
has the reputation of wisdom,
and the substance of rewards and punishments.
When both reputation and substance are achieved,
then good fortune is surely known.
48.6 Listening to Laws
If listening is not verified,
then there is no basis to hold subordinates accountable;
if words are not checked for utility,
then deceitful talk confounds the ruler.
Words as things gain credibility through numbers;
for something untrue,
if ten people say it, doubt arises;
if a hundred agree, it seems true!
A thousand cannot untangle it.
The hesitant speak with doubt,
the eloquent speak with credibility.
Villains who deceive the ruler
draw resources from the crowd,
rely on eloquence for trust,
and use categories to disguise their selfishness.
If the ruler does not suppress anger and waits to verify,
the situation benefits the subordinates.
The principled ruler listens to words,
checks their utility,
examines their results,
and from examination, rewards and punishments arise;
thus, useless debates do not remain at court.
If those in office lack sufficient knowledge to perform duties,
then the position is reclaimed.
For grandiose and exaggerated claims, trace to the source,
so villains are exposed and punished.
Unjustified failure is deceit,
and deceit incriminates the minister.
Every statement must have a response,
every proposal must be held accountable for utility;
thus, cliquish words do not reach the ruler.
The way of listening overall:
ministers' loyal discussions reveal villains,
broad discussions unify internally;
if the ruler is unwise,
then villains gain advantage.
The way of an enlightened ruler is such that,
when he is pleased,
he seeks what led to the acceptance;
when he is angered,
he examines what caused the provocation.
Deliberating after changes have occurred,
he thereby obtains evidence of censure or praise, public or private.
Multiple remonstrances are offered to display wisdom and cunning,
making the ruler choose one to avoid blame.
Thus, when multiple remonstrances fail,
it is the ruler's choice.
There should be no contradictory words to the superior
to preempt future events,
but align words with outcomes
to discern deceitful or truthful speech.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
ministers cannot offer dual advice,
they must commit to one statement;
they cannot act arbitrarily,
but must align with verification,
thus, treacherous schemes find no way to advance.
48.7 Analogous to the handle,
without law,
the law's decline
stems from the ruler's obscurity.
If the ruler is obscure and without standards,
officials act on their own authority;
officials acting arbitrarily
lead to excessive emoluments without precedent;
excessive emoluments
result in numerous levies;
numerous levies thus bring wealth.
When officials are wealthy and powerful,
it breeds chaotic achievements.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
select based on capability,
esteem based on office,
reward based on merit.
If words meet the standard,
and the ruler is pleased,
all must benefit;
if not fitting,
and the ruler is angered,
all must suffer harm;
then people will not favor their own kin
but recommend even their enemies.
Authority sufficient to enforce laws,
emoluments adequate for duties,
and no room for private interests,
thus the people labor diligently and hold office lightly.
Do not burden with heavy responsibilities,
but ensure their honor lies in rank;
those in office should have no private gains,
ensuring their benefits come from salary,
thus the people respect rank and value salary.
Rank and salary
are means of reward;
if the people value these rewards,
the state is well-governed.
Punishments become excessive,
reputations become erroneous.
If rewards and praises are misapplied, the people doubt,
for they value reputation as much as reward.
If rewards come with slander,
they cannot encourage;
if punishments come with praise,
they cannot prohibit.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
rewards must stem from public benefit,
reputation must align with service to the superior.
Rewards and praises follow the same path,
censures and punishments are applied together.
Then the people find no glory outside rewards.
Those heavily punished bear ill repute,
thus the people fear.
Punishment
is means of prohibition;
if the people fear what prohibits,
the state is well-governed.
48.8 Sovereign's Dignity
If righteousness is displayed, the sovereign's dignity is divided;
if compassion is heeded, laws and regulations are destroyed.
The people fear the superior through regulations,
yet the superior lowers themselves with power to inferiors,
so inferiors act recklessly and take pride in disrespecting the ruler,
thus the sovereign's dignity is divided.
The people find it hard to offend the superior through law,
yet the superior bends the law with compassion,
so inferiors openly practice favor-giving
and engage in bribery and graft,
thereby laws and decrees decay.
Honoring private actions divides the sovereign's dignity,
practicing bribery and graft undermines the law.
If heard, it disrupts governance;
if not heard, it slanders the ruler,
thus the ruler is belittled in position
and laws are confused among officials,
this is called a state without constancy.
The way of an enlightened ruler:
ministers cannot gain honor through righteous deeds,
nor achieve merit through private benefits.
Merit and fame must arise
from official laws.
Outside the law,
even if there are difficult deeds,
they are not recognized,
thus the people have no means to private fame.
Establish laws and standards to unify the people,
trust in rewards and punishments to exhaust the people's abilities,
clarify censure and praise to encourage and deter.
Reputation, rewards and punishments, laws and decrees form three corners.
Thus, when ministers act,
they honor the ruler;
when the common people achieve merit,
it benefits the superior—this is called a state with the Way.
In high antiquity,
people were few and beasts numerous,
people could not overcome beasts, insects, and snakes.
A sage arose,
built wooden nests
to avoid various harms,
and the people rejoiced in him,
making him rule the world,
calling him Yǒu Cháo Shì.
People ate fruits, melons, clams, and mussels,
foul and putrid,
harming stomachs and intestines,
many people fell ill.
A sage arose,
drilled wood for fire
to transform the foul smells,
and the people delighted in him,
making him rule the world,
calling him Suì Rén Shì.
In middle antiquity,
the world had great floods,
and Gǔn
and Yǔ dredged waterways.
In recent antiquity,
Jié and Zhòu were tyrannical and chaotic,
and Tāng
and Wǔ waged campaigns.
If today someone built nests or drilled for fire
in the age of the Xià Hòu,
they would be laughed at by Gǔn
and Yǔ;
if someone dredged waterways
in the Yīn
or Zhōu eras,
they would be laughed at by Tāng
and Wǔ.
Then, if today someone praises the ways of Yáo,
Shùn, Tāng,
Wǔ, and Yǔ
in the current age,
they will be laughed at by new sages.
Thus, sages do not aspire to emulate antiquity,
do not take constant norms as law,
but discuss the affairs of their time,
and prepare accordingly.
A man of Sòng was plowing a field,
in the field was a tree stump,
a rabbit ran into the stump,
broke its neck and died,
so he left his plow to guard the stump,
hoping to get another rabbit,
but no more rabbits came,
and he became the laughingstock of Sòng.
Now, to wish to govern the people of today
with the policies of former kings
is all of the guard-the-stump variety.
In ancient times, men did not plow,
for the fruits of plants were enough to eat;
women did not weave,
for the skins of beasts were enough to wear.
Without toiling, sustenance was ample,
people were few and wealth abundant,
so the people did not contend.
Thus, generous rewards were not used,
heavy punishments were not applied,
and the people governed themselves.
Nowadays, having five sons is not considered too many,
and each son has five sons,
so before the grandfather dies, he already has twenty-five grandsons.
As a result, the population is large but goods and wealth are scarce,
labor is strenuous but provisions are meager,
hence the people contend.
Even with doubled rewards and repeated punishments,
disorder cannot be avoided.
When Yáo ruled the world,
his thatched roof was left untrimmed,
and the wooden rafters were unhewn;
he ate coarse grains,
and his soup was made of greens;
in winter he wore deerskin,
in summer, hemp cloth;
even the clothing and sustenance of a gatekeeper
were no worse than this.
When Yǔ ruled the world,
he personally carried the plough and spade to lead the people,
his thighs were without flesh,
and the hair on his shins had worn away.
Even the toil of a slave or captive
was not harsher than this.
Thus it is said,
those in ancient times who abdicated the position of Son of Heaven
were merely giving up the sustenance of a gatekeeper
and escaping the labor of a slave,
so relinquishing the world in antiquity was not praiseworthy.
Nowadays, when a county magistrate dies,
his descendants for generations can still ride in carriages,
hence people value the position.
Therefore, when it comes to abdication,
people easily declined being the ancient Son of Heaven
but find it hard to give up being a modern county magistrate—
this is because the realities of benefit and hardship differ.
Those who dwell in the mountains and draw water from the valleys
offer water to each other during the Lóu and Là festivals;
those who live in marshy lands and suffer from water
hire laborers to dig channels.
Thus, in the spring of a famine year,
even a younger brother is not fed;
in the autumn of a abundant year,
even distant visitors are sure to be fed.
It is not that one treats one's own flesh and blood with indifference
and loves passersby more,
but that the realities of abundance and scarcity differ.
Hence, the easy relinquishment of wealth in ancient times
was not due to benevolence,
but because wealth was plentiful;
the contention and seizure nowadays
are not due to greed,
but because wealth is scarce.
The light dismissal of the Son of Heaven
was not due to nobility,
but because his authority was slight;
the struggle for official positions
is not due to baseness,
but because the power is great.
Therefore, the sage deliberates on abundance and scarcity,
assesses the weight of authority,
and governs accordingly.
Thus, light punishments are not due to kindness,
severe executions are not due to cruelty,
but are in accordance with the customs of the time.
So affairs change with the age,
and measures are adapted to the affairs.
In ancient times,
King Wén dwelled between Fēng and Hào,
with a territory of a hundred li square,
practiced benevolence and righteousness,
won over the Xīróng,
and thus became king of the world.
King Yǎn of Xú resided east of the Hàn River,
with a territory of five hundred li square,
practiced benevolence and righteousness,
and thirty-six states ceded land and came to pay homage.
King Wén of Jīng, fearing that he would harm himself,
raised an army to attack Xú,
and thus destroyed it.
Hence, King Wén practiced benevolence and righteousness
and became king of the world,
while King Yǎn practiced benevolence and righteousness
and lost his state—
this shows that benevolence and righteousness were effective in antiquity
but not in the present.
Therefore it is said:
When the age differs, affairs change.
In the time of Shùn,
the Yǒumiáo did not submit,
and Yǔ was about to attack them.
Shùn said:
"It cannot be.
When virtue above is not profound and one resorts to force,
it is not the Way."
So he cultivated education for three years,
then took up shield and battle-axe in a dance,
and the Yǒumiáo then submitted.
In the battle against Gōnggōng,
those with short iron spears reached the enemy,
and those whose armor was not strong were wounded in the body.
This shows that shields and battle-axes were effective in antiquity
but not in the present.
Therefore it is said:
When affairs change, measures must alter.
In high antiquity, competition was through morality,
in the middle ages, pursuit was by wisdom and strategy,
and in the present age, contention is by strength and force.
When Qí was about to attack Lǔ,
Lǔ sent Zǐgòng to persuade them.
The people of Qí said:
"Your words are not without eloquence,
but what we desire is land,
not what these words refer to."
So they raised an army to attack Lǔ,
and pushed the border to within ten li of the gate.
Thus, King Yǎn's benevolence and righteousness led to Xú's destruction,
and Zǐgòng's eloquence and wisdom led to Lǔ's diminishment.
From this it is said,
benevolence, righteousness, eloquence, and wisdom
are not the means to sustain a state.
Abandoning King Yǎn's benevolence,
ceasing Zǐgòng's wisdom,
and following the strength of Xú and Lǔ
to resist a state of ten thousand chariots,
then the desires of Qí and Jīng
could not be imposed on these two states.
Ancient and modern customs differ,
and new and old measures vary.
To wish to govern the people of a troubled age with lenient and relaxed policies
is like driving a fierce horse without reins or whip—
this is the calamity of ignorance.
Now the Confucians and Mohists both praise the former kings
for loving all under heaven equally,
and thus regarding the people as their parents.
How is this demonstrated?
They say:
"When the minister of justice carries out an execution,
the ruler refrains from music for it;
upon hearing the report of a death sentence,
the ruler sheds tears."
This is what they cite about the former kings.
If considering ruler and minister as like father and son
would surely bring order,
then by extension,
there would be no disorderly fathers and sons.
In human nature, none come before parents,
yet all are loved and not necessarily well-ordered;
even with deep love,
how can disorder be avoided?
Now the former kings' love for the people
did not exceed parents' love for their children;
if children are not necessarily without disorder,
then how can the people be well-ordered?
Moreover, carrying out punishments according to law,
while the ruler weeps for it,
is to display benevolence,
not to use it as a means of governance.
Shedding tears and unwilling to punish is benevolence;
yet having to punish is law.
The former kings upheld their laws
and did not heed their tears;
thus, that benevolence cannot be used for governance
is also clear.
Moreover, the people are naturally submissive to power
and rarely influenced by righteousness.
Zhòngní was a sage of the world,
who cultivated conduct and clarified the Way
to travel across the realm;
the realm praised his benevolence,
admired his righteousness,
yet those who served him were only seventy.
Thus, those who value benevolence are few,
and those capable of righteousness are rare.
Thus in the vastness of the world,
only seventy served under its rule,
and but one embodied benevolence and righteousness.
Lǚ Āigōng,
a ruler of low caliber,
faced south to govern his state,
and none among the people within its borders dared not submit.
The people inherently yield to power;
power indeed easily subdues others.
Thus, Zhòngní instead became a subject
while Āigōng remained the ruler.
Zhòngní did not embrace his righteousness
but submitted to his power.
So, by righteousness,
Zhòngní would not have submitted to Āigōng;
wielding power,
Āigōng made Zhòngní his subject.
Now, when scholars advise rulers,
they do not advocate employing certain power,
but insist that practicing benevolence and righteousness
can make one a true king.
This demands that rulers must match Zhòngní
and that all common people be like his disciples,
a certainty that cannot be achieved.
Now, take an unworthy son:
his parents' anger does not change him,
his villagers' reproaches do not move him,
his teachers' instructions do not alter him.
With the love of parents,
the conduct of villagers,
and the wisdom of teachers,
these three excellences applied to him
yet he remains unmoved in the end,
not a hair on his shin altered.
But when the local officers,
wielding official troops,
enforcing public laws,
come to arrest criminals,
then he becomes fearful,
changes his conduct,
and alters his behavior.
Thus, parental love is insufficient to educate a child;
one must await the strict penalties of the state:
the people are inherently spoiled by love
and submit to authority.
Hence, a wall ten ren high
even Lóu Jì cannot overclimb,
because it is steep;
a mountain a thousand ren high,
even a lame ewe can be pastured on it,
because it is gentle.
Thus, an enlightened ruler makes his laws steep and his punishments severe.
A piece of cloth or silk, even if ordinary,
common folk will not discard it;
molten gold worth a hundred yì,
even Dào Zhí would not pick it up.
If not necessarily harmful,
they won't discard the ordinary cloth;
if certain to harm the hand,
they won't pick up the hundred yì of gold.
Thus, an enlightened ruler ensures his punishments are certain.
Therefore, no reward is better than generous and trustworthy,
making the people benefit from it;
no punishment is better than heavy and inevitable,
making the people fear it;
no law is better than uniform and steadfast,
making the people know it.
Thus, when the ruler bestows rewards without change,
carries out punishments without pardon,
praise accompanies the rewards,
blame follows the punishments,
then both the worthy
and the unworthy will exert their full efforts.
Now, it is not so:
they ennoble him for his achievements,
yet despise his official rank;
they reward him for his farming,
yet belittle his family enterprise;
they ostracize him for not accepting office,
yet praise his disdain for the world;
they punish him for violating prohibitions,
yet admire his courage.
The application of blame, praise, reward, and punishment
is mutually contradictory and erroneous,
so laws and prohibitions are ruined, and the people become more disorderly.
Now, if a brother is wronged,
and one must retaliate,
it is deemed integrity;
if a close friend is insulted,
and one seeks revenge,
it is deemed loyalty.
When integrity and loyalty are established,
the laws of the ruler are violated.
If the ruler honors acts of loyalty and integrity,
yet overlooks the crime of breaking prohibitions,
then the people compete in bravery,
and officials cannot overcome them.
Those who do not labor yet have food and clothing
are called capable;
those without military achievements yet are honored
are called worthy.
When such worthy and capable conduct is established,
the military weakens and lands lie fallow.
If the ruler delights in worthy and capable conduct,
yet forgets the disasters of a weak military
and barren lands,
then private conduct thrives
and public benefit perishes.
Confucians use culture to disrupt the law,
knights-errant use force to violate prohibitions,
yet the ruler honors both,
this is the cause of chaos.
Those who deviate from the law should be condemned,
yet various scholars are employed for their literary learning;
those who break prohibitions should be punished,
yet bands of knights are supported for their private swordsmanship.
Thus, what the law condemns,
the ruler employs;
what the officials punish,
the superior supports.
Law, interest, superior, and subordinate,
these four are in mutual opposition,
with no fixed standard,
even with ten Huángdìs,
it would be impossible to govern.
Therefore, those who practice benevolence and righteousness should not be praised,
praising them harms achievements;
those engaged in literary learning should not be employed,
employing them disrupts the law.
In Chǔ, there was a man named Zhígōng;
his father stole a sheep,
and he reported it to the officials.
The district ruler said:
"Execute him!"
Considering him upright to the ruler but unfilial to his father,
he was convicted and punished.
From this perspective,
the ruler's upright subject
is the father's violent son.
A man from Lǔ followed his ruler to war,
fled three times in three battles.
Zhòngní asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"I have an old father;
if I die, no one will support him."
Zhòngní considered this filial,
and promoted him.
From this perspective,
the father's filial son
is the ruler's traitorous subject.
Thus, the prime minister's execution
caused Chǔ's crimes to go unreported,
and Zhòngní's reward made Lǔ's people prone to surrender and flee.
The interests of superior and subordinate
are so divergent,
yet the ruler simultaneously praises commoners' conduct
and seeks to bring blessings to the state,
it is certainly hopeless.
In ancient times, when Cāngjié created writing,
self-circling was called private (sī),
and turning away from private was called public (gōng).
The opposition between public and private
was inherently known by Cāngjié.
Now, to consider them as having the same interest
is the fault of lack of examination.
Thus, for a commoner's strategy,
nothing is better than cultivating righteousness and practicing literary learning.
Cultivate benevolence and righteousness, and one will be trusted;
trusted, then given official duties;
master literary learning, and one becomes a brilliant teacher;
a brilliant teacher, then achieves fame and honor:
this is the beauty for a commoner.
Yet, to receive duties without merit,
to gain fame and honor without rank,
if governance is like this,
then the state will surely be in chaos, and the ruler in peril.
Therefore, incompatible matters
cannot coexist.
Those who behead enemies receive rewards,
yet acts of profound kindness are esteemed;
those who capture cities are granted ranks and emoluments,
yet doctrines of integrity and compassion are trusted;
sturdy armor and sharpened weapons are prepared for defense against calamity,
yet the adornments of officials are admired;
enriching the state through agriculture,
resisting enemies by relying on soldiers,
yet scholars of literature and learning are honored;
the people who revere superiors and fear the law are cast aside,
while wandering knights and private swordsmen are nurtured.
If conduct is such,
order and strength cannot be attained.
In times of peace, Confucian scholars and knights are nurtured,
but when difficulties arise, armored warriors are employed;
those who are benefited are not those who are used,
and those who are used are not those who are benefited.
Hence, those engaged in service neglect their duties,
while wandering scholars increase daily;
this is the reason the world is in chaos.
Moreover, what the world calls worthy
are acts of loyalty and trustworthiness;
what it calls wise
are subtle and profound words.
Subtle and profound words
are difficult for even the wisest to understand.
Now, to establish laws for the masses
with what the wisest find hard to comprehend,
then the people will have no means to recognize them.
Thus, those not sated with bran and husks do not seek fine grains and meat;
those without whole short hemp garments
do not await embroidered silks.
In governing the affairs of the world,
if the urgent cannot be obtained,
then the non-urgent should not be pursued.
Now, in the governance of administration and the affairs among the people,
what is clearly understood by common men and women is not used,
yet the theories of the supremely wise are admired;
this is contrary to good governance.
Therefore, subtle and profound words
are not the people's concern.
As for honoring those with loyal and trustworthy conduct,
one must value men who do not deceive;
men who do not deceive
also have no art of not being deceived.
Commoners in their interactions
have no wealth to benefit each other,
no authority to intimidate each other,
hence they seek men who do not deceive.
Now, the ruler occupies a position to control others,
possesses the wealth of a state,
with heavy rewards and strict punishments,
able to wield his power,
and cultivate the clarity of methods to illuminate all;
even if there are ministers like Tián Cháng or Zǐ Hǎn,
they would not dare to deceive him;
why wait for men who do not deceive?
Now, loyal and trustworthy men do not number ten,
yet officials within the borders number in the hundreds;
if loyal and trustworthy men must be appointed,
then there are not enough men for the offices.
If there are not enough men for the offices,
then those who bring order are few and those who cause chaos are many.
Therefore, the way of an enlightened ruler
is to unify laws and not seek wisdom,
to solidify methods and not admire trustworthiness;
thus, the laws are not corrupted,
and all officials are free from deceit.
Now, when it comes to speech, the ruler
delights in its eloquence without seeking its appropriateness;
in its application to action,
he admires its reputation without demanding achievement.
Therefore, among the masses of the world,
those who engage in discourse strive to be eloquent
without being practical in use,
so those who cite the ancient kings speaking of benevolence and righteousness
fill the court,
yet governance cannot avoid chaos;
those cultivating themselves compete to be lofty
without aligning with merit,
so wise men retreat to caves and cliffs,
declining salaries and refusing offers,
and the military cannot avoid weakness.
If the military cannot avoid weakness,
and governance cannot avoid chaos,
what is the reason for this?
What the people praise,
and what the superiors honor,
are methods that lead the state to chaos.
Now, all the people within the borders speak of governance,
and households possess the laws of Shāng Yāng
and Guǎn Zhòng,
yet the state grows poorer—
because many speak of farming,
but few hold the plow.
All within the borders speak of military affairs,
and households possess the books of Sūn Wǔ
and Wú Qǐ,
yet the military grows weaker—
because many speak of war,
but few don armor.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler uses their strength,
not heeding their words;
he rewards their achievements,
and must prohibit the useless,
so the people exhaust their utmost strength
in following their superiors.
Farming requires laborious effort,
yet the people do it,
saying:
"It can lead to wealth."
Warfare is a dangerous affair,
yet the people engage in it,
saying:
"It can lead to nobility."
Now, if one cultivates literature and learning,
practices speech and debate,
then there is no toil of farming yet the reality of wealth is attained,
no peril of war
yet the honor of nobility is gained—
then who would not do it?
Thus, a hundred men engage in intellectual pursuits
while one man exerts physical strength;
if those in intellectual pursuits are many,
then the laws are corrupted;
if those exerting strength are few,
then the state is impoverished—
this is the reason the world is in chaos.
Therefore, in the state of an enlightened ruler,
there are no texts of bamboo slips,
but the law is taught as instruction;
there are no words of the ancient kings,
but officials serve as teachers;
there is no defiance of private swordsmen,
but beheading enemies is considered courage.
Thus, all the people within the borders,
those who speak and debate must conform to the law,
those who act must dedicate themselves to merit,
and those who are brave must exhaust their efforts in the army.
Therefore, in times of peace, the state is rich;
in times of trouble, the military is strong—
this is called the kingly resource.
Once the kingly resource is accumulated
and one capitalizes on the vulnerabilities of enemy states,
to surpass the Five Emperors and equal the Three Kings—
it must be through this method.
Now, it is not so;
scholars and people act recklessly within,
those who engage in discourse seek power abroad,
internal and external alike perpetrate evil,
awaiting a strong enemy—
is this not perilous?
Therefore, among the ministers who speak of external affairs,
some have affiliations with the Vertical or Horizontal factions,
others have loyalties of personal enmity,
and they borrow the state's power for their own ends.
The Vertical alliance
unites the weak to attack the strong;
and the Horizontal alliance
serves the strong to attack the weak;
neither is a way to maintain the state.
Now, among the ministers who advocate the Horizontal alliance,
all say:
"If we do not serve the great,
then we will encounter enemies and suffer calamity."
Serving the great
may not have substance,
yet we present maps and surrender territory,
offer the seal and request troops.
Presenting maps reduces territory,
offering the seal degrades our name;
reduced territory means the state is weakened,
a degraded name means governance is chaotic.
Serving the great under the Horizontal alliance
shows no benefit,
yet we lose land and disrupt governance.
Those among the ministers who advocate alliances
all say:
"If we do not rescue small states and attack large ones,
we will lose the support of the world,
losing the world's support endangers the state,
and with the state endangered, the ruler is humbled."
Yet rescuing small states may not yield tangible gains,
while it prompts raising armies to confront great powers.
Saving small states does not ensure their survival,
and attacking large ones
is not without risks;
once risks arise, the state falls under the control of a strong power.
Sending out troops leads to military defeat,
retreating to defend results in cities being captured.
Rescuing small states through alliances
shows no benefit,
yet it causes loss of territory and defeat of armies.
Therefore, serving a strong power
allows officials to gain internal positions through external influence;
rescuing small states
enables the use of internal power to seek profit abroad.
Before the state's benefits are secured,
noble titles and generous salaries are already awarded;
though the ruler is humbled,
the ministers are honored;
though the state's territory is reduced,
private households grow wealthy.
If the endeavor succeeds,
they maintain long-term influence through power;
if it fails,
they retire with their wealth.
When the ruler listens to his ministers' persuasions,
ranks and emoluments are elevated even before the task is completed;
if the endeavor fails without punishment,
then among the itinerant persuaders,
who would not use cunning rhetoric
to gamble on future chances?
Hence, states are destroyed and rulers lost
due to believing in the empty talk of persuaders.
What is the reason for this?
It is that the ruler does not understand the distinction between public and private interests,
does not scrutinize the appropriateness of words,
and fails to enforce punishments consistently thereafter.
They all say:
"In external affairs,
at best, one can become a king,
at least, secure safety."
Now, to be a king
means being able to attack others;
and to be safe
means being unassailable.
Strength
enables attacking others,
while good governance
makes one unassailable.
Good governance and strength cannot be demanded from external affairs,
but arise from internal administration.
If laws and methods are not applied internally,
but wisdom is devoted to external matters,
then the state will not achieve good governance and strength.
A common proverb says:
"Long sleeves are good for dancing,
much money is good for trading."
This means ample resources make tasks easier.
Thus, a well-governed and strong state finds it easy to devise strategies,
while a weak and disordered one struggles to plan.
Therefore, for those employed in Qín,
even ten changes
rarely lead to failed plans;
for those in Yān, one change
seldom yields a successful plan,
not because those in Qín are necessarily wiser,
or those in Yān necessarily foolish,
but because the conditions of order and disorder differ.
Thus, when Zhōu broke with Qín to join an alliance,
it was conquered within a year;
when Wèi left Wèi for a horizontal alliance,
it perished in half a year.
So Zhōu was destroyed by the vertical alliance,
and Wèi fell by the horizontal alliance.
Had Zhōu and Wèi
slowed their alliance strategies,
and strengthened internal governance,
clarified their laws and prohibitions,
enforced rewards and punishments strictly,
maximized land productivity to increase reserves,
and motivated the people to die in defense, fortifying city guards,
then if others seized their land
the gain would be small,
and attacking their state would cause great losses,
so no state of ten thousand chariots
would dare stall under sturdy walls,
allowing a strong enemy to exploit their weakness,
this is the method to ensure no destruction.
Abandoning the method of certain survival
for actions leading to certain ruin
is the error of those who govern states.
When wisdom is exhausted abroad and governance disordered at home,
the state's collapse is irreversible.
The common people's calculations
always seek safety and profit
and avoid danger and poverty.
Now, if they are made to attack and fight,
advancing means death by the enemy,
retreating means death by execution,
that is dangerous.
Abandoning private affairs
to endure the toils of war,
with families in distress and the ruler showing no concern,
that is poverty.
Where poverty and danger lie,
how can the people avoid fleeing?
Therefore, they serve powerful families
and seek exemptions from service,
exemptions secured mean avoiding war,
avoiding war means safety.
By bribing those in power
they achieve their desires,
achieving desires brings personal security,
and where personal security lies,
how can they not gravitate there?
Thus, public-minded citizens decrease
while private-serving individuals increase.
An enlightened king's way of governing
ensures that merchants, artisans, and itinerant people are few
and of low status,
discouraging neglect of fundamental duties
for peripheral trades.
In today's world, if requests from close associates are heeded,
official titles can be bought,
official titles bought,
then merchants and artisans are not lowly.
If illicit wealth and goods are usable in the market,
then merchants are not few.
Accumulating wealth twice that of farmers
and gaining more honor than tillers and warriors,
then upright scholars become few
and merchant people many.
Therefore, the customs of a disordered state:
its scholars
praise the ways of ancient kings under the guise of righteousness,
adorn themselves in fine robes and embellish their arguments,
to cast doubt on current laws,
and confuse the ruler's mind.
Its persuaders
fabricate tales and false claims,
relying on external forces,
to achieve private ends,
abandoning the state's interests.
Its swordsmen
gather followers,
establish codes of honor,
to glorify their names,
and violate the prohibitions of the state.
Its avoiders of service
cluster around powerful families,
exhausting bribes,
using influential recommendations,
to evade the toils of war.
Its merchants and artisans
craft shoddy implements,
amass extravagant wealth,
hoard goods awaiting opportunities,
to exploit the farmers' profits.
These five groups are the vermin of the state.
If the ruler does not eliminate these five types of vermin,
and does not nurture upright scholars,
then even if within the seas there are ruined states,
or annihilated courts,
it should be no surprise.
The prominent schools of the age are
the Rú (Confucian) and Mò (Mohist).
The ultimate source of the Rú
is Kǒng Qiū.
The ultimate source of the Mò
is Mò Dí.
Since the death of Confucius,
there has been the Rú of Zǐzhāng,
the Rú of Zǐsī,
the Rú of the Yán clan,
the Rú of the Mèng clan,
the Rú of the Qīdiāo clan,
the Rú of the Zhòngliáng clan,
the Rú of the Sūn clan,
the Rú of the Yuèzhèng clan.
Since the death of Mòzǐ,
there has been the Mò of the Xiànglǐ clan,
the Mò of the Xiàngfū clan,
the Mò of the Dènglíng clan.
Thus after Kǒng
and Mò,
the Rú split into eight,
the Mò divided into three,
their acceptances and rejections being contradictory and different,
yet all claiming to be the true Kǒng and Mò.
Kǒng
and Mò cannot be born again;
who shall decide the learning of the age?
Confucius
and Mòzǐ both spoke of Yáo
and Shùn,
yet their acceptances and rejections differed,
both claiming to be the true Yáo
and Shùn.
Yáo
and Shùn cannot be born again;
who shall determine the genuineness of the Rú
and Mò?
From Yīn to Zhōu is over seven hundred years,
from Yú to Xià over two thousand years,
and yet we cannot determine the truth of the Rú
and Mò;
now we wish to examine the Way of Yáo
and Shùn
from over three thousand years ago—
I fear it cannot be certain!
To affirm something without testing and verification
is foolishness;
to rely on what cannot be affirmed
is deception.
Thus, to clearly rely on the former kings
and affirm Yáo and Shùn
is either foolish or deceptive.
Foolish and deceptive learning,
mixed and contradictory conduct—
an enlightened ruler does not accept them.
The Mòists in burial
use winter clothes in winter,
summer clothes in summer,
a coffin of tong wood three inches thick,
and three months of mourning;
the lords of the age consider this frugal and honor them.
The Rúists bankrupt their families to bury,
observe three years of mourning,
become greatly emaciated and lean on canes;
the lords of the age consider this filial and honor them.
Now to approve Mòzǐ’s frugality
is to condemn Confucius’ extravagance;
to approve Confucius’ filial piety
is to condemn Mòzǐ’s cruelty.
Now filial piety, cruelty, extravagance, and frugality
all exist in the Rú and Mò,
yet the ruler honors them all.
The teachings of Qīdiāo
say: do not yield in expression,
do not flee with the eyes,
if one’s conduct is crooked, flee even from slaves,
if one’s conduct is straight, defy even the feudal lords;
the lords of the age consider this incorruptible and honor him.
The teachings of Sòng Róngzǐ
establish no fighting,
take no revenge,
feel no shame in prison,
see insult as not disgraceful;
the lords of the age consider this tolerant and honor him.
Now to approve Qīdiāo’s integrity
is to condemn Sòng Róng’s forbearance;
to approve Sòng Róng’s tolerance
is to condemn Qīdiāo’s violence.
Now tolerance,
integrity, forbearance,
and violence
all exist in these two men,
yet the ruler honors them both.
Since foolish and deceptive learning
and mixed, contradictory debates contend,
and the ruler listens to them all,
thus the scholars of the world
have no fixed doctrine in speech,
no constant standard in conduct.
Now ice and charcoal cannot long share the same vessel,
cold and heat cannot arrive together in the same season,
mixed and contradictory schools cannot both stand and bring order.
Now to simultaneously listen to mixed learning, erroneous conduct,
and divergent arguments—
how can there not be chaos?
If listening and conduct are like this,
then in governing the people it will surely be the same.
The scholars of today who speak of governance
mostly say:
"Give land to the poor to fill their lack of resources."
Now, if people are similar in circumstances,
have no extra income from bumper years,
and yet some alone are fully provided for,
it is due either to hard work or frugality.
If people are similar in circumstances,
suffer no calamities of famine,
disease,
misfortune, or crime,
and yet some alone are poor,
it is due either to extravagance or laziness.
The extravagant and lazy are poor,
the hardworking and frugal are rich.
Now if the ruler levies taxes from the rich
to distribute to poor families,
this is to rob the hardworking and frugal
and give to the extravagant and lazy;
and to expect the people to work diligently and economize
is impossible.
Suppose there is a person here
who, for righteousness, will not enter a dangerous city,
not join the army,
not exchange one hair from his shin for the great benefit of the world;
the lords of the age will surely follow and honor him,
esteem his wisdom and praise his conduct,
considering him
one who despises material things and values life.
Now the reason the ruler displays fine fields and large houses,
establishes ranks and emoluments,
is to exchange them for the people’s lives and efforts.
If the ruler honors those who despise material things and value life,
and expects the people to risk death
and sacrifice themselves for the ruler’s affairs,
it is impossible.
To store books and texts,
practice debating,
gather disciples,
devote oneself to literature and discuss theories—
the lords of the age will surely follow and honor this,
saying:
"Respect the worthy scholars—
this is the Way of the former kings."
Now, those taxed by the officials
are the farmers;
and those supported by the ruler
are the scholars.
The farmers are heavily taxed,
the scholars are richly rewarded;
and to expect the people to work hard and speak little
is impossible.
To establish integrity conspicuously,
hold to principles without yielding,
so that upon hearing a slighting word,
one must follow it with a sword—
the lords of the age will surely follow and honor this,
considering them self-respecting men.
Now, the toil of decapitating enemies in war goes unrewarded,
while the courage of private quarrels is honored and exalted;
and to expect the people to fight fiercely and resist enemies
without private fights
is impossible.
When the state is at peace,
it nurtures Rúists and knights-errant;
when trouble comes,
it uses armored soldiers.
Those nurtured are not those used,
those used are not those nurtured—
this is the cause of chaos.
Moreover, when a ruler listens to learned discourse,
if the words are correct,
he should promulgate them through official channels and employ the speaker;
if the words are incorrect,
he should dismiss the speaker and suppress their origins.
Now if something is deemed correct,
yet not promulgated officially;
if deemed incorrect,
yet its origins are not suppressed.
To recognize correctness but not use it,
to recognize error but not extinguish it—
this is the path to chaos and ruin.
Dàntái Zǐyú
had the appearance of a noble man,
and Confucius nearly selected him based on this,
but after long association
his conduct did not match his appearance.
Zǎi Yǔ's speech
was refined and elegant,
and Confucius nearly selected him based on this,
but after long association
his wisdom fell short of his eloquence.
Hence Confucius said:
"To select men by appearance—
I missed with Zǐyú;
to select men by speech—
I missed with Zǎi Yǔ."
Thus even with Confucius' wisdom
there were instances of misjudgment.
Nowadays new sophists surpass even Zǎi Yǔ in excess,
while contemporary rulers' hearing is more dazzled than Confucius',
delighting in their words,
they consequently appoint them to office—
how could they avoid errors?
Thus Wei employed Mèng Mǎo's eloquence
and suffered the disaster at Huàxià;
Zhào employed Mǎfú's rhetoric
and met with the calamity at Chángpíng.
These two cases
exemplify the error of trusting eloquence.
Inspecting the tempering and examining the color
cannot enable Ōuyě to guarantee a sword's quality;
but striking waterfowl in flight
or severing colts on land
would leave even slaves in no doubt of its sharpness.
Examining teeth and appearance
cannot enable Bó Lè to guarantee a horse's quality;
but hitching it to a carriage
and observing its performance at journey's end
would leave even slaves in no doubt of its worth.
Observing appearance and dress,
listening to speech and words—
not even Confucius could thereby ascertain a scholar's quality;
but testing them in official duties,
examining their achievements,
would leave even ordinary people in no doubt of their foolishness or wisdom.
Therefore the officials of an enlightened ruler—
ministers must arise from local administration,
fierce generals must emerge from the ranks.
When the meritorious are invariably rewarded,
then noble ranks and emoluments being generous
increasingly encourages effort;
promoting offices and advancing grades,
then with official positions greater
governance improves further.
When noble ranks and emoluments are substantial
and official duties well administered,
this is the way of true kingship.
A thousand lǐ of barren rock
cannot be called wealth;
a million human figurines
cannot be called strength.
The stones are not insufficiently large,
the numbers not insufficiently numerous,
yet they cannot be called wealthy and strong—
because rocks yield no grain,
and figurines cannot be deployed against enemies.
Now merchants, officials, artisans, and technicians
also eat without cultivating land,
making the land uncultivated
just like the barren rocks.
Confucians and knights without military service
yet achieving prominence and honor
make the people unusable,
identical to the human figurines.
Those who recognize the harm of rocks and figurines
but fail to recognize the harm of merchant-officials, Confucians and knights
as uncultivated land
and unusable people
understand not the nature of things.
Thus the rulers of rival states
may admire our righteousness,
yet we cannot make them pay tribute and submit;
but marquises within our borders
may criticize our conduct,
yet we can surely make them present gifts and attend court.
Therefore when strength is great
others come to our court,
when strength is small
we attend others' courts.
Hence enlightened rulers concentrate on power.
In strict households there are no violent bullies,
while indulgent mothers produce wayward sons.
From this I know that authority can prohibit violence,
while abundant virtue cannot stop disorder.
When sages govern the state,
they do not rely on people being good to me,
but make use of their inability to do wrong.
Relying on people being good to me,
there are not ten in the entire realm;
making people unable to do wrong,
the whole state can be unified.
Those who govern
employ what works for the many and discard what works for the few,
therefore they do not cultivate virtue
but enforce laws.
If one must rely on arrows that are naturally straight,
there would be no arrows for a hundred generations;
if one must rely on wood that is naturally round,
there would be no wheels for a thousand generations.
Arrows naturally straight,
wood naturally round
—not one appears in a hundred generations,
yet why does the world still have chariot riders and archers?
Because the way of straightening devices is employed.
Even if there were naturally straight arrows
and naturally round wood
without relying on straightening devices,
skilled craftsmen would not value them.
Why?
Riders are not just one person,
archers do not shoot just one arrow.
Not relying on rewards and punishments
but relying on people who are naturally good
is not valued by enlightened rulers.
Why?
State laws cannot be neglected,
and those governed are not just one person.
Therefore rulers with methods
do not follow accidental goodness,
but practice inevitable ways.
Suppose someone tells a person:
"I can make you inevitably wise and long-lived."
The world would certainly consider them mad.
Wisdom
is innate nature;
longevity
is destiny.
Innate nature and destiny
cannot be learned from others,
yet to promise people what one cannot deliver
is why the world calls such people mad.
To say someone cannot do something
is simply description,
describing their nature.
Teaching people with benevolence and righteousness
is like promising them wisdom and longevity—
measured rulers do not accept this.
So praising the beauty of Máo Qiáng
and Xī Shī
does not improve my own face;
using cosmetics and powders
doubles one's original appearance.
Extolling the former kings' benevolence and righteousness
brings no benefit to governance;
clarifying our laws and regulations,
enforcing our rewards and punishments
is also the state's cosmetics and powders.
Therefore enlightened rulers prioritize practical aids
and delay empty praises,
hence they do not preach benevolence and righteousness.
Nowadays, when sorcerers and invokers bless people, they say:
"May you live for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years."
The sound of "thousand autumns and ten thousand years" fills the ears,
but not a single day of extended life is actually bestowed upon anyone.
This is why people despise sorcerers and invokers.
In our time, when Confucian scholars persuade rulers,
they do not discuss effective methods for governance,
but instead talk about the achievements of past governance;
they do not examine the affairs of official laws,
nor do they investigate the circumstances of wickedness and corruption,
but all speak of
the legendary praises of ancient times
and the successes of former kings.
The Confucians embellish their words, saying:
"Listen to my words,
and you can become a hegemon or a true king."
Such persuaders are like sorcerers and invokers,
and a ruler with standards does not accept them.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler promotes practical deeds,
eliminates the useless,
does not speak of the reasons for benevolence and righteousness,
and does not listen to the words of scholars.
Now, those who do not understand governance inevitably say:
"Win the hearts of the people."
If winning the people's hearts were sufficient for governance,
then figures like Yī Yǐn
and Guǎn Zhòng would have no use,
and one would merely follow the people's wishes.
But the people's wisdom is not reliable,
just like the mind of an infant.
If an infant's head is not lanced, it will suffer abdominal pain;
if a boil is not cut open, it will gradually worsen.
When lancing the head
or squeezing a boil,
someone must hold the child,
and a loving mother treats it,
yet the child still cries incessantly,
because the infant does not understand that enduring a small discomfort
leads to great benefit.
Now, when the ruler urgently promotes farming and land reclamation
to enrich the people's livelihood,
he is considered cruel by them;
when he institutes punishments and heavy penalties to prohibit evil,
he is deemed harsh;
when he levies taxes in money and grain to fill the granaries and treasuries,
intending to relieve famine
and prepare for military campaigns,
he is called greedy;
when he ensures that all within the borders know armor
and do not seek private exemptions,
uniting in swift combat
to capture enemies,
he is regarded as violent.
These four measures
are for achieving stability and order,
yet the people do not appreciate them.
Seeking sagely and insightful scholars
is necessary because the people's knowledge is not worthy of being followed or used.
In the past, when Yǔ dredged the rivers,
the people gathered tiles and stones against him;
when Zǐchǎn opened fields and planted mulberries,
the people of Zhèng slandered him.
Yǔ benefited the world,
and Zǐchǎn preserved the people of Zhèng,
yet both were criticized;
thus, the inadequacy of the people's wisdom is clear.
Therefore, selecting scholars while seeking the wise and intelligent,
and governing while hoping to please the people,
are both sources of chaos,
and cannot be used to achieve order.
All under heaven consider the ways of filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and obedience
to be right,
but none know to examine
the ways of filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and obedience
and practice them carefully;
hence, the world is in chaos.
All consider the ways of Yáo and Shùn to be right
and emulate them,
leading to regicide
and disobedience to fathers.
Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ sometimes inverted the righteousness between ruler and minister,
disrupting the teachings for later generations.
Yáo, as a ruler, treated his minister as a ruler;
Shùn, as a minister, had his ruler treated as a minister;
Tāng and Wǔ, as ministers,
killed their lords and punished their corpses,
yet the world praises them;
this is why the world remains in disorder to this day.
What is called an enlightened ruler
is one who can nurture his ministers;
what is called a worthy minister
is one who can clarify laws and regulations,
manage official duties, and support his ruler.
Now, Yáo considered himself enlightened
but could not nurture Shùn;
Shùn considered himself worthy
but could not support Yáo;
