Tāng and Wǔ considered themselves righteous
but killed their lords and superiors;
these are cases where enlightened rulers are often given away to,
and worthy ministers often take from.
Hence, to this day, there are sons who seize their fathers' households,
and ministers who seize their rulers' states.
Fathers yielding to sons,
rulers yielding to ministers—
this is not the way to establish fixed positions and uniform teachings.
I have heard it said:
"Ministers serve the ruler,
sons serve the father,
wives serve the husband.
When these three are in harmony, the world is orderly;
when these three are inverted,
the world is in chaos.
This is the constant way of the world."
If enlightened kings and worthy ministers do not change this,
then even if the ruler is unworthy,
ministers dare not encroach.
Now, exalting the worthy and employing the wise without constancy
is contrary to the way,
yet the world often considers it governance.
Thus, the Tián clan seized the Lǚ clan's power in Qí,
and the Dài clan seized the Zǐ clan's power in Sòng.
These were acts of the worthy and wise;
how could they be foolish and unworthy?
Therefore, abandoning constancy to exalt the worthy
leads to chaos;
discarding laws to employ the wise
leads to danger.
Hence it is said:
Exalt laws, not the worthy.
The records say:
"When Shùn met Gǔsǒu,
his expression became troubled.
Confucius said:
'At that time,
how perilous!
The world was on the brink!
For a man of the Way,
a father indeed cannot treat him as a son,
nor a ruler as a minister.'"
I say:
Confucius fundamentally did not understand
the ways of filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and obedience.
If so, then for a man of the Way,
in advancement, he does not act as a minister to his ruler,
and in retreat, he does not act as a son to his father?
The reason a father desires a worthy son
is that if the family is poor, he enriches it;
if the father suffers, he brings him joy;
the reason a ruler desires a worthy minister
is that if the state is chaotic, he brings order;
if the ruler is humbled, he elevates him.
Now, if there is a worthy son who does not act for the father,
then the father's management of the household is bitter;
if there is a worthy minister who does not act for the ruler,
then the ruler's position is perilous.
Thus, a father having a worthy son,
or a ruler having a worthy minister,
may indeed become a harm—
how can it be beneficial?
What is called a loyal minister
does not endanger his ruler;
a filial son does not criticize his parents.
Now, Shùn, being worthy, took his ruler's state,
and Tāng and Wǔ, being righteous, exiled or killed their rulers;
these are cases where worthiness endangered the lords,
yet the world considers them worthy.
The determined scholars of old,
in advancement, did not serve the ruler as ministers,
in retreat, did not manage the family—
thus, in advancement, they criticized their ruler,
and in retreat, they criticized their parents.
Moreover, those who in advancement do not serve their ruler as subjects,
and in retirement do not manage their households,
follow the path that leads to the extinction of lineage in a chaotic age.
Therefore, to regard Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ as worthy
and to affirm martyrs,
is a method that brings chaos to the world.
Gǔsǒu was Shùn's father, yet Shùn exiled him;
Xiàng was Shùn's younger brother, yet Shùn killed him.
Exiling one's father and killing one's brother cannot be called benevolent;
marrying the two daughters of the emperor to gain the world,
cannot be called righteous.
Having neither benevolence nor righteousness,
one cannot be called enlightened.
The Book of Songs says:
"Under the vast heaven,
all is the king's land;
within the borders of the land,
all are the king's subjects."
If we truly believe the words of the Book of Songs,
then Shùn, when abroad, made his ruler his subject,
and at home, made his father his subject,
treating his mother as a concubine and marrying his lord's daughters.
Thus, martyrs internally do not manage their households,
leading to the extinction of lineage in a chaotic age;
and externally deceive their ruler,
with decaying bones and rotting flesh,
scattered upon the land,
flowing in rivers and valleys,
not avoiding treading through water and fire.
If the world follows and imitates them,
then the world would universally die
and wish for an early death.
These all abandon the world
and do not bring order to it.
Those whom the world calls martyrs,
detach themselves from the masses and act alone,
seeking to be different from others,
practicing the learning of indifference and tranquility
and discussing obscure and vague statements.
I consider indifference and tranquility
to be teachings of no utility;
obscurity and vagueness,
to be statements without standards.
Statements that arise from having no standards,
and teachings that come from having no utility,
the world calls perceptive.
I believe that in human life,
one must serve the ruler and support one's parents;
serving the ruler and supporting parents
cannot be done through indifference and tranquility;
governing people
must involve discussions of loyalty, trust, laws, and methods;
discussions of loyalty, trust, laws, and methods
cannot be obscure and vague.
Obscure and vague statements,
and the learning of indifference and tranquility,
are deceptive methods in the world.
A filial son serving his father
does not compete to take over his father's household;
a loyal minister serving his ruler
does not compete to seize his ruler's state.
If a person as a son
often praises the parents of others, saying:
"So-and-so's parents,
rest late and rise early,
exerting themselves to generate wealth
to support their children, grandchildren, and servants."
This is to slander his own parents.
If a minister often praises the virtuous kindness of former kings
and aspires to it,
this is to slander his own ruler.
To criticize one's parents is known to be unfilial,
yet those who criticize their ruler
are all regarded as worthy by the world;
this is the cause of chaos.
Therefore, ministers should not praise the worthiness of Yáo and Shùn,
not commend the campaigns of Tāng and Wǔ,
not speak of the loftiness of martyrs,
but exert their strength in upholding the law,
and focus their minds on serving their lord—these are loyal ministers.
In ancient times, the common people were simple, reserved, and foolish,
so they could be won over by empty reputations.
Now the people are clever, investigative, and wise,
wishing to act on their own,
and not obeying their superiors.
The ruler must encourage them with rewards,
then they can be advanced;
and also make them fear punishments,
then they will not dare to retreat.
Yet the world all says:
"Xǔ Yóu declined the empire,
so rewards are insufficient to encourage;
Dào Zhí violated penalties and faced dangers,
so punishments are insufficient to restrain."
I say:
Those who do not possess the empire
and have no regard for the empire,
Xǔ Yóu is such a one;
those who already possess the empire
and have no regard for the empire,
Yáo and Shùn are such;
those who destroy their integrity to seek wealth,
violate penalties to pursue profit,
and forget the risk of death,
Dào Zhí is such.
These two types
are perilous extremes.
The way to govern the state and employ the people
should not take these two as measures.
Governing means
governing the constant norms;
the Way means
guiding the constant norms.
Perilous extremes and subtle words
are harmful to governance.
The highest-minded scholars in the world
cannot be encouraged by rewards;
the lowest-minded scholars in the world
cannot be restrained by punishments.
Yet if for the highest-minded no rewards are established,
and for the lowest-minded no punishments are set,
then the way to govern the state and employ the people is lost.
Therefore, many in the world do not speak of state laws
but speak of vertical and horizontal alliances.
The feudal lords who speak of vertical alliances say:
"If vertical alliances succeed, one will surely become hegemon."
And those who speak of horizontal alliances say:
"If horizontal alliances succeed, one will surely become king."
East of the mountains, discussions of vertical and horizontal alliances
have not ceased for a single day,
yet achievements and fame are not accomplished,
and hegemony or kingship is not established,
because empty words cannot bring about order.
The king acts alone and is called a true king;
thus, the Three Sovereigns did not engage in alliances or divisions
yet achieved correctness,
and the Five Hegemons did not rely on vertical or horizontal alliances
yet achieved clarity,
for they governed internally to control externally.
The reasons why rulers endanger themselves and lose their states
are that the great ministers become too noble,
and the attendants too powerful.
What is called nobility
is acting without law and arbitrarily,
wielding the state's authority for personal convenience.
What is called power
is monopolizing authority and manipulating weights and measures.
These two
must not be overlooked.
The reason horses can bear heavy loads
and pull carts over long distances
is their physical strength.
The ruler of ten thousand chariots,
the lord of a thousand chariots,
controls the world and subjugates the feudal lords
through his authority and power.
Authority and power are the physical strength of the ruler.
Now if great ministers gain authority,
and attendants monopolize power,
then the ruler loses his strength;
for a ruler who has lost his strength to still possess the state—
not one in a thousand exists.
The reason tigers and leopards can overcome humans
and capture all beasts
is their claws and teeth;
if tigers and leopards were to lose their claws and teeth,
then humans would surely control them.
Now, weight of authority
is the claws and teeth of the ruler;
if a ruler loses his claws and teeth,
he is like a tiger or leopard.
The ruler of Sòng lost his claws and teeth to Zǐ Hǎn,
Duke Jiǎn lost his claws and teeth to Tián Cháng,
and because they did not seize them back early,
they died and their states perished.
Now, rulers without method
all clearly know the errors of the Sòng ruler
and Duke Jiǎn,
yet do not realize their own faults,
failing to examine the similarity of circumstances.
Moreover, men of method and statecraft
are incompatible with ministers in power.
How can this be demonstrated?
When the ruler has such strategists,
great ministers cannot monopolize decisions,
and intimate attendants dare not peddle influence;
once the power of great ministers and courtiers is extinguished,
the way of the sovereign becomes clear.
But now it is not so:
those ministers in power, having gained influence and control over affairs,
use them to serve their private interests,
while intimate attendants form cliques and collude
to manipulate the distant and estranged.
Under such circumstances, when would men of method and statecraft ever get to advance and be employed,
and when would the sovereign ever get to deliberate and decide?
Hence, even if one possesses statecraft, it may not be used,
and since the situations are mutually exclusive,
how can men of method and statecraft avoid danger?
Therefore, if the ruler of men cannot dismiss the arguments of great ministers
and reject the pleas of his courtiers,
to align solely with words that accord with the Way,
then how could men of method and statecraft
risk the peril of death
to present their counsel?
This is why the world is not well-governed.
An enlightened ruler,
assessing achievements, bestows ranks and emoluments,
and according to ability, assigns official duties.
Those recommended must be worthy,
and those employed must be capable.
When worthy and capable men advance,
then private solicitations cease.
If those with merit receive high emoluments,
and the capable hold high office,
then how could men of private swordsmanship
fail to abandon their personal bravery
and swiftly confront the enemy,
and how could wandering scholars
fail to resist the pull of private factions
and strive for integrity?
This is the means to gather worthy and capable men
and disperse the followers of private factions.
Now, intimate attendants are not necessarily wise,
yet when the sovereign encounters someone
with knowledge and listens to him,
he then discusses that person's words with his intimates.
Listening to the intimates without considering their wisdom
is to discuss the wise with the foolish.
Those in power are not necessarily worthy,
yet when the sovereign encounters someone
deemed worthy and honors him,
he then discusses that person's conduct with those in power.
Listening to their words and not employing the worthy
is to discuss the worthy with the unworthy.
Thus, if the wise have their strategies decided by fools,
and worthy men have their conduct judged by the unworthy,
then when would worthy and wise men ever get employed,
and the clarity of the sovereign is blocked.
In the past, Guān Lóngpáng advised Jié and had his limbs injured,
Prince Bǐgān remonstrated with Zhòu and had his heart cut out,
and Wǔ Zīxū, loyal and straightforward to Fūchāi,
was executed with the sword Shǔlòu.
These three men,
as ministers, were not without loyalty,
and their counsel was not inappropriate,
yet they could not avoid the misfortune of death.
The reason is that the sovereign did not examine the words of the worthy and wise,
but was blinded by the harm of the foolish and unworthy.
If today's sovereign
is unwilling to employ men of method and statecraft,
but listens to foolish and unworthy ministers,
then which of the worthy and wise
would dare to face the peril of those three
and offer their wisdom and abilities?
This is why the world is in chaos.
When decrees are strictly enforced,
laws do not change;
when laws are fair,
officials have no wickedness.
Once the law is established,
do not harm it with fine words.
Appointing by merit
makes the people speak less,
while appointing by rhetoric
makes them talk more.
Applying the law with precise judgments:
ruling within five lǐ makes one kingly,
within nine lǐ makes one strong,
but delayed governance leads to decline.
Govern with punishment,
reward for battle,
and generous emoluments to employ statecraft.
If the capital's faults are addressed,
then the capital has no corrupt markets.
If goods are many and non-essentials abound,
agriculture slackens and wickedness prevails,
then the state will surely decline.
When the people have surplus grain,
let them exchange it for ranks,
ensuring it comes from their labor,
so farmers do not become idle.
A three-inch pipe without a bottom
cannot be filled.
Granting offices and emoluments without regard to merit
is like having no bottom.
If the state grants offices and ranks based on merit,
this is called using wisdom to achieve,
and awe to encourage bravery in battle,
making the state invincible.
When the state grants offices and ranks based on merit,
governance becomes simplified,
and rhetoric is blocked.
This is called using governance to eliminate complexity,
words to eliminate talk,
through merit and rank.
Thus, the state becomes powerful,
and no one in the world can invade it.
When the army marches, it must capture;
what it captures, it must hold.
If it holds back from attack, it will surely grow rich.
In court affairs,
minor matters are not neglected,
and official ranks are awarded for proven merit.
Even if there are clever arguments in court,
they cannot interfere,
which is called governing by fixed rules.
Attacking with force yields one and gains ten;
attacking with words expends ten and loses a hundred.
If the state values force,
this is called attacking with difficulty;
if it values rhetoric,
this is called attacking with ease.
If one can
overcome its harms,
lighten its burdens,
and spare mental energy for the Way,
without bearing the ruler's blame for official duties.
With no hidden resentments within,
and the clear-minded not interfering with each other,
thus there are no disputes;
with scholars not holding multiple posts,
thus skills are honed;
with people not sharing achievements,
thus there is no contention.
This is called easy to attack.
Severe punishments and few rewards
show the ruler's love for the people,
and the people will die for rewards;
many rewards and light punishments
show the ruler does not love the people,
and the people will not die for rewards.
When benefits come from one source,
the state is invincible;
from two sources,
its army is half-effective;
from ten sources,
the people will not defend it.
Severe punishments enlighten the people,
great systems direct them,
then the ruler benefits.
In administering punishments,
heavily penalize minor offenses:
then minor offenses do not occur,
and major ones do not come,
which is called using punishment to eliminate punishment.
If crimes are heavy but punishments light,
light punishments lead to more offenses,
which is called using punishment to invite punishment,
and the state will surely decline.
The sage in governing the people
considers the fundamentals,
not indulging their desires,
aiming only to benefit them.
Thus, in imposing punishments upon them,
it is not because he dislikes the people,
but stems from love for them.
When punishments prevail, the people are tranquil;
when rewards are excessive, wickedness arises.
Therefore, in governing the people,
the supremacy of punishment
is the foremost principle of governance;
excessive rewards
are the root of chaos.
Now, the nature of the people is to delight in disorder and not adhere to the laws.
Hence, an enlightened ruler in governing the state
establishes clear rewards
so that the people are encouraged to achieve merits,
and enforces strict punishments
so that the people respect the laws.
When encouraged to achieve merits,
public affairs are not violated,
and when they respect the laws,
evil has no chance to sprout.
Thus, those who govern the people
prohibit evil before it sprouts;
and those who employ military force
instill the will to fight in the people's hearts.
Prohibiting at the root leads to order,
and military action that wins hearts leads to victory.
When a sage governs the people,
he who governs first becomes strong,
he who fights first achieves victory.
Now, state affairs must prioritize
unifying the people's hearts,
focus exclusively on public good
so that private interests do not prevail,
reward informants so that evil does not arise,
and clarify laws so that governance is not troublesome.
He who can employ these four becomes strong,
he who cannot employ these four becomes weak.
Now, the reason a state is strong
lies in its governance;
the reason a ruler is honored
lies in his authority.
Thus, an enlightened ruler has authority and governance,
and a chaotic ruler also has authority and governance,
but their accumulation differs,
which is why they stand apart.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler wields authority and is esteemed above,
unifies governance and the state is well-ordered.
Hence, laws
are the foundation of kingship;
punishment
is the origin of love.
Now, the nature of the people
is to dislike toil and enjoy ease.
Ease leads to neglect,
neglect leads to disorder,
disorder leads to chaos,
and if rewards and punishments are not implemented under heaven,
it will surely be blocked.
Thus, he who wishes to achieve great merits
but finds it hard to muster the people's strength,
cannot expect to accomplish great merits;
he who wishes to govern with laws
but finds it hard to change old habits,
cannot expect to bring order to a chaotic people.
Therefore, governing the people has no constant rule,
only law brings order.
When laws evolve with the times, there is order;
when governance suits the world, there is achievement.
Thus, if the people are simple and restrained by reputation
they are governed,
if the world is wise and bound by punishment
they comply.
If times change but governance does not adapt, there is chaos;
if abilities multiply but prohibitions do not change,
there is decline.
Hence, when a sage governs the people,
he evolves laws with the times
and changes prohibitions with abilities.
He who can maximize strength from the land becomes rich,
he who can rouse strength against enemies becomes strong,
and if strong without obstruction, he becomes king.
Thus, the way of kingship lies in what is opened,
and what is blocked,
and he who blocks evil will surely become king.
Therefore, the art of kingship does not rely on the absence of external chaos,
but on being unshakable.
Relying on external order
to establish governance leads to decline,
while relying on being unshakable
to enforce laws leads to prosperity.
Thus, a worthy ruler in governing the state
adopts the method of being unshakable.
Valuing ranks
ensures the ruler's esteem,
so by rewarding merit and conferring ranks
evil finds no entry.
He who values strength honors ranks,
and honored ranks
bring ruler's dignity,
and ruler's dignity
ensures kingship.
A state that does not value strength but relies on private studies
devalues ranks,
and devalued ranks
bring ruler's humility,
and ruler's humility leads to decline.
Hence, the way to establish a state and employ the people
is to close external influences and block private interests
so that the ruler relies on himself,
and kingship can be achieved.
Now, all states that are vast and rulers honored
have never failed to enforce heavy laws to achieve order and prohibitions under heaven.
Therefore, the ruler allocates ranks and regulates emoluments,
so laws must be strict and emphasized.
When the state is well-ordered, the people are secure;
when affairs are chaotic, the state is endangered.
Heavy laws capture human sentiments,
light prohibitions lose touch with reality.
Moreover, the people's capacity for utmost effort
is inherent,
and their sentiment is to exert this effort
to attain what they desire;
while likes and dislikes
are controlled by the ruler,
for the people like profit and emoluments
and dislike punishments.
The ruler masters likes and dislikes
to harness the people's strength,
and thus should not lose touch with reality;
yet if prohibitions are light and affairs go astray,
it is due to errors in punishment and reward.
If governing the people does not uphold laws for good,
then thus,
it is as if there are no laws.
Therefore, the principle of order and chaos
should focus on distinguishing punishments and rewards as urgent,
and every ruler of a state has laws,
yet some endure and some perish.
Those that perish
do not distinguish
in regulating punishments and rewards.
In a well-governed state,
punishments and rewards are always distinguished.
If one holds to differences as distinction,
it cannot be called true distinction.
As for the distinction of a perceptive ruler,
it is unique distinction.
Thus, his people respect laws and fear prohibitions,
wishing to avoid crime and not daring to expect rewards.
Hence it is said:
without awaiting punishments or rewards,
the people undertake tasks.
Therefore, in the most well-ordered state,
it is essential to excel at stopping evil,
why is that?
Because its laws connect with human sentiments,
and relate to the principles of governance.
Then, how to eliminate subtle evil?
It务必 ensures that people monitor each other's true conditions.
Then, how to make them spy on each other?
The answer is:
through the principle of collective responsibility.
If prohibitions involve implications for oneself,
one inevitably spies on others,
fearing only to not avoid punishment.
Those with evil intentions are not allowed to forget,
for there are many spies.
In this way,
they are cautious of themselves and spy on others,
exposing the secrets of evil.
Those who report offenses are exempt from punishment
and receive rewards,
while those who fail to report evil are punished
with implicated penalties.
Thus,
evil kinds are exposed.
No evil, however minor, is tolerated,
due to private reporting and collective responsibility.
The most enlightened method of governance
relies on systems rather than individuals.
Thus, in states that possess such art,
without employing praise, there is no proper direction,
yet the realm is inevitably well-ordered,
because they rely on systems.
A doomed state allows enemy troops to march openly across its land
and cannot prevent or stop them,
due to relying on individuals without systematic methods.
To attack oneself is due to human factors,
to attack others relies on systematic methods.
Therefore, states with effective governance
abandon empty talk and adhere to laws.
Generally, irregular achievements that follow contracts are hard to discern,
and faults concealed by rhetoric are difficult to detect,
leading to confusion in punishments and rewards due to duplicity.
What is called hard-to-discern contractual compliance
refers to treacherous accomplishments;
ministers' faults that are hard to detect
stem from hidden roots of error.
If following principles fails to reveal empty achievements,
and assessing circumstances misses treacherous roots,
how can these two aspects avoid dual failures?
Thus, empty scholars establish reputations internally,
while persuaders devise strategies externally,
so foolishness, timidity, courage, and cunning interconnect,
using hollow doctrines to conform to customs
and gain acceptance in the world.
Hence, their laws go unenforced,
and punishments do not reach the condemned.
Under such conditions,
how can punishments and rewards avoid duplicity?
Reality has its inherent limits,
yet principles lose their measure,
and this loss of measure
is not caused by the law itself,
but by fixed laws relying on cunning.
Those who discard laws and trust cunning
—how can officeholders fulfill their duties?
When duties do not align with affairs,
how can laws avoid failure,
and punishments avoid complexity?
Thus, rewards and punishments become disordered,
the state's path errs,
due to the indistinct application of penalties and rewards.
